If he chooses the first child, he will add (a_1=2) to (X) to get (X=2); if he chooses the second child, he will subtract (a_2=-3) from (X) to get (X=3). Thus, the answer is (3). In the second test case, it is optimal to select the first child in all three operations
2178C.editorial_text:
2178C - First or Second
Note that $$$n - 1$$$ of the children will be chosen by Santa, and one will remain unchosen. We can compute the best possible answer for each option of unchosen child and compute the answer at the end.
First, note that the first child in line will always have a contribution of $$$+a_i$$$ (unless they are the unchosen child).
For any child to the right of the unchosen child, the only way they can be chosen is to be put on the naughty list (as the unchosen child will always be ahead of them in line). This means that all of their contribution to $$$X$$$ must be $$$-a_i$$$.
For any child in between the first child and the unchosen child, if their niceness is $$$a_i$$$, the contribution added by assigning them to the nice or naughty list will always be $$$+a_i$$$ or $$$-a_i$$$. It turns out that for each of the children in this range, we can choose each of their signs independently (and no matter what we choose, it is a valid assignment). We shall show this by construction. After determining what sign we want each child to be, we perform the following strategy: If we want the second child to be negative, perform an operation of type 2 (putting the second child on the naughty list). Otherwise, perform an operation of type 1 and put the first child on the nice list. Whenever we do the second case the new child in the first position will either be one from whom we want a positive contribution, or the fixed unchosen child.
As we wish to maximize the total score, for each child between the first and unchosen child we will make their value equal to $$$\max(+a_i, -a_i) = |a_i|$$$.
Now if we naively compute the optimal value for each choice of unchosen child, this will take $$$\mathcal{O}(n^2)$$$ time. To optimize this we can employ prefix/suffix sums. If we pre-compute the prefix sums of $$$|a_i|$$$ (except $$$a_1$$$ which does not have an absolute value), and compute the suffix sums of $$$-a_i$$$ then for any fixed unchosen child we can compute the maximum value of $$$X$$$ by adding the prefix sum of $$$|a_i|$$$ before the unchosen child and the suffix sum of $$$-a_i$$$ after the unchosen child (adding in $$$a_1$$$ if the unchosen child is not the first child).
After computing these $$$n$$$ values, we can take the maximum to find the overall maximum value of $$$X$$$.

2178D.title: Xmas or Hysteria
2178D.statement_text: Franklin is plotting a Christmas attack where he casts the spell Mass Hysteria on a village of elves. There are (n) elves numbered (1) to (n), where elf (i) has a health value of (h_i) and an attack value of (a_i). Initially, (h_i=a_i) for all (i), and all (a_i) are distinct. Elf (i) is alive if and only if its health is positive (i.e., (h_i>0)). When Franklin casts Mass Hysteria , the following process is repeated: Choose a pair of distinct living elves (x) and (y) ((h_x,h_y>0)) such that elf (x) has not attacked before. If no such pair exists, terminate the process. Then, elf (x) attacks elf (y), decreasing (h_y) by (a_x). Additionally, due to recoil, (h_x) is decreased by (a_y). Note that (a_x) and (a_y) remain unchanged. The process will repeat until it is impossible to choose a valid pair of elves. It can be shown that Mass Hysteria terminates after at most (n) iterations. Given an integer (m), construct a valid sequence of attacks such that exactly (m) elves are alive when the process ends; or determine that no such sequence exists. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (m) ((2\le n\le 2\cdot 10^5, 0\le m\le n)) — the number of elves in the village and the number of elves to be left alive. The second line contains (n) integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) ((1\le a_i\le 10^9)) — the initial attack and health values of the elves. It is guaranteed that all (a_i) are distinct. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2\cdot 10 ^ 5). For each test case, if it is impossible for exactly (m) elves to remain alive, print (-1). Otherwise, output a valid sequence of attacks as follows: On the first line,
2178D.editorial_text:
2178D - Xmas or Hysteria
Note that in each attack, at least one elf dies. The elf with smaller attack value must die, as its health is always at most its attack, which in turn is less than the other elf's attack.
Consider the elves that survive at the end. They each must attack once, and since they survived, each elf they attacked must have died. Furthermore, each target elf can only be attacked by one surviving elf, as they will die immediately upon being attacked. Therefore, for every surviving elf, there must be a corresponding dead elf. This means that no more than $$$\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$$$ elves can survive, so if $$$2m \gt n$$$, output $$$-1$$$.
Now, suppose $$$2m \le n$$$. $$$m$$$ elves survive and they attack $$$m$$$ smaller target elves, which die. We need the $$$n - 2m$$$ leftover elves to die. How can we do this?
We can sort the leftover elves from left to right. Then, each leftover elf attacks the larger elf immediately after it from left to right. This causes all leftover elves to die except for the largest. If there is a target elf which dies ($$$m \gt 0$$$), we can also kill the largest elf — let it attack a larger target elf before that target elf is attacked by some larger surviving elf. This will kill the largest leftover elf, while allowing the target elf it attacks to still be alive for the larger surviving elf.
This idea solves the problem for $$$0 \lt m \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$$$ — a construction always exists in this case. One clean way to implement this is by sorting all elves by their size, letting the largest $$$m$$$ elves be the surviving elves, the next largest $$$m$$$ elves be the target elves, and the remaining (smallest) $$$n-2m$$$ elves be the leftover elves. Each leftover elf attacks the elf to its right, and then each surviving elf attacks a different target elf. In the end, every surviving elf has attacked.
For $$$m = 0$$$, the idea to kill the leftover elves is not sufficient because the largest leftover elf has no one larger to attack and thus will not die. To kill the largest elf, we need some elves to attack it; all of them will die. We can then deal with the remaining elves using the same idea for the leftover elves above.
To implement the $$$m = 0$$$ case, sort the elves. Iterate through the elves in decreasing order from the second-largest elf until their sum reaches the largest elf's health; save these elves to attack the largest elf at the end. Each remaining smaller elf should attack the (larger) elf to its right and die in the process; then let the saved elves should attack the largest elf so that all elves die.
If all other elves attacking the largest elf is not sufficient to kill the largest elf (i.e., the sum of all elves except the largest is less than the largest elf), there is no way to kill the largest elf. In this case it is not possible for $$$0$$$ elves to survive, so output $$$-1$$$.
This solves the problem in all cases in $$$\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$$$.

2178E.title: Flatten or Concatenate
2178E.statement_text: This is an interactive problem. While procrastinating at work, Dilhan the elf stumbled upon two arrays (a) and (b). Initially, both of them consist of a single integer (2^k) (i.e., (a=b=2^k)), where (k) is a non-negative integer. Dilhan then applied the following two types of operations an arbitrary number of times (possibly zero), in any order: Flatten — Choose either (a) or (b), and select any element (x) that is maximal within that array ((x) does not need to be maximal in the other array). Then, replace (x) with two copies of (\frac x2) in the same position. This operation can only be applied if (x) is even. Concatenate — Set both (a) and (b) to be (a+b), where (+) denotes array concatenation. After performing these operations, Dilhan discards (b), hides (a) from you, and challenges you to a game. Let (n) be the length of the hidden array (a). You may make the following query: Choose an interval (l, r) ((1\le l\le r\le n)), and Dilhan will tell you the sum (a_l+a_{l+1}+\cdots+a_r). Determine the value of the maximum element of (a) by making at most (300) queries. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 100)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 10^5)) — the length of (a). It is guaranteed that (1\le a_i\le 2^{30}), and the array (a) can be generated by the process described in the statements. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (10^5). For each test case, you are first given an integer (n) — the length of the hidden array (a). You may then make up to (300) queries. To make a query, print a line in the following format: (?\;l\;r) ((1\le l\le r\le n)) — the indices chosen for the query. After you print a
2178E.editorial_text:
2178E - Flatten or Concatenate
Define $$$ab$$$ to be the concatenation of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$.
Observe that flattening an array preserves its sum. In addition, $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ initially have the same sum, and they have the same sum after concatenation. Therefore, $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ always have the same sum when applying the given operations.
All flatten operations after the final concatenate can be considered to be before the concatenate, as any flatten operations on $$$ab$$$ are also legal flatten operations on either $$$a$$$ or $$$b$$$ (the maximum of $$$ab$$$ is a maximum of either $$$a$$$ or $$$b$$$). Thus, assume the final operation is a concatenate.
Consider the arrays $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ before the final concatenate, so that the hidden final array is $$$ab$$$. Since $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ have the same sum, we can find where the split point in $$$ab$$$ is using binary search on prefix sums. The maximum of $$$ab$$$ must be in either $$$a$$$ or $$$b$$$. How can we determine which one it is in?
Claim: The shorter of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ must contain a maximum of $$$ab$$$.
Some number of flatten operations before the final concatenate, $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ were identical — either after the previous concatenate, or at the beginning of the process (when $$$a = b = [2^k]$$$) if no prior concatenate existed. Since flattening increases the size of an array by $$$1$$$, the shorter of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ was flattened fewer times. Intuitively, flattening reduces the maximum over time, so the array that is flattened fewer times contains the maximum. More formally, suppose one array is flattened $$$x$$$ times and the other is flattened $$$y$$$ times, with $$$x \ge y$$$. After each array is flattened $$$y$$$ times, both arrays contain the same multiset of elements. Flattening the array the remaining $$$x - y$$$ times cannot increase its maximum, so the maximum of the array that is flattened more times cannot exceed the maximum of the other array. Therefore, the shorter of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$, which is flattened fewer (or equal) times, contains a maximum of $$$ab$$$.
Now, for a final array $$$ab$$$, we know which of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ is guaranteed to contain a maximum of $$$ab$$$. Note that $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ are both arrays that can be generated by the given operations. This means we can recurse on whichever contains the maximum.
This leads to the following algorithm: 

Using binary search on prefix sums, find the split point of the final $$$ab$$$ — i.e., find $$$m$$$ such that $$$2(a_1 + \cdots + a_m) = a_1 + \cdots + a_n$$$. 
Recurse on the shorter of $$$[a_1, \ldots, a_m]$$$ and $$$[a_{m+1}, \ldots, a_n]$$$. 
In the base case of this recursive algorithm, we have an array $$$a$$$ which was never concatenated. If $$$a$$$ was never flattened, then its length is $$$1$$$, and we can simply query and return its only element. Otherwise, the array $$$a = [2^k]$$$ was flattened at some point into $$$[2^{k-1}, 2^{k-1}]$$$ and has length at least $$$2$$$. But $$$[2^{k-1}, 2^{k-1}]$$$ can be generated by starting with $$$[2^{k-1}]$$$ and concatenating, so if $$$a$$$ has length at least $$$2$$$, we can assume there were more concatenates and continue recursing. Thus, the only base case we need is $$$n = 1$$$.
Since the size of the array decreases by at least a factor of $$$2$$$ in each recursive step, this algorithm makes at most $$$\log_2 n$$$ recursive calls. In each recursive call, a binary search is done that takes at most $$$\log_2 n$$$ queries. Thus, the algorithm uses at most $$$(\log_2 n)^2 \lt 300$$$ queries in total.
Optionally, one can derive a tighter bound as follows. The sizes of the arrays are at most $$$n, n/2, n/4, \ldots$$$; then the total number of queries is at most $$$$$$ \log_2 n + \log_2 (n/2) + \log_2 (n/4) + \cdots + 1 = \log_2 n + (\log_2 (n) - 1) + (\log_2 (n) - 2) + \cdots + 1, $$$$$$ which is the sum of the integers from $$$1$$$ to $$$\log_2 n$$$ (assume, e.g., we are taking the ceilings of the logs), $$$$$$\frac{(\log_2 n)(\log_2 n - 1)}{2} \lt \frac{(\log_2 n)^2}{2} \lt 145.$$$$$$ Therefore, our recursive algorithm actually fits very comfortably within the query limit.

2178F.title: Conquer or of Forest
2178F.statement_text: Define the unique ornamental coloring of a rooted tree(^{\text{∗}}) as the following vertex coloring: A vertex (v) is colored white if the number of vertices in the subtree(^{\text{†}}) rooted at (v) is even; Otherwise, (v) is colored black. On his quest to conquer a forest of Christmas trees, Yuuki encountered an ornamentally colored tree (T) with (n) vertices labeled from (1) to (n), rooted at vertex (1). Yuuki considers the tree conquered if and only if at least one of the following conditions holds: There are no white vertices in the tree, or There exists some vertex (v) such that all white vertices lie on the simple path from the root (1) to (v). To conquer the tree, Yuuki can apply the following operation on (T) an arbitrary number of times (possibly zero): First, choose a vertex (w) that is colored white and is not the root of (T). Let (p_w) be the parent of (w). Then, remove the edge connecting (p_w) and (w), and add an edge between any two vertices such that (T) remains a tree. Finally, recolor the vertices of (T) such that it is ornamentally colored. Note that (T) is always rooted at vertex (1). Compute the number of distinct(^{\text{‡}}) conquered trees that Yuuki can construct by applying the above operation an arbitrary number of times on (T). Since the answer may be large, output it modulo (998\,244\,353). Note that Yuuki cannot stop midway through an operation (in particular, he must recolor the tree before checking if it is conquered ). Additionally, Yuuki is allowed to apply the operation even if the tree is already conquered . (^{\text{∗}})A tree is a connected graph without cycles. (^{\text{†}})A subtree of vertex (v) is the subgraph of (v), all its descendants, and all the edges between them. (^{\text{‡}})Two trees are considered distinct if and only if there exists a pair of vertices such that there is an edge
2178F.editorial_text:
2178F - Conquer or of Forest
Read the hints for an intuitive walkthrough!
Consider the components formed after removing all edges connecting a white vertex and its parent. Note that naturally, every component has exactly one white vertex and it is the vertex closest to the root. 
Claim: The above property is an invariant of the operation (that is, the components will always remain the same and a vertex is white iff it is the one closest to the root within a component).
Proof: In order to prove this, we will use the fact that every component has even size and every vertex has odd degree (with the exception of the component containing vertex $$$1$$$). You should try to prove why this is the case!
Suppose the operation was applied a single time, we will show that the invariant still holds. First, note that a single operation cannot break apart a component as the only removable edge is one connecting a white vertex and its parent (which is in a different component). After the operation, consider any component that is a leaf (that is, does not have any other component as a descendant).

If this is the component containing vertex $$$1$$$, note that this component could not have changed as a result of the operation and thus we are done. 
Otherwise, the component has even size and thus the root of the subtree (that is, the vertex closest to the root) is colored white. It suffices to show that there are no other white vertices. Assume otherwise for the sake of contradiction that there exists another white vertex and consider the white vertex with greatest depth. The degree of this vertex is odd and thus it must have an even number of children. However, every child must be colored black since otherwise there would be a white vertex with greater depth. If a vertex has an even number of odd sized subtrees, its own subtree must also have odd size and we have a contradiction. 
Now, in the latter case, because a subtree of even size does not affect the colors of any of its ancestors, we can remove the component and repeatedly apply the above reasoning. Thus, we've shown that the invariant holds. $$$\square$$$
So what kinds of trees can Yuuki construct? A corollary of the above claim is that any edge within a component cannot be removed. It turns out Yuuki can make any tree as long as no edges are removed within a component. Here is one possible method of constructing any tree: remove leaf components one by one and attach them to vertex $$$1$$$, then reassemble the now independent components as desired.
Let there be $$$k$$$ components $$$c_1\ldots c_k$$$ and their sizes be $$$s_1\ldots s_k$$$ (where $$$c_1$$$ contains vertex $$$1$$$). In order to satisfy the conquered condition, the components must be in a line with $$$c_1$$$ as an endpoint. 

If $$$k=1$$$, then no operations can be applied and the answer is $$$1$$$. 
Otherwise, $$$c_1$$$ must be one endpoint of the line and suppose $$$c_i$$$ ($$$2\le i\le k$$$) is the other endpoint. First, we get to reorder the internal components of the line in any way. For the two endpoint components, we must choose one vertex that is connected to its neighbor. For the internal components, we must choose two vertices, one for each neighbor. Therefore, the number of conquered trees is $$$$$$(k-2)!\cdot s_1\cdot s_i\cdot \prod_{j\not\in\{1, i\}}s_j^2$$$$$$ Taking the sum over all $$$i$$$, we get $$$$$$\sum_{i=2}^k\left((k-2)!\cdot s_1\cdot s_i\cdot \prod_{j\not\in\{1, i\}}s_j^2\right)=(k-2)!\cdot s_1\cdot \left(\sum_{i=2}^k\frac{1}{s_i}\right)\left(\prod_{i=2}^ks_i^2\right)$$$$$$ 
The sizes of the components can be found via DFS which, along with the above formula, can be computed in $$$O(n)$$$.

2178G.title: deCH OR Dations
2178G.statement_text: Due to supply chain issues in the North Pole (allegedly caused by a lazy elf), Santa is planning to give out hand-drawn circles as presents this Christmas. Please help him decorate them! There are (2n) equally spaced points around the circle, labeled (1,2,\ldots,2n) in clockwise order. Santa has chosen (n) chords with distinct endpoints, where chord (i) connects the points (a_i) and (b_i). He draws these chords onto the circle one by one, in order. After Santa has drawn the first (\ell) chords, consider any non-empty subset (S) of the (\ell) chords and let (1\leq c_1<c_2<\cdots<c_{|S|}\leq \ell) be their indices. (S) is defined to be a chain if and only if chord (c_k) intersects chord (c_{k+1}) for all (1\leq k < |S|). Note that (S) is always a chain if (|S|=1). Santa does not want any chord to be the odd one out. Therefore, he considers the chords to be tight-knit if and only if every chord appears in an even number of chains , taken over all chains that are subsets of the first (\ell) chords. For each (\ell) from (1) to (n), help Santa determine whether his chords are tight-knit . Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((2\le n\le 5\cdot 10^5)) — the number of chords. Then (n) lines follow, the (i)-th line containing two integers (a_i) and (b_i) ((1\le a_i<b_i\le 2n)) — the endpoints of the (i)-th chord. It is guaranteed that all endpoints are distinct. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (5\cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a string of length (n) — the (\ell)-th character should be (1) if the first (\ell) chords are tight-knit and (0) otherwise. In the first test case, n
2178G.editorial_text:
2178G - deCH OR Dations
The first key observation is that computation in $$$\mathbb{Z}_2$$$ works very nicely with chords. In particular, if you have bit string of length $$$2n$$$ and set the bits $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ to $$$1$$$ for some chord $$$i$$$, a range XOR query over the range $$$[x_j,y_j]$$$ for some chord $$$j$$$ will only count the contribution from chord $$$i$$$ if chord $$$i$$$ intersects chord $$$j$$$ (if they do not intersect, the indices $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ will appear either not appear or appear twice and cancel itself out). By this observation, using an XOR Fenwick Tree, we can compute $$$f(i)=(\text{number of }\textit{chains}\text{ ending at chord }i)\text{ mod } 2$$$ efficiently.
Now, consider the following solution that is too slow. For every $$$1\le i, j\le n$$$, let $$$$$$g(i,j)=(\text{number of }\textit{chains} \text{ containing chord }j\text{ and ending at chord }i)\text{ mod } 2$$$$$$ We can check whether the chords are tight-knit by checking whether $$$$$$\oplus_{i=j}^\ell g(i,j)=0\qquad\forall 1\leq j\leq \ell$$$$$$ We can compute the values of $$$g(i,j)$$$ as follows: $$$$$$ g(i,j)= \begin{cases} 0 & i \lt j\\ f(i) & i=j\\ \oplus_{k \lt i\text{ and chord }k\text{ intersects chord } i} g(k, j)& \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$$$$$ Notably, computing for the last case can be optimized using the initial key observation. Using a Fenwick Tree of ✨ bitsets ✨, we can speed up the solution to $$$O(\frac{n^2}{w})$$$, but it will MLE/TLE.
In order to speed this up further, we will use the fact that we need every chord to appear an even number of times (and do not necessarily need to know the parities of each individual one). Define $$$$$$h(i)=\{j : f(i,j)=1\}$$$$$$ Now, we want to check whether $$$$$$\oplus_{i=1}^\ell h(i)=\emptyset$$$$$$ and we can compute $$$$$$ h(i)=\left(\oplus_{k \lt i\text{ and chord }k\text{ intersects chord } i} h(k)\right)\oplus \left(\{i\}\text{ if }f(i)=1\text{ else }\{\}\right) $$$$$$
However, it is obviously not possible to store and update these sets naively. What magical method can we use to store these sets efficiently? XOR Hashing!
If we compute a random $$$64$$$-bit hash for each chord, we can express a set as the XOR of the hashes of its elements. We can compute a symmetric difference of two sets by taking the XOR of its hashes. Thus, if we maintain two XOR Fenwick Trees (one for $$$f(i)$$$ and one for the hashes of $$$h(i)$$$), we can perform all updates in $$$O(\log n)$$$ and solve the problem in $$$O(n\log n)$$$.

2178H.title: Create or Duplicate
2178H.statement_text: Santa realized that hand-drawing circles takes too long, so he has turned to magic to meet his production quotas. There are three types of presents with distinct values (a), (b), and (c). Initially, Santa has exactly one present of each type. You are given two integers (m) and (k), representing Santa's favorite number and the cost of duplication, respectively. Santa can cast the following two types of spells any number of times (possibly zero): Create — Choose a type of present and create one additional present of that type. This spell costs (x) mana, where (x\in \{a,b,c\}) is the value of the chosen type. Duplicate — Choose a type of present and duplicate all presents of that type. This spell costs (k) mana. Santa wants to perform a sequence of spells such that the sum of the values of all presents is a multiple of (m) after the spells. Determine the minimum amount of mana Santa needs to achieve this. It can be shown that, under the given constraints, such a sequence of spells always exists. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains five integers (a), (b), (c), (m), and (k) ((1\leq a< b< c< m\leq 5\cdot 10^5), (1\leq k\leq 5\cdot 10^5)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (m) over all test cases does not exceed (5\cdot 10^5). It is guaranteed that the sum of (k) over all test cases does not exceed (5\cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the minimum amount of mana Santa needs to make the sum of the values of all presents a multiple of (m). Let (\ell) be the list of values of presents and (\operatorname{sum}(\ell)) be the sum of all elements in (\ell). In the first test case, below is an optimal sequence of operations: In the second test case, it is optimal to not perform any operat
2178H.editorial_text:
2178H - Create or Duplicate
The operations are independent for each present so we'll consider them separately. First, we will solve the easier version of only one present type with value $$$a$$$.
When applying an operation, we only care about the current residue of the total sum modulo $$$m$$$. This motivates us to have some DP with this residue as the state. Let $$$dp[x]$$$ denote the minimum cost of a sequence of operations to get to $$$x\text{ mod }m$$$. We have $$$dp[a]=0$$$ and the transitions 

$$$dp[x+a\text{ mod } m]=\min(dp[x + a\text{ mod } m], dp[x] + a)$$$ for the Create spell 
$$$dp[x\cdot 2\text{ mod } m]=\min(dp[x \cdot 2\text{ mod } m], dp[x] + k)$$$ for the Duplicate spell 
Because there is no nice way to iterate over $$$x$$$ in computing these transitions, we must consider a weighted graph representation (states as vertices and transitions as edges). In this graph representation, we can use Dijkstra's algorithm to find the shortest paths from vertex $$$0$$$ which give us the desired $$$dp$$$ values.
We could try to combine the results from above for $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, and $$$c$$$. However, this would require a $$$(\min, +)$$$ convolution without a nice structure, which will take $$$O(n^2)$$$.
The issue that prevents us from making a graph representation that combines $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, and $$$c$$$ is that we must maintain separate residues for each value in order to perform updates for the Duplicate spell. For instance, consider the following sequence of spells 

Step123456789
$$$a$$$DuplicateCreateDuplicate
$$$b$$$DuplicateDuplicateDuplicate
$$$c$$$CreateDuplicateCreate
cost$$$k$$$$$$k$$$$$$c$$$$$$a$$$$$$k$$$$$$k$$$$$$k$$$$$$k$$$$$$c$$$
If we only maintain a single combined residue, we do not know how to update our total value when duplicating a single present. To fix this, instead of considering the operations independently, we will perform them together. For instance, consider the following modification of the same sequence 
Step123456
$$$a$$$DuplicateCreateDuplicate
$$$b$$$DuplicateDuplicateDuplicate
$$$c$$$CreateDuplicateCreate
cost$$$k$$$$$$2k$$$$$$a$$$$$$c$$$$$$3k$$$$$$c$$$
This almost works, where we can duplicate presents together and simply double the combined residue. However, because we started with one of each present, we would be duplicating presents that we do not wish to. To fix this, we can just start with no presents and eventually force ourselves to create one of each present (and subtract $$$a+b+c$$$ from the cost at the end). 
Step123456789
$$$a$$$CreateDuplicateCreateDuplicate
$$$b$$$CreateDuplicateDuplicateDuplicate
$$$c$$$CreateCreateDuplicateCreate
cost$$$b$$$$$$k$$$$$$a$$$$$$2k$$$$$$c$$$$$$a$$$$$$c$$$$$$3k$$$$$$c$$$

Thus, consider the graph with vertices $$$(\text{current residue}, \text{mask of presents we have at least one of})$$$. Then, we can create the following edges 

$$$(x, \text{mask}) \to (x + a\text{ mod } m, \text{mask }|\ 100)$$$ with cost $$$a$$$ 
$$$(x, \text{mask}) \to (x + b\text{ mod } m, \text{mask } |\ 010)$$$ with cost $$$b$$$ 
$$$(x, \text{mask}) \to (x + c\text{ mod } m, \text{mask } |\ 001)$$$ with cost $$$c$$$ 
$$$(x, \text{mask}) \to (x \cdot 2\text{ mod } m, \text{mask})$$$ with cost $$$k\cdot \text{popcount}(\text{mask})$$$ 
The desired answer is the shortest path from $$$(0, 000)$$$ to $$$(0, 111)$$$, subtracted by $$$a+b+c$$$. This can be found using Dijkstra's algorithm in $$$O(8m\log m)$$$.

2178I.title: Numbers or Fireworks
2178I.statement_text: Now that all the presents have been delivered, the North Pole is finally at peace — and it's time to celebrate with a spectacular New Year's fireworks show! The North Pole is modeled as the Cartesian plane, with (n) cities located at distinct lattice points. You are also given an integer (k). For a proper subset(^{\text{∗}}) (T) of the cities ((T) may be empty), we define its explosiveness as follows: A firework is launched from every city in (T). For each city (c) not in (T), let (f) be the number of fireworks launched from cities that are exactly (\sqrt{k}) Euclidean distance(^{\text{†}}) away from (c). Assign the number ((f+1)) to this city (c). The explosiveness of (T) is the product of all numbers assigned in Step 2. Compute the sum of the explosiveness of (T) over all (2^n-1) proper subsets (T) of the cities. Since the answer may be large, output it modulo (998\,244\,353). (^{\text{∗}})A proper subset is any subset which is not equal to the whole set. (^{\text{†}})The Euclidean distance between two points ((x, y)) and ((p, q)) is defined as (\sqrt{(x - p)^2 + (y - q)^2}). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 1000)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (k) ((2\le n\le 31), (1\leq k \leq2\cdot 10^4)). Then (n) lines follow, the (i)-th line containing two integers (x_i) and (y_i) ((1\leq x_i, y_i\leq 100)) — the (x) and (y) coordinates of the (i)-th city, respectively. It is guaranteed that the coordinates of the cities are pairwise distinct. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n^3) over all test cases does not exceed (31^3). For each test case, print a single integer — the sum, modulo (998\,244\,353), of the explosiveness over all proper subsets (T) of
2178I.editorial_text:
2178I - Numbers or Fireworks
Consider a graph on $$$n$$$ vertices corresponding to the cities in the input, where two cities have an edge between them if they have distance $$$\sqrt{k}$$$. 
The first thing to note is that the graph is bipartite. To see this, note that if $$$k$$$ is odd and we color the board in a checkerboard pattern then all edges will be between a black and a white cell. The graph is thus bipartite. On the other hand, if $$$k$$$ is even, note that all edges will be between two white cells or between two black cells. We can consider these cases to be independent graphs. If we rotate either of these graphs by 45 degrees and scale down by a factor of $$$\sqrt{2}$$$, we again get a new lattice, except $$$k$$$ has halved. If we repeatedly do this until $$$k$$$ is odd, we can see that the original graph is a disjoint union of bipartite graphs and thus must be bipartite.
From here we can 2-color the graph into two parts $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$. We can assign them such that $$$|A| \leq |B|$$$ (so $$$|A| \leq 15$$$). We iterate over subsets of $$$A'$$$ of $$$A$$$ that we place fireworks in. Note that the product of $$$1+[\text{number of adjacent fireworks}]$$$ can be reformulated as: the number of ways to select $$$0$$$ or $$$1$$$ adjacent fireworks for each city not in $$$T$$$. In other words, for each element not in $$$T$$$ we choose either nothing, or an adjacent city with fireworks.
Thus, we get the following dp approach: $$$\text{dp}[i][\text{mask}]$$$ is the sum of explosiveness after accounting for $$$b_1,\dots,b_i$$$ and mask represents which of the unplaced points in $$$A \setminus A'$$$ have selected an adjacent firework.
The transition from $$$i$$$ to $$$i+1$$$ is: $$$$$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask}]~\text{+=}~\text{dp}[i][\text{mask}] \cdot [1+\text{number of fireworks in }A\text{ that are adjacent to }b_{i+1}]$$$$$$ for the cases where we don't place a firework at $$$b_{i+1}$$$. When we do place a firework, the transition is $$$$$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask} | s]~\text{+=}~\text{dp}[i][\text{mask}]$$$$$$ where $$$s$$$ is a submask of the unplaced points adjacent to $$$b_{i+1}$$$ and $$$s\&mask=0$$$ (this corresponds to the points represented by $$$s$$$ selecting $$$b_{i+1}$$$ as their adjacent firework).
The final total that we want is the sum of $$$\text{dp}[|B|-1][\text{mask}]$$$ over all masks (and then we sum that value over all subsets $$$A'$$$ of $$$A$$$). For each $$$A'$$$, the time complexity is $$$\mathcal{O}(|B|*3^{|A'|})$$$. Summing over all $$$A'$$$, the overall complexity is $$$\mathcal{O}(|B|*4^{|A|})$$$, which needs to be optimized.
In order to speed this up note that the bottleneck is iterating over $$$s$$$ for the $$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask}|s]~\text{+=}~\text{dp}[i][\text{mask}]$$$ transition. In particular, $$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask1}]$$$ gets incremented by $$$\text{dp}[i+1][\text{mask2}]$$$ if and only if $$$\text{mask1}\wedge\text{mask2}$$$ is a submask of the unplaced points adjacent to $$$b_{i+1}$$$. This is exactly the result of a sum-over-subsets dp over the points adjacent to $$$b_{i+1}$$$. This means that the trasition for each $$$b_i$$$ will run in time $$$\mathcal{O}(\deg{b_i}2^{|A'|})$$$, so for each $$$A'$$$, the complexity will be $$$\mathcal{O}(\sum_{b_i \in B} \deg{b_i}\cdot 2^{|A'|}) = \mathcal{O}(|E(G)| \cdot 2^{|A'|})$$$. Summing over all $$$A'$$$ we get that the overall complexity is $$$\mathcal{O}(|E(G)| \cdot 3^{|A|})$$$ which we can upper bound by $$$|A||B|\cdot3^{|A|} = 240 \cdot 3^{15} \approx 3 \cdot 10^9$$$ which should pass with the given time limit (especially given that out innerloop contains only simple operations from the sum-over-subsets DP if we take care to mod only at the end). 
To be more sure the above solution passes, we can show a better bound for $$$|E(G)|$$$. Note that the input graph cannot contain a $$$K_{2, 3}$$$ (as two circles in a plane intersect in at most two points). This means that $$$\sum \deg(b_i)^2 \leq 2 \binom{|A|}{2}$$$, so in the worst case $$$|A| = 15$$$ we get that $$$\sum \binom{\deg{b_i}}2 \leq 210 = 10 \cdot 15 + 6 \cdot 10$$$, so $$$\sum \deg(b_i) \leq 10 \cdot 6 + 6 \cdot 5 = 90$$$. (Note the inequality follows from seeing that if we look at pairs of adjacent vertices from each $$$b_i$$$, each pair of $$$a_i$$$ appears at most twice. The second inequality follows from convexity of $$$\binom{x}{2}$$$). 
This gives us a bound of $$$|E(G)| \leq 90$$$. In the actual testdata, the worst case we found was $$$|E(G)| = 76$$$. Plugging in this value tells us that our same solution from before runs in under $$$10^9$$$ operations (which are mainly arithmetic and bitwise), which should easily pass.

2182A.title: New Year String
2182A.statement_text: We will call a string consisting of characters 0 , 2 , 5 , and/or 6 a New Year string if at least one of the two conditions is met: it contains the string 2026 as a continuous substring; it does not contain the string 2025 as a continuous substring. For example, the strings 20252026 , 21026 , 20262026 , 000 are New Year strings. The strings 2025 , 20256 , 20252025 , 000202500020226 are not New Year strings. You are given a string (s). You can perform the following operation any number of times (possibly zero): choose a character in the string (s) and replace it with 0 , 2 , 5 , or 6 (you can choose any one of these four characters). Calculate the minimum number of operations needed to make the string (s) a New Year string. The first line contains one integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. Each test case consists of two lines: the first line contains one integer (n) ((4 \le n \le 20)) — the number of characters in (s); the second line contains (s) — a sequence of (n) characters 0 , 2 , 5 , and/or 6 . For each test case, output one integer — the minimum number of operations needed to make the string (s) a New Year string. In the second example from the statement, you can replace the (2)-nd character of the string with 2 . Then the string will become 2225 . In the fifth example from the statement, you can replace the (4)-th character with 6 . Then the string will become 20262025 . In the sixth example from the statement, you can replace the (8)-th character with 6 . Then the string will become 202520266 .
2182A.editorial_text:
2182A - New Year String
The main observation you need to solve this problem is that an occurrence of 2025 can be turned into 2026 using only one operation. So, if the given string does not meet any of the conditions from the statement, you need only one operation to create an occurrence of 2026 (since $$$s$$$ contains 2025 if it is not a New Year string already).
Thus, the answer to the problem is either $$$0$$$ or $$$1$$$. To check if the string meets at least one of the conditions (which is exactly the case when the answer is zero), you can use built-in tools to search for an occurrence of a substring, like string::find in C++ or in in Python.

2182B.title: New Year Cake
2182B.statement_text: Monocarp is going to bake a New Year cake. The cake must consist of at least one layer. The size of the top layer of the cake must be (1); the size of the layer below it must be (2); the layer below that must be (4), and so on (each layer, except for the top one, is twice the size of the layer above it). Additionally, each layer must be covered with either white or dark chocolate. To cover a layer of size (k), Monocarp will need (k) kilograms of chocolate. Each layer must be covered with exactly one type of chocolate, and these types must alternate (if some layer is covered with dark chocolate, both the layer directly below it and the layer directly above it must be covered with white chocolate, and vice versa). Monocarp has (a) kilograms of white chocolate and (b) kilograms of dark chocolate. He wants to calculate the maximum number of layers that the cake can consist of, ensuring that he has enough chocolate of both types. The first line contains one integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. Each test case consists of one line containing two integers (a) and (b) ((1 \le a, b \le 10^6)). For each test case, output one integer — the maximum possible number of layers in the cake. In the first example, Monocarp can bake a cake with one layer of size (1) and cover it with any type of chocolate. In the second example, Monocarp can bake a cake with two layers: the top layer of size (1) with white chocolate, and below it a layer of size (2) with dark chocolate. In the third example, Monocarp can bake a cake with two layers: the top layer of size (1) with dark chocolate, and below it a layer of size (2) with white chocolate. In the fourth example, Monocarp can bake a cake with two layers: the top layer of size (1) with dark chocolate, and below it a layer of size (2) with white chocolate. Note that a cake with three layers, where the top layer of size (1) and the la
2182B.editorial_text:
2182B - New Year Cake
The sizes of the cake layers grow exponentially: each subsequent layer is twice the size of the previous one. This means that the answer to the problem is not very large — it does not exceed $$$\log_2{\max(a, b)}$$$, which under the problem constraints is no more than $$$20$$$. This allows us to write a solution with runtime proportional to the answer.
For example, we can write a loop that maintains the current total size of the "even" and "odd" layers (by "even", we mean the top layer and all layers of the same type with it, and by "odd", we mean all the other layers). During each iteration, we can increase one of these total sizes by the current power of two and check that we have enough chocolate for the current sizes of the layers (depending on the implementation, two cases may be required here, as the top layer can be covered with chocolate of any type). As soon as we run out of chocolate, we can break the loop — in the next iteration, another layer will be added, and if we did not have enough chocolate for $$$k$$$ layers, we will not have enough for $$$(k+1)$$$ layers either.
Another solution is to iterate over the number of layers in the cake and check if there is enough chocolate for a cake of that many layers. Although this solution is slower, it is still fast enough for the problem constraints.

2182C.title: Production of Snowmen
2182C.statement_text: To create a truly festive atmosphere, Santa's helpers have opened a factory for producing snowmen! Each snowman consists of three snowballs — a head, a torso, and legs. For the snowman to be stable, the ball forming the legs must be strictly larger than the ball forming the torso; in turn, the ball forming the torso must be strictly larger than the ball forming the head. Formally, if we denote the sizes of the head, torso, and legs as (a, b, c) respectively, the snowman will be stable if and only if (a < b < c). At the snowman production factory, there are three conveyors, each containing (n) snowballs. The first conveyor contains balls of sizes (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n); the second contains balls of sizes (b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n); the third contains balls of sizes (c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n). The conveyors are cyclic; in other words, after the element numbered (n), the element numbered (1) follows again, and we can consider that the ball numbered (i) and the ball numbered (i+n) (as well as the ball numbered (i+2n), (i+3n), and so on) are the same ball. To produce snowmen, it is necessary to specify three parameters (i, j, k) ((1 \le i, j, k \le n)), indicating which balls on each conveyor the production starts from. After that, the snowmen will be assembled from the balls as follows: the first snowman will have a head of size (a_i), a torso of size (b_j), and legs of size (c_k); the second snowman will have a head of size (a_{i+1}), a torso of size (b_{j+1}), and legs of size (c_{k+1}); and so on; the (n)-th (last) snowman will have a head of size (a_{i+n-1}), a torso of size (b_{j+n-1}), and legs of size (c_{k+n-1}). The parameters (i, j, k) must be chosen in such a way that all (n) snowmen are stable. Your task is to count the number of suitable combinations of parameters. The first line contains one integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 5000)) — the number of test

2182D.title: Christmas Tree Decoration
2182D.statement_text: A group of (n) people decided to decorate the Christmas tree. They have ((n+1)) boxes of decorations, numbered from (0) to (n). Initially, the (i)-th box contains (a_i) decorations. We say that a permutation (p) of size (n) (an array of size (n) where each number from (1) to (n) appears exactly once) is fair if it is possible to hang all the decorations on the tree using the following process: person (p_1) takes a decoration either from box (0) or from box (p_1), and hangs it on the tree; person (p_2) takes a decoration either from box (0) or from box (p_2), and hangs it on the tree; and so on; after person (p_n), person (p_1) follows, and the process repeats until all the decoration are on the tree. During this process, there should never be a situation where person (i) needs to hang a decoration, but both box (0) and box (i) are empty. If such a situation cannot be avoided, the permutation is not fair. However, if the people can choose from which box to take a decoration during each step in such a way that this situation does not arise, then the permutation is fair. Your task is to calculate the number of fair permutations. Since the answer may be large, output it modulo (998244353). The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 5000)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 50)). The second line contains ((n+1)) integers (a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n) ((0 \le a_i \le 10^6)). For each test case, print a single integer — the number of fair permutations, taken modulo (998244353). In the first example, the fair permutations are (1, 2, 3) and (1, 3, 2). Let's take a closer look at the Christmas tree decoration for permutation (1, 3, 2): the person (p_1=1) hangs a decoration from the box (1); the person (p_2=3) hangs a decoration from the
2182D.editorial_text:
2182D - Christmas Tree Decoration
Note that it is optimal for each person to hang decorations first from their own box, and only when it becomes empty, they should start hanging decorations from the $$$0$$$-th box.
Each person will hang at least $$$k = \lfloor\frac{s}{n}\rfloor$$$ decorations, where $$$s = \sum\limits_{i=0}^{n} a_i$$$ is the total number of decorations. Let $$$b_0, b_1, \dots, b_n$$$  represent the remaining number of decorations after $$$k$$$ full rounds. If $$$b_0 \lt 0$$$ (indicating someone did not have enough decorations for $$$k$$$ rounds) or if there is an $$$i \gt 0$$$ such that $$$b_i \gt 1$$$ (meaning there is a person who cannot hang all their decorations), then fair permutations are impossible.
During the last round, $$$s \bmod n$$$ decorations remain. Let $$$z$$$ denote the number of people with empty boxes, and $$$x = z - b_0$$$ be the number of people who will not hang decorations during this round. If $$$x \lt 0$$$, there are too many decorations in the $$$0$$$-th box, and $$$z$$$ people cannot hang them all. In this case, there are no fair permutations either. Otherwise, the number of fair permutations can be calculated using simple combinatorial formula: $$$\binom{z}{x} x! (n - x)!$$$. This involves selecting $$$x$$$ people out of $$$z$$$ who will not hang decorations (placing them at the end of the permutation) and arranging their order, as well as ordering the remaining $$$(n-x)$$$ people who will hang the decorations.

2182E.title: New Year's Gifts
2182E.statement_text: Monocarp has (n) friends and decided to give a New Year's gift to each of them. He has also prepared (m) boxes to place the gifts in; the beauty of the (i)-th box is (a_i). Every box can contain at most one gift. Monocarp wants to give a gift worth at least (y_i) coins to the (i)-th friend. Additionally, he knows that the (i)-th friend will be happy if at least one of the following conditions holds: the gift is in a box with beauty at least (x_i); the gift is worth at least (z_i) ((z_i > y_i)). Your task is to help Monocarp calculate the maximum possible number of friends he can make happy if he has (k) coins. Note that Monocarp must purchase a gift for each friend, and the gift may not necessarily come in a box . The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains three integers (n), (m) and (k) ((1 \le n, m \le 2 \cdot 10^5); (1 \le k \le 10^{15})). The second line contains (m) integers (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m) ((1 \le a_i \le m)). Then (n) lines follow; the (i)-th of them contains three integers (x_i), (y_i) and (z_i) ((1 \le x_i \le m); (1 \le y_i < z_i \le 10^9)). Additional constraints on the input: (\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} y_i \le k). the sum of (n) over all test cases doesn't exceed (2 \cdot 10^5); the sum of (m) over all test cases doesn't exceed (2 \cdot 10^5); For each test case, print a single integer — the maximum possible number of friends Monocarp can make happy if he has (k) coins. In the first example, Monocarp can make both friends happy as follows: give the first friend a gift for (3) coins, and give the second friend a gift for (2) coins in a box with (1) beauty. In the second example, Monocarp cannot make any of his friends happy, because he does not have enough money to buy a gift for (z_i) coins for even o
2182E.editorial_text:
2182E - New Year's Gifts
Let's reformulate the problem a bit: we'll immediately spend $$$\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}$$$ coins on gifts for each friend. Now, we can make the $$$i$$$-th friend happy if we use some box $$$j$$$ with a beauty $$$a_j \ge x_i$$$ or if we pay extra $$$z_i - y_i$$$ coins.
Let's say we put some gifts in boxes, and now we want to pay extra for some gifts. Obviously, to do this, we will sort the remaining friends in ascending order of the values of $$$z_i - y_i$$$ and take some prefix of friends. From here, we can see that for the box $$$j$$$, we want to put a gift $$$i$$$ such that $$$x_i \le a_j$$$, and $$$z_i - y_i$$$ is as big as possible, so that you have to pay less extra for the remaining gifts.
Therefore, we can solve the problem using the following greedy algorithm: let's go through the beauty $$$j$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$m$$$ and maintain a set (sorted by value $$$z_i - y_i$$$) of unpacked gifts with $$$x_i \le j$$$. Then for a box with beauty $$$j$$$, we can take a gift from the set with the maximum value of $$$z_i - y_i$$$. After such a pass, it is impossible to match any box with any gift, which means we will have to pay extra for several gifts (the cheapest ones) that are left in the set, as long as the value of $$$k$$$ allows it.

2182F1.title: Christmas Reindeer (easy version)
2182F1.statement_text: This is the easy version of the problem. The only difference between the versions is the upper bound on (n) and (m). In this version, (n \le 500) and (m \le 500). You have a herd of (n) Christmas reindeer. The strength of the (i)-th reindeer is (2^{c_i}). The carrying capacity of a group of (k) Christmas reindeer is calculated as follows: the strengths of the reindeer are sorted in non-increasing order. Let's denote the sorted list of strengths as (c'_1, c'_2, \dots, c'_k), where (c'_i \ge c'_{i+1}); then, the carrying capacity of this group of reindeer is equal to (c'_1 + \lfloor\frac{c'_2}{2}\rfloor + \lfloor\frac{c'_3}{4}\rfloor + \dots + \lfloor\frac{c'_k}{2^{k - 1}}\rfloor). Note that some reindeer may contribute zero to the carrying capacity of the group. You have to process queries of three types: add a reindeer with strength equal to (2^x) to the herd; remove a reindeer with strength equal to (2^x) from the herd of reindeer; calculate the number of ways to choose some of the reindeer from the herd (possibly all of them) so that the carrying capacity of the chosen group is at least (x) . If there are multiple reindeer with the same strength in the herd, they are considered different. For example, if you have two reindeer with strength (1) each, and you need to calculate the number of ways to choose a group with carrying capacity of at least (1), there are (3) ways to choose it: choose the first reindeer, the second reindeer, or both of them. The first line contains two integers (n) and (m) ((1 \le n, m \le 500)) — the initial number of reindeer in the herd and the number of queries, respectively. The second line contains (n) integers (c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n) ((0 \le c_i \le 60)) denoting the strengths of the reindeer in the herd: the strength of the (i)-th reindeer is (2^{c_i}). The next (m) lines describe the queries in one of the following formats

2182F2.title: Christmas Reindeer (hard version)
2182F2.statement_text: This is the hard version of the problem. The only difference between the versions is the upper bound on (n) and (m). In this version, (n \le 3 \cdot 10^5) and (m \le 3 \cdot 10^5). You have a herd of (n) Christmas reindeer. The strength of the (i)-th reindeer is (2^{c_i}). The carrying capacity of a group of (k) Christmas reindeer is calculated as follows: the strengths of the reindeer are sorted in non-increasing order. Let's denote the sorted list of strengths as (c'_1, c'_2, \dots, c'_k), where (c'_i \ge c'_{i+1}); then, the carrying capacity of this group of reindeer is equal to (c'_1 + \lfloor\frac{c'_2}{2}\rfloor + \lfloor\frac{c'_3}{4}\rfloor + \dots + \lfloor\frac{c'_k}{2^{k - 1}}\rfloor). Note that some reindeer may contribute zero to the carrying capacity of the group. You have to process queries of three types: add a reindeer with strength equal to (2^x) to the herd; remove a reindeer with strength equal to (2^x) from the herd of reindeer; calculate the number of ways to choose some of the reindeer from the herd (possibly all of them) so that the carrying capacity of the chosen group is at least (x) . If there are multiple reindeer with the same strength in the herd, they are considered different. For example, if you have two reindeer with strength (1) each, and you need to calculate the number of ways to choose a group with carrying capacity of at least (1), there are (3) ways to choose it: choose the first reindeer, the second reindeer, or both of them. The first line contains two integers (n) and (m) ((1 \le n, m \le 3 \cdot 10^5)) — the initial number of reindeer in the herd and the number of queries, respectively. The second line contains (n) integers (c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n) ((0 \le c_i \le 60)) denoting the strengths of the reindeer in the herd: the strength of the (i)-th reindeer is (2^{c_i}). The next (m) lines describe the queries in o
2182F2.editorial_text:
2182F2 - Christmas Reindeer (hard version)
In this editorial, we wiil refer to a deer with strength $$$2^i$$$ as a deer of type $$$i$$$ for convenience.
The first observation needed to solve the problem is as follows: if we replace a deer of type $$$i$$$, which contributes a non-zero amount to the carrying capacity, with any number of deer of lower types, the total carrying capacity will decrease. We will prove this: suppose there were $$$k$$$ other deer before this one in sorted order, and it is the last deer of type $$$i$$$. Then its contribution is $$$\frac{2^i}{2^k}$$$. If we replace it with any number of deer of lower types, the contribution of the strongest of these deers will be at most $$$\frac{2^{i-1}}{2^k}$$$, the contribution of the next one will be at most $$$\frac{2^{i-1}}{2^{k+1}}$$$, the contribution of the next one will be at most $$$\frac{2^{i-1}}{2^{k+2}}$$$, and so on. If we sum the maximum possible contributions of all subsequent deer, we get $$$(\frac{2^i}{2^k} - 1)$$$, which is less than the contribution of the deer of type $$$i$$$. Let's remember this observation; we will need it soon.
Now let's try to understand how to achieve a carrying capacity of exactly $$$x$$$, ensuring that there are no deers with zero contribution. This will help us later understand when the carrying capacity is at least $$$x$$$.
Consider the highest non-zero bit of $$$x$$$; let this be the bit corresponding to $$$2^i$$$. Also, consider the strongest deer in the group; let its type be $$$j$$$:

If $$$j \lt i$$$, then we cannot achieve a total carrying capacity of $$$2^i$$$ with deer of types $$$j$$$ and lower, so the total carrying capacity will definitely be less than $$$x$$$; 
If $$$j \gt i$$$, then the deer of type $$$j$$$ definitely provides a carrying capacity strictly greater than $$$x$$$; 
If $$$j = i$$$, then we can subtract $$$2^i$$$ from $$$x$$$, remember that we had one deer of type $$$i$$$, and move to the next bit. 
For the next bit (let's say it corresponds to $$$2^{i'}$$$), the situation is the same, but since the contribution of the next deer is half as much, instead of comparing with $$$i'$$$, we need to compare with $$$(i'+1)$$$. For the bit after that (let's say it corresponds to $$$2^{i"}$$$), we need to compare with $$$(i"+2)$$$, and so on. Note that since $$$i'+1 \le i$$$, each subsequent deer will definitely not be stronger than the previous one.
Thus, we can determine how many deer of each type are needed so that the total carrying capacity is exactly $$$x$$$, and no deer contributes zero. Let's say we obtained an array $$$[r_0, r_1, r_2, \dots, r_{60}]$$$, where $$$r_i$$$ is the required number of deer of type $$$i$$$.
Now, let's understand how to check that the carrying capacity of a group of deer, where there are $$$[k_0, k_1, k_2, \dots, k_{60}]$$$ deer of types $$$0, 1, 2, \dots, 60$$$, is at least $$$x$$$. We find the last position where $$$r_i \ne k_i$$$ (if there is none, then the carrying capacity equals $$$x$$$). If in this position $$$r_i \gt k_i$$$, then we are lacking a deer of this type, and the carrying capacity is less than $$$x$$$. If $$$r_i \lt k_i$$$, then this "extra" deer covers the remaining carrying capacity, and the carrying capacity of the group is at least $$$x$$$.
Now we can solve the problem. We will maintain an array $$$[f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{60}]$$$, where $$$f_i$$$ is the number of deer of type $$$i$$$. Queries of the first and second types are handled trivially. To process a query of the third type, let's iterate over how many of the last elements in the arrays $$$r$$$ (the required number of deer of each type) and $$$k$$$ (the number of deer of each type in the group we are building) match. Let's say $$$r_i \ne k_i$$$, but all subsequent values match; we will count the number of ways to assemble a group of deer such that the array $$$k$$$ satisfies this condition:

for deer of all types $$$j \gt i$$$, we definitely know their counts, so the number of ways to choose them is $$$\prod\limits_{j=i+1}^{60} {{f_j}\choose{r_j}}$$$; 
for deer of all types $$$j \lt i$$$, we are fine with any number, so the number of ways to choose them is $$$2^{f_0 + f_1 + \dots + f_{i-1}}$$$; 
for deers of type $$$i$$$, their count must be more than $$$r_i$$$, so the number of ways to choose them is $$$\sum\limits_{j=r_i+1}^{f_i} {{f_i}\choose{j}}$$$. 
The first and second values can be recalculated in $$$O(1)$$$ for each $$$i$$$. But what about the third value? Let's use the fact that $$$\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n} {{n}\choose{k}} = 2^n$$$, and transform it as follows (assuming $$$r_i \le f_i$$$):
$$$$$$\sum\limits_{j=r_i+1}^{f_i} {{f_i}\choose{j}} = 2^{f_i} - \sum\limits_{j=0}^{r_i} {{f_i}\choose{j}}$$$$$$
This value can now be computed in $$$O(r_i)$$$, and since the sum $$$r_i$$$ does not exceed the number of bits in $$$x$$$, we can process the query in $$$O(\log x)$$$. Don't forget that the arrays $$$r$$$ and $$$k$$$ may not necessarily differ, so we also need to add the number of ways to choose a group of deer with the specified array of counts (but this is calculated trivially).

2182G.title: Short Garland
2182G.statement_text: Monocarp wants to hang a garland on the Christmas tree. The Christmas tree is a tree with (n) vertices rooted at vertex (1). The distance between two vertices of the tree is the number of edges on the shortest path between them, and the depth of a vertex is the distance from it to the root. The garland consists of (n) bulbs connected by wire and numbered from (1) to (n). The length of the wire between every two adjacent bulbs is (k). The garland must be hung on the tree according to the following rules: every bulb must be placed on one of the vertices of the tree, and every vertex must have exactly one bulb on it; bulb (1) must be placed on the root of the tree; each subsequent bulb has to be placed on such a vertex that its parent vertex has a bulb on it. If there are multiple such vertices, the vertex with the largest depth is chosen. If there are still multiple options, any of them can be chosen; for each pair of subsequent bulbs, the distance between the vertices they are placed on must not exceed (k). Your task is to count the number of ways to hang the garland while following all the rules and output it modulo (998244353). Two ways are considered different if there exists at least one integer (i \in 1, n) such that the (i)-th bulb is placed on different vertices in these two ways. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (k) ((2 \le n \le 3 \cdot 10^5); (1 \le k < n)) — the number of vertices in the tree and the distance constraint between two consecutive bulbs. The second line contains (n-1) integers (p_2, p_3, \dots, p_n) ((1 \le p_i < i)), where (p_i) is the parent of the (i)-th vertex in the tree. Additional constraint on the input: the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (3 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output one integer
2182G.editorial_text:
2182G - Short Garland
The procedure in the problem statement describes a depth-first search, where a vertex is written down upon entry. Accordingly, the choice we are allowed to make is the order of traversing the children of each vertex.
Let's think about the condition that the distance must not exceed $$$k$$$. It follows that when we have traversed all vertices in the subtree of one child of vertex $$$v$$$, and there are still other unvisited children, the last visited vertex in the subtree must be at a distance of no more than $$$k-1$$$ from $$$v$$$.
Let's try to fit this into dynamic programming. Let $$$\mathit{dp}[v][k]$$$ store the number of ways to traverse the subtree of vertex $$$v$$$ such that the last visited vertex is at a distance exactly $$$k$$$ from $$$v$$$. This dynamic programming can be computed as follows. Fix the last visited child of the vertex and the depth of the last vertex in its subtree. Then, the other children can be visited in any order, as long as the condition that the depth does not exceed $$$k-1$$$ is satisfied. That is, for each child, we need to sum $$$\mathit{dp}[u][t]$$$ for all $$$t \lt k$$$, multiply the obtained sums, and multiply by the factorial of the number of remaining children to fix their order.
In fact, in such dynamic programming, it is often more convenient to store not the dp array itself, but its prefix sum directly. Thus, we can say that $$$\mathit{dp}[v][k]$$$ will store the number of ways to traverse the subtree of vertex $$$v$$$ such that the last visited vertex is at a distance no more than $$$k$$$ from $$$v$$$. Then, for recalculation, it is enough to take the value $$$\mathit{dp}[u][k-1]$$$. Thus, the transitions in the dynamic programming look as follows: $$$\mathit{dp}[v][t+1] = \sum\limits_{u \in g_v}\mathit{dp}[u][t] \cdot (|g_v|-1)! \cdot \mathit{prod}_u$$$, where $$$\mathit{prod}_u = \prod\limits_{w \in g_v; w \neq u}\mathit{dp}[w][k-1]$$$.
We have obtained a polynomial solution to the problem, but so far it is too slow. Since the depth (the second state of the dynamic programming) is of the order of $$$O(n)$$$, the complexity in the most optimal implementation will be $$$O(n^2)$$$.
The first difficulty is obtaining the product $$$\mathit{dp}[u][k-1]$$$ for all children of $$$v$$$, except for the current one. Of course, we can precompute the product for all children and then divide by the value for the current child to remove its contribution to the product. The modulo in the problem is prime, so dividing is not too difficult; however, there is a problem with zero values. When multiplying by zero, all information about the other factors is lost, and it cannot be retrieved. There are two popular ways to solve this problem. The first solution is to compute the product on the prefix and on the suffix of the children. To obtain the product without one factor, we multiply the prefix up to it and the suffix after it. The second solution is to compute the product without zeros and also keep track of the number of zeros. If there are at least two zeros, the product will always be zero, regardless of which factor we remove. With one zero, we can carefully consider whether we are removing a zero or a non-zero value.
Now, regarding the optimization of the dynamic programming itself. It is quite natural to try to optimize it using small-to-large. The contributions of the children, except for the heaviest one, are calculated in the same way. For them, we can iterate through all depths and add them with the corresponding coefficients. To avoid adding the contribution of the heaviest child, we can multiply the values of its dynamic programming by a correct coefficient and make this an initial dp for the vertex $$$v$$$.
Unfortunately, we cannot afford to iterate over all values for the heaviest child. Let's perform the multiplication lazily instead. In addition to the dynamic programming array, we will also store two values: $$$\mathit{ml}$$$ — what to multiply all elements of the array by and $$$\mathit{ad}$$$ — what to add to them. Then, the heaviest child can be recalculated by multiplying both $$$\mathit{ml}$$$ and $$$\mathit{ad}$$$ by the necessary coefficient.
To add values for the other children, we need to divide them by $$$\mathit{ml}$$$ in advance. This means that $$$\mathit{ml}$$$ should not be zero, which could potentially happen when recalculating the heaviest child. Let's solve this problem. If we need to multiply $$$\mathit{ml}$$$ by zero, we can set all values of dp to zero with a loop and only leave as many values as there are in the second largest child. Then the heaviest child is still the heaviest, but the complexity of small-to-large is preserved.
The value of $$$\mathit{ad}$$$ is needed for adding the other children. Since we maintain the prefix sum of the dynamic programming, we need to update all dp values for $$$v$$$ for each child. That would break the small-to-large complexity if performed directly. However, all values beyond the depth of the child change by the same value. Therefore, we can lazily add this number to the variable $$$\mathit{ad}$$$.
This variation of small-to-large, where the number of dynamic programming values is limited by the height of the vertex, works in $$$O(n)$$$. In my implementation, the asymptotic complexity turned out to be $$$O(n \log A)$$$ because it is necessary to compute the inverse element for $$$\mathit{ml}$$$ at each vertex.

2183D1 — Tree Coloring (Easy Version)
Idea & Preparation: jiazhichen844

Rate The Problem!

[likes: 5, option1] Good Problem

[likes: 5, option2] Okay Problem

[likes: 5, option3] Bad Problem

[likes: 5, option4] Didn't Solve

Hint 1
Consider which points cannot be colored in the same operation.

Hint 2
Find a lower bound for the number of operations.

Solution
Suppose the number of points at depth $$$i$$$ is $$$t_i$$$. First, points at the same depth cannot be colored simultaneously, so the lower bound for the answer is $$$\max t_i$$$.
However, note that if points in layer $$$x$$$ share a common parent, they and their parent also cannot be colored simultaneously. Thus, the answer must also be compared with $$$\max(t_x + 1)$$$.
We claim this is the answer. Proof follows from the constructive proof in D2.
