2193A.title: DBMB and the Array
2193A.statement_text: DBMB had a birthday yesterday. He was gifted an array (a) of (n) elements and a number (x). But there is one problem: he only likes arrays where the sum of the elements equals (s). To make the array appealing to him, you can perform the following operation any number of times: Choose an index (i) ((1 \le i \le n)) and add (x) to the number (a_i). Each test consists of several test cases. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 1000)) — the number of test cases. The following describes the test cases. The first line of each test case contains three integers (n), (s), (x) ((1 \le n, x \le 10), (1 \le s \le 100)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \dots a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le 10)) — the elements of the array gifted to DBMB. For each test case, output " YES " if the array can appeal to DBMB. Otherwise, output " NO ". You can output each letter in any case (lowercase or uppercase). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES " will be accepted as a positive answer. In the second test case, (a = 1, 2, 3), applying the operation on (a_2) gives us (a = 1, 4, 3). The sum of the array equals (s).

2193B.title: Reverse a Permutation
2193B.statement_text: A permutation of length (n) is an array consisting of (n) distinct integers from (1) to (n) in arbitrary order. For example, (2,3,1,5,4) is a permutation, but (1,2,2) and (1,3,4) are not permutations. You are given a permutation (p) of length (n). You can perform the following operation exactly once : Choose two integers (l,) (r) ((1\le l\le r\le n)). Reverse the segment (l, r) in the permutation (p). Each test consists of several test cases. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1\le t\le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains the number (n) ((1\le n\le 2\cdot 10^5)). The second line of each test case contains (n) distinct integers (p_1, p_2,...,p_n) ((1\le p_i\le n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of the values of (n) across all test cases does not exceed (2\cdot 10^5). For each test case, output the lexicographically maximum permutation that can be obtained with one operation. For the first test case, the best segment is (1, 4). After reversing, (a = 4, 1, 2, 3). For the second test case, the best segment is (2, 3). After reversing, (a = 3, 2, 1).

2193C.title: Replace and Sum
2193C.statement_text: Today, KQ has an exam at the Grail Academy. A strict teacher gave a task that KQ could not solve. He was given two arrays (a) and (b) of length (n). KQ is allowed to perform the following operations on the arrays: Choose an index (i) ((1\le i\lt n)) and replace (a_i) with (a_{i+1}). Choose an index (i) ((1\le i\le n)) and replace (a_i) with (b_i). Each test consists of several test cases. The first line contains one integer (t) ((1\le t\le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n), (q) ((1\le n, q\le 2 \cdot 10^5)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2,...,a_n) ((1\le a_i\le 10^4)). The third line of each test case contains (n) integers (b_1, b_2,...,b_n) ((1\le b_i\le 10^4)). The following (q) lines contain two integers (l) and (r) ((1\le l\le r\le n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of the values of (n) and the sum of the values of (q) across all test cases do not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output (q) numbers separated by spaces — the maximum values of the sums ((a_l + a_{l+1} + a_{l+2} + \dots + a_r)). Consider the first test case. Replace (a_3) with (b_3), (a = 3, 2, 3). Replace (a_2) with (a_3), (a = 3, 3, 3). The sum (a_1 + a_2 + a_3 = 9).

2193D.title: Monster Game
2193D.statement_text: You have been gifted a new game called "Elatyh". In the game, you are given (n) swords, each with its own strength. In particular, the sword numbered (i) has a strength of (a_i). The game consists of (n) levels, each of which features a monster. You start at level (1) and progress further. To pass level (i) and move on to level (i + 1), you need to defeat the monster at level (i). To defeat the monster at level (i), you need to deal it (b_i) sword strikes. The swords in the game are very fragile, so they can only deal one strike before breaking. If you complete level (n) or run out of swords, you can finish the game and proceed to score calculation. Before the game, you are allowed to choose the difficulty level. If you choose difficulty (x), swords with a strength less than (x) will not affect the monsters. The game score in this case is equal to (x) multiplied by the number of levels completed. Your task is to choose the game difficulty in such a way as to maximize the game score. Each test consists of several test cases. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1\le t\le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The following describes the test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1\le n\le 2 \cdot 10^5)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) ((1\le a_i\le 10^9)). The third line of each test case contains (n) integers (b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n) ((1\le b_i\le n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of the values of (n) across all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the maximum game score. Consider the first test case. Optimal difficulty to choose is (3). If difficulty is (3), you can deal strikes with swords number (2) and (3). With (2) swords you can complete (1) level, so the game score is (3\cdot 1 = 3).

2193E.title: Product Queries
2193E.statement_text: Today, Sabyrzhan was called to the board with an array (a) of length (n) and was assigned an officer's task — to answer (n) questions. In the (i)-th question, it is required to determine the minimum number of elements from the array that need to be selected from the board (it is allowed to use the same element multiple times) so that their product is exactly equal to (i), or to report that it is impossible to achieve such a product. Note that at least one element must be selected. Each test consists of several test cases. The first line contains one integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains one integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 3 \cdot 10 ^ 5)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of the values of (n) across all test cases does not exceed (3 \cdot 10 ^ 5). For the (i)-th question, output one integer — the minimum number of elements from the array required to obtain a product equal to (i), or (−1) if it is impossible to achieve such a product. Consider the first test case. The products can be obtained as follows: (1) cannot be obtained. (2) can be obtained by selecting (a_2). (3) can be obtained by selecting (a_1). (4) can be obtained by selecting (a_2) twice. (5) cannot be obtained. (6) can be obtained by selecting (a_7). (7) can be obtained by selecting (a_5). (8) can be obtained by selecting (a_2) three times.

2193H.title: Remove the Grail Tree
2193H.statement_text: The Great Grail Tree has stood in the kingdom for (315) years. It takes up a lot of space, so King Ila decided to get rid of it as soon as possible. The tree itself is an acyclic, connected, undirected graph with (n) vertices, each having its own value (a_v). The tree can be removed in the following way: Let (S_v) be the sum of the values of all remaining neighbors of (v). If (v) has no remaining neighbors, then (S_v) is (0). Choose a vertex (v) such that (a_v) and (S_v) differ in parity (i.e., either (a_v) is even and (S_v) is odd, or (a_v) is odd and (S_v) is even). If there are no such vertices, stop the process. Remove vertex (v) and all edges connected to it from the tree. Each test consists of several test case. The first line contains one integer (t) ((1\le t\le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The description of the test cases follows. The first line contains the number (n) ((1\le n\le 2\cdot 10^5)) — the number of vertices in the Grail Tree. The second line describes the array (a) ((1\le a_i\le 10^9)) — the values of the vertices in the tree. Next, there are (n - 1) lines, each containing 2 numbers (v) and (u) ((1\le v, u\le n, v\neq u)), indicating that vertices (v) and (u) are connected by an edge in the tree. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) across all test cases does not exceed (2\cdot 10^5). For each test case, output "YES" if it is possible to completely remove the Grail Tree. Otherwise, output "NO". If the answer is "YES", output any sequence of removals. You can output each letter in any case (lowercase or uppercase). For example, the strings "yEs", "yes", "Yes", and "YES" will be accepted as a positive answer.

You are given an array (a) of length (n). For an integer (k), we call it piggy if and only if it is possible to sort (a) in non-descending order by performing the following operation an arbitrary number of times (possibly zero): First, select two indices (i) and (j) ((1 \le i < j \le n)) such that (|a_i - a_j| \ge k); Then, swap (a_i) and (a_j). You need to determine the largest piggy integer (k). If such an integer does not exist, output (-1). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the length of (a). The second line contains (n) integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le 10^9)) — the elements of (a). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2\cdot10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the largest piggy integer (k). If such an integer does not exist, output (-1) instead. In the first and the second test case, no matter how large (k) is, you can always sort (a) in non-descending order by not performing any operations. In the third test case, the largest piggy (k) is (2). We can select (i=2) and (j=3) in the first operation, since (|a_2-a_3|=|4-2|=2 \ge k), and (a) is sorted in non-descending order. It can be proven that no piggy integers larger than (2) exist.

2187A.editorial_text:
2187A - Restricted Sorting
Firstly, if $$$a$$$ is already sorted, then any integer $$$k$$$ is piggy, we can simply output $$$-1$$$.
Let $$$b$$$ be the array obtained by sorting $$$a$$$. For some $$$1 \le i \le n$$$, if $$$a_i=b_i$$$, we do not need to touch it. For $$$i$$$ with $$$a_i\ne b_i$$$, we need to swap them to their correct places. Let $$$mx=\max(a)$$$ and $$$mn=\min(a)$$$. Consider for an integer $$$k$$$, how do we check if it is piggy:
If $$$mx-mn \lt k$$$, we can swap none of the elements, so $$$k$$$ is not piggy.
If there exists some $$$i$$$ such that $$$a_i \ne b_i$$$ and $$$mx-a_i \lt k$$$ and $$$a_i - mn \lt k$$$, we can never swap this element, so $$$k$$$ is not piggy.
Otherwise, we claim that $$$k$$$ is piggy. This is because we can indirectly swap any pair of $$$a_i$$$ and $$$a_j$$$, with help from $$$mn$$$ and $$$mx$$$. Without loss of generality, consider two cases: 
If $$$a_i-mn\ge k$$$ and $$$a_j-mn \ge k$$$, we can perform the following swaps (elements are shown by their relation positions): 
$$$a_i$$$, $$$a_j$$$, $$$mn$$$
$$$a_i$$$, $$$mn$$$, $$$a_j$$$
$$$mn$$$, $$$a_i$$$, $$$a_j$$$
$$$a_j$$$, $$$a_i$$$, $$$mn$$$ 
If $$$a_i-mn \ge k$$$ and $$$mx-a_j \ge k$$$: 
$$$a_i$$$, $$$a_j$$$, $$$mn$$$, $$$mx$$$
$$$mn$$$, $$$a_j$$$, $$$a_i$$$, $$$mx$$$
$$$mx$$$, $$$a_j$$$, $$$a_i$$$, $$$mn$$$
$$$a_j$$$, $$$mx$$$, $$$a_i$$$, $$$mn$$$
$$$a_j$$$, $$$mn$$$, $$$a_i$$$, $$$mx$$$
$$$a_j$$$, $$$a_i$$$, $$$mn$$$, $$$mx$$$ 
As shown in Hint 1, if we can swap any two elements, we can always sort the array.
With the above analysis, we can binary search for the largest piggy $$$k$$$, and check the answer in $$$O(n)$$$, with overall complexity $$$O(n \log n)$$$. In fact, we do not even need to perform binary search. The answer can be shown to be:
$$$$$$\min_{a_i \ne b_i}(\max(a_i-mn, mx-a_i))$$$$$$

Shortest Statement Ever
PROGRAMMING
bitmasks constructive algorithms dp greedy

Add tag

You are given two non-negative integers (x), (y). Find two non-negative integers (p) and (q) such that (p\;\&\;q=0), and (|x-p|+|y-q|) is minimized. Here, (\&) denotes the bitwise AND operation . Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains two non-negative integers (x) and (y) ((0 \le x,y < 2^{30})). For each test case, output two non-negative integers (p) and (q) you found. If there are multiple pairs of (p) and (q) satisfying the conditions, you may output any of them. It can be proven that under the constraints of the problem, any valid solution satisfies (\max(p,q)<2^{31}). In the first test case, one valid pair would be (p=0) and (q=0), as (0\,\&\,0=0) and (|x-p|+|y-q|=|0-0|+|0-0|=0) is the minimum over all pairs of (p) and (q). In the third test case, one valid pair would be (p=3) and (q=8), as (3\,\&\,8=0) and (|x-p|+|y-q|=|3-3|+|8-6|=2) is the minimum over all pairs of (p) and (q). Note that ((p,q)=(3,4)) is also a valid pair.

2187B.editorial_text:
2187B - Shortest Statement Ever
This is the intended solution. 
Find the highest bit $$$b$$$ such that both $$$p$$$ and $$$q$$$ have a $$$1$$$. We need to modify $$$p$$$ and $$$q$$$ such that one of $$$p$$$ or $$$q$$$ has a $$$0$$$ on this bit. Without loss of generality, there are two ways to do this:
Increment $$$p$$$ until this bit is $$$0$$$, and let $$$y=q$$$. In this case, if $$$x\,\&\,y=0$$$, update the answer.
Let $$$x=\underbrace{..}_{\text{high bits same as }p}1\underbrace{00..000}_{b-1 \text{ zeroes}}$$$, and $$$y=\underbrace{..}_{\text{high bits same as }q}0\underbrace{11..111}_{b-1 \text{ ones}}$$$. It can be shown that $$$x\,\&\,y=0$$$. 
It can be proven that this greedy leads to an optimal solution. Overall complexity $$$O(1)$$$ per test case.
There is another interesting fact: there always exists a solution where $$$p=x$$$ or $$$q=y$$$. You may also build a greedy solution on top of this observation.
There is also a dynamic programming solution, which is significantly more tedious.

2187C.title: Jerry and Tom
2187C.statement_text:
Problems

Solved
Index
Name
Type
Tags
Community Tag
Rating

( 1515 ) 
C
Jerry and Tom
PROGRAMMING
data structures dfs and similar games graphs greedy trees

Add tag

Jerry and Tom are playing a game on a directed graph (G) with (n) vertices, numbered from (1) to (n). For every vertex (1 \le u < n), there is a directed edge from (u) to (u+1). In addition, there are (m) extra directed edges. The (i)-th extra edge goes from (u_i) to (v_i), where (1 \le u_i < v_i \le n). The graph (G) has the following special property: there do not exist two directed edges ((u_i\to v_i)) and ((u_j\to v_j)) such that (u_i < u_j < v_i < v_j). At the beginning of the game, Jerry and Tom stand on vertices (x) and (y), respectively, where (x \ne y). The game proceeds in turns. In each turn, the players behave according to the following rules, with Jerry going first, followed by Tom: Jerry must choose one outgoing edge from his current vertex and move along it to its end. If his current vertex has no outgoing edges, he stays where he is. Tom may choose one outgoing edge from his current vertex and move along it to its end, or choose not to move and stay where he is. If at the end of any turn, Jerry and Tom are at the same vertex ( including at vertex (n) ), the game ends immediately and Tom wins. Otherwise, if Jerry is initially at vertex (n), or reaches vertex (n) at the end of any turn, Jerry wins. Note that if after a turn, both Jerry and Tom are at vertex (n), then Tom wins . Throughout the entire game, both players know each others' locations. It can be proven that the game will end in a finite number of turns. 2187C.editorial_text:
2187C - Jerry and Tom
Observation: Both players will always take the outgoing edge that goes the furthest.
Suppose there are two edges $$$(u \to v)$$$ and $$$(u \to w)$$$ with $$$v \lt w$$$. If a player takes the edge $$$(u \to v)$$$, due to the special property of $$$G$$$ (no crossing edges), the player will never reach any vertices beyond $$$w$$$ faster than if he were to take the edge $$$(u \to w)$$$.
Let the furthest vertex reachable from $$$u$$$ be $$$a(u)$$$. If we connect all edges $$$(u \to a(u))$$$, we get a tree rooted at $$$n$$$. Let the depth of $$$u$$$ be $$$d(u)$$$. There are two cases:

If $$$d(x) \lt d(y)$$$, Tom can never catch Jerry before Jerry reaches $$$n$$$, thus $$$f(x,y)=0$$$.
Otherwise, Tom can move to the lowest common ancestor (lca) of $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$, denoted by $$$\operatorname{lca}(x,y)$$$. To reach $$$n$$$, Jerry eventually has to move to $$$\operatorname{lca}(x,y)$$$, where Tom will catch him. Thus, $$$f(x,y)=d(y)-d(\operatorname{lca}(x,y))$$$. 
Simplifying things a little:
$$$$$$\begin{aligned}\sum_{1 \le x,y \le n, x\ne y}f(x,y) &= \sum_{1 \le x,y \le n,x \ne y, d(x )\ge d(y)} \left(d(y)- d(\operatorname{lca}(x,y))\right) \\ &= \sum_{1 \le x \lt y \le n} \left(\min(d(x),d(y))-d(\operatorname{lca}(x,y)) \right) + \sum_{1 \le x \lt y \le n,d(x)=d(y)} \left(d(y)- d(\operatorname{lca}(x,y))\right) \\ &= \sum_{1 \le x \lt y \le n} \min(d(x),d(y)) - \sum_{1 \le x \lt y \le n} d(\operatorname{lca}(x,y)) - \sum_{1 \le x \lt y \le n,d(x)=d(y)} \left(d(y)- d(\operatorname{lca}(x,y))\right) \end{aligned} $$$$$$
The first sum can be calculated by sorting the depth array. Let the sorted depth array be $$$b$$$, then the first sum is $$$\sum_{i=1}^n (n-i-1)\cdot b_i$$$. 
The second sum can be calculated by precomputing subtree sizes. Let the size of the subtree of $$$u$$$ be $$$s(u)$$$. The number of pairs of vertices with $$$\operatorname{lca}=u$$$ is $$$\sum_{v,w \in \text{children of }u} s(v) \cdot s(w) = \frac{s(u)\cdot (s(u)-1)}{2}-\sum_{v \in \text{children of }u}\frac{s(v) \cdot (s(v)-1)}{2}$$$. 
The third sum can be calculated similarly, by separating the two components. There are many ways to optimize this process. The standard solution uses dsu on tree, with overall complexity $$$O(n \log^2 n)$$$.

2187D.editorial_text:
2187D - Cool Problem
Note that we can rewrite the formula as follows:
$$$c_i-\frac{x+y}{2}=c_{i-1}-\frac{y-x}{2}$$$, if $$$s_i=\texttt{0}$$$;
$$$c_i-\frac{x+y}{2}=\frac{y-x}{2}-c_{i-1}$$$, if $$$s_i=\texttt{1}$$$.
From this, we can see that
$$$$$$\left( c_i - \frac{x+y}{2}\right)^2=\left(c_{i-1}-\frac{y-x}{2}\right)^2$$$$$$
$$$$$$$$$$$$
always holds. Thus,
$$$$$$\left(c_i^2-c_{i-1}^2\right)-y \cdot \left(c_i-c_{i-1}\right)+xy=x \cdot \left(c_i+c_{i-1}\right)$$$$$$
So,
$$$$$$\sum \left(c_i^2-c_{i-1}^2\right) - \sum y \cdot \left(c_i-c_{i-1}\right) + nxy=x \cdot \sum \left(c_i+c_{i-1}\right)$$$$$$
This implies
$$$$$$f(r)=\frac{c_n^2+(x-y)\cdot c_n + nxy}{2x}$$$$$$
Thus, we can use dynamic programming to calculate all reachable $$$c_n$$$. Note that the coefficient of $$$y$$$ in $$$c_n$$$ is either $$$1$$$ or $$$0$$$, we may define $$$dp_{i,j,k}$$$ as whether the coefficient of $$$x$$$ can be $$$j$$$, considering the first $$$i$$$ characters of $$$s$$$, and the current coefficient of $$$y$$$ is $$$k$$$, which can be optimized to $$$O(\frac{n^2}{w})$$$ using bitset.

Doors and Keys
PROGRAMMING

Add tag

There are (n+1) rooms arranged in a line, numbered from (1) to (n+1) from left to right. There are also (n) doors numbered from (1) to (n), where the (i)-th door connects rooms (i) and (i+1). Each door (i) has an associated non-negative integer (a_i). You are given a binary string(^{\text{∗}}) (s) of length (n). For each (1 \le i \le n): If (s_i=1), then room (i) initially contains one key. Otherwise, room (i) contains no key. At the beginning of the (0)-th second, you are in room (1), and all doors are closed. For each (k \ge 0), the following events will happen in order in the (k)-th second: At the beginning of the (k)-th second, all doors (j) with (a_j=k) will open. Suppose you are in room (i): If you are not carrying any keys and there is at least one key in room (i), you may pick it up and carry it with you. If you are carrying a key, you may drop it in room (i). If you are not carrying any keys and there is at least one key in room (i), you may pick it up and carry it with you. If you are carrying a key, you may drop it in room (i). At the end of the (k)-th second: You may move to room (i+1). If door (i) is still closed, you have to be carrying a key to move to room (i+1). 2187E.editorial_text:
2187E - Doors and Keys
Important Transformation: The constraint of carrying at most one key is annoying. It can actually be transformed into something else: 

You may carry any number of keys with you. However, the time required to move to an adjacent room is $$$\max(1,2k-1)$$$, where $$$k$$$ is the number of keys you can carrying. 
This is because you can repeatedly move between rooms $$$i$$$ and $$$i+1$$$, which requires $$$k$$$ trips to take all the keys with you. 
Thus, we can design a dynamic programming solution. Let $$$dp_{i,j}$$$ be the minimum time required to reach room $$$i$$$, carrying $$$j$$$ keys. The base case is $$$dp_{0,0}=0$$$. 
Consider the transitions:

If there is a key in room $$$i$$$, you can choose to carry it with you or not. Thus, $$$dp_{i,j+1}=\min(dp_{i,j+1},dp_{i,j})$$$. 
If $$$dp_{i,j} \ge a_i$$$, door $$$i$$$ is already open. Thus, $$$dp_{i+1,j}=\min(dp_{i+1,j},dp_{i,j}+\max(1,2j-1))$$$.
Otherwise:
We can use one key to open door $$$i$$$. Thus, $$$dp_{i+1,j-1}=\min(dp_{i+1,j-1},dp_{i,j}+\max(1,2j-1))$$$.
We can also wait for door $$$i$$$ to open automatically at $$$t=a_i$$$. Thus, $$$dp_{i+1,j}=\min(dp_{i+1,j},a_i+\max(1,2j-1))$$$.

The above solution runs in $$$O(n^2)$$$. Suppose you are carrying $$$k$$$ keys; in an optimal solution, all of these keys need to be used, otherwise you can simply carry fewer keys to achieve a not worse solution. The time required to move while carrying those keys is at least $$$k+(k-1)+(k-2)+\ldots+1=O(k^2)$$$. Thus, if we let $$$V=\max(a)$$$, it is never optimal to carry more than $$$O(\sqrt{V})$$$ keys, as the doors would have opened automatically by then. The second dimension will be only up to $$$O(\sqrt{V})$$$. The overall complexity should be $$$O(n \min(n,\sqrt{V}))$$$.

2188A.editorial_text:
2188A - Divisible Permutation

Idea: __baozii__, Tobo

Solution: __baozii__

Editorial: __baozii__

Solution
For $$$|p_{n-1}-p_n|$$$ to be divisible by $$$n-1$$$, either $$$p_{n-1}=1$$$ and $$$p_n=n$$$, or $$$p_{n-1}=n$$$ and $$$p_n=1$$$. Either way, we can construct $$$p$$$ backwards. For $$$i$$$ from $$$n-2$$$ to $$$1$$$, there will only by one possible choice for $$$p_i$$$, where $$$p_i$$$ is either $$$p_{i+1}-i$$$ or $$$p_{i+1}+i$$$, depending on the parity of $$$i$$$.

Code (Python)
for _ in range(int(input())):
n = int(input())
p = [1, n]
used = {1, n}
for i in range(n - 2, 0, -1):
prev = p[-1]
if 1 <= prev - i <= n and prev - i not in used:
p.append(prev - i)
used.add(prev - i)
else:
p.append(prev + i)
used.add(prev + i)
p.reverse()
print(*p)

Cordell manages a row of (n) seats at the Scuola Comunale di Musica Piova where students are strictly forbidden from sitting next to each other. You are given a binary string(^{\text{∗}}) (s), where (s_i = \mathtt{1}) indicates that the (i)-th seat has been occupied by a student, and (s_i = \mathtt{0}) indicates that it is free now. It is guaranteed that no two adjacent seats are occupied currently. Cordell needs to add more students until it is impossible to seat anyone else in the row. However, she wants to achieve this state with as few students as possible. Your task is to calculate the minimum total number of students seated when it is impossible to seat anyone else in the row. (^{\text{∗}})A binary string is a string where each character is either (\mathtt{0}) or (\mathtt{1}). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the number of seats in the row. The second line of each test case contains the binary string (s) of length (n) ((s_i \in \{\mathtt{0}, \mathtt{1}\})). It is guaranteed that no two adjacent characters are both (\mathtt{1}). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the minimum total number of seated students. In the first test case, (n = 1) and the hall is initially empty. Because the row is still possible to seat any student, Cordell must place one student at seat (1). Therefore, the minimum number of seated students is (1). In the third test case, Cordell can place two students at seats (1) and (4). Lawn Mower
PROGRAMMING
math

Add tag

The exit from the summer cottage is fenced with a fence consisting of (n) boards, each (1) meter wide. To the left and right of the exit are the fences of other plots. Some of the boards of the fence want to be removed for the construction of a bathhouse (possibly all or none), while there is an automatic lawn mower on the plot that is (w) meters wide and must not leave the plot through a hole in the fence. The lawn mower will be able to exit the plot if there are at least (w) consecutive removed boards among the numbers of the removed boards. Determine the maximum number of boards that can be removed from the fence. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (w) ((1 \leq n \leq 10^{9}), (1 \leq w \leq 10^{9})) — the number of boards in the fence and the width of the lawnmower in meters, respectively. For each test case, output a single number — the maximum number of boards that can be removed from the fence. In the first test case, the fence consists of (9) boards. You can remove (6) boards and leave only the boards numbered (2), (5), and (8). Then the lawn mower will not be able to leave the boundaries of the territory. In the second test case, you can remove (10) boards, a possible arrangement is shown below.

2194A.editorial_text:
2194A - Lawn Mower
Note that the optimal way to remove the boards is to remove a consecutive $$$w-1$$$ boards and then leave one. Thus, every $$$w$$$-th board will remain. Therefore, the answer is $$$\displaystyle n - \left\lfloor \frac{n}{w} \right\rfloor$$$.

Mark loves money very much, and he keeps most of it in the bank. He stores his money in (n) different banks. In the (i)-th bank, he has (a_i) rubles. One day, Mark decided to gather all his money in one bank, so he will be transferring money from one bank account to another. All interbank transfers are arranged the same way: he can transfer only (x) rubles in one transfer, and considering all fees, (y) rubles will be credited to the other account (since banks want to make a profit, it holds that (y \leq x)). 2194B.editorial_text:
2194B - Offshores
Let us assume we want to make the $$$i$$$-th element the maximum. We will calculate $$$S_i = \sum\limits_{j = 1 \dots n}^{j \neq i} \lfloor \frac{a_j}{x} \rfloor$$$. Notice that the maximum number of transfers we can make to the $$$i$$$-th account from all the others is exactly this amount (since the condition $$$y \le x$$$ holds, if we make a transfer from some account $$$u$$$ to some account $$$v$$$, then $$$\lfloor \frac{a_u}{x} \rfloor$$$ will decrease by exactly $$$1$$$, while $$$\lfloor \frac{a_v}{x} \rfloor$$$ will increase by at most $$$1$$$, so intermediate transfers between accounts will not help increase $$$S_i$$$). Thus, the problem reduces to learning how to quickly compute $$$S_i$$$ for each $$$i$$$. To do this, we can calculate $$$S_{all} = \sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n} \lfloor \frac{a_j}{x} \rfloor$$$, then $$$S_i = S_{all} - \lfloor \frac{a_i}{x} \rfloor$$$

2194C.editorial_text:
2194C - Secret message
Let's iterate over $$$d$$$ (divisor of $$$n$$$) and check if we can obtain a string with informativeness $$$d$$$. For this, for each $$$1 \leq i \leq d$$$, we need to check that there is a common letter at positions $$$i, i+d, i+2d, \dots$$$. To do this, we will iterate over the letter at position $$$i$$$ and check that this letter is also present at positions $$$i+d, i+2d, \dots$$$. For position $$$i$$$, the check can be done in $$$O\left(\frac{n}{d} \cdot k^2\right)$$$, and for all $$$i$$$, it will work in $$$O(n k^2)$$$. In total, across all $$$d$$$, the algorithm will run in $$$O(n \cdot d(n) \cdot k^2)$$$ (where $$$d(n)$$$ is the number of divisors of the number $$$n$$$, which does not exceed $$$100$$$ in the problem constraints). With careful implementation, such a solution can pass all tests, but it can be improved.
The idea: instead of storing $$$k$$$ letters at each position, let's store an array of length 26, where for each letter it is recorded whether it is present at this position or not. Now, for each $$$i$$$, we can check in $$$O\left(26 \cdot \frac{n}{d}\right)$$$ whether there is a common letter at positions $$$i, i+d, i+2d, \cdots$$$ (iterate over one of the letters at position $$$i$$$ and check that it fits for $$$\frac{n}{d}$$$). Thus, the overall asymptotic complexity of the algorithm will be $$$O(26 \cdot n \cdot d(n))$$$.

Table Cut
PROGRAMMING
constructive algorithms greedy

Add tag

Given a table of size (n \times m), where each cell contains either (0) or (1). The task is to divide it into two parts with a cut that goes from the top left corner to the bottom right corner. The cut lines can only go right or down. Let (a) be the number of ones in one part of the table after the cut, and (b) be the number of ones in the other part of the table. The goal is to maximize the value of (a \cdot b). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (m) ((1 \leq n, m \leq 3 \cdot 10^{5}), (2 \leq n \cdot m \leq 3 \cdot 10^{5})) — the number of rows and columns in the table, respectively. Each of the following (n) lines contains (m) integers, where the (j)-th number in the (i)-th line corresponds to the value (a_{i, j}) ((0 \leq a_{i, j} \leq 1)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n \cdot m) across all test cases does not exceed (3 \cdot 10^{5}). For each test case, output a single number in the first line of the output data — the maximum value of the product. In the second line, output a string consisting of (n) characters ' D ' and (m) characters ' R ', representing the direction of the next cut, where ' D ' means a cut downwards, and ' R ' — a cut to the right. The images show the correct cuts for each of the first and second test cases, at which the maximum value of the product is achieved.

2194D.editorial_text:
2194D - Table Cut
Let there be $$$k$$$ ones in the table. Then the maximum possible product is $$$\displaystyle \left\lfloor \frac{k}{2} \right\rfloor \cdot \left( k - \left\lfloor \frac{k}{2} \right\rfloor \right)$$$. We will show that the answer is always achievable. We want to separate the part with $$$\displaystyle x = \left\lfloor \frac{k}{2} \right\rfloor$$$. We will find the last row such that the sum of ones in the prefix of the rows is $$$\leq x$$$.

In the next row, we will take the necessary number of elements from the suffix so that the sum above becomes equal to $$$x$$$.
After that, the cut is restored from the figure above.

2194E.editorial_text:
2194E - The Turtle Strikes Back
Let us start with a basic solution. First, consider some path with the maximum total enjoyment from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$. Observe that Raphael must block one of the cells on this path. For each cell that Raphael may block, we can independently compute the maximum enjoyment that Michelangelo can obtain by moving from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$ while avoiding this cell. This approach is naturally implemented using standard grid dynamic programming and leads to a time complexity of $$$O(nm(n + m))$$$.
To further optimize the solution, fix one of the maximum-enjoyment paths $$$S$$$ from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$ on the original grid. Denote the cells of this path by $$$s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n + m - 1}$$$. Observe that if Raphael does not block any of these cells, Michelangelo can follow the path $$$S$$$ and obtain the maximum possible enjoyment. Therefore, an optimal move for Raphael always consists of blocking some cell $$$s_k$$$.
Let us consider what happens when the cell $$$(i, j) = s_k$$$ is blocked. Michelangelo has two options: 

follow the same path $$$S$$$, losing exactly $$$2 a_{i,j}$$$ enjoyment, which results in the value $$$maxS - 2 a_{i,j}$$$; 
choose a path from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$ that does not pass through the cell $$$(i, j)$$$. 
The first option can be computed directly. The second requires determining the maximum enjoyment of a path that bypasses the blocked cell.
Observe that a path does not pass through the cell $$$(i, j)$$$ if and only if it contains some cell $$$(a, b)$$$ such that either $$$a \lt i$$$ and $$$b \gt j$$$, or $$$a \gt i$$$ and $$$b \lt j$$$. This allows us to consider all such cells $$$(a, b)$$$ as possible bypass points.
We introduce two auxiliary dynamic programming tables: 

$$$dpS[x][y]$$$ — the maximum enjoyment on a path from $$$(1, 1)$$$ to $$$(x, y)$$$; 
$$$dpT[x][y]$$$ — the maximum enjoyment on a path from $$$(x, y)$$$ to $$$(n, m)$$$. 
Then the contribution of a path passing through the cell $$$(a, b)$$$ is equal to $$$dpS[a][b] + dpT[a][b] - a[a][b]$$$.
For each cell $$$s_k$$$, we store the maximum of this value over all valid bypass points and denote it by $$$dp[k]$$$. The final answer is then given by $$$\min_k \left( \max\bigl(dp[k],\; maxS - 2 a[s_k]\bigr) \right)$$$.
It remains to optimize the computation of the values $$$dp[k]$$$. For a fixed cell $$$(i, j)$$$, it is sufficient to consider only the cells $$$(i + 1, q \lt j)$$$ and $$$(p \lt i, j + 1)$$$. For these cells, we need to quickly find the maximum value of the expression $$$dpS[x][y] + dpT[x][y] - a[x][y]$$$.
Note that such maxima are queried over prefixes of rows and columns, so they can be precomputed in $$$O(nm)$$$. After that, for each cell $$$(i, j)$$$, the value of the best bypassing path can be obtained in $$$O(1)$$$ time.
Thus, the final solution runs in $$$O(nm)$$$ time and uses $$$O(nm)$$$ memory.

2194F2.editorial_text:
2194F2 - Again Trees... (hard version)
Let $$$dp[v][x]$$$ be the number of ways to select a set of edges from the subtree of this vertex, including the edge from vertex $$$v$$$ to its ancestor, such that the XOR of the cut-off vertices in the subtree (vertices which is not connected to $$$v$$$ now) equals $$$x$$$. To recompute $$$dp$$$, we first need to calculate the XOR convolution of the $$$dp$$$ values of the children. The XOR convolution of arrays $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ of length $$$2^k$$$ is an array $$$c_i = \sum a_j \times b_{j \oplus i}$$$. For now, we will compute it in $$$O(len(a) \times len(b))$$$. After performing the XOR convolution for all children, we must process the option of removing the edge from $$$v$$$ to its ancestor. For this, we iterate over $$$x$$$, and if xor_subtree[$$$v$$$] $$$\oplus$$$ $$$x \in b$$$, then we need to add $$$dp[v][x]$$$ to $$$dp[v][0]$$$. Thus, this solution works in $$$O(n \times 2^{30} \times 2^{30})$$$, since $$$0 \leq x \lt 2^{30}$$$, and naive convolution works in $$$O(len(a) \times len(b))$$$. Of course, we are not satisfied with this time complexity, but note that $$$x$$$ in this $$$dp$$$ is an XOR combination of the set $$$b$$$.
Let's choose a basis from the set $$$b$$$ and store $$$dp$$$ in this basis. Now, the number of possible $$$x$$$ in $$$dp$$$ is $$$2^k$$$, and naive XOR convolution works in $$$4^k$$$, so the solution runs in $$$O(n \times 4^{k})$$$, which is sufficient to pass F1. There are also several other approaches for solving F1, but they cannot be optimized to solve F2.
The first optimization that improves the complexity is to perform XOR convolution using the Hadamard transform (FWHT). Then, the complexity becomes $$$O(n \times 2^k \times k)$$$, but this is still insufficient to pass F2.
We want to get rid of the multiplication by $$$k$$$. One XOR convolution via Hadamard looks like this: compute the Hadamard transform of both arrays, then compute the element-wise multiplication, and finally apply the inverse Hadamard transform. Instead of storing $$$dp[v][x]$$$, let's store $$$hadamard(dp[v][x])$$$, i.e., the Hadamard transform. Its formula is: $$$hadamard(a)[i] = \sum a_j \times (-1)^{popcount(i \ AND \ j)}$$$. Then, convolution is performed in $$$O(2^k)$$$ via element-wise multiplication. Now, the difficulty arises with the second recomputation step, where we wanted to compute the value $$$dp[v][x]$$$ at certain points $$$x$$$ and add it to $$$dp[v][0]$$$.
Let's start with the first step. We need to compute $$$\sum dp[v][b_i \oplus$$$ xor_subtree[v]$$$]$$$. It is worth noting that if xor_subtree[$$$v$$$] cannot be expressed in the basis, then such recomputation is unnecessary. First, let's compute this sum assuming xor_subtree[v] = 0. Let $$$p$$$ be an array of size $$$2^k$$$, where the positions corresponding to $$$b_i$$$ are set to 1, and all others are zeros. Then, the sum we need to compute is the zero element of the XOR convolution of $$$dp[v]$$$ and $$$p$$$. We cannot compute the convolution of $$$dp[v]$$$ and $$$p$$$ directly, but we can compute $$$q = hadamard($$$convolution of $$$dp[v]$$$ and $$$p$$$), since this is the element-wise product of $$$hadamard(dp[v])$$$ and $$$hadamard(p)$$$, and $$$hadamard(p)$$$ can be computed once at the beginning of the program. Now, we are interested in the zero element of the inverse transform of $$$q$$$, which is simply $$$(\sum q_i) / 2^k$$$. Now, recall that we have xor_subtree[$$$v$$$], but to account for it, it is enough to include in the convolution of $$$dp[v]$$$ and $$$p$$$ an array where only the position xor_subtree[$$$v$$$] is set to one. The $$$hadamard$$$ of such an array can be computed in $$$O(2^k)$$$ by definition. Thus, we have computed the required sum in $$$O(2^k)$$$.
Now, we need to compute the new $$$hadamard(dp[v])$$$ after adding the computed sum to $$$dp[v][0]$$$. But by the definition of the Hadamard transform, we can find the coefficients with which the added sum contributes to the old value of $$$hadamard(dp[v])$$$.
Thus, in this solution, the Hadamard transform needs to be explicitly computed only for calculating $$$hadamard(p)$$$, while in the rest, we explicitly compute the necessary coefficients by definition and obtain a solution in $$$O(n \times 2^k + t \times 2^k \times k)$$$, where the second term comes from computing $$$hadamard(p)$$$ for each test dataset.

A
Game with a Fraction
PROGRAMMING
games math

Add tag

Alice and Bob have two integers (p) and (q), and they are playing a game with these numbers. The players take turns, with Alice going first. On their turn, a player can do one of two actions: decrease (p) by one (this action is possible if (p \gt 0)); decrease (q) by one (this action is possible if (q \gt 1)). The game ends when (p = 0) and (q = 1). Bob wins if at any point during the game the fraction (\frac{p}{q}) is equal to in value the fraction (\frac{2}{3}). Otherwise, Alice wins. Given the initial values of (p) and (q), determine the winner of the game if both players play optimally. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. Each input case consists of a single line containing two integers (p) and (q) ((1 \le p, q \le 10^{18})). For each input case, output: " Alice " if Alice wins; " Bob " if Bob wins. In the first input case, the fraction is already equal to (\frac{2}{3}) by value, so Bob wins. In the second input case, one possible sequence of the game is as follows: initially (p = 10, q = 14); after Alice's turn (p = 9, q = 14); after Bob's turn (p = 9, q = 13); after Alice's turn (p = 9, q = 12); after Bob's turn (p = 8, q = 12). Bob wins, as (\frac{8}{12}) is equal to (\frac{2}{3}). It can be shown that in this example, with optimal play from both players, Bob always wins. For the third input case, Alice's optimal strategy will be to decrease (q) as long as possible. In this case, the game will end in favor of Alice regardless of Bob's actions.

2196A.editorial_text:
2196A - Game with a Fraction
The solution is very simple, it is necessary to check that:

$$$p \lt q$$$ 
$$$\texttt{min}(\frac{p}{2}, \frac{q}{3}) \ge q - p$$$ 
If both conditions are met, then Bob wins, otherwise, Alice wins.
The first condition is quite obvious, if it is not met, then Alice will always decrease $$$q$$$ if possible, leading to $$$p \ge q$$$, so the fraction will always be either $$$ \gt \frac{2}{3}$$$ or $$$= 0$$$ (after all moves).
The second condition states that no matter what move Alice makes, there is always a move for Bob that maintains the original difference $$$q - p$$$. There will be a moment during the game when $$$p = 2 \cdot \texttt{min}(\frac{p}{2}, \frac{q}{3})$$$, because $$$2 \cdot \texttt{min}(\frac{p}{2}, \frac{q}{3}) \le p$$$, and at that moment, with such a difference, the fraction will exactly equal $$$\frac{2}{3}$$$.
The solution works in $$$O(1)$$$

In the array (a), we call a pair of indices (i), (j) beautiful if the following condition holds: (a_{i} \cdot a_{j} = j - i). Count the number of beautiful pairs in the array (a). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^{5})). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_{i}) ((1 \le a_{i} \le 10^{9})). Additional constraints on the input: The sum of (n) across all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the answer to the problem. In the first example, there are (3) beautiful pairs: ((1, 2)), ((1, 3)), and ((1, 5)). In the second example, there are (7) beautiful pairs: ((1, 3)), ((1, 5)), ((2, 4)), ((2, 6)), ((3, 4)), ((3, 5)), and ((4, 6)).

This is the simple version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, you can ask no more than (32 \cdot (n + m)) questions, and (n \leq 15). You can hack only if you solved all versions of this problem. This is an interactive problem. The jury has thought of a directed acyclic graph without loops and multiple edges, which has (n) vertices and (m) edges. Your task is to determine which edges are in this graph. To do this, you can ask questions of the form: what does the (k)-th path look like in the lexicographically(^{\text{∗}}) sorted list of all paths in the graph. A path in the graph is a sequence of vertices (u_{1}, u_{2}, \dots, u_{l}), such that for any (i \lt l), there exists an edge ((u_{i}, u_{i + 1})) in the graph. Your task is to accomplish this by asking no more than (32 \cdot (n + m)) questions. 2196C1.editorial_text:
2196C1 - Interactive Graph (Simple Version)
Let's solve the problem using binary search. For each edge, there exists a path that consists solely of that edge, so let's simply find that path and remember that this edge is in our graph. Initially, we set the boundaries $$$l = 0$$$ and $$$r = 2^{30}$$$ and will search for the first path consisting of $$$1$$$ edge that starts at vertex $$$1$$$. Once we find it, we will add the corresponding edge to the answer. After that, we continue searching for the next path of one edge that starts at vertex $$$1$$$ with a new binary search, taking into account that all paths starting from the first found edge are no longer of interest to us. When two edges are known, we will ignore all paths that start on them, and so on. Ultimately, we will find all edges from vertex $$$1$$$ (the last binary search will not find an edge from vertex $$$1$$$). After this, we will continue searching for all edges from vertex $$$2$$$, $$$3$$$, and so on.
As a result, we will need $$$\log A \cdot (n + m)$$$ queries. Since $$$A = 2^{30}$$$, this fits well within the query limits of the problem

2196C2.editorial_text:
2196C2 - Interactive Graph (Hard Version)
Let's start asking for paths in order starting from $$$2$$$, since path $$$1$$$ consists of a single vertex $$$1$$$. If we ask for paths one by one (that is, each subsequent one), then during our questioning, the path will change in one of two ways:

a vertex has been added to the previous path; 
a suffix of vertices has been removed from the previous path and a new one has been added. 
Note that when the second point occurs, for all the vertices that are removed from the suffix, we can determine the number of paths that start from this vertex and end at some other vertex, let's denote this as $$$C_v$$$. Therefore, if at some point we visit a vertex for the second time, we can immediately skip these $$$C_v$$$ paths and move on to the next one in lexicographic order. Thus, for each query, we either learn about one edge or move to another connected component, so we need exactly $$$n + m$$$ questions

2196D.editorial_text:
2196D - Double Bracket Sequence
The problem has a fairly simple solution with a time complexity of $$$O(|s|^{3})$$$ using dynamic programming of the form $$$\texttt{dp}[i][bal_1][bal_2]$$$—the minimum number of changes required after processing the first $$$i$$$ characters, where the balance of the subsequence of round brackets is $$$bal_1$$$, and the balance of the subsequence of square brackets is $$$bal_2$$$. The transitions are quite trivial (from each state, we try to process the next bracket by either changing it or not changing it).
However, this solution does not help when the constraints are $$$|s| \lt = 10^{6}$$$ (though it is useful for stress testing).
Another solution suggests using a greedy approach. Ultimately, each bracket must have a pair, and for each pair, either $$$0$$$, $$$1$$$, or $$$2$$$ actions are needed to make the pair correct. For example, for the pair "()", $$$0$$$ actions are needed; for the pair "[)", $$$1$$$ action is needed; and for the pair "][", $$$2$$$ actions are needed. Let's assume we have optimally paired the brackets (such that this pairing achieves the minimum number of actions); then an important observation is that there can be at most one pair that requires $$$2$$$ actions, because otherwise, we could form pairs differently, which would not worsen the answer.
We would also like to maximize the number of pairs that require $$$0$$$ actions. The simplest way to do this is to find a subsequence of round brackets that forms the longest valid parentheses subsequence (LPS), and do the same for square brackets. The remaining brackets that do not belong to any LPS will form pairs that require either $$$1$$$ or $$$2$$$ actions. Here, we need to check whether there will be that one pair that requires $$$2$$$ actions or not. It turns out that it is sufficient to check that the remaining brackets form a sequence where closing brackets come first, followed by opening brackets, with an odd number of closing and opening brackets, for example:
"))]))[[("
Here, the opening brackets ($$$5$$$ in total) come first, followed by the closing brackets ($$$3$$$ in total), and for such a sequence, there will be a pair that requires $$$2$$$ actions.
In any other case, there will be no pairs requiring $$$2$$$ actions.
This solution works in $$$O(|s|)$$$

2196E1.editorial_text:
2196E1 - Fuzzy Concatenation (Easy Version)
The following greedy algorithm works: we will find the longest prefix of the string $$$t$$$ such that this prefix is contained in $$$s$$$ as a substring (possibly with one character replaced), and then remove this prefix from $$$t$$$ and repeat until $$$t$$$ is empty. The number of such "pieces" will be the answer. This greediness is correct because if we take a prefix of shorter length, the next piece can only decrease in size, not increase.
Now we need to learn how to quickly solve the following problem:
For a fixed number $$$l$$$, find the maximum $$$r$$$ such that there exists a number $$$i$$$ and a string $$$c$$$, for which the string $$$t_l t_{l + 1} \ldots t_{i - 1} c t_{i + 1} \ldots t_{r}$$$ is a substring of the string $$$s$$$.
Solving this problem involves using root optimization. Let $$$B$$$ be the constant we chose for our root. Let $$$d$$$ denote $$$r - l + 1$$$ for optimal $$$i, c$$$ (in other words, how many characters we processed in one iteration of the greedy algorithm). We want to handle the case $$$d \lt B$$$ in $$$O(d)$$$ time.
Let's store the hash of each substring of the string $$$s$$$ of length at most $$$B$$$, where we have removed one of the elements. There are a total of $$$O(n \cdot B^2)$$$ such segments. Thus, for fixed $$$i, d$$$, where $$$d \lt B$$$, we can check in $$$O(1)$$$ time whether a given string is a substring of $$$s$$$ by verifying that the hash of the string without the character $$$c$$$ is in the set of precomputed hashes. This allows us to solve the case when $$$d \lt B$$$ in $$$O(d^2)$$$ time. We can iterate $$$i$$$ from $$$l$$$ to the maximum accumulated length and increase the optimal $$$d$$$ by exactly $$$1$$$ if we find this substring for the given $$$i$$$. Smaller $$$r$$$ values are not of interest to us. Overall, this part of the solution works in $$$O(m \cdot B)$$$ time, as we increase $$$r$$$ no more than $$$m$$$ times in total, and each check works in $$$d$$$ time, since there are at most $$$B$$$ interesting values of $$$i$$$ in each iteration.
If $$$d \geq B$$$, we can explicitly iterate over the starting point of the substring in the string $$$s$$$. Let's denote this starting point of the substring as $$$j$$$. Let $$$d_1$$$ be $$$\operatorname{lcp}(s_j \ldots s_n, t_l \ldots t_m)$$$. Then for a fixed starting point $$$j$$$, we can add at most $$$d_1 + 1 + \operatorname{lcp}(s_{j + d_1 + 1} \ldots s_n, t_{l + d_1 + 1} \ldots t_m)$$$. The $$$\operatorname{lcp}$$$ can be easily computed in $$$O(1)$$$ time using a suffix array for the string $$$s\text{\#}t$$$. Thus, this part of the solution works in at most $$$O(\frac{n \cdot m}{B})$$$ time, as this search algorithm will be run no more than $$$\frac{m}{B}$$$ times, and the iteration itself works in $$$O(n)$$$ time.
The asymptotic complexity of the solution is $$$O(n \cdot B^2 + \frac{n \cdot m}{B} + m \cdot B)$$$. With $$$B=50$$$, this solution should fit well within the problem's constraints.
There is also a solution that runs in $$$26 \cdot m \cdot \log^2(n + m) + \log(n) \cdot (n + m)$$$, which is based on a complete solution but uses hashes

2196E2.editorial_text:
2196E2 - Fuzzy Concatenation (Hard version)
The following greedy algorithm works: we will find the longest prefix of the string $$$t$$$ such that this prefix is contained in $$$s$$$ as a substring (possibly with one character replaced) and then remove this prefix from $$$t$$$ and repeat until $$$t$$$ is empty. The number of such "pieces" will be the answer. This greediness is correct because if we take a prefix of shorter length, the next piece can only decrease in size, not increase.
To efficiently find the longest prefix, we will use the following algorithm:
We will start from the beginning of the prefix and try to change the current character to some character from the alphabet, and then attempt to find the LCP of the string $$$t$$$ with the modified character and some suffix of the string $$$s$$$. Let $$$f(t', pos)$$$ denote the time to find such an LCP if a character in the string is changed at position $$$pos$$$ to some character from the alphabet; then the time complexity of the entire algorithm can be estimated as $$$O(|t| \cdot \sum_{i = 1}^{|t|} f(t', i))$$$.
We will use a suffix array. We will construct it for the string $$$s + "\#" + t$$$, and also compute the LCP for this array. Additionally, we will compute the reverse array $$$sa\_rev$$$: that is, such that $$$sa\_rev[i]$$$ contains the position of the suffix of length $$$i$$$ in the suffix array $$$sa$$$.
Let $$$t_{suff}$$$ be the suffix of the original $$$t$$$, where we need to search for the maximum "piece". Also, let $$$t_{suff, ps}$$$ be the suffix of the original $$$t$$$, in which one character was changed at position $$$ps$$$.
In the suffix array, there are two classes of suffixes: for $$$s$$$ and for $$$t$$$. We will separate the positions of all suffixes for $$$s$$$ into a separate array. Now let's search for our maximum "piece" in $$$t_{suff, ps}$$$. We will perform a binary search on the suffix array to determine where the position of the string $$$t_{suff, ps}$$$ would be in it if we wanted to insert $$$t_{suff, ps}$$$ into the suffix array constructed solely from $$$s$$$.
Next, we need to understand how the check for this binary search will look. Suppose we want to check during the binary search whether the position after $$$sa_i$$$ is the position we need; let $$$sa_{j}$$$ and $$$sa_{k}$$$ be the positions of the nearest suffixes to the left and right that belong to $$$s$$$. We need to check that $$$sa_{j} \le t_{suff, ps} \le sa_{k}$$$. It seems that comparing such strings cannot be done faster than $$$\log$$$, but since we do not have arbitrary strings, we can do the following:
We will find the LCP of $$$sa_{j}$$$ and $$$t_{suff}$$$ (we can do this because $$$sa$$$ is constructed from all suffixes of $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$, and we can find the LCP of any two arbitrary suffixes in the suffix array in $$$O(1)$$$). If this LCP is greater than $$$ps$$$ for the current $$$t_{suff, ps}$$$, then we know the relationship between the strings $$$sa_{j}$$$ and $$$t_{suff, ps}$$$ (greater, less, or equal). If the LCP is less, we will check that the corresponding character of $$$sa_{j}$$$ at position $$$ps$$$ is equal to the corresponding character in $$$t_{suff, ps}$$$ (if it is not equal, we again know the relationship between the strings).
If it turns out to be equal, we need to compare the strings $$$sa_{sa\_rev_{sa_{j} + ps}}$$$ and $$$t_{suff + ps}$$$. This can also be done in $$$O(1)$$$ by looking at their positions in the suffix array $$$sa$$$.
After we have found the required position in the suffix using binary search, we can similarly calculate the maximum LCP of $$$t_{suff, ps}$$$ and the substring of $$$s$$$ also in $$$O(1)$$$.
Thus, $$$f(t', pos)$$$ can be estimated as $$$O(\log (|s| + |t|) \cdot k)$$$, where $$$k$$$ is the size of the alphabet.
Therefore, the problem can be solved in $$$O(|t| \cdot \log (|s| + |t|) \cdot k)$$$

You are given two numbers (n) and (m). An undirected graph is called beautiful if it satisfies the following conditions: It has no loops or multiple edges. It has exactly (n) vertices and (m) edges. Its vertices cannot be divided into (2) sets such that the sums of the degrees of all vertices in the first set and the sums of the degrees of all vertices in the second set are equal. You need to either report that a beautiful undirected graph with the given (n, m) does not exist, or provide one. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains two integers (n, m) ((12 \leq n \leq 10^5, 1 \leq m \leq \min(2 \cdot 10^5, \frac{n(n-1)}{2}))) — the number of vertices and edges in the graph. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) across all test cases does not exceed (10^5), and the sum of (m) across all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output "No" if such a graph does not exist. Otherwise, output "Yes" , and then, in the following (m) lines — the edges of the beautiful graph in arbitrary order. If there are multiple answers, you may output any of them. In the first test case, the graph is a simple cycle of (7) vertices. The degrees of the vertices are (\{2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0\}). It is easy to see that in such a graph, it is impossible to divide the vertices into (2) parts with equal sums of degrees. In the second test case, since (m = 1), it is easy to see that the vertices can always be divided into (2) parts with equal sums of degrees. Therefore, no solution exists.

2196F.editorial_text:
2196F - Indivisible
First solution:
Let's start by solving the problem for odd $$$n$$$. Intuitively, if for an odd $$$n$$$ we can make all vertex degrees almost equal and as large as possible, there should be a good chance that the set of degrees will be indivisible.
We divide the sum of all degrees, $$$2m$$$, by $$$n$$$ with a remainder. Let $$$2m = q \cdot n + r$$$. $$$0 \le r \lt n$$$.
We can make the vertex degrees almost equal if they are $$$q, \ldots, q, q+1, \ldots, q+1$$$, where $$$q+1$$$ appears $$$r$$$ times, and $$$q$$$ appears $$$n-r$$$ times. A graph with such degrees can always be constructed; let's consider two cases:
$$$q$$$ and $$$r$$$ are even numbers. Mentally arrange the vertices in a circle from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, where $$$n$$$ and $$$1$$$ will also be neighboring vertices. Connect vertices $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ with an edge if the minimum distance between them around the circle does not exceed $$$\frac{q}{2}$$$. After this, each vertex will have a degree equal to $$$q$$$. Then we add $$$\frac{r}{2}$$$ edges between pairs of vertices $$$1 \lt = \gt \frac{n}{2}+1, \ldots, r \lt = \gt \frac{n}{2}+r$$$.
$$$q$$$ and $$$r$$$ are odd numbers. Since $$$n$$$ is odd and $$$q \lt n$$$, it is also true that $$$q+1 \lt n$$$, which means we can construct a configuration from the first case where each vertex degree is $$$q+1$$$. After that, we remove edges $$$1 \lt = \gt 2, \ldots, n-r-1 \lt = \gt n-r$$$.
There are no other cases since $$$n$$$ is odd, and $$$2m = q \cdot n + r$$$, which means modulo two, $$$q + r$$$ equals $$$0$$$.
Let's analyze in which cases this graph will meet the problem's condition. For the condition to be violated, there must be a solution to the equation $$$qa + (q+1)b = m$$$, where $$$0 \leq a \leq n-r, 0 \leq b \leq r$$$. Additionally, we fix the condition $$$a+b \lt \frac{n}{2}$$$; this must be satisfied for one of the halves of the partition (since the total number of vertices is $$$n$$$, the smaller half has fewer than $$$\frac{n}{2}$$$ vertices when $$$n$$$ is odd). We transform the equation:
$$$$$$qa + (q+1)b = m$$$$$$
$$$$$$q(a+b) + b = m$$$$$$
$$$$$$2q(a+b) + 2b = 2m$$$$$$
$$$$$$2q(a+b) + 2b = qn + r$$$$$$
$$$$$$q(2a+2b-n) = r - 2b$$$$$$
$$$$$$q(n - 2a - 2b) = 2b - r$$$$$$
Let's take a closer look at the rewritten equation. The left side is guaranteed to be an integer $$$\geq q$$$, since $$$n \gt 2a+2b$$$. 
We will show that when $$$r \lt q$$$, the equation has no solutions. When $$$r \lt q$$$, since $$$b \le r$$$, we get that $$$2b - r \le r$$$, meaning the right side of the equation $$$\le r$$$, while the left side equals $$$q$$$, and in the case $$$r \lt q$$$, such an equation is unsolvable. Thus, if $$$r \lt q$$$, we have shown that the graph satisfies the problem's condition.
Let's continue the chain of inequalities, each time weakening the inequality.
$$$$$$(q + 1) \cdot (n - 2a - 2b) = n - 2a - r$$$$$$
$$$$$$q + 1 \le n - 2a - r$$$$$$
$$$$$$q + 1 + 2a + r \le n$$$$$$
$$$$$$q + r \lt n$$$$$$
It follows that from the assumption that a solution to the equation exists, we derive the fact that $$$q + r \lt n$$$. From this, it follows that when $$$n \le q + r$$$, there is no solution to the equation, and the graph satisfies the problem's condition.
Let's consider the following strategy: while $$$\frac{(n-2)(n-3)}{2} \geq m$$$, we decrease $$$n$$$ by $$$2$$$ and reduce the problem to $$$(n-2, m)$$$, isolating two vertices of degree $$$0$$$. In the end, we will obtain a problem where $$$n(n-1) \ge 2m$$$ and $$$(n-2)(n-3) \lt 2m$$$, while $$$n$$$ is still odd.
We will show that in this case (when $$$n(n-1) \ge 2m$$$ and $$$(n-2)(n-3) \lt 2m$$$) one of the two conditions ($$$n \le q+r$$$ or $$$r \lt q$$$) will always be satisfied, except for the case when $$$m \in \{1, 2, 4, 6, 12\}$$$.
$$$$$$n(n-1) \geq 2m \gt n^2-5n+6$$$$$$
$$$$$$n-1 \geq \lfloor \frac{2m}{n} \rfloor \gt n-5+\frac{6}{n}-1$$$$$$
$$$$$$n-1 \geq q \gt n-6+\frac{6}{n}$$$$$$
Let's analyze the cases.
$$$q = n-1$$$
In this case, the graph must be complete, and for it $$$r=0$$$, thus the condition $$$r \lt q$$$ is satisfied.
$$$q = n-2$$$
If $$$r \lt n-2$$$, then $$$r \lt q$$$.
If $$$2 \le r$$$, then $$$n \le q + r$$$.
The extreme case where both conditions are not satisfied is $$$n=3$$$, then $$$m=2$$$.
$$$q = n-3$$$
If $$$r \lt n-3$$$, then $$$r \lt q$$$.
If $$$3 \le r$$$, then $$$n \le q + r$$$.
The extreme cases where both conditions are not satisfied are $$$n=3$$$, $$$m=1$$$ and $$$n = 5$$$, $$$m = 6$$$. 
$$$q = n-4$$$
If $$$r \lt n-4$$$, then $$$r \lt q$$$.
If $$$4 \le r$$$, then $$$n \le q + r$$$.
The extreme cases where both conditions are not satisfied are $$$n = 7$$$, $$$m = 12$$$ and $$$n = 5$$$, $$$m = 4$$$.
$$$q = n-5$$$
The unweakened condition: $$$2m \gt n^2-5n+6$$$, thus $$$2m - qn \gt 6$$$, meaning $$$r \gt 6$$$. Therefore, the condition $$$n \le q+r$$$ in this case is always satisfied.
Thus, our strategy has been proven to yield an indivisible graph for odd $$$n$$$, and $$$m \notin \{1,2,4,6,12\}$$$!
By bruteforce, it is easy to show that all possible graphs with $$$m \in \{1,2,4,6\}$$$ will be divisible. For example, for $$$m=2$$$, the possible vertex degrees are either $$$\{1,1,1,1\}$$$ or $$$\{1,1,2\}$$$.
And for $$$m=12$$$, it is possible to create a graph on $$$6$$$ vertices (and for all $$$n \gt 6$$$, we can take this graph and $$$n-6$$$ isolated vertices) that satisfies the indivisibility condition, with degrees $$$\{3,3,3,5,5,5\}$$$, which is $$$K_6$$$ without three edges between the first three vertices.
Thus, the solution for odd $$$n$$$ is No for $$$m \in \{1,2,4,6\}$$$, with the case $$$m=12$$$ handled separately; otherwise, the strategy works: take the densest graph with $$$m$$$ edges and $$$\le n$$$ vertices, supplemented with isolated vertices.
Now let's solve the problem for even $$$n$$$. Immediately, we can discard a cluster of cases using the solution for odd:
If $$$m \in \{1,2,4,6\}$$$, the answer is still no.
If $$$m = 12$$$, the same example will work.
If $$$m \le \frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}$$$, we can isolate one vertex and reduce the problem to $$$(n-1, m)$$$, and $$$n-1$$$ will be odd, thus we know that with such parameters a solution always exists.
The only remaining case: $$$2m \gt (n-1)(n-2)$$$.
Notice that in this case, if the graph has a partition of vertices into two sets with equal sum of degrees, then both of these sets must have size $$$\frac{n}{2}$$$, otherwise, the smaller set has size $$$\le \frac{n}{2}-1$$$, and thus the maximum sum of degrees of this set: $$$(n-1)(\frac{n}{2}-1) = (n-1)\frac{n-2}{2}$$$, while $$$m$$$ is strictly greater than this number.
Knowing this, we note that in this case, the condition of indivisibility for this graph is equivalent to the condition of indivisibility for the reverse graph, but with the added condition that the vertex sets must have equal size.
In the reverse graph, there will be $$$\frac{n(n-1)}{2} - m \lt n - 1$$$ edges. If $$$\frac{n(n-1)}{2} -m$$$ is not equal to $$$0, 1, 2, 4, 6$$$, we can take an indivisible reverse graph on $$$n-1$$$ vertices and $$$\frac{n(n-1)}{2} - m$$$ edges, using the construction above. Since this graph is indivisible in general form, it is also indivisible under the added condition of equal set sizes.
It remains to deal with the cases when $$$\frac{n(n-1)}{2} - m \in \{0,1,2,4,6\}$$$. Here we can recall the restriction $$$n \ge 12$$$. It turns out that for $$$n \ge 12$$$, any graph with $$$0,1,2,4,6$$$ edges is not just always divisible, but always divisible into two sets of equal size. This is true because in a regular partition, the sizes of both sets do not exceed $$$6$$$ (if we only take non-isolated vertices), thus we can take a regular partition and supplement it with isolated vertices so that both sets have size $$$6$$$. And for $$$n \gt 12$$$, we can take a pair of isolated vertices in different sets and reduce the problem to $$$n - 2$$$. Thus, in this case, there is no solution to the problem.
Second solution (thanks to [user:SomethingNew] for the alternative solution!):
Let's note/guess/suppose that the graph answer cannot have more than 3 different degrees. More precisely, it is sufficient to consider only graphs with no more than 3 different degrees to cover all possible $$$(n,m)$$$ where a solution exists.
Let's bruteforce all possible sets of degrees and use the Erdős–Gallai theorem to check whether a graph can be formed from these degrees, in $$$O(n \log n)$$$. Checking the indivisibility criterion can also be done quite quickly, given that there are no more than $$$3$$$ different degrees (they can be arranged in $$$O(\log n)$$$ knapsack items), and using a bitset.
Such a solution already works, but is obviously too slow. However, we can cleverly "tweak" the parameters of the enumeration, trying to guess the properties of the construction so that it works in terms of time.
Enumerate the actual $$$n$$$ (without isolated vertices) in increasing order, starting from the first such that $$$\frac{n(n-1)}{2} \ge m$$$.
Enumerate the maximum degree value only from $$$n$$$ to $$$n-5$$$.
Honestly enumerate the number of vertices with the maximum degree, as well as the minimum degree, after which we honestly enumerate the average degree. Of course, add as many break as possible.
It is claimed that such bruteforce will run in $$$O(m \sqrt m \log m)$$$ time, as all considered values of $$$n$$$ will be $$$O(\sqrt m)$$$

2197A.title: Friendly Numbers
2197A.statement_text: For an integer (x), we call another integer (y) friendly if the following condition holds: (y - d(y) = x), where (d(y)) is the sum of the digits of (y). For a given integer (x), determine how many friendly numbers it has. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 500)). The description of the test cases follows. Each test case consists of a single line containing one integer (x) ((1 \le x \le 10^{9})). For each test case, output one integer — the answer to the problem. The number (1) does not have any friendly numbers. The number (18) has (10) friendly numbers: These are all the numbers from (20) to (29). For example, (20 - d(20) = 20 - 2 = 18). The number (998\,244\,360) has (10) friendly numbers: (998\,244\,400) (998\,244\,401) (998\,244\,402) (998\,244\,403) (998\,244\,404) (998\,244\,405) (998\,244\,406) (998\,244\,407) (998\,244\,408) (998\,244\,409)
2197A.editorial_text:
2197A - Friendly Numbers
To solve this problem, it is sufficient to explicitly check that the number $$$i$$$ meets the condition for all $$$i$$$ from $$$x$$$ to $$$x + 83$$$. To verify this, we need to explicitly calculate $$$i - d(i)$$$. Now let's prove this.
Notice that numbers greater than $$$2 \cdot 10^9$$$ definitely do not suit us, since the sum of the digits of the number $$$2 \cdot 10^9 + y \cdot 10^9$$$ does not exceed $$$9 \cdot 9 + 2 + y = 83 + y$$$, while the value of $$$i$$$ in this case will be at least $$$(2 + y) \cdot 10^9$$$, which obviously cannot be suitable.
Thus, the maximum sum of the numbers we are interested in does not exceed $$$83$$$, which means that checking is relevant between $$$x$$$ and $$$x + 83$$$

2197B.title: Array and Permutation
2197B.statement_text: Given a permutation (p) of length (n)(^{\text{∗}}) and an array (a) of length (n). We call the permutation (p) generating for the array (a) if the array (a) can be obtained from the permutation (p) by applying some number of operations (possibly zero) of the following type: Choose an index (i) ((1 \le i \lt n)) and perform one of two replacements: (p_{i} := p_{i + 1}); (p_{i + 1} := p_{i}). In other words, in one operation, you can choose two adjacent elements of the array and copy the value of one into the other. You are required to report whether the permutation (p) is generating for the array (a). (^{\text{∗}})A permutation of length (n) is an array consisting of (n) distinct integers from (1) to (n) in arbitrary order. For example, (2,3,1,5,4) is a permutation, but (1,2,2) is not a permutation ((2) appears twice in the array), and (1,3,4) is also not a permutation ((n=3) but there is (4) in the array). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^{5})) — the length of the array and the permutation. The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n) ((1 \le p_{i} \le n)) — the elements of the permutation. The third line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) ((1 \le a_{i} \le n)) — the elements of the array. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) across all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^{5}). For each test case, output " YES " if the permutation (p) is generating for the array (a), otherwise output " NO ". You may output each letter in any case (lowercase or uppercase). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES "
2197B.editorial_text:
2197B - Array and Permutation
Let's take a closer look at what the array looks like after such operations. I claim that it will have the form $$$q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_n$$$, where the element at position $$$q_i$$$ in permutation $$$p$$$ is not to the right of the element $$$q_{i + 1}$$$. The intuition and proof are as follows:
Essentially, at each iteration, each element of the permutation is located on some segment of the array $$$a$$$, in the corresponding initial order. Then, after each operation, one segment simply increases in length by $$$1$$$, while the other decreases by $$$1$$$ (or is removed). Therefore, these segments cannot change their order. This means that the array after any number of operations will have the form stated above. It is also clear how to obtain any such array using the operations described in the problem statement

2195A.title: Sieve of Erato67henes
2195A.statement_text: You are given (n) positive integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n). Please determine if it is possible to select any number of elements in (a), so that their product is (67). Note that you may not select zero elements, as the product of zero elements is not defined in this problem. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 5)). The second line of each test case contains (n) positive integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le 67)). If it is possible to select elements so that their product is (67), output " YES " on one line. Otherwise, output " NO " on one line. You can output the answer in any case. For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", and " Yes " will also be recognized as positive responses. In the first test case, you can select (a_1) and (a_5) to get (a_1\cdot a_5 = 1 \cdot 67 = 67). In the second test case, it is impossible to select any number of elements so that their product is (67).
2195A.editorial_text:
2195A - Sieve of Erato67henes
Note that $$$67$$$ is a prime number. Therefore, if you want a number of elements to have a product of $$$67$$$, at least one of them must be $$$67$$$. And if there is $$$67$$$ in the sequence $$$a$$$, you know that you can select that element to make $$$67$$$.
Therefore, you can simply check if $$$67$$$ appears in the sequence $$$a$$$.
Alternatively, you can run an algorithm similar to knapsack to get a solution in $$$\mathcal{O}(67n)$$$, but this is overkill compared to the intended solution.

2195B.title: Heapify 1
2195B.statement_text: You are given a permutation (a) of length (n)(^{\text{∗}}). You can perform the following operation any number of times (possibly zero): Select an index (i) ((1 \le i \le \frac{n}{2})), and swap (a_i) and (a_{2i}). For example, when (a=1,4,2,3,5), you can swap (a_2) and (a_4) to make it (1,3,2,4,5), but you cannot swap (a_2) and (a_3). Please determine if the sequence (a) can be sorted in increasing order. (^{\text{∗}})A permutation of length (n) is an array consisting of (n) distinct integers from (1) to (n) in arbitrary order. For example, (2,3,1,5,4) is a permutation, but (1,2,2) is not a permutation ((2) appears twice in the array), and (1,3,4) is also not a permutation ((n=3) but there is (4) in the array). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)). The second line of each test case contains (n) distinct integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). If (a) can be sorted in increasing order, output " YES " on a separate line. Otherwise, output " NO " on a separate line. You can output the answer in any case. For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", and " Yes " will also be recognized as positive responses. In the first test case, (a) is (1,4,3,2,5). You can sort (a) in increasing order by swapping (a_2) and (a_4). Therefore, the answer is " YES ". In the second test case, (a) is (1,4,2,3,5). It is impossible to sort (a) in increasing order. Therefore, the answer is " NO ".

2195C.title: Dice Roll Sequence
2195C.statement_text: Consider the following cube (D) where numbers (x) and (7-x) lie on opposite sides : A sequence (b) of integers from (1) to (6) is called a dice roll sequence if it satisfies the following condition: All pairs of adjacent elements lie on adjacent(^{\text{∗}}) sides of the cube. For example, (1,4,2) is a dice roll sequence, while (3,4,6,3) is not because (3) and (4) are not on adjacent sides of the dice.
