It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (3 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output the minimum number of operations required to make (a) a dice roll sequence. For the first test case, the sequence (a) is (1,4,2). As this is already a dice roll sequence, the answer is (0). For the second test case, the sequence (a) is (3,4,6,3). Changing exactly one element, you can get (3,\color{red}{5},6,3), which is
2195C.editorial_text:
2195C - Dice Roll Sequence
Note how two integers $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$ are on adjacent sides if $$$s \neq t$$$ and $$$s+t \neq 7$$$.
Now we introduce a simple observation derived from the dice itself:

Theorem 1: For any two sides $$$S$$$ and $$$T$$$: there is a third side $$$U$$$ adjacent to both. 
This can be shown in a case-work manner:

If $$$S$$$ and $$$T$$$ are adjacent, $$$U$$$ is any side that shares a corner with $$$S$$$ and $$$T$$$. 
If $$$S=T$$$, $$$U$$$ is a side adjacent to $$$S$$$. 
If $$$S$$$ and $$$T$$$ are opposite to each other, any other side can be $$$U$$$. 
Let's split the sequence $$$a$$$ into subsegments made of two opposite sides of the dice. For example, $$$[1,6,1,1,2,5,2,5,2,3,4,1,1]$$$ becomes $$$[1,6,1,1]+[2,5,2,5,2]+[3,4]+[1,1]$$$.
For each subsegment of $$$k$$$ indices, you need to change at least $$$\left \lfloor k/2 \right \rfloor$$$ indices to fix it. For example, $$$[1,6,1,1]$$$ can be turned into $$$[1,\color{red}{5},1,\color{red}{3}]$$$, and $$$[2,5,2,5,2]$$$ can be turned into $$$[2,\color{red}{4},2,\color{red}{4},2]$$$.
Then, there is always a way to use exactly $$$\left \lfloor k/2 \right \rfloor$$$ indices to remove all violations in this subsegment without making new violations. For odd $$$k$$$, changing the $$$\left \lfloor k/2 \right \rfloor$$$ indices greedily removes all violations in the subsegment without causing new violations. For even $$$k$$$, you can change all elements on odd indices. Now you will never use two adjacent indices at the same time, and each used index fixes violations with both of its adjacent elements.
Thus, after splitting the sequence, we have a lower bound which is always achievable, and the problem is solved in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ time.
Alternatively, there are DP solutions that work in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ time; feel free to use them if they are easier for you.

2195D.title: Absolute Cinema
2195D.statement_text: There is a hidden sequence (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) of (n) integers ((n \ge 2)). It is guaranteed that (|a_i| \le 1000) for all (1 \le i \le n). Let's define a function (f(x)) as follows: ()f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \cdot |i-x|() Given (n) values (f(1),f(2),\ldots,f(n)), please determine the values of (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n). It is guaranteed that the values (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) can be determined uniquely. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((\color{red}{2} \le n \le 300\,000)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (f(1),f(2),\ldots,f(n)) ((-10^{14} \le f(i) \le 10^{14})). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (300\,000). For each test case, output (n) integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) on a separate line ((|a_i| \le 1000)). It is guaranteed that the values (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) can be determined uniquely. In the first test case, the hidden sequence is (a=1,4,2,3). The values (f(1),f(2),\ldots,f(n)) are as follows: (f(1) = 1 \cdot |1-1| + 4 \cdot |2-1| + 2 \cdot |3-1| + 3 \cdot |4-1| = 0+4+4+9 = 17); (f(2) = 1 \cdot |1-2| + 4 \cdot |2-2| + 2 \cdot |3-2| + 3 \cdot |4-2| = 1+0+2+6 = 9); (f(3) = 1 \cdot |1-3| + 4 \cdot |2-3| + 2 \cdot |3-3| + 3 \cdot |4-3| = 2+4+0+3 = 9); (f(4) = 1 \cdot |1-4| + 4 \cdot |2-4| + 2 \cdot |3-4| + 3 \cdot |4-4| = 3+8+2+0 = 13).
2195D.editorial_text:
2195D - Absolute Cinema
Let's plot the graph for $$$y=f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i \cdot |i-x|$$$ and look at the slopes. How is the $$$a_i \cdot |i-x|$$$ term different from all of the other terms?
In the function $$$f(x)$$$, the only term that changes slope at $$$x=i$$$ is the $$$a_i \cdot |i-x|$$$ term. In other words, the slope difference near $$$x=i$$$ is related to $$$a_i$$$. Let's do some math with these slopes.

The slope left to $$$x=i$$$ is $$$f(i)-f(i-1)$$$; 
The slope right to $$$x=i$$$ is $$$f(i+1)-f(i)$$$; 
We know that the slope changed by $$$2a_i$$$ near $$$x=i$$$; 
Therefore, $$$a_i = \frac{(f(i+1)-f(i))-(f(i)-f(i-1))}{2} = \frac{f(i+1)+f(i-1)-2f(i)}{2}$$$ when $$$1 \lt i \lt n$$$. 
Now we know $$$a_2,a_3,\ldots,a_{n-1}$$$. How about $$$a_1$$$ and $$$a_n$$$? Let's define a new function as follows.
$$$$$$g(x)=a_1 \cdot |1-x| + a_n \cdot |n-x|$$$$$$
One value of $$$g(x)$$$ can be found in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ time by subtracting $$$n-2$$$ terms from $$$f(x)$$$.
Now note the following:

$$$g(1) = (n-1) \cdot a_n$$$; 
$$$g(n) = (n-1) \cdot a_1$$$. 
Therefore, $$$a_1$$$ and $$$a_n$$$ can be found from $$$g(1)$$$ and $$$g(n)$$$ in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ time.

2195E.title: Idiot First Search
2195E.statement_text: There is a binary tree of (n+1) vertices ( (n) is odd ), with vertices labeled (0,1,\ldots,n). At most one letter can be written on each vertex of the tree, and all vertices initially have nothing written on them. The root of the tree is vertex (0). In the tree, vertex (0) is the parent of vertex (1), while all other vertices have either (2) children or (0) children. Bob is lost in one vertex of the tree and wishes to escape the tree by reaching vertex (0). This is very easy for most people with common sense. However, since Bob is an idiot, he created a new way of traversing the tree; introducing the "Idiot First Search". When Bob is on vertex (v) ((1 \le v \le n)), Bob's movement is determined as follows: If vertex (v) is a leaf, Bob always moves to the parent of (v); otherwise, check the next few conditions. If nothing is written on vertex (v), Bob writes ' L ' on vertex (v) and moves to the left child of (v); If ' L ' is written on vertex (v), Bob overwrites it to ' R ' and moves to the right child of (v); If ' R ' is written on vertex (v), Bob erases it and moves to the parent of (v). It takes exactly (1) second for Bob to move to an adjacent vertex, so Bob will take exactly (x) seconds to perform (x) moves. It has been shown that regardless of which vertex Bob starts on, Bob can reach vertex (0) in a finite (though possibly inexplicably large) amount of time. We don't know who proved it; surely it can't be Bob, but it is definitely proven. For each vertex (k=1,2,\ldots,n), please determine the total time it takes to reach vertex (0) if Bob started on vertex (k), in seconds. As the values may be huge, you are only asked to compute them modulo (10^9+7). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test
2195E.editorial_text:
2195E - Idiot First Search
Can we recursively define Bob's path? Say, what happens when Bob moves to a vertex $$$v$$$ and then its subtree was empty? Then, he must traverse the entire subtree and then move up to the parent.
Note the following things:

When he started on vertex $$$k$$$, its subtree was empty. 
When he traverses the entire empty subtree of $$$v$$$ and moves up to the parent, the subtree of $$$v$$$ becomes empty again. 
Let's define $$$\mathtt{dp}_1[v]$$$ as the time to traverse the subtree of $$$v$$$ and move to the parent. Then $$$\mathtt{dp}_1$$$ can be computed using a simple "bottom-up" DP on tree. If $$$v$$$ is a leaf, then $$$\mathtt{dp}_1[v]=1$$$. Otherwise, it satisfies $$$\mathtt{dp}_1[v]=\mathtt{dp}_1[l_v]+\mathtt{dp}_1[r_v]+3$$$.
Now, Bob's path from vertex $$$v$$$ to vertex $$$0$$$ is as follows:
$$$$$$v \to \ldots \to v \to p(v) \to \ldots \to p(v) \to p(p(v)) \to \ldots p(p(v)) \to \ldots \to 0 $$$$$$
Therefore, Bob's path can be described by values of $$$\mathtt{dp}_1$$$ from vertex $$$v$$$ to vertex $$$0$$$.
Let's define $$$\mathtt{dp}_2[v]$$$ as the sum of $$$\mathtt{dp}_1$$$ over the path $$$v \to \ldots \to 1$$$. This can be computed using a "top-down" DP similarly to a prefix sum. Now the answer to vertex $$$v$$$ is equal to $$$\mathtt{dp}_2[v]$$$.
The problem is solved in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ time.

2195F.title: Parabola Independence
2195F.statement_text: You are given a set of (n) quadratic functions (F=\{f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_n \}), where (f_i(x)=a_i x^2 + b_i x + c_i). Two functions (f) and (g) are called independent if (f(x) \neq g(x)) for all (x \in \mathbb{R}). Also, a set of functions (G=\{g_1,g_2,\ldots,g_k\}) is called organized if the two functions (g_i) and (g_j) are independent for all (1 \le i \lt j \le |G|). For each (i=1,2,\ldots,n), please find the size of the largest organized subset of (F) that contains (f_i) as an element. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 3000)). Each of the (n) following lines contains three integers (a_i), (b_i), (c_i) denoting the function (f_i) ((-10^6 \le a_i, b_i, c_i \le 10^6), (a_i \neq 0)). It is guaranteed that the functions in one test case are pairwise distinct. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n^2) over all test cases does not exceed (3000^2). For each test case, output (n) integers (s_1,s_2,\ldots,s_n), where (s_i) is the size of the largest organized subset that contains (f_i). In the first test case, the functions are as follows: (f_1(x)=x^2+2x-1); (f_2(x)=-3x^2-3); (f_3(x)=-x^2+4x-5); (f_4(x)=x^2+2x-4). The functions' graphs are as shown below: The largest organized subsets of (F) containing each function are as follows: (\{f_1,f_3,f_4\}) is the largest organized subset that contains (f_1); (\{f_1,f_2\}) is the largest organized subset that contains (f_2); (\{f_1,f_3,f_4\}) is the largest organized subset that contains (f_3); (\{f_1,f_3,f_4\}) is the largest organized subset that contains (f_4).
2195F.editorial_text:
2195F - Parabola Independence
Let's consider a graph $$$G$$$ where $$$u\leftrightarrow v$$$ is an edge if and only if $$$f_u$$$ and $$$f_v$$$ are independent. Then, by the problem definition, an organized subset is a clique (complete subgraph) in the graph $$$G$$$. The issue is that the clique problem is famously known to be NP-complete. Can we use any other property to our advantage?
The given functions are continuous functions. That is, if $$$f_i(x) \neq f_j(x)$$$ for all $$$x \in \mathbb{R}$$$, then either of the following holds:

$$$f_i(x) \gt f_j(x)$$$ for all $$$x \in \mathbb{R}$$$. 
$$$f_i(x) \lt f_j(x)$$$ for all $$$x \in \mathbb{R}$$$. 
Let's denote that $$$u \prec v$$$ if $$$f_u(x) \lt f_v(x)$$$ for all $$$x \in \mathbb{R}$$$. We will consider the unique properties of this relation.

The relation $$$\prec$$$ is transitive. That is, if $$$a \prec b$$$ and $$$b \prec c$$$, then $$$a \prec c$$$. 
If $$$u \prec v$$$, then trivially $$$v \prec u$$$ cannot be true. 
$$$u \prec u$$$ cannot hold for any $$$u$$$. 
Such a relation is also called a strict partial order in mathematics.
Let's construct a directed graph $$$D$$$ where $$$u \to v$$$ is an edge if and only if $$$u \prec v$$$. All indices from an organized subset can be ordered by $$$\prec$$$, so organized subsets of size $$$k$$$ correspond to paths of $$$k$$$ vertices in $$$D$$$. Therefore, now we reduced the problem to a longest path problem in $$$D$$$.
Due to the properties of $$$\prec$$$, the graph $$$D$$$ cannot have cycles, meaning the graph $$$D$$$ is a directed acyclic graph (DAG). As we already know, the longest path problem on a DAG can be solved using DP.
Let's define two DP states. $$$\mathtt{dp}_l[v]$$$ is defined as the length (the number of vertices) of the longest path ending on $$$v$$$, and $$$\mathtt{dp}_r[v]$$$ is defined as the length of the longest path starting on $$$v$$$. Then the length of the longest path containing vertex $$$v$$$ is exactly $$$\mathtt{dp}_l[v]+\mathtt{dp}_r[v]-1$$$. We can compute both $$$\mathtt{dp}_r[v]$$$ and $$$\mathtt{dp}_r[v]$$$ in $$$\mathcal{O}(n^2)$$$ time, and the problem is solved.

2195G.title: Idiot First Search and Queries
2195G.statement_text: This problem shares the definitions with problem E. However, it does not ask for the same answer. There is a binary tree of (n+1) vertices ( (n) is odd ), with vertices labeled (0,1,\ldots,n). At most one letter can be written on each vertex of the tree, and all vertices initially have nothing written on them. The root of the tree is vertex (0). In the tree, vertex (0) is the parent of vertex (1), while all other vertices have either (2) children or (0) children. Bob is lost in one vertex of the tree and wishes to escape the tree by reaching vertex (0). This is very easy for most people with common sense. However, since Bob is an idiot, he created a new way of traversing the tree; introducing the "Idiot First Search". When Bob is on vertex (v) ((1 \le v \le n)), Bob's movement is determined as follows: If vertex (v) is a leaf, Bob always moves to the parent of (v); otherwise, check the next few conditions. If nothing is written on vertex (v), Bob writes ' L ' on vertex (v) and moves to the left child of (v); If ' L ' is written on vertex (v), Bob overwrites it to ' R ' and moves to the right child of (v); If ' R ' is written on vertex (v), Bob erases it and moves to the parent of (v). It takes exactly (1) second for Bob to move to an adjacent vertex, so Bob will take exactly (x) seconds to perform (x) moves. It has been shown that regardless of which vertex Bob starts on, Bob can reach vertex (0) in a finite (though possibly inexplicably large) amount of time. We don't know who proved it; surely it can't be Bob, but it is definitely proven. 2195G.editorial_text:
2195G - Idiot First Search and Queries
We assume that you already read and understand the editorial of problem E.
What does $$$\mathtt{dp}_2$$$ tell you about, other than its definition? Specifically, what does it tell you about the structure of the path?
Let's assume a vertex $$$w$$$ that is an ancestor of vertex $$$v$$$. Then, the path defined by $$$\mathtt{dp}_2[w]$$$ is a suffix of the path defined by $$$\mathtt{dp}_2[v]$$$. Before reaching vertex $$$w$$$ for the first time, Bob has been traversing subtrees of descendants of $$$w$$$ (which never include $$$w$$$). Therefore, the first time Bob reaches an ancestor vertex $$$w$$$ from vertex $$$v$$$ can be simply written as $$$\mathtt{dp}_2[v]-\mathtt{dp}_2[w]$$$.
Let's say vertex $$$u$$$ is the lowest ancestor of $$$v$$$ such that $$$\mathtt{dp}_2[v]-\mathtt{dp}_2[u] \le k$$$. Then, we can say Bob was traversing the subtree of $$$u$$$ (including vertex $$$u$$$) after $$$k$$$ moves. Naively finding this vertex has a time complexity of $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$. Instead, using binary lifting, we can binary search directly on ancestors of $$$v$$$, finding vertex $$$u$$$ in $$$\mathcal{O}(\log n)$$$ time.
Now we have to find the vertex Bob is on after $$$k-(\mathtt{dp}_2[v]-\mathtt{dp}_2[u])$$$ moves from vertex $$$u$$$. This can be solved by preprocessing the Euler Tour order of the tree.
Let's record the path that Bob traverses after starting from vertex $$$1$$$. For the second example test case, it looks like the following:
$$$$$$1 \to 2 \to 1 \to 3 \to 4 \to 3 \to 5 \to 3 \to 1 \to 0$$$$$$
Then, any subtree traversal order appears contiguously in this record.
$$$$$$(1 \to (2) \to 1 \to (3 \to (4) \to 3 \to (5) \to 3) \to 1) \to 0$$$$$$
By also preprocessing the first index where vertex $$$v$$$ appears, we can find the $$$i$$$-th vertex in the subtree traversal of vertex $$$v$$$ in $$$\mathcal{O}(1)$$$ time. So we have solved the rest of the problem in $$$\mathcal{O}(1)$$$ time per query.
The problem is solved with time complexity $$$\mathcal{O}((n+q) \log n)$$$.
Challenge: There are also $$$\mathcal{O}((n+q) \log^2 n)$$$ solutions which use HLD instead of binary lifting and Euler tour technique. I was unable to hack these solutions without making the TL extremely tight, so I deliberately did not hack them yet. Can you hack them?

2195H.title: Codeforces Heuristic Contest 001
2195H.statement_text: There is a grid of (3n \times 3n) points, consisting of all integer points ((x,y)) such that (1 \le x,y \le 3n). Find a largest set of triangles satisfying the following conditions: Each triangle has its vertices on exactly three points on the grid. Each triangle has an area of exactly (\frac{1}{2}). Note that they do not have to be right triangles. No two triangles share a common intersection point, including their vertices. If there exist multiple largest such sets of triangles, you may output any of them. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 30)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 166)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n^2) over all test cases does not exceed (166^2). Output the maximum size (m) of the set of triangles on one line ((0 \le m \le 3n^2)). Then, output (m) lines in the following format: (x_{i,1}\;y_{i,1}\;x_{i,2}\;y_{i,2}\;x_{i,3}\;y_{i,3}): The vertices of the (i)-th triangle are ((x_{i,1},y_{i,1})), ((x_{i,2},y_{i,2})), ((x_{i,3},y_{i,3})). You may output the vertices of one triangle in any order (clockwise or counterclockwise). Your output will be accepted if it satisfies all conditions and the maximum size given is correct. In the first test case, the example output has (2) triangles as shown in the following image: In the second test case, the example output has (12) triangles as shown in the image on the left: As the triangles are not required to be right triangles, the set of triangles shown in the image on the right will also be considered valid.
2195H.editorial_text:
2195H - Codeforces Heuristic Contest 001
Is it possible to find a recurrence to reduce a problem into a smaller problem? Formally, can we find a construction for $$$n=k$$$ using a construction for some $$$n=k-c$$$?
The $$$2 \times 3$$$ rectangle has an interesting property that we can use. By placing two $$$(2 \times 3)$$$-s horizontally, you can get a $$$2 \times 6$$$ rectangle. Also, by placing three $$$(3 \times 2)$$$-s horizontally, you can get a $$$3 \times 6$$$ rectangle. By a corollary to the Frobenius coin problem, we can get a $$$k \times 6$$$ or $$$6 \times k$$$ rectangle for any $$$k \ge 2$$$ using these rectangles.
Now we can split a $$$3n \times 3n$$$ square into the following three rectangles:

A $$$6 \times 3n$$$ rectangle; 
A $$$3(n-2) \times 6$$$ rectangle; 
A $$$3(n-2) \times 3(n-2)$$$ square. 
The first two rectangles can be constructed as they are $$$6 \times k$$$ and $$$k \times 6$$$ rectangles. The third square is precisely the subproblem for $$$n-2$$$. Therefore, if there is a construction for $$$n=m-2$$$ having $$$3(m-2)^2-k$$$ triangles, we can also find a construction for $$$n=m$$$ having $$$3m^2-k$$$ triangles.
For even $$$n$$$, a $$$3n \times 3n$$$ square is easily tiled using $$$2 \times 3$$$ and $$$3 \times 2$$$ rectangles. For odd $$$n$$$, we know that we can use two triangles on $$$n=1$$$, and that gives us a construction with $$$3n^2-1$$$ triangles in the general case. Is that the maximum value? Can we do better for some $$$n$$$?
Yes, in fact, we can use $$$27$$$ triangles for $$$n=3$$$.

Therefore, we have shown that we can use $$$3n^2$$$ triangles for all $$$n \ge 2$$$. The $$$3n^2$$$ triangles can be constructed by implementing the aforementioned recursion with base condition $$$n \le 3$$$. Alternatively, it doesn't have to be implemented recursively; just keep the base condition in mind and it's easy to write an iterative construction. The problem has been solved in $$$\mathcal{O}(n^2)$$$ time.
As the $$$n=3$$$ case has only $$$27$$$ triangles, it is convenient to encode them in an array of strings with $$$27$$$ different characters and decode them at runtime.

2192A.editorial_text:
2192A — String Rotation Game

Hint 1
By performing the operation, try to break a block into $$$2$$$ blocks.

Solution
The only way to increase the count of blocks is to break a block into $$$2$$$ blocks by performing an operation such that some characters of a block are present at the start of the string and some characters at the end of the string. For us to be able to achieve this, there must exist at least one block with a size greater than or equal to $$$2$$$. But, if in the original string, the first and the last character are already equal, this means a block is already broken into $$$2$$$ block (in some other rotation, it will be one block). Hence in this case the answer will be the score of the original string.
Inshort, if first and the last character of the string are equal, or no $$$2$$$ adjacent characters are equal, then the answer will be score of the original string. Else the answer will be score of the original string $$$+ 1$$$.
Time complexity: $$$O(n)$$$

B
Flipping Binary String
PROGRAMMING
constructive algorithms strings

Add tag

You are given a binary string (s) of length (n). You can perform the following operation on the string: Choose an index (i), and flip the bit present at all other indices except for the index (i). In other words, choose an integer (i) ((1 \le i \le n)), and for all (j) such that (1 \le j \le n) and (j \ne i), if (s_j = 0), then set (s_j:=1), otherwise set (s_j:=0). You can perform the operation any number of times, but each index can be chosen by at most one operation. Your task is to make all bits present in the string (s) equal (0), or report that it is impossible to do so. You don't have to minimize the number of operations. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)). The second line of each test case contains the binary string (s) of length (n). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output (-1) if it is impossible to transform all bits to (0). Otherwise, output two lines in the following format: In the first line, print the number of operations (x) ((0 \leq x \leq n)). In the second line of each test case, print (x) numbers – the indices you select in each operation in order. You should guarantee that each index is chosen at most once. If there are multiple possible solutions, you may output any. In the first test case, performing the operation on index (2) means flipping bits present at index (1) and (3). So the new string formed will be (000). In the second test case, it can be shown that we cannot make string (a) equal to (000) using the described operations.

2192B.editorial_text:
2192B — Flipping Binary String

Hint 1
What is the condition for -1?

Hint 2
If the length of the string is odd and the count of 1 is odd, then and only then the answer will be -1.

Solution
First of all, flipping a bit an even number of times is equivalent to not flipping the bit at all, and flipping a bit an odd number of times is equivalent to flipping the bit just one time. So, to make all the bits equal to $$$0$$$, we have to make sure we flip all the $$$0$$$ bits an even number of times and all the $$$1$$$ bits an odd number of times.
One of the ways to achieve this is, if the count of $$$0$$$ bits in the string is odd, then apply the operation on all the $$$0$$$ bits. If the count of $$$0$$$ bits in the string is even and the count of $$$1$$$ bits in the string is also even, then apply the operation on all the $$$1$$$ bits. If the count of $$$0$$$ bits in the string is even and the count of $$$1$$$ bits in the string is odd, then after applying any operation, the count of $$$0$$$ bits will always stay even. But the length of the string in this case is odd which means we cannot make all the bits equal to $$$0$$$. Hence in this case the answer will be $$$-1$$$.
Time complexity: $$$O(n)$$$

You are developing a new shooter game, but since there are a lot of shooter games out there, you decide to have something unique in your game. You have an all-in-one gun that shoots bullets in a fixed order. There are (n) bullets in the magazine, the (i)-th of which deals (a_i) damage. The enemy starts with (h) health and dies when its health becomes (\le 0). The gun shoots one bullet per second. After firing all (n) bullets, it must reload, which takes (k) seconds. Reloading always restores the same sequence of bullets (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n). You cannot reload early; you must empty the magazine first. At the start, the magazine is already full. Before the fight begins, you may perform at most one swap: pick any indices (1 \le i \lt j \le n) and exchange (a_i) with (a_j). Your task is to find the minimum number of seconds needed to kill the enemy, taking into account this optional single swap. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each testcase contains three integer (n), (h) and (k) ((2 \le n \le 2\cdot 10^5), (1 \le h, k \le 10^9)) — the size of magazine, health of your enemy and time required to reload the magazine. The second line of each testcase contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le 10^9)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5) over all test cases. For each testcase, output a single integer denoting the minimum time required to kill the enemy. In the first test case, you swap the bullets present at index (2) and (5). This makes array (a) as (4, 3, 3, 5, 2). After (3) seconds, the health of your enemy will be (10 - 4 - 3 - 3 = 0), hence the enemy dies in (3) seconds. 2192C.editorial_text:
2192C — All-in-one Gun

Hint 1
If an entire magazine is used, then the operation does not change the total damage dealt or the time used by that magazine. Hence, the operation mainly impacts only the last magazine.

Hint 2
For us to be able to kill the enemy using only $$$i$$$ bullets from the last magazine, what is the necessary condition? Also, what would be the most optimal operation for this?

Solution
First, calculate the total damage an entire magazine deals, which is sum of the array $$$a$$$. We will have to use at least $$$h/sum$$$ magazines. Now, the remaining health of the enemy would be $$$h$$$ modulo $$$sum$$$. If the remaining health is $$$0$$$, then we don't need to worry about the operation.
If the remaining health is greater than $$$0$$$, then we will try to perform an operation that can minimise the number of bullets required in the last magazine. For every $$$i$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, we will check if we can kill the enemy using only $$$i$$$ bullets from the last magazine. When checking for the index $$$i$$$, the most optimal operation will always be to swap $$$min(a_0, a_1,\ldots a_i)$$$ and $$$max(a_{i+1}, a_{i+2},\ldots a_n)$$$. If $$$min(a_0, a_1,\ldots a_i) \gt max(a_{i+1}, a_{i+2},\ldots a_n)$$$, then it is optimal to not perform the operation for this $$$i$$$. After performing the operation (or not performing), if $$$sum(a_0, a_1,\ldots a_i)$$$ becomes less than or equal to the remaining health, then it is possible to kill the enemy using only $$$i$$$ bullets from the last magazine. The smallest $$$i$$$ satisfying this condition gives us the most optimal answer.
Time complexity: $$$O(n)$$$
Code: 363909342

For a tree (T) with root (r), where each node (u) has a value (a_u) associated with it, the cost of the tree defined as: ()\sum_{u\in T} (a_u \cdot d(r,u))() Here, this sum is taken over all nodes (u) in the tree (T), and (d(r,u)) denotes the number of edges on the shortest path from node (r) to node (u) on a tree. You are given a tree consisting of (n) nodes, rooted at node (1). Each node (i) has a value (a_i) assigned to it. For each (r) from (1) to (n), please solve the following problem independently: Consider the subtree of node (r) with respect to node (1). Formally, the subtree of node (r) is the tree consisting of all nodes (u) such that the shortest path from (1) to (u) contains (r). Find the maximum cost of the subtree after performing at most one operation of the following type on the subtree: Choose any node (u) ((u \neq r)). Remove the edge from (u) to the parent of node (u)(^{\text{∗}}). Then, add an edge from (u) to any node (v) that is still reachable from (r). It can be shown that after this operation, the graph remains a tree. (^{\text{∗}})Formally, remove the edge from (u) to (p), where (p) is the unique node satisfying (d(u,p)=1) and (d(u,r)=d(p,r)+1) Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each testcase contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the count of nodes in the tree. The second line of each testcase contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le 2 \cdot 10^5)). Then (n − 1) lines follow, the (i)-th line containing two integers (u) and (v) ((1 \le u, v \le n)) — the two nodes that the (i)-th edge connects. It is guaranteed that the given edges form a tree.

2192D.editorial_text:
2192D — Cost of Tree

Hint 1
How to solve the problem for all subtrees without considering the operation?

Hint 2
Answer of hint $$$1$$$: If $$$cost(i)$$$ represents the cost of subtree with root $$$i$$$, and $$$sum(i)$$$ represents the sum of value of all nodes present in the subtree with root $$$i$$$, then $$$cost(i)$$$ is the summation of $$$cost(j) + sum(j)$$$ for all nodes $$$j$$$ that are children of node $$$i$$$.

Hint 3
Now for the operation, for a chosen node $$$u$$$, once the edge between node $$$u$$$ and the parent of node $$$u$$$ is removed, always choose node $$$v$$$ as the node present in the subtree with root as parent of node $$$u$$$, and having maximum $$$d($$$parent of node $$$u$$$, $$$v)$$$ (distance from partent of node $$$u$$$). Do this for all possible node $$$u$$$.

Solution
This problem can be solved in a single DFS on the tree. In the DFS, each node will calculate $$$2$$$ things for it's subtree, cost without performing operation and the maximum cost with operation already performed in the subtree. 
For calculating cost without performing operation, as compared to the child, the value of $$$d(r, i)$$$ (distance of $$$i$$$ from $$$r$$$) increases by $$$1$$$ for the parent, where $$$i$$$ are all the nodes present in the subtree of child. $$$d(r, i)$$$ increasing by $$$1$$$ means adding $$$a_i$$$ once, as per the equation of the cost of the tree. And adding $$$a_i$$$ once for all nodes present in the subtree means adding sum of values of all nodes present in the subtree once. So, cost of parent $$$=$$$ summation of cost of $$$j$$$ + $$$sum(j)$$$ for all nodes $$$j$$$ that are children of the parent, where $$$sum(j)$$$ represents the sum of value of all nodes present in the subtree of $$$j$$$.
For calculating the maximum cost with operation already performed in the subtree, what the operation does is, it changes the value of $$$d(r, i)$$$ for all nodes $$$i$$$ present in the subtree of node $$$u$$$ (nodes $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ are described in the operation). To maximize the cost, we have to increase $$$d(r, i)$$$ by the maximum possible value. And if the value of $$$d(r, i)$$$ is increased by $$$x$$$, for all nodes $$$i$$$ present in the subtree of node $$$u$$$, it means the cost of tree increases by $$$sum(u) * x$$$. Hence, for a chosen node $$$u$$$, node $$$v$$$ should be the node with the maximum depth in the remaining tree. At this point, if node $$$v$$$ does not lie in the subtree of parent of node $$$u$$$, then it will always be optimal to choose parent of $$$u$$$ as node $$$u$$$ (because this increases $$$sum(u)$$$). We can keep doing this, until node $$$v$$$ lies in the subtree of parent of node $$$u$$$. Hence, if we try performing operation for each node $$$u$$$, and node $$$v$$$ is always chosen as the node with the maximum depth present in the remaining subtree of parent of node $$$u$$$, and we take the maximum cost across all these operations, we will always get the maximum cost of the tree we can achieve. In the DFS, for subtree of $$$r$$$, we only need to calculate cost by performing operations for node $$$u$$$, where node $$$u$$$ are children of node $$$r$$$. For all other nodes present in subtree that can be the node $$$u$$$, the maximum cost with operation already performed in the subtree of children of node $$$r$$$ would have already taken care of this.
Time complexity: $$$O(n)$$$
Code: 363909632

Swap to Rearrange
PROGRAMMING

You are given (2) arrays, (a) and (b), both of length (n). You can perform the following operation: Choose an index (i) ((1 \le i \le n)) and swap (a_i) with (b_i). You can perform the operation any number of times (possibly zero), but each index can be chosen by at most one operation. Your task is to make (a) a rearrangement of (b) after all operations, or state that it is impossible. You do not have to minimize the number of operations. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 10^6)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) ((1 \leq a_i \leq n)). The third line of each test case contains (n) integers (b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n) ((1 \leq b_i \leq n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (10^6). For each test case, output (-1) if it is impossible to make (a) a rearrangement of (b). Otherwise, output two lines in the following format: In the first line, print the number of operations (s) ((0 \leq s \leq n)). In the second line of each test case, print (s) numbers – the indices you select in each operation in order. You should guarantee that each index is chosen at most once. If there are multiple possible answers, you many output any. In the first test case, the operations performed are swap((a_2, b_2)) and swap((a_4,b_4)), which will make (a = 1,2,3,4) and (b = 2,1,4,3). Now it is possible to achieve (a) by rearranging the elements of (b). In the second test case, it can be shown that no matter what operations we do, we cannot make (a) a rearrangement of (b).

2192E.editorial_text:
2192E — Swap to Rearrange

Hint 1
Graph problem?

Hint 2
Eulerian cycle?

Solution
Make $$$a$$$ a rearrangement of $$$b$$$ means the frequency of all numbers present in array $$$a$$$ should be equal to the frequency of all numbers present in array $$$b$$$. For this to be possible, the combined frequency of all numbers present in array $$$a$$$ and array $$$b$$$ should be even. If at least one number has combined frequency as odd, the answer will be $$$-1$$$.
Now, if the answer is not $$$-1$$$, let's see how to perform the operations. Create a graph with $$$n$$$ nodes and $$$n$$$ directed edges from node $$$a_i$$$ to $$$b_i$$$. The operation swap $$$a_i$$$ and $$$b_i$$$ means the direction of the $$$i$$$-th edge is reversed in the graph. This means, for each edge any direction is possible. Hence, we can consider the graph as an undirected graph, which we need to convert to a directed graph. In other words, we need to decide the direction of all the edges.
In the directed graph, the indegrees and outdegrees of a node $$$i$$$ actually mean the frequency of $$$i$$$ in array $$$a$$$ and array $$$b$$$ respectively. Our problem is to make the frequency of each number in array $$$a$$$ equal to array $$$b$$$, which means to make the indegrees of each node equal to its outdegree.
Since, the combined frequency of all numbers is even, it means the degree of each node in the undirected graph is even. This means the graph contains Eulerian cycles. Each connected component can be treated like a separate graph (because it is possible that our graph is not a single connected component), and find Eulerian cycle in all these graphs. Keep assigning direction to the edges in the direction used in the Eulerian cycle and hence accordingly perform the operations.
Time complexity: $$$O(n)$$$

2192F.editorial_text:
2192F — Fish Fight

Hint 1
DP?

Hint 2
Try solving the problem in $$$2$$$ phases. Phase $$$1$$$, when Alice's fish and Bob's fish are not adjacent to each other, and phase $$$2$$$, when they are adjacent to each other. 

Solution
First, let's solve the problem for phase $$$1$$$ (fish $$$A$$$ (Alice's fish) and fish $$$B$$$ (Bob's fish) are not adjacent to each other):
We will maintain $$$2$$$ separate $$$dp$$$, one for each player. Both the $$$dp$$$ work independently of each other. Each $$$dp$$$ will have $$$2$$$ states $$$l$$$ and $$$r$$$, denoting the fish has eaten all other fishes present in the range $$$[l, r]$$$, and $$$dp[l][r]$$$ stores the probability of this happening (without considering the turns played by the other player's fish). This means, the size of the fish has increased by the sum of $$$b_i$$$ for all $$$i$$$ present in the range $$$[l, r]$$$ and $$$i$$$ not equal to the original position of the fish ($$$x$$$ for fish $$$A$$$ and $$$y$$$ for fish $$$B$$$).
From $$$dp[l][r]$$$ we can go to $$$dp[l - 1][r]$$$ and $$$dp[l][r + 1]$$$. But if both the adjacent fishes (fish $$$(l - 1)$$$ and fish $$$(r + 1)$$$) have a larger size and can't be eaten, then in this case the player's fish gets eaten and loses. Hence this directly contributes to the answer without going to the phase $$$2$$$ (only if due to this the fish $$$A$$$ wins). But in this case, we can't directly add $$$dp[l][r]$$$ to the answer as we need to ensure that the other fish is still alive.
Let's say, $$$dpA$$$ and $$$dpB$$$ represents $$$dp$$$ of fish $$$A$$$ and fish $$$B$$$ respectively, and $$$la$$$ and $$$lb$$$ represent $$$l$$$ of fish $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$ respectively, and $$$ra$$$ and $$$rb$$$ represent $$$r$$$ of fish $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$ respectively.
If from $$$dpB[lb][rb]$$$ the fish $$$B$$$ can't eat any of the adjacent fish and hence fish $$$B$$$ is going to get eaten, then
$$$probabiliityB = dpB[lb][rb]$$$
At this point, fish $$$B$$$ occupies subarray of length $$$rb - lb + 1$$$, which means fish $$$B$$$ has played a total of $$$rb - lb$$$ turns. Corresponding to this, the fish $$$A$$$ would have played $$$rb - lb + 1$$$ turns (since they play alternate turns starting from fish $$$A$$$). So, we need to find the probability that the fish $$$A$$$ is not a neighbor of fish $$$B$$$ and fish $$$A$$$ is still alive (fish $$$A$$$ occupies subarray of length $$$rb - lb + 2$$$). Considering fish $$$A$$$ is present to the right of fish $$$B$$$, for fish $$$A$$$ to not be a neighbour of fish $$$B$$$, $$$la$$$ should be at least $$$rb + 2$$$. And for fish $$$A$$$ to occupy subarray of length $$$rb - lb + 2$$$, $$$ra$$$ should be equal to $$$la + (rb - lb + 1)$$$. Hence,
$$$probabiliityA =$$$ summation of $$$dpA[la][ra]$$$ (for all $$$la \ge rb + 2$$$ and corresponding $$$ra \le n$$$)
We can similarly calculate when fish $$$A$$$ is towards the left of fish $$$B$$$. We can maintain prefix sum and suffix sum to get these summations in $$$O(1)$$$ time.
We will add $$$probabiliityA * probabiliityB$$$ directly to the final answer without going to the second phase.
No need to do these things when fish $$$A$$$ can't eat any of the adjacent fish and hence fish $$$A$$$ is going to get eaten, because this increases the answer by $$$0$$$ as we need to calculate the probability of fish $$$A$$$ winning and not the probability of $$$A$$$ losing.
Now, let's solve the problem for phase $$$2$$$ (fish $$$A$$$ and fish $$$B$$$ are adjacent to each other):
For this, we will maintain a single $$$dp$$$. The states of the $$$dp$$$ will be $$$la$$$ and the total number of turns played (combined of both fish $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$). Since both the fishes are adjacent to each other, from only these $$$2$$$ states we can calculate all $$$4$$$ states ($$$la, ra, lb, rb$$$). In phase $$$1$$$, when fishs $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$ get adjacent to each other, the corresponding probability $$$(probabilityA * probabilityB)$$$ can be added to this $$$dp$$$ of phase $$$2$$$. If the total number of turns played is $$$c$$$, then in this $$$dp$$$, either we can move to $$$dp$$$ with state $$$c + 1$$$ (and correspondingly the other state $$$la$$$ can also change), or the fish eats the other player's fish, or it gets eaten by it's adjacent fishes. In the latter $$$2$$$ cases, if the fish $$$A$$$ wins, then we can add the probability of this happening in the final answer.
Time complexity: $$$O(n^2)$$$
Space complexity: $$$O(n^2)$$$
Code: 363912044

2201A1.editorial_text:
2201A1 - Lost Civilization (Easy Version)
There are two solutions to the easy version. They both utilize one observation:

Each element of the initial sequence corresponds to a subsegment of the returned sequence. 
The two solutions are as follows:

Solution 1: Process in the order of left to right. 
Let's check for each element if it must be a new subsegment or should be merged into the previous subsegment. Let's say the first element of the previous subsegment was $$$x$$$, and the last element was $$$y$$$. We definitely know that $$$x \le y$$$. Let's think of it in a case-by-case analysis:

If $$$a_i \le x$$$, then nothing in the previous subsegment could add $$$a_i$$$. This must be a new subsegment. 
If $$$a_i = y+1$$$, then you can construct $$$a_i$$$ from the last element. This can be merged into the previous subsegment. 
If $$$x+1 \le a_i \le y$$$, then we can perform until $$$a_i-1$$$ is found in the previous subsegment, add $$$a_i$$$, then perform the rest of the operations. This can be merged into the previous subsegment. 
If $$$y+1 \lt a_i$$$, then nothing could add $$$a_i$$$. Note that the maximum value of the previous subsegment does not matter. This is because adding $$$a_i$$$ and then inserting smaller values right before it is impossible. 
Therefore, $$$a_i$$$ can be merged into the previous subsegment if and only if $$$x+1 \le a_i \le y+1$$$.
Greedily merging according to this rule yields the optimal initial sequence in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ time.

Solution 2: Process in the order of right to left. 
Let's maintain a stack of elements. For each earlier element $$$a_i$$$ we see, we will eliminate all occurrences of $$$a_i+1$$$ on top of the stack. Afterwards, we push $$$a_i$$$ to the top of the stack.
This can be seen as performing the operations in reverse order, and thus this algorithm only gets sequences that can construct the given sequence.
The stack after this algorithm finishes (from top to bottom) gives you the optimal initial sequence. The algorithm has time complexity $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$.

2201A2.editorial_text:
2201A2 - Lost Civilization (Hard Version)
Please read the editorial of the easy subtask and understand both solutions.
Let's use the stack solution, while we will observe something from both solutions.

The stack solution maintains the shortest sequence for all suffixes. 
The prefix solution maintains the shortest sequence for all prefixes. 
Note how both algorithms performed iterations in an online manner. That being said, by the proof of the prefix solution, we know that a prefix of the shortest constructing sequence is a shortest constructing sequence for some prefix. In other words, when we use the stack solution, the stack contains the shortest constructing sequences for all prefixes of this suffix (which are subsegments of the sequence!).
Therefore, let's record at which index each element in the stack gets added. Then we can record the contribution of each element, and find the sum of all prefixes in $$$\mathcal{O}(1)$$$ at any moment. As we found the sum of all prefixes for every suffix, we have effectively found the sum of all subsegments in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ time.

2201B.editorial_text:
2201B - Recollect Numbers
The value $$$k$$$ can't be less than $$$n$$$ because each pair needs to be flipped at least once, and can't be greater than $$$2n$$$ because each pair will be flipped in at most two operations. What is the actual maximum number of operations?
Let's simulate the algorithm to look at how the number of operations is computed. We classify elements into "unseen" and "seen"; for each value the first occurrence is "unseen" ('u') and the second occurrence is "seen' ('s').
The number of operations accumulated in the algorithm is as follows:

If the next element is seen ('s'), then a pair is flipped and $$$1$$$ operation is accumulated for $$$1$$$ index. 
Otherwise, the next element is unseen ('u?'). 
If the following element is seen ('us'), there are two cases: 
If the element was the same as the previously flipped element, this pair is already flipped and $$$1$$$ operation is accumulated for $$$2$$$ indices. 
If the element was different from the previously flipped element, you need to flip again and $$$2$$$ operations are accumulated for $$$2$$$ indices. 

If the following element is unseen ('uu'), nothing is flipped yet and $$$1$$$ operation is accumulated for $$$2$$$ indices. 

Which case would waste the most number of operations? It's certainly either 's' or 'us' when two elements are different. But 's' cases make the other operations use less on average, because the unseen card of the pair should have appeared from either 'us' or 'uu'. If we record correct operations as $$$1$$$ flip for that pair and wasted operations as $$$0.5$$$ flips for both pairs, the real contribution is as follows:

's': $$$1$$$ flip for this pair; 
'us' (same value): $$$1$$$ flip for this pair; 
'us' (different value): $$$0.5$$$ flips for the unseen, $$$1.5$$$ flips for the seen; 
'uu': $$$0.5$$$ flips for both pairs. 
Therefore, we can see that using the 's' case can only allow $$$1.5$$$ flips for this pair, while the 'us' (different value) case allows $$$2$$$ flips for this pair.
Let's try using as many 'us' cases as possible. The first consideration would be $$$\mathtt{ususus}\ldots\mathtt{ususus}$$$, but this makes every case have the same value and only uses $$$n$$$ operations in total. The respective sequence would be $$$1,1,2,2,\ldots,n,n$$$.
Instead, if we use $$$\mathtt{uuusus}\ldots\mathtt{ususss}$$$, then we can achieve $$$2n-1$$$ operations. One respective sequence would be as follows:

$$$1,2,3,1,4,2,5,3,\ldots,n,n-2,n-1,n$$$ 
As we have shown that not every pair can get $$$2$$$ flips as contribution, we can see that $$$2n-1$$$ is the maximum possible number of operations.
Now to construct every possible $$$k$$$ for the given $$$n$$$, we concatenate the $$$k=n$$$ case and the $$$k=2n-1$$$ case. By concatenating the construction for $$$(x,2x-1)$$$ and the construction for $$$(n-x,n-x)$$$, we achieve a construction for $$$(n,n+x-1)$$$. By setting $$$x=k-n+1$$$, we can construct every possible value of $$$k$$$.
The problem is solved in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ time.

For example, the sequence " ()(()()) " is a regular bracket sequence, while " ())(() " or " (() " are not regular bracket sequences. You are given a regular bracket sequence (S). Let us consider shifting a subsequence (^{\text{∗}}) to the right. In other words, the element of the (j)-th chosen index gets reassigned to the (((j-2) \bmod k + 1))-th chosen character. 2201C.editorial_text:
2201C - Rigged Bracket Sequence
Let's observe how the prefix sums (when '(' and ')' are substituted with $$$+1$$$ and $$$-1$$$) change when you shift a subsequence.
Let's say $$$S$$$ was $$$\mathtt{()(()())}$$$ and we shifted the subsequence $$$S_2 S_4 S_7$$$. The prefix sums before and after the shift are as follows:

Before ($$$\mathtt{()(()())}$$$): $$$[0,1,0,1,2,1,2,1,0]$$$ 
After ($$$\mathtt{(\color{red}{)}(\color{red}{)})(\color{red}{(})}$$$): $$$[0,1,0,1,0,-1,0,1,0]$$$ 
How did the number of brackets in the first five indices change? Let's look at them side by side:
$$$$$$\mathtt{\underline{(\color{blue}{)}(\color{blue}{(})}(\color{blue}{)})} \\ \mathtt{\underline{(\color{red}{)}(\color{red}{)})}(\color{red}{(})}$$$$$$
We can observe that $$$S_7$$$ got moved into the prefix as $$$S_2$$$, and $$$S_4$$$ moved out from the prefix as $$$S_7$$$. Generalizing this, we get the following:

If a prefix either doesn't include any index or includes all indices of the subsequence, then the number of brackets doesn't change. 
If a prefix only partially includes the indices of the subsequence, then the number of brackets changes: 
The last chosen element within the prefix moves out of the prefix. 
The last chosen element of the subsequence moves into the prefix. 

If the last chosen element of the subsequence was a '(', this always keeps the string regular. If it was a ')', it might make the string not regular because a '(' moving out and a ')' moving in means that the prefix sum changes by $$$-2$$$.
Let's maintain a DP defined as $$$\mathtt{DP}_i = (\text{number of non-trivial subsequences in prefix containing index }i)$$$, where non-trivial means that the subsequence ends with a ')'. Then, $$$\mathtt{DP}_j$$$ affects $$$\mathtt{DP}_i$$$ ($$$j \lt i$$$) if either:

$$$S_j$$$ was ')'; 
or the prefix sums between $$$j$$$ and $$$i$$$ never dropped below $$$2$$$. 
One can implement this DP in time complexity $$$\mathcal{O}(n^2)$$$ trivially, and by using prefix sums on DP values, it is possible to optimize condition $$$2$$$ (by binary search or two pointers) to make the DP run in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ or $$$\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$$$ time.
Now the final answer can be computed as follows:

If $$$S_k$$$ was '(', then add $$$2^{k-1}$$$ to the answer. 
If $$$S_k$$$ was ')', then add the corresponding value of $$$\mathtt{DP}$$$ to the answer. 
The problem is solved in time complexity $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ or $$$\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$$$.

2201D.editorial_text:
2201D - Binary Not Search and Queries
Let's observe how it is possible to compute $$$k_\max$$$:
For every two indices $$$i \lt j$$$ such that $$$a_i=a_j$$$, we know that $$$(i,i+1,j-i)$$$ is an element in $$$S(a)$$$. From this we claim:

$$$k_\max$$$ is the maximum value of $$$|i-j|$$$ such that $$$a_i=a_j$$$. 
Let's say this maximum value is $$$d$$$, and then suppose there is a good tuple such that $$$k \gt d$$$. In that case, $$$a_i$$$ must appear in the part unique to the left segment, but cannot appear in the part unique to the right segment. This is a contradiction. Therefore, $$$k_\max=d$$$.
Let's see how we can count $$$f(a)$$$ and also maintain it over updates. For each distinct value in $$$a$$$, we can simply find one (and not more than one) candidate of $$$k_\max$$$. If we maintain all such candidates in a set, it takes only $$$\mathcal{O}(\log n)$$$ time to add and remove candidates. Finding the removed/added candidates of $$$k_\max$$$ can be done by maintaining a set of indices for each distinct value; there are $$$n$$$ elements throughout $$$n$$$ distinct values, so this also takes only $$$\mathcal{O}(\log n)$$$ time to maintain.
How can we maintain $$$f(a)$$$ then? Observe that if $$$(i,i+1,k_\max),(i+1,i+2,k_\max),\ldots,(i+x-1,i+x,k_\max)$$$ are all found from candidates of $$$k_\max$$$ that we know, then any $$$(p,q,k_\max)$$$ where $$$i \le p \lt q \le i+x$$$ are also elements of $$$S(a)$$$. Therefore, if we know these "chains" of tuples then we can count $$$f(a)$$$ by sums of $$$\binom{x}{2}$$$-s. Now we maintain these chains as intervals. For example, $$$(i,i+1,k_\max),(i+1,i+2,k_\max),\ldots,(i+x-1,i+x,k_\max)$$$ becomes interval $$$[i,i+x-1]$$$. Now these can be maintained in a set of intervals; adding a tuple becomes inserting the interval $$$[i,i]$$$ and removing a tuple becomes removing the interval $$$[i,i]$$$.
That was about maintaining $$$f(a)$$$ for one $$$k_\max$$$. However, our complexity does not change even if we maintain it for all $$$k_\max$$$. Because there's just at most one candidate tuple for each distinct value, there's still only $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ intervals maintained at any moment, and the time complexity didn't suffer.
Now we can maintain all of this and then simply take the value of $$$f(a)$$$ from the set with the actual current value of $$$k_\max$$$.
The time complexity is $$$\mathcal{O}((n+q) \log n)$$$.

2201E - ABBA Counting
To solve the problem, first observe the following:

$$$S$$$ can be factored into $$$A+B+B+A$$$ if and only if the first half is a cyclic rotation of the second half. 
Let's count the strings that can be the second half with respect to the first half. Think of rotation; if you rotated the first half by $$$k$$$ indices and then found $$$x$$$ coinciding '?'s without any 'a' coinciding with a 'b', then we can say that there are $$$2^x$$$ second halves that match when rotated $$$k$$$ times. We can consider adding this up.
But this counting has a flaw. Let's think of "abaababaabaa". The second half "baabaa" must have been counted twice on $$$k=0$$$ and $$$k=3$$$! Therefore, we must find a way to deal with this overcounting issue. For this, we consider the minimal period of the first half.
For each divisor $$$d$$$ of $$$n/2$$$, we want to count minimal periods of length $$$d$$$. We can collapse the first and second halves of the string into two length-$$$d$$$ strings. Then, similarly to when we overcounted, we can count for each rotation from $$$k=0,1,\ldots,d-1$$$. Then, strings with minimal period length $$$d$$$ are counted in divisor $$$d$$$ exactly once. The unfortunate part is that our "abaababaabaa" is still counted twice in $$$d=6$$$.
But that's fine! Thankfully, if the minimal period length is $$$d$$$ for some period, then we know that it's overcounted $$$2$$$ times for $$$2d$$$, $$$3$$$ times for $$$3d$$$, and $$$x$$$ times for $$$xd$$$. Therefore, we can perform an "inclusion-exclusion" kind of elimination; for $$$d_1 \lt d_2$$$ and $$$d_1 \mid d_2$$$, we subtract $$$(d_2/d_1)$$$ times the answer for $$$d_1$$$ from the answer for $$$d_2$$$. Then we actually have the correct count for each minimal period length, and adding them up gives us the answer.
Counting fast for one period length is considered (relatively) standard practice. Formally, you can reverse the second half and find a cyclic "convolution" with the first half. That is, we modify $$$\sum_{i+j=k} a_i \cdot b_j$$$ into $$$\sum_{i-j=k} a_i \cdot b_j = \sum_{i=j+k} a_i \cdot b_j$$$. By FFT, we can count for a divisor $$$d$$$ in $$$d \log d$$$ time.
As we took $$$\mathcal{O}(n+d \log d)$$$ time while counting for divisor $$$d$$$, the total time complexity is $$$\mathcal{O}(n \, d (n/2) + \sum d \log d)$$$. It can be shown that $$$\sum d$$$ is actually of order $$$\mathcal{O}(n \log \log n)$$$, and therefore our time complexity boils down to $$$\mathcal{O}(n \, d (n/2) + n \log n \log \log n)$$$.

2201F2.editorial_text:
2201F2 - Monotone Monochrome Matrices (Hard Version)
For the Easy subtask, you may observe the following reduction of the problem.

If there is no violation between two rows $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$, it holds true that either row is a submask of the other. 
This is because if there is a black column in row $$$i$$$ that is not in $$$j$$$, and a black column in row $$$j$$$ that is not in $$$i$$$, this is both equivalent to a violation in the problem and a violation to both $$$M_i \subseteq M_j$$$ and $$$M_j \subseteq M_i$$$.
Let's try to sort the rows and count the adjacent violations. If you maintain the rows sorted, then the number of adjacent violations can be maintained by looking at adjacent elements in a std::set.
The issue is on how to sort rows. For this, we can see that if $$$M_1 \subseteq M_2 \subseteq \ldots \subseteq M_n$$$, then $$$|M_1| \le |M_2| \le \ldots \le |M_n|$$$. Therefore, if the answer is YES, then sorting by cardinality is equivalent to sorting so that subsets come before supersets.
By dealing with adjacent violations using bitsets, one can achieve a time complexity of $$$\mathcal{O}((n+q)(\frac{n}{w}+\log n))$$$.
The difference between Easy and Medium is not very intuitive. The biggest issue of Easy is that it uses $$$\mathcal{O}(\frac{n^2}{w})$$$ memory. There are various facts one can use to resolve this and hopefully achieve $$$\mathcal{O}(q \sqrt {q})$$$ time complexity:

There are only $$$\mathcal{O}(\sqrt q)$$$ different cardinalities at any moment. 
If the answer is YES, then either the number of active rows or the number of active columns is $$$\mathcal{O}(\sqrt {q})$$$. 
If there are two different contents of rows with the same cardinality, the answer is NO. 
Each of these facts lead to a different solution that optimizes the solution. For example, we can use the second observation, and find the final moment $$$k$$$ such that either the number of rows or the number of columns was at most $$$\sqrt{k}$$$. Then, any moment after this the answer is NO, and we can solve up to this moment only using the active rows/columns of the smaller side. As the smaller side has cardinality $$$\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{q})$$$, one can achieve a time complexity of $$$\mathcal{O}(q \sqrt{q})$$$ or $$$\mathcal{O}(\frac{q\sqrt{q}}{w})$$$.
In order to achieve a solution to the Hard subtask, we would want to drastically change our approach, because large bitmasks are fundamentally hard to manage anyways.
Here is an observation that solves the problem:

If you push the $$$1$$$-s forcefully into one direction (think of gravity), then it's equivalent to sorting if and only if the answer is YES. 
Proving equivalence is not easy, but the general idea of the proof is:

If the answer is YES, then the algorithm to simulate gravity always pulls supersets into subsets, so it becomes equivalent to selection sort. 
If the answer is NO, then any sorting order yields a floating $$$1$$$, whereas gravity doesn't allow a floating $$$1$$$. 
It is now quite easy to maintain a sorted order (respective to cardinality) and the orientation due to gravity at the same time, because we have done the former by std::set (Note that we don't have to use a std::set, and can simply swap two indices each time) and the latter is just placing cells at the rightmost possible column.
Then, by either comparing the column cardinalities, or simply hashing both matrices, we can bookkeep equivalence of sorting and gravity in $$$\mathcal{O}(1)$$$ time. By the time complexity to maintain the sorted order, the total time complexity is $$$\mathcal{O}((n+q)\log n)$$$.

2201G.editorial_text:
2201G - Codeforces Heuristic Contest 1001
One quick disclaimer before getting into what we're actually trying to do in the solution: the value $$$1/e$$$ didn't really have anything to do with the real solution. That's just for a little fun factor in the problem; the actual model solution aims for a density of $$$0.4 - o(1)$$$. It uses $$$385\,160$$$ vertices, where at least $$$368\,615$$$ vertices are required to get accepted.
The main concept that you would need to understand in order to solve this problem would be "gadgets". In Wikipedia, it is defined as "subunit of a problem instance that simulates the behavior of one of the fundamental units of a different computational problem". You don't have to be scared about terminology right now, though; understanding "subunit of a problem" "simulating units of another computational problem" is enough for this problem.
Let's look at the following example:

We can call that a "gadget" that simulates an edge in a path graph, considering that it can be extended arbitrarily and looks like an edge (well, close enough)..... though we don't really have something that we would call a vertex. So what we're trying to do in a nutshell is to find a pattern that repeats well without making violations with other patterns. And it would be great if they can interconnect with some other patterns as well.
One nice pattern made of gadgets, though it doesn't get AC on the problem, would be the following:

This pattern doesn't make any inner cycles, repeats well enough, and is made of easily extensible gadgets. That's why gadgets are important in solving this problem; they make up the framework of the main pattern in any construction.
Now, constructing a good gadget can be done in two ways in general:

Draw on paper until you get a good one. This is not impossible, but it's hard in general. Definitely not impossible though, sammyuri did it in this way! 
Define the "rules" that the gadget must satisfy, and optimize that using heuristics or optimization libraries. Trying out some solvers such as PuLP (free) or Gurobi (proprietary) would be a good start. It's still not easy, but at least it must be less manual labor, right? 
The advantage of the second method is that those algorithms and libraries will optimize for you according to the rules you set; so your role changes from laying out the pattern to planning how the pattern should behave.
Now the final objective of the problem is to find good gadgets and weave a pattern that achieves at least $$$0.4-o(1)$$$ density. $$$0.4-o(1)$$$ means that it converges to $$$0.4$$$ from below, so small amounts of empty areas can be wasted without much concern; in the end, you will see the forest, not the trees. How will you do that? That's up to you. Good luck, and have fun!

Today, Alex wants to build a parkour course for Steve to train his parkour skills on. A parkour course is a sequence (p_0 \to p_1 \to \ldots \to p_k) of integer coordinates on the plane. Here, a contiguous pair of coordinates is called a move , denoted as (p_{i-1} \to p_i). Alex knows that Steve can only perform the following types of moves: ((x_i,y_i) \to (x_i+2,y_i+1)); ((x_i,y_i) \to (x_i+3,y_i)); ((x_i,y_i) \to (x_i+4,y_i-1)). Note that Steve will not perform any other type of moves. For example, Steve can perform ((0,0) \to (2,1)) and ((2,1) \to (5,1)), but will never perform moves such as ((2,1) \to (3,2)), ((3,0) \to (5,-1)), or ((4,-1) \to (6,-1)) (even though they may look very easy). You are given an integer coordinate ((x,y)) on the plane. Please determine if it is possible to make a parkour course (q_0,q_1,\ldots,q_k) that satisfies the following conditions: (q_0=(0,0)); (q_k=(x,y)); The parkour course only consists of moves that Steve can perform. 2202A.editorial_text:
2202A - Parkour Design
Notice how these three paths end up on the same coordinate:

$$$(0,0) \to (2,1) \to (6,0)$$$ 
$$$(0,0) \to (3,0) \to (6,0)$$$ 
$$$(0,0) \to (4-1) \to (6,0)$$$ 
Because of this, using both $$$(+2,+1)$$$ and $$$(+4,-1)$$$ types of moves is meaningless because they can be substituted into two $$$(+3,0)$$$ moves. Now we can simply align the $$$y$$$ coordinate using only one type of move, and then check if the given coordinate is reachable by checking the $$$x$$$ coordinate.
Alternatively, one can show that the answer is YES if $$$(x,y)$$$ satisfies the following two conditions:

$$$x+y \equiv 0 \pmod 3$$$ 
$$$-\frac{x}{4} \le y \le \frac{x}{2}$$$ 
The proof is left as a practice for the reader.

2202B.editorial_text:
2202B - ABAB Construction
Notice that the states $$$T=\mathtt{abab}\ldots\mathtt{abab}$$$ and $$$T=\mathtt{baba}\ldots \mathtt{baba}$$$ (with the same length) are equivalent by reflection (you can simply use the opposite operation for the rest of the iteration).
Initially, if $$$n$$$ is odd, you can only append a to $$$S$$$. Therefore, $$$S_1$$$ needs to be a if $$$n$$$ is odd. The rest of the string is equivalent to when $$$n$$$ is even, so WLOG we will assume that $$$n$$$ is even.
When $$$T=\mathtt{abab}\ldots\mathtt{abab}$$$, you can't use the same letter twice in a row because the first and last letters of $$$T$$$ will be the same on the next iteration. Therefore, when you look at the letters of $$$S$$$ in groups of $$$2$$$, they should be either ab or ba.
Therefore, the string $$$S$$$ generated by the algorithm must satisfy the following conditions:

$$$S_1$$$ is a if $$$n$$$ is odd; 
$$$S_{2i} \neq S_{2i+1}$$$ if $$$n$$$ is odd; 
$$$S_{2i-1} \neq S_{2i}$$$ if $$$n$$$ is even. 
The '?'-s in the input don't make a difference in the solution after this observation. The problem is solved in $$$\mathcal{O}(n)$$$ time.

This is the easy version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, the constraints on (n) and (q) are smaller. You can hack only if you solved all versions of this problem. A monochrome matrix of size (n \times n) is a matrix of (n) rows and (n) columns, where each cell is colored either black or white. Let the color of cell ((r,c)) in a monochrome matrix (C) be denoted as (Cr,c). Let's call such a matrix (C) monotone if it satisfies the following condition: There exist no two rows (1 \le i \lt j \le n) and two columns (1 \le k \lt l \le n) that satisfy the following three conditions: (Ci,k=Cj,l); (Cj,k=Ci,l); (Ci,k \neq Cj,k). (Ci,k=Cj,l); (Cj,k=Ci,l); (Ci,k \neq Cj,k). There is a monochrome matrix (M) of size (n \times n), where all cells are initially white. Please solve (q) queries of the following kind: (r\;c): Change the color of the cell ((r,c)) in (M) to black . Then, determine if (M) is monotone or not. For each query, it is guaranteed that the color of the cell ((r,c)) was white before the query. Do note that the updates are persistent. In other words, the change in color from one query affects the later queries as well. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^3)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (q) ((2 \le n \le 25\,000), (1 \le q \le \min(n^2,200\,000))). Each of the (q) following lines contains two integers (r_i), (c_i) denoting the (i)-th query ((1 \le r_i,c_i \le n)). For each query, it is guaranteed that the color of the cell ((r,c)) was white before the query. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (25\,000).
