2203A.title: Towers of Boxes
2203A.statement_text: Monocarp has (n) identical boxes. The weight of each box is (m), and the durability of each box is (d). To save space, Monocarp wants to build several "towers" of boxes by stacking them on top of each other. Each tower will consist of a positive (greater than (0)) integer number of boxes stacked on top of each other. To ensure that no box breaks, the following condition must be met: for each box, the total weight of all boxes above it must not exceed the durability of that box. Help Monocarp calculate the minimum number of towers he can achieve, given that each of the (n) boxes must be used. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. Each test case consists of a single line containing three integers (n, m, d) ((1 \le n, m, d \le 50)). For each test case, print one integer — the minimum number of towers. In the first example, it is possible to build three towers consisting of (3), (2), and (3) boxes, respectively. In the second example, all boxes are durable enough to build one tower of (8) boxes. In the third example, the weight of the box exceeds its durability, so they cannot be stacked on top of each other. As a result, (5) separate towers will have to be built.
2203A.editorial_text:
2203A - Towers of Boxes
The main idea of this problem is to calculate how many boxes can be in one tower. Suppose we want to build a tower of $$$k$$$ boxes; then if we consider the very bottom box, there will be $$$k-1$$$ boxes on top of it, and their total weight is $$$m(k-1)$$$. This means that the constraint $$$d \ge m(k-1)$$$ must hold, and then the maximum possible $$$k$$$ is equal to $$$\lfloor \frac{d}{m} \rfloor + 1$$$. If there should be no more than $$$k$$$ boxes in the tower, then the minimum number of towers is $$$\lceil \frac{n}{k} \rceil$$$.
When it is necessary to compute a quotient with rounding down or up, it is not recommended to use floating-point numbers and functions like ceil, as this can cause precision issues. For integer division with rounding down, all programming languages have standard operators; if rounding up is needed, you can use the relation $$$\lceil \frac{x}{y} \rceil = \lfloor \frac{x+y-1}{y} \rfloor$$$.

2203B.title: Beautiful Numbers
2203B.statement_text: Let's define (F(x)) as the sum of the digits of (x). An integer (x) is considered beautiful if (F(F(x)) = F(x)). You are given an integer (x). In one move, you can choose any digit in the number and replace it with another. The resulting number cannot have leading zeros. Your task is to calculate the minimum number of moves (possibly zero) required to make the given number beautiful. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The only line of each test case contains a single integer (x) ((1 \le x \le 10^{18})). For each test case, print a single integer — the minimum number of moves (possibly zero) required to make the given number beautiful. In the first example, the given number is already beautiful. In the second example, in one move, we can get the beautiful number (3\underline{3}) (the changed digit is underlined). In the third example, in two moves, we can get the beautiful number (\underline{1}4\underline{0}) (the changed digits are underlined).
2203B.editorial_text:
2203B - Beautiful Numbers
Note that $$$F(x) \lt x$$$ for $$$x \ge 10$$$, and $$$F(x) = x$$$ otherwise. Therefore, a number is beautiful only if $$$F(x) \le 9$$$.
Consider a number represented by the sequence of digits $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$. For each position, we can calculate how much the sum of digits can be reduced by changing that position (let's call it $$$d_i$$$ for the $$$i$$$-th position). We can set $$$0$$$ in every position except the first one (since leading zeros are not allowed). Therefore, $$$d_i = a_i$$$ for $$$i \gt 1$$$ and $$$d_1 = a_1 - 1$$$.
To minimize the number of moves, we can sort the array $$$d$$$ in non-ascending order. Then, find the minimum $$$k$$$ such that the sum of all digits minus the sum of the first $$$k$$$ elements of $$$d$$$ is at most $$$9$$$ (i. e. $$$\displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} a_i - \displaystyle\sum\limits_{j=1}^{k} d_j \le 9$$$). This value of $$$k$$$ is the answer to the problem.

2203C.title: Test Generator
2203C.statement_text: You are developing a test generator. It takes two integers (s) and (m) as input. You need to construct an array of non-negative integers (a = a_{1}, a_{2}, \dots, a_{n}) such that: (\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i = s); for each (i), the condition (a_i \,\&\, m = a_i) holds, where (\&) denotes the bitwise AND operator. In other words, in each number (a_i), the bits that are set to one can only be in the positions where the bits in the number (m) are also set to one. Determine whether there exists at least one such array. If it exists, find the minimum possible length (n). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. Each test case consists of a single line containing two integers (s) and (m) ((1 \le s, m \le 10^{18})) — parameters of the generator. For each test case, print one integer: if such an array does not exist, print (-1); otherwise, print the minimum possible value of (n) — the length of the array. Let's analyze some examples: For (s = 13, m = 5), the answer is (3), as there is a suitable array (a = 5, 4, 4); For (s = 13, m = 3), the answer is (5), as there is a suitable array (a = 3, 3, 3, 3, 1); For (s = 13, m = 6), the answer is (-1), as there is no suitable array.
2203C.editorial_text:
2203C - Test Generator
Let's remove the condition on the minimum possible $$$n$$$ and try to solve the problem where we simply need to answer whether such an array $$$a$$$ exists or not.
Consider an example for $$$s = 147$$$ and $$$m = 57$$$.
Let's write our number $$$s$$$ in binary representation:
$$$$$$[\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{1}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{0}, \color{green}{1}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{1}, \color{green}{1}]$$$$$$
Here, we color the bits green that are allowed by the condition (i.e., these are the set bits of $$$m$$$), and the other bits are colored red. If there were no red set bits in the binary representation of $$$s$$$, we would be guaranteed to be able to create the array $$$a$$$. But what should we do if that is not the case?
Let's transition from the binary representation of $$$s$$$ to an array $$$c$$$, such that $$$\sum c_{i} \cdot 2^{i} = s$$$. This is necessary so that we can perform the following operation for $$$i \gt 0$$$:

subtract one from $$$c_{i}$$$ and then add two to $$$c_{i - 1}$$$. 
For such an operation, the sum of $$$c$$$ does not change, and we can use it to eliminate red set bits:
Let's perform the operation with $$$i = 7$$$:
$$$$$$[\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{2}, \color{green}{0}, \color{green}{1}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{1}, \color{green}{1}]$$$$$$
Now, let's perform the operation with $$$i = 6$$$:
$$$$$$[\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{1}, \color{green}{2}, \color{green}{1}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{1}, \color{green}{1}]$$$$$$
Next, let's perform the operation with $$$i = 6$$$ again:
$$$$$$[\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{4}, \color{green}{1}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{1}, \color{green}{1}]$$$$$$
Now, let's perform the operation with $$$i = 1$$$:
$$$$$$[\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{4}, \color{green}{1}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{3}]$$$$$$
After removing the red set bits, we can construct the array $$$a$$$ as follows:
We will form the numbers $$$a_{i}$$$ one by one. For the next $$$a_{i}$$$, we will go through $$$c$$$ and if $$$c_{j}$$$ is greater than $$$0$$$, we will subtract one from $$$c_{j}$$$ and add $$$2^{j}$$$ to $$$a_{i}$$$ (i.e., we will set the $$$j$$$-th bit to one).
For our example:
$$$a_{0} = 2^{5} + 2^{4} + 2^{0} = 49$$$ and after this:
$$$$$$c = [\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{3}, \color{green}{0}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{2}]$$$$$$
$$$a_{1} = 2^{5} + 2^{0} = 33$$$ and after this:
$$$$$$c = [\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{2}, \color{green}{0}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{1}]$$$$$$
$$$a_{2} = 2^{5} + 2^{0} = 33$$$ and after this:
$$$$$$c = [\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{1}, \color{green}{0}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{0}]$$$$$$
$$$a_{3} = 2^{5} = 32$$$ and after this:
$$$$$$c = [\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{0}, \color{green}{0}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{0}]$$$$$$
It is clear that this method generates a valid array $$$a$$$. We also note that the number of elements in the resulting array is $$$n = \max c_{j}$$$.
We have learned to construct $$$a$$$, but when will we not be able to construct it? It is easy to see that this happens when some bit of $$$s$$$ is a red set bit and there is no green bit lower down, for example:
$$$$$$s = [\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{1}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{0}, \color{green}{1}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{1}, \color{red}{1}]$$$$$$
Okay, we have learned to solve the simplified problem. Now let's return to the original problem, meaning we will restore the condition on the minimum $$$n$$$.
Simply removing the red set bits is now insufficient, as we would like to minimize $$$\max c_{j}$$$. For our example, the minimum $$$\max c_{j}$$$ is $$$3$$$, since after we have removed all the red set bits, we can apply the operation at $$$i = 5$$$:
$$$$$$[\color{red}{0}, \ldots, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{3}, \color{green}{3}, \color{green}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{red}{0}, \color{green}{3}]$$$$$$
Let's try to apply binary search! This can be done since the monotonicity condition holds (if we can create a suitable $$$a$$$ from $$$n$$$ elements, we can also create a suitable $$$a$$$ from $$$n + 1$$$ elements, for example by adding $$$a_{n} = 0$$$).
Now we have a plan for the solution:
We will iterate over $$$n$$$ using binary search. In the checking function for $$$n = mid$$$, we will go through the bits from the most significant to the least significant and form the array $$$c$$$, with the constraint that $$$c_{i} \le mid$$$.
This works quite quickly, as the binary search performs $$$O(\log s)$$$ checks and each check operates in $$$O(\log s)$$$ (since we go through the bits, and the number of bits is $$$\log s$$$).
Asymptotic complexity: $$$O(t \cdot \log^2 s)$$$
Bonus: Think about how to solve the problem in $$$O(t \cdot \log s)$$$

2203D.title: Divisibility Game
2203D.statement_text: Alice and Bob are playing a game. They have an array (a) of (n) elements and an array (b) of (m) elements. The players take turns. Alice goes first. On their turn, each player chooses a number (x) from array (a) and a number (y) from array (b). Alice has her own rule for choosing (x) and (y), and Bob has his: Alice must choose (x) and (y) such that (y) is divisible by (x). Bob must choose (x) and (y) such that (y) is not divisible by (x). After choosing (x) and (y), (y) is removed from the array (b) (but (x) remains in (a)). When (y) is removed from (b), if there are multiple occurrences of (y), only one is removed. The player who cannot make a move loses. Who will win if both players play optimally? Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (m) ((1 \le n, m \le 10^{6})). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_{i}) ((1 \le a_{i} \le n + m)) — the elements of the array (a). The last line of each test case contains (m) integers (b_{i}) ((1 \le b_{i} \le n + m)) — the elements of the array (b). Additional constraints on the input: the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (10^6); the sum of (m) over all test cases does not exceed (10^6). For each test case, print one word: Alice if Alice wins; Bob if Bob wins. Consider the first test case. Let's show how Alice wins through the moves: Alice's move: (x = 3, y = 6) (after this, (6) will be removed from (b), resulting in (b = 7, 12)) Bob's move: (x = 3, y = 7) (Bob will choose (y = 7) on his turn anyway, since there is no (x) that does not divide (y = 12), after this move (b = 12)) Alice's move: $
2203D.editorial_text:
2203D - Divisibility Game
We will divide the numbers from the array $$$b$$$ into three classes:

Numbers that can only be removed by Alice (they are divisible by every number in the array $$$a$$$), we will call them Alice's numbers; 
Numbers that can only be removed by Bob (none of the numbers in the array $$$a$$$ divide them evenly), we will call them Bob's numbers; 
Numbers that can be removed by both Alice and Bob, we will call them common numbers. 
It is easy to guess that the optimal strategy for each player will be to first remove the common numbers and only then remove their own.
The main difficulty of the problem is to learn how to quickly determine to which class each number from $$$b$$$ belongs.
Let's take an arbitrary number from $$$b$$$ and denote it as $$$y$$$. We will try to check whether it is Bob's number or Alice's number; if it is neither, then it is a common number.
Let's look at all the divisors of the number $$$y$$$. For $$$y$$$ to be Alice's number, the array $$$a$$$ must consist only of its divisors, that is:
$$$$$$\displaystyle\sum_{d|y} \text{cnt}[d] = n$$$$$$
where $$$\text{cnt}[d]$$$ denotes the number of occurrences of the number $$$d$$$ in the array $$$a$$$.
Similarly, for $$$y$$$ to be Bob's number, there should not be any of its divisors in the array $$$a$$$:
$$$$$$\displaystyle\sum_{d|y} \text{cnt}[d] = 0$$$$$$
Now we can already write a solution that finds all the divisors of the number and directly checks these two conditions. However, this is slow and works in $$$O(\sqrt{(n + m)} \cdot m)$$$.
Instead of checking each number from $$$b$$$ separately, let's try to calculate an array $$$c$$$ such that:
$$$$$$c_{i} = \displaystyle\sum_{d|i} \text{cnt}[d]$$$$$$
How can we do this? With a simple nested loop:
for(int i = 1; i <= n + m; i++){
for (int j = 1; i * j <= n + m; j++){
c[i * j] += cnt[i];
}
}
In this loop, we iterate over the number $$$i$$$ and add $$$\text{cnt}[i]$$$ to all numbers that are divisible by it. After that, using the array $$$c$$$, we can check the class of a number in $$$O(1)$$$.
This works faster than iterating over all divisors of each number. Let's estimate the number of operations of these nested loops: for $$$i = 1$$$, the inner loop will make $$$n + m$$$ iterations; for $$$i = 2$$$: $$$\frac{n + m}{2}$$$; for $$$i = 3$$$: $$$\frac{n + m}{3}$$$, and so on. Thus, the total number of operations is:
$$$$$$\displaystyle\sum_{i = 1}^{n + m} \frac{n + m}{i} = (n + m) \cdot \displaystyle\sum_{i = 1}^{n + m} \frac{1}{i}$$$$$$
The last factor is the harmonic series. It is known that asymptotically it is equal to $$$\ln (n + m) + \gamma$$$, where $$$\gamma$$$ is a constant, so the number of operations of the nested loops, and thus the entire problem, is solved in $$$O((n + m) \cdot \log (n + m))$$$.

2203E.title: Probabilistic Card Game
2203E.statement_text: Alice and Bob have a deck of cards, which is initially empty. They play a game that lasts for (m) rounds. In the (i)-th round, the following events occur: a card with the value (a_i) is added to the deck (it is guaranteed that no card with this value was previously in the deck); if there are fewer than (3) cards in the deck, the round ends; otherwise, Alice chooses a card from the deck; then Bob chooses a card (knowing which card Alice chose; he cannot choose the same one); one more card is chosen from the remaining (i-2) cards uniformly at random; at the end, all three chosen cards are returned to the deck. Let (a) be the value on Alice's card, (b) be the value on Bob's card, and (c) be the value on the randomly chosen card. Then Bob receives: (0) points if (|a - c| \le |b - c|) (where (|x|) denotes the absolute value of (x)); (0) points if card (c) is between cards (a) and (b) (i. e., (a \lt c \lt b) or (b \lt c \lt a)); (|b-c|) points otherwise. Alice's goal in each round is to minimize Bob's expected score, while Bob's goal is to maximize it. What will be the expected score for Bob in each round if both Alice and Bob play optimally? Print the expected score modulo (998\,244\,353). Note that the players minimize or maximize the real value of the expected score, not the result taken modulo (998\,244\,353). The first line contains a single integer ((3 \le m \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the number of rounds. The second line contains (m) integers (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_m) ((1 \le a_i \le 10^{12}); all (a_i) are distinct). Print (m-2) integers: the (i)-th number should be equal to the expected score for Bob in the round (i+2) with optimal play from both players modulo (998\,244\,353) (i. e., let the expected score be an irreducible fraction (\frac{x}{y}); you need to output (x \cdot y^{-1} \bmod 998\,244\,353), where (y^{-1}) is such a num
2203E.editorial_text:
2203E - Probabilistic Card Game
Since the third card is chosen uniformly at random, the expected value is equal to the sum of the scores that Bob will receive for each of the cards, divided by $$$i-2$$$, where $$$i$$$ is the index of the round. Therefore, it is sufficient for us to minimize or maximize the sum. For output, multiply the sum by the inverse element of $$$i-2$$$, which can be found using Fermat's little theorem.
Let Alice choose some card $$$a$$$. Which card is most optimal for Bob to choose? Let's show that it's a card nearest to $$$a$$$ by value (either on the lesser or greater side). We can represent the cards as points on a number line. Suppose Bob chooses a card $$$b \gt a$$$, i. e., to the right of Alice's card. Then for all cards to the left of $$$a$$$, he will definitely receive a score of $$$0$$$. If there is at least one card $$$b'$$$ between $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$, then it is surely better for Bob to take it. Indeed, all cards between $$$b'$$$ and $$$b$$$ previously gave a score of $$$0$$$, but now they will give a positive score. All cards to the right of $$$b$$$ will give an even greater score. Therefore, the sum will increase.
We define two functions $$$\mathit{cost}_l(a)$$$ and $$$\mathit{cost}_r(a)$$$, which return the total score of the nearest card to the left of $$$a$$$ and the nearest card to the right of $$$a$$$, respectively. Then Alice wants to choose a card $$$a$$$ that minimizes the value of $$$\max(\mathit{cost}_l(a), \mathit{cost}_r(a))$$$.
Let's consider the function $$$\mathit{cost}_l$$$. Note that this function is monotonically increasing. As the value of card $$$a$$$ increases, the value of the nearest card to the left also increases, and the distance from it to the other cards on the left also grows. Similarly, the function $$$\mathit{cost}_r$$$ is monotonically decreasing.
Now, let's look at the graph of the function $$$\max(\mathit{cost}_l(a), \mathit{cost}_r(a))$$$. This function monotonically decreases until the intersection point of the functions $$$\mathit{cost}_l(a)$$$ and $$$\mathit{cost}_r(a)$$$, and then it monotonically increases. Thus, the minimum of this function is found at the intersection. Since the functions are discrete, the answer can be either the largest point for which $$$\mathit{cost}_l(a) \lt \mathit{cost}_r(a)$$$ or the next one after it (the smallest point for which $$$\mathit{cost}_l(a) \ge \mathit{cost}_r(a)$$$).
These candidates can be found using binary search. If we learn to quickly compute $$$\mathit{cost}_l(a)$$$ and $$$\mathit{cost}_r(a)$$$, then by comparing them, we can understand from which side the intersection occurs.
The first problem: with each round, cards are added in arbitrary order, and we need to perform binary search on them. That is, we need to be able to quickly look up the $$$k$$$-th largest card, as well as the previous and next cards from it. The jury's solution uses ordered_set from pbds for this, but any data structure that can answer $$$k$$$-th order statistic queries can be used.
Now, let's learn to quickly compute $$$\mathit{cost}_l(a)$$$. Suppose we have found the nearest card to the left $$$b$$$. Let $$$b$$$ be the $$$k$$$-th card in increasing order. Then we need to compute $$$\sum\limits_{i=1}^{k} (b - \mathit{card}_i)$$$. We can break this down into two sums. $$$\sum\limits_{i=1}^{k} b = k \cdot b$$$. The sum $$$\sum\limits_{i=1}^{k} -\mathit{card}_i$$$ can be maintained using a data structure like a Fenwick tree or a segment tree. $$$\mathit{cost}_r(a)$$$ is computed similarly. It will be convenient to use coordinate compression beforehand: renumerate the points in increasing order as $$$0, 1, 2, \dots$$$ and update the value at the renumerated index in the data structure.
Overall complexity: $$$O(m \log^2 m)$$$.
Instead of binary search, we can also use sqrt decomposition on the renumbered cards. In each block of size $$$\sqrt{m}$$$, we can maintain the rightmost card that's already added, the sum of the card values, and their count. The previous and next cards can be maintained in a doubly linked list.
Then the intersection point of the functions can be found iteratively in $$$O(\sqrt{m})$$$. We check the rightmost card of the block: if it lies to the left of the intersection, we move to the next block; otherwise, we go one card at a time until we reach the intersection.
Overall complexity: $$$O(m\sqrt{m})$$$.

2203F.title: Binary Search with One Swap
2203F.statement_text: Consider the following algorithm for searching for an integer (x) in an array (a) of length (n), where the elements are numbered from (1) to (n): initialize (l = 1) and (r = n); if (l \gt r), terminate the algorithm and report that the desired element was not found; compute (m = \lfloor \frac{l + r}{2} \rfloor); if (a_m = x), terminate the algorithm and report that the desired element was found; if (a_m \lt x), set (l = m + 1), otherwise set (r = m - 1); go to step (2). It can be shown that if the array (a) is sorted in non-decreasing order, then any element of (a) will be successfully found by this algorithm. Your task is as follows: for a given number (n), consider all pairs ((i, j)) such that (1 \le i \lt j \le n). For each of these pairs, you need to calculate its beauty — the number of integers (x) from (1) to (n) that can be successfully found by the described algorithm if we take the array (a = 1, 2, 3, \dots, n) and swap the elements (a_i) and (a_j). After that, for each (k) from (0) to (n), you need to output (p_k) — the number of pairs with beauty (k). The only line of the input contains one integer (n) ((3 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^6)). Print (n+1) integers (p_0, p_1, \dots, p_n), where (p_k) is the number of pairs ((i, j)) with beauty (k). Consider an example where (n = 4): if we swap (a_1) and (a_2), then (1), (3), and (4) can be successfully found; if we swap (a_1) and (a_3), then (2) and (4) can be successfully found; if we swap (a_2) and (a_3), then (1), (3), and (4) can be successfully found; if we swap (a_1) and (a_4), then (2) and (3) can be successfully found; if we swap (a_2) and (a_4), then (1) and (4) can be successfully found; if we swap (a_3) and (a_4), then (1), (2), and (4) can
2203F.editorial_text:
2203F - Binary Search with One Swap
Let's call the integer $$$\lfloor \frac{l + r}{2} \rfloor$$$ the center of the segment $$$[l, r]$$$. We say that the center of the segment controls every integer in the segment.
Consider the binary tree that defines the binary search process. The root controls $$$c = \lfloor \frac{1+n}{2} \rfloor$$$ the whole segment $$$[1, n]$$$, the left child of the root controls its left part — the segment $$$[1, c-1]$$$, the right child of the root controls its right part — the segment $$$[c+1, n]$$$, and so on.
Suppose we are swapping $$$a_i$$$ with $$$a_j$$$. Let $$$k$$$ be the LCA of $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ in this tree. If an integer $$$x$$$ is not controlled by $$$k$$$, then searching for the integer $$$x$$$ will not go to $$$k$$$ or its subtree; so, every integer outside of $$$k$$$'s subtree will be successfully found.
This allows us to use the following approach: iterate on $$$k$$$ (the LCA of $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$), and consider only the subtree of $$$k$$$ as integers which might not be found. For this fixed $$$k$$$, we are going to build an array $$$[p_0, p_1, \dots, p_{f(k)}]$$$, where $$$f(k)$$$ is the size of the segment that $$$k$$$ controls, and $$$p_x$$$ is the number of pairs $$$(i, j)$$$ such that their LCA is $$$k$$$ and swapping them makes exactly $$$x$$$ elements impossible to find.
If $$$k$$$ is the LCA of $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$, then there are three possible cases for the location of $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$:

$$$i$$$ is in the left subtree, $$$j = k$$$; 
$$$i = k$$$, $$$j$$$ is in the right subtree; 
$$$i$$$ is in the left subtree, $$$j$$$ is in the right subtree. 
We will consider the first and the third case; the second case is symmetric to the first one and can be solved in the same way.
Case $$$1$$$: let's say that we swap $$$k$$$ with $$$i$$$, and $$$i$$$ belongs to the left subtree of $$$k$$$. Which integers won't be found? I claim that these are all integers from $$$i+1$$$ to $$$k$$$: we will go to the right subtree of $$$k$$$ while searching for them (since the vertex $$$k$$$ now has value $$$i$$$), but they are all in the left subtree. For all integers less than $$$i$$$ or greater than $$$k$$$, nothing will change, and for $$$i$$$ itself, it will be found as soon as we arrive to the vertex $$$k$$$. So, the number of integers we won't find if we swap $$$k$$$ with $$$i$$$ is exactly $$$k-i$$$.
Case $$$3$$$: let's say that we swap $$$i$$$ with $$$j$$$, $$$i$$$ belongs to the left subtree of $$$k$$$, and $$$j$$$ belongs to the right subtree of $$$k$$$. Let $$$g(i)$$$ be the number of integers in the left subtree of $$$k$$$ which won't be found if we replace $$$i$$$ with some integer greater than $$$k$$$, and $$$h(j)$$$ be the number of integers in the right subtree of $$$k$$$ which won't be found if we replace $$$j$$$ with some integer less than $$$k$$$. I claim that $$$g(i)$$$ is equal to the size of the right subtree of $$$i$$$, plus one: obviously, $$$i$$$ won't be found; but also, when we arrive at the subtree which $$$i$$$ controlled, we have to go to the right if we are looking for some integer from the right subtree, but we will go to the left instead. Similarly, $$$h(j)$$$ is equal to the size of the left subtree of $$$j$$$, plus one.
This allows us to calculate all of the values of $$$g(i)$$$ and $$$h(j)$$$ in $$$O(n)$$$, but how do we "merge" them? This looks like a FFT problem, but FFT is too slow. Instead, let's analyze the possible values of $$$g(i)$$$ and $$$h(j)$$$. I claim that there are only $$$O(\log n)$$$ different values of $$$g(i)$$$ and $$$h(j)$$$, because there are $$$\log_2 n$$$ layers in our tree and the sizes of subtrees in each layer differ at most by $$$1$$$. So, we can simply build two frequency maps which, for every $$$g(i)$$$ and $$$h(j)$$$, store the number of vertices having this value of $$$g(i)$$$ or $$$h(j)$$$ in the subtree, and merge them naively. The sizes of these maps are at most $$$\log n$$$, so processing every $$$k$$$ works in $$$O(f(k) \log \log n + \log^2 n)$$$.
And our final optimization will be as follows: if two vertices which we choose as LCAs of $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ have the same subtree sizes, then the search in their subtrees behaves exactly the same. So we don't need to calculate everything for each possible vertex $$$k$$$; instead, for every $$$f(k)$$$, let's count the number of vertices having this $$$f(k)$$$, calculate the answers for that value of $$$f(k)$$$, and multiply them. There are only $$$O(\log n)$$$ different values of $$$f(k)$$$, and their sum is $$$O(n)$$$, so now our solution works in $$$O(n \log \log n + \log^3 n)$$$.

For a permutation(^{\text{∗}}) (r) of length (m), we call an index (i) ((1\le i\le m)) ugly if and only if (i=\max(\{r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_i\})). Simons has a permutation (p) of length (n), and he can perform the following operation on (p) at most once : Choose two indices (i) and (j) ((1\le i\ne j\le n)), then swap (p_i) and (p_j). Find a permutation (q) that can be obtained from (p) by performing the above operation at most once, such that the number of ugly indices in (q) is minimized. (^{\text{∗}})A permutation of length (n) is an array consisting of (n) distinct integers from (1) to (n) in arbitrary order. For example, (2,3,1,5,4) is a permutation, but (1,2,2) is not a permutation ((2) appears twice in the array), and (1,3,4) is also not a permutation ((n=3) but there is (4) in the array). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 100)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line contains an integer (n) ((1\le n\le 500)) — the length of (p). The second line contains (n) integers (p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n) ((1\le p_i\le n), all (p_i)-s are distinct) — the elements of (p). For each test case, print (n) integers (q_1,q_2,\ldots,q_n) — the permutation you found. If there are multiple possible permutations, you may output any. In the first test case, Simons can obtain only two possible permutations: (1,2) and (2,1). For permutation (1,2), we can see (1=\max(\{1\})) and (2=\max(\{1,2\})). So there are two ugly indices. For permutation (2,1), we can see (1\ne\max(\{2\})) and (2=\max(\{2,1\})). So there is only one ugly index. Thus, permutation (2,1) has the minimum count of ugly indices. In the second test case, Simons can obtain permutation (2,4,1,3) by choosing indices $$$2$

Simons and Cakes for Success
PROGRAMMING
implementation math

Add tag

Simons has (n) friends and a huge amount of cakes. To divide the cakes fairly, you are asked to help him solve the following problem: Find the minimum positive integer (k) such that (n) is a divisor of (k^n). It can be proved that the answer always exists under the given constraints. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 100)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((2\le n\le 10^9)) — the number of friends Simons has. For each test case, output a single integer — the minimum (k) you found. In the first test case: (1^8=1), and (8) is not a divisor of (1); (2^8=256), and (8) is a divisor of (256), because (256 = 8\cdot 32). Thus, the minimum possible (k) is (2). In the second test case, (12) is a divisor of (6^{12}=2\,176\,782\,336), because (2\,176\,782\,336=12\cdot 181\,398\,528).

C
Simons and Posting Blogs
PROGRAMMING
greedy sortings

Add tag

There are (n) blogs. The (i)-th blog mentioned (l_i) users in order as an array (a_i=a_{i,1},a_{i,2},\ldots,a_{i,l_i}). You are going to post all (n) blogs. Let us maintain a sequence (Q) that describes the list of users you have recently mentioned. You need to perform the following operation exactly (n) times: Choose an unposted blog (i) ((1\le i\le n)), then post it. This will cause the following operations for each (1\le j\le l_i) in order: If (a_{i,j}) already exists in (Q), then move (a_{i,j}) to the beginning of (Q). Otherwise, insert (a_{i,j}) at the beginning of (Q). If (a_{i,j}) already exists in (Q), then move (a_{i,j}) to the beginning of (Q). Otherwise, insert (a_{i,j}) at the beginning of (Q). Find the lexicographically smallest(^{\text{∗}}) (Q) after all (n) operations. (^{\text{∗}})An array (x) is lexicographically smaller than an array (y) if and only if one of the following holds: (x) is a prefix of (y), but (x \ne y); or in the first position where (x) and (y) differ, the array (x) has a smaller element than the corresponding element in (y). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 1000)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line contains a single integer (n) ((1\le n\le 3000)) — the number of blogs. Then (n) lines follow, the (i)-th line starting with an integer (l_i) ((1\le l_i\le 3000)), describing the number of users mentioned in the (i)-th blog, which is followed by (l_i) integers (a_{i,1},a_{i,2},\ldots,a_{i,l_i}) ((1\le a_{i,j}\le 10^6)) — the list of users mentioned in the (i)-th blog. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (3000). Denote (\sum\limits_{i=1}^n l_i) as (L). It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$L$

We call an array (b) of length (m) cool if and only if: There exists no index (i) ((1 \lt i \lt m)) such that (b_i=\max(\{b_{i-1}, b_i, b_{i+1}\})). Simons has an array (a) of size (n). Initially, the array is a permutation(^{\text{∗}}). He must perform the following operation until the array is cool : Choose an index (i) ((1 \lt i \lt n)) such that (a_i=\max(\{a_{i-1}, a_i, a_{i+1}\})). Then, he can remove either (a_{i-1}) or (a_{i+1}) from the array. After removal, a gap appears in the array, and the left and right sides of the gap will be rejoined. Find the minimum number of operations for Simons to perform. (^{\text{∗}})A permutation of length (n) is an array consisting of (n) distinct integers from (1) to (n) in arbitrary order. For example, (2,3,1,5,4) is a permutation, but (1,2,2) is not a permutation ((2) appears twice in the array), and (1,3,4) is also not a permutation ((n=3) but there is (4) in the array). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 5\cdot 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line contains an integer (n) ((3\le n\le 5\cdot 10^5)) — the size of (a). The second line contains (n) integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) ((1\le a_i\le n), all (a_i)-s are distinct) — the array Simons has initially. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (5\cdot 10^5). For each test case, print a single integer — the minimum number of operations for Simons to perform. In the first test case, the array is cool initially, so Simons can't perform any operation. The answer is (0). Simons and Reconstructing His Roads
PROGRAMMING

Add tag

There are (n \times m) crossroads in the city, named crossroad ((1, 1), (1, 2),\ldots, (n, m)). The first number represents the row, and the second represents the column. There exists and only exists streets between ((i,j)) and ((i+1,j)) or between ((i,j)) and ((i,j+1)). The street between ((i, j)) and ((i + 1, j)) has a weight of (w_{i,j}), and the street between ((i, j)) and ((i, j + 1)) has a weight of (v_{i,j}). Simons wants some streets reconstructed. Due to some accidents, some of the streets cannot be reconstructed, while others are optional to be reconstructed. For each crossroad, if the number of reconstructed streets adjacent to it is even , Simons calls the crossroad elegant . If all the crossroads are elegant , Simons calls the reconstruction nice . The beauty of a reconstruction is calculated as follows: At first, the beauty is (0). For each row (i) from (1) to (n - 1), let the columns of the streets reconstructed be (c_1 \lt c_2 \lt c_3 \lt \cdots), add (w_{i, c_1} - w_{i, c_2} + w_{i, c_3} - w_{i, c_4}+\cdots) to the beauty . Similarly, for each column (j) from (1) to (m - 1), let the rows of the streets reconstructed be (r_1 \lt r_2 \lt r_3 \lt \cdots), add (v_{r_1, j} - v_{r_2, j} + v_{r_3, j} - v_{r_4, j}+\cdots) to the beauty . In other words, if a street is an odd-indexed one reconstructed in its row or column, add its weight to the beauty ; else subtract it from the beauty . For example, consider the streets and crossroads below without any streets that cannot be reconstructed: We can have a nice reconstruction as follows: The beauty of the reconstruction is (3+4+2-(-9)-(-2)+9+1-(-1)-(-3)-(-4)=38). Simons and Diophantus Equation
PROGRAMMING
bitmasks brute force data structures number theory

Add tag

Simons has given you two integers (n) and (m). Count the number of ordered tuples ((i, j, k)), such that: (0\le i, j, k\le m), and There exist two integers (x) and (y), such that ((i \oplus j) \cdot x + (j \oplus k) \cdot y = n), where (\oplus) denotes the bitwise XOR operation . Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line contains two integers (n) and (m) ((1\le n\le 10^9), (1\le m\le 3\cdot 10^5)) — the given integers. It is guaranteed that the sum of (m) over all test cases does not exceed (3\cdot10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the number of ordered tuples ((i,j,k)) that satisfy the condition. In the first test case, there are (18) tuples that satisfy the conditions. For example: ((2,1,2)) is a valid tuple because the equation ((2\oplus 1)\cdot x+(1\oplus 2)\cdot y=3) has an integer solution (x=3), (y=-2). ((1,1,0)) is also a valid tuple because the equation ((1\oplus 1)\cdot x+(1\oplus 0)\cdot y=3) has an integer solution (x=100), (y=3). ((2,0,2)) is not a valid tuple because the equation ((2\oplus 0)\cdot x+(0\oplus 2)\cdot y=3) has no integer solution. ((1,1,1)) is not a valid tuple because the equation ((1\oplus 1)\cdot x+(1\oplus 1)\cdot y=3) has no integer solution. ((3,2,1)) is not a valid tuple because (3 \gt 2).

2200A.title: Eating Game
2200A.statement_text: There are (n) players playing a game at a circular table. The (i)-th player has (a_i) dishes to eat. They take turns eating the food, and any player can go first. During their turn, if player (i) has any dishes remaining, they must eat exactly one dish. Then, player ((i \bmod n) + 1) starts their turn. This continues until all dishes are finished. The player who eats the last dish is considered the winner. Determine the number of players that can possibly be winners. The first line contains an integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 5000)), the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains an integer (n) ((1 \leq n \leq 10)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers, the elements of (a) ((1 \leq a_i \leq 10)). For each test case, output a line with the answer. In the first test case, player (1) wins for every starting player. In the second test case, player (2) wins for every starting player. In the third test case, players (2) and (4) can win.
2200A.editorial_text:
2200A - Eating Game
Let $$$m$$$ be the maximum value in $$$a$$$. After $$$n(m-1)$$$ moves, only players with $$$a_i=m$$$ will have dishes remaining, so no other players can win. If $$$a_i=m$$$, then player $$$i$$$ can win if the first player is player $$$(i\bmod n) + 1$$$. Hence, the answer is the number of maximums of $$$a$$$.

2200B.title: Deletion Sort
2200B.statement_text: AksLolCoding is playing a game on an array (a) of (n) positive integers. During each turn: If (a) is non-decreasing (^{\text{∗}}), the game ends. Otherwise, AksLolCoding can choose any single element and remove it from the array. Determine the minimum possible number of elements that can be remaining in the array after the game ends. (^{\text{∗}})(a) is non-decreasing if (a_i\leq a_{i+1}) for all (1\leq i\leq m-1), where (m) is the length of (a). The first line contains an integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 1000)), the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains an integer (n) ((1 \leq n \leq 10)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers, the elements of (a) ((1 \leq a_i \leq 100)). For each test case, output an integer: the minimum possible number of elements left once the array is sorted. In the first test case, the minimum of (1) element can be achieved by removing (1), (2), and (3) in that order. In the second and third test cases, no elements can be removed.
2200B.editorial_text:
2200B - Deletion Sort
If $$$a$$$ is non-decreasing at the start, then the answer is trivially $$$n$$$. Otherwise, there exists an $$$i$$$ such that $$$a_i \gt a_{i+1}$$$. We can delete all elements besides these two and then delete $$$a_i$$$ to get to $$$1$$$ remaining element, so the answer is $$$1$$$ in this case.

2200C.title: Specialty String
2200C.statement_text: AksLolCoding is playing a game on a string (s) of length (n). Initially, (s) contains only lowercase Latin characters. In one turn, AksLolCoding can choose any pair of integers ((i,j)) such that: (1 \leq i \lt j \leq n); (s_i = s_j \neq *); and (s_k = *) for all (i \lt k \lt j). Once the game ends, AksLolCoding wins if and only if every character in (s) is equal to (*). Determine if it is possible for AksLolCoding to win. Note: (*) represents ASCII character 42. The first line contains an integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 100)), the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains an integer (n) ((1 \leq n \leq 5000)), the length of the string. The second line of each test case contains a string (s) consisting of lowercase Latin characters. The sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (5000). Output the answer to each test case on its own line. If AksLolCoding can win, output " YES " (without quotes). Else, output " NO " (without quotes). You can output the answer in any case (upper or lower). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES " will be recognized as positive responses. In the first test case, it can be shown that it is impossible for AksLolCoding to win. In the second test case, AksLolCoding can win by making the following moves: llmllm (\rightarrow) llm**m (\rightarrow) **m**m (\rightarrow) ****** In the third test case, AksLolCoding can win by making the following moves: uwuuwu (\rightarrow) uw**wu (\rightarrow) u****u (\rightarrow) ******
2200C.editorial_text:
2200C - Specialty String
Instead of replacing characters with *s, just delete them from the string. Then, the operation becomes deleting two adjacent characters that are equal. AksLolCoding wins if the string becomes empty. Since deleting a pair can never disrupt another pair, the order in which we do the operations does not matter.
We search through the array $$$\frac{n}{2}$$$ times, removing a pair of equal elements whenever we find one. At the end, just output whether the string is empty.
The problem can also be solved in $$$O(n)$$$ using a stack.

2200D.title: Portal
2200D.statement_text: You are given a permutation(^{\text{∗}}) (p) of length (n). There are also two portals located at positions (x) and (y) ((x \lt y)). A portal at position (i) is initially located between the (i)-th and ((i+1))-th elements of the array. Specifically, if (i=0), then the portal is located before the first element of the array, and if (i=n), then the portal is located after the last element. You may perform either of the following two operations as many times as you like: Remove the element to the immediate left of one portal and insert it to the immediate right of the other portal. Remove the element to the immediate right of one portal and insert it to the immediate left of the other portal. Let (\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}}) denote a portal. For example, if (p) is (3,\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}},2,4,\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}},1): Using operation (1) on the left and right portals respectively results in the arrays (\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}},2,4,\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}},3,1) and (3,\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}},4,2,\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}},1). Using operation (2) on the left and right portals respectively results in the arrays (3,\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}},4,2,\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}},1) and (3,1,\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}},2,4,\mathbf{\color{red}{\mathcal{O}}}). Find the lexicographically(^{\text{†}}) smallest permutation you can obtain using these operations. Note that portals do not affect the lexicographical comparison of permutations. (^{\text{∗}})A permutation of length (n) is an array of length (n) containing each integer from (1) to (n) exactly once. (^{\text{†}})A permutation (a) is lexicographically smaller than permutation (b) if there exists an index (i) such that (a_j = b_j) for all indices (1 \leq j \lt i) and (a_i \lt b_i). The first lin
2200D.editorial_text:
2200D - Portal
Let $$$A$$$ denote the subarray of elements between the two portals and $$$B$$$ denote the remaining elements. The operations can cyclically shift $$$A$$$. They cannot change the order of elements of $$$B$$$, but they can change the position of $$$A$$$ within $$$B$$$. Importantly, an element cannot move from $$$A$$$ to $$$B$$$ or vice versa.
To make the lexicographically minimum permutation, we should cyclically shift $$$A$$$ until its leftmost element is its minimum element. Then, insert $$$A$$$ to the left of the leftmost element in $$$B$$$ that is greater than the minimum of $$$A$$$ (or after $$$A$$$ if no such element exists).

2200E.title: Divisive Battle
2200E.statement_text: Alice and Bob are playing game on array (a) initially containing (n) positive integers, with Alice going first. On each player's turn, if (a) is non-decreasing(^{\text{∗}}), the game immediately ends. Otherwise, the player can choose an element (x) from the array and positive integers (1 \lt y,z \lt x) such that (x=yz) and replace (x) in the array with two elements (y) and (z) (in any order at the original location of (x)). If no such move is possible, the game ends. Once the game ends, if (a) is non-decreasing, then Bob wins. Otherwise, Alice wins. Determine who will win the game if both players play optimally. (^{\text{∗}})(a) is non-decreasing if (a_i\leq a_{i+1}) for all (1\leq i\leq m-1), where (m) is the length of (a). The first line contains an integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 10^4)), the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains an integer (n) ((1 \leq n \leq 10^5)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) ((1 \leq a_i \leq 10^6)). The sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (10^5). For each test case, output a line containing "Alice" if Alice wins or "Bob" if Bob wins. The grader is case-sensitive. In the first test case, Alice will win if both players play optimally. In the second test case, Bob can always win no matter what moves Alice makes. In the third test case, Alice can win by replacing (6) with (3) and (2). In the fourth test case, the game ends immediately and Bob wins.
2200E.editorial_text:
2200E - Divisive Battle
If the $$$a$$$ is non-decreasing, Bob wins immediately. Otherwise:
If there exists an element $$$x$$$ in $$$a$$$ that is divisible by two distinct primes $$$p \lt q$$$, then Alice can ensure her victory by replacing $$$x$$$ with $$$\frac{x}{p}$$$ and $$$p$$$. Since $$$\frac{x}{p}$$$ is a multiple of $$$q$$$, there will always be a multiple of $$$q$$$ that appears before $$$p$$$ and is greater than $$$p$$$, so the array will never be non-decreasing.
If no such element exists, all elements in the array are either $$$1$$$ or prime powers of the form $$$p^e$$$ for some prime $$$p$$$. Define an array $$$b$$$ such that $$$b_i$$$ is $$$1$$$ if $$$a_i=1$$$ and is the unique prime factor of $$$a_i$$$ otherwise. If $$$b_i$$$ is non-decreasing, then Bob will win (since $$$a$$$ will be non-decreasing once no moves are possible). Otherwise, there exists an $$$i$$$ such that $$$b_{i-1} \gt b_i$$$. Alice can replace $$$a_i=p^e$$$ with $$$p$$$ and $$$p^{e-1}$$$ if $$$e \gt 1$$$. By similar logic to the above paragraph, this will make it impossible for Bob to win, so Alice will win.

2200F.title: Mooclear Reactor 2
2200F.statement_text: Bessie needs to produce energy as possible in her mooclear reactor. She has (n) different particles. Each particle is defined by two integers (x) and (y). The particle generates (x) units of energy but has a reactivity (y), meaning that it can only exist together with at most (y) other particles in the reactor. Formally, if this particle is chosen to generate energy, then at most (y) particles (other than itself) can also be chosen to generate energy. Bessie must choose a subset of particles that satisfy this constraint to generate energy. The amount of energy that she generates is equal to the sum of the energies of the particles in the subset. There is a shop with (m) particles. Bessie can buy exactly one particle from the shop. For each particle in the shop , determine the maximum total energy that Bessie would be able to produce if she were to buy only that particle from the shop. Bessie is not required to use the particle that is purchased from the shop. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (m) ((1 \leq n, m \leq 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the number of particles that Bessie has and the number of particles in the shop, respectively. The (i)-th of the next (n) lines contains two integers (x) and (y) ((1 \leq x \leq 10^9), (0 \leq y \leq n)) — the energy and reactivity of Bessie's (i)-th particle. The (j)-th of the next (m) lines contains two integers (x) and (y) ((1 \leq x \leq 10^9), (0 \leq y \leq n)) — the energy and reactivity of the shop's (j)-th particle. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases and the sum of (m) over all test cases do not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, print (m) integers. The (i)-th integer should be the maximum total energy that Bessie can produce if she purchases
2200F.editorial_text:
2200F - Mooclear Reactor 2
Consider solving the problem without any shop particles. We can iterate on the number of energy generating particles $$$k$$$ from $$$n$$$ to $$$1$$$. We can only use particles with $$$y\geq k-1$$$. Store a set or min heap of the $$$k$$$ largest $$$x$$$ values. As $$$k$$$ decreases, we add particles to the set/heap, removing the smallest element whenever the size of the set/heap exceeds $$$k$$$. We can store the sum of the elements in the set/heap in a variable $$$s$$$. The answer $$$a$$$ will be the max of $$$s$$$ over all values of $$$k$$$.
To handle shop particles, we can run the algorithm again, but using a maximum set size of $$$k-1$$$ instead of $$$k$$$, reserving an extra slot for the shop particle. We can store the sum $$$s$$$ for each $$$k$$$ in an array $$$f$$$. We can then take the prefix max of $$$f$$$ by setting $$$f[k]:=max(f[k],f[k-1])$$$. For each shop particle, we can: 

choose to not use it, resulting in $$$a$$$ energy, or 
pair it with any other subset of size at most $$$y+1$$$, resulting in $$$x+f[y+1]$$$ energy. 
The answer for each shop particle is just the maximum of these two values.

2200G.title: Operation Permutation
2200G.statement_text: AksLolCoding has an integer (x) and a list of (n) operations. Each operation is a string starting with one of the symbols +,-,x, or / (representing addition, subtraction, multiplication, and real number division respectively), followed immediately by a positive integer (y) ((1 \leq y \leq 10^9)). For example, the operation x3 represents multiplying (x) by (3). AksLolCoding will randomly permute the operations and then apply all operations sequentially to (x) in the permuted order. Help AksLolCoding compute the expected(^{\text{∗}}) final value of (x) modulo (10^9+7). Formally, let (M = 10^9 + 7). It can be shown that the answer can be expressed as an irreducible fraction (\frac{p}{q}), where (p) and (q) are integers and (q \not\equiv 0 \pmod M). Output the integer equal to (p \cdot q^{-1} \pmod M). In other words, output such an integer (a) that (0 \le a \lt M) and (a \cdot q \equiv p \pmod M). (^{\text{∗}})The expected final value of (x) is the average of the final value of (x) over all (n!) permutations. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 1000)), the number of test cases. For each test case, the first line contains two integers (n) and (x) ((1 \leq n \leq 3000), (1 \leq x \leq 10^9)). The second line of each test case contains (n) strings, each representing an operation in the format described above. The sum of (n^2) over all test cases does not exceed (3000^2). Note: x is used to represent multiplication, not * For each test case, output a single integer: the expected final value of (x) modulo (10^9+7). In the first test case, (x) can either be ((10\cdot 2)-10=10) or ((10-10)\cdot 2=0), resulting in an expected value of (5). In the second test case, all possible permutations result in (x=2). In the third test case, the expected value of (x) is (\frac{55}{6}).
2200G.editorial_text:
2200G - Operation Permutation
Replace each - operation with +(-y) and /y with x(1/y) $$$\pmod{10^9+7}$$$.
Consider the contribution of each +y operation to the final answer. Its contribution is equal to the product of $$$y$$$ and the expected value of the product of x operations that come after it. Let there be $$$m$$$ x operations in total. Then, since all permutations are equally likely, there is a $$$\frac{1}{m+1}$$$ chance for there to be $$$k$$$ x operations after the +y operation for all $$$0\leq k\leq m.$$$
For each $$$k$$$, we need to compute the expected value of the sum of a random subset of $$$k$$$ of the $$$m$$$ x operations. To do this, we can use a DP where $$$dp[i][j]$$$ is the sum of the products of all subsets of size $$$j$$$ using only the first $$$i$$$ x operations. If $$$b_i$$$ is the value of the $$$i$$$-th x operation, then the DP transition is $$$dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j]+b_i\cdot dp[i-1][j-1]$$$. Calculating $$$dp$$$ takes $$$O(m^2)$$$ time.
The expected value of the sum of a random subset of $$$k$$$ x operations is $$$\frac{dp[m][k]}{\binom{m}{k}}$$$, so the expected value of the product of the x operations after a + operation is
$$$$$$S=\frac{1}{m+1}\sum_{k=0}^m \frac{dp[m][k]}{\binom{m}{k}}.$$$$$$
For each +y operation, its contribution to the final answer is $$$S\cdot y$$$. After summing contributions of the +y terms, we just need to add the contribution of $$$x$$$, which is $$$x\cdot dp[m][m]$$$, to get the final answer.
The time complexity is $$$O(n^2)$$$ since $$$m\leq n$$$.

2200H.title: Six Seven
2200H.statement_text: For positive integers (i) and (j), define (f_i(j)) as the maximum integer (k) such that (i^k) divides (j). A number (j) is considered special if (f_6(j) \gt f_7(j)). For example, (6) is special , but (67) and (7) are not. You are given an array (a) of (n) positive integers. In one operation, you must increase every element in the array by (1). Your task is to find the minimum number of operations needed to make all elements in (a) special at the same time, or determine that it is impossible. The first line contains an integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 10^4)), the number of test cases. For each test case, the first line contains an integer (n) ((1 \leq n \leq 2 \cdot 10^5)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) ((1 \leq a_i \leq 10^9)). The sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a single integer: the minimum number of operations to make all elements special at the same time, or (-1) if it is impossible. In the first test case, all elements cannot be made special at the same time. In the second test case, performing (5) operations results in the array (30,72), whose elements are all special. In the fourth test case, the array becomes (9557358) after (7) operations.
2200H.editorial_text:
2200H - Six Seven
Consider a recursive definition of being special. If a number $$$x$$$ is not divisible by $$$42$$$, it is special if and only if it is divisible by $$$6$$$. Otherwise, since $$$f_6(\frac{x}{42})=f_6(x)-1$$$ and $$$f_7(\frac{x}{42})=f_7(x)-1$$$, $$$x$$$ is special if and only if $$$\frac{x}{42}$$$ is special.
Let the number of operations performed be $$$m$$$. For each value of $$$k=m\bmod{42}$$$, let us find the minimum possible $$$m$$$. For each $$$i$$$, if $$$42\nmid a_i+k$$$, this value of $$$k$$$ is impossible unless $$$6$$$ divides $$$a_i+k$$$. Otherwise, $$$\frac{a_i+m}{42}$$$ must be special. Create an array $$$b$$$ of the values of $$$\frac{a_i+k}{42}$$$ for all $$$i$$$ such that $$$42\mid a_i+k$$$. Finding the minimum $$$m$$$ congruent to $$$k\bmod{42}$$$ is equivalent to solving the original problem for the array $$$b$$$, so we can use recursion to find $$$m'$$$, the minimum number of operations to make all elements in $$$b$$$ special. (Make sure to create a base case in the recursion!) Then, the minimum $$$m$$$ for this case is $$$m=42m'+k$$$. Our final answer is just the minimum of these values over all possible $$$k$$$.
To see why this runs in the time limit, observe that each $$$a_i$$$ corresponds to exactly one array element at each recursion depth. Hence, each recursion depth is processed in a total of $$$O(n)$$$ time. Since each recursion divides values by $$$42$$$ compared to the previous recursion, the maximum recursion depth is $$$O(\log_{42} 10^9)$$$. Thus, the total time complexity is $$$O(n\log_{42} 10^9)$$$, though it may vary based on implementation.

2207A.editorial_text:
2207A - 1-1
Note that no zeroes that are adjacent to other zeroes will ever become ones, and it is not possible to create adjacent zeroes. So, we look at runs of ones that have only gaps of at most one zero in between. If such a run has length $$$L$$$, we can easily convert it to all ones. The minimum number of zeroes you can create in such a run is $$$\left\lfloor \frac{L-1}{2} \right\rfloor$$$. To solve, we can now just sum these values over all such runs.

Let (n, m, \ell) be positive integers. You have made the unfortunate decision to work as a night guard at Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria, where there are (m) animatronics numbered (1, \ldots, m) waiting to jumpscare you. The night consists of (\ell) seconds, numbered (1, \ldots, \ell). The (j)-th of the (m) animatronics has a danger level (d_j), and initially (d_1 = \ldots = d_m = 0). Every second, the danger level of exactly one animatronic will increase by (1), and throughout the night, you are able to observe all values of (d_j) at the current time. For example, if (m = 2), one possible list of danger levels after (5) seconds is (d_1, d_2 = 2, 3). You are not defenseless, however. At each of the (n) fixed times (a_i) ((1 \leq a_1 \lt \ldots \lt a_n \leq \ell)), you can shine your flashlight on exactly one animatronic (j_i) of your choice. This occurs immediately after the (a_i)-th second and sets its danger level back to zero, i.e. (d_{j_i} := 0). Note that this choice is made independently for each flashlight use (a_i). Continuing the example from before, if (a_1 = 5) and you choose to flash the second animatronic at that time, the danger levels after (5) seconds will be (d_1, d_2 = 2, 0). Let the overall danger be the maximum danger across all animatronics, i.e. (\max_{1 \leq j \leq m} d_j). You will lose if the overall danger at the end of the night (after (\ell) seconds) is greater than (x). 2207B.editorial_text:
2207B - One Night At Freddy's
We make a series of observations. First, we will solve the night guard's strategy. Suppose he sees danger levels $$$d_1 \leq \ldots \leq d_m$$$. Then, flashing any animatronic $$$j$$$ will result in danger levels $$$[0, d_1, \dots, d_{j-1}, d_{j+1}, \dots, d_m]$$$. Of these, choosing $$$j = m$$$ simultaneously minimizes all of the danger values, so he will always flash the animatronic with the current highest $$$d_j$$$.
Notice that if there are $$$k$$$ flashes remaining, there is no reason to increment any animatronic outside the top $$$k + 1$$$ danger levels. Once there are less than $$$m$$$ flashes remaining, the animatronic that gets flashed will no longer be incremented as it is outside the top $$$k + 1$$$ danger levels after the flash. This means that we will eventually flash at least $$$\min(n, m - 1)$$$ different animatronics.
Due to this, the final danger level will only be accumulated on one animatronic, which means it is equal to $$$\ell$$$ minus the sum of the flashed animatronic values. So, our goal is to minimize this sum, which is clearly done by greedily incrementing the current minimum. 
This process may be simulated naively to arrive at an $$$O(m \ell)$$$ solution.

2207C.editorial_text:
2207C - Where's My Water?
Before we begin, note that there are many solution paths to this problem. We include a particularly elegant one here.
First, we attempt to solve the problem for just one drain, located at index $$$1 \leq i \leq n$$$. We notice that a water tile is drained if it has an unobstructed path right and down to the drain, by definition.
Define $$$m_{i,j}$$$ to be $$$\max(a_i, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_j)$$$. Then, a water tile at location $$$(x,y)$$$ is drained if $$$m_{\min(x,i),\max(x,i)} \leq y$$$, that is the maximum elevation between $$$x$$$ and $$$i$$$ is at most $$$y$$$.
Thus, to solve the problem for one drain placed at location $$$i$$$, we can move to the right while keeping a current maximum $$$curr$$$ which is initially $$$a_i$$$, and add $$$h-curr$$$ to our total at each column, and repeat the process to the left. Call this amount of water that a drain can drain at location $$$i$$$ be $$$cnt_i$$$.
Now, let us investigate how we can solve the problem for two drains placed at locations $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$. We can start with the total $$$cnt_i + cnt_j$$$, but we notice that this overcounts water tiles that are drained by both drains. Let us split up the columns into three ranges, $$$[1,i), [i,j], (j,n]$$$. We investigate each range independently.
Consider water tile $$$(x,y)$$$ with $$$x \in [1,i)$$$. Note that by our definition this water tile is drained by both drains if $$$m_{x,i},m_{x,j} \leq y \implies \max(m_{x,i},m_{i,j}) \leq y$$$.
Consider water tile $$$(x,y)$$$ with $$$x \in [i,j]$$$. Note that by our definition this water tile is drained by both drains if $$$m_{i,x},m_{x,j} \leq y \implies m_{i,j} \leq y$$$.
Consider water tile $$$(x,y)$$$ with $$$x \in (j,n]$$$. Note that by our definition this water tile is drained by both drains if $$$m_{i,x},m_{j,x} \leq y \implies \max(m_{i,j},m_{j,x}) \leq y$$$.
From here, we notice that a drain located at elevation $$$m_{i,j}$$$ between $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ perfectly encompasses this overcount, as per our definition of draining earlier. Thus, if we let $$$k = \arg \max(a_i,a_{i+1},\dots,a_j)$$$, then our answer for drains $$$i,j$$$ is $$$cnt_i + cnt_j - cnt_k$$$.
Thus, to solve the problem, we can compute $$$cnt_i$$$ for each drain $$$i$$$ with the earlier algorithm. Then, we fix drain $$$i$$$ and iterate over all choices $$$j$$$ to the right of $$$i$$$ from left to right, updating our argument max $$$k$$$ if necessary, and then computing $$$cnt_i + cnt_j - cnt_k$$$. Our answer is the maximum over all such values.
Our algorithm is linear for each drain, so computing all values of $$$cnt_i$$$ is $$$O(n^2)$$$. Then iterating over all pairs of drains $$$i,j$$$ is $$$O(n^2)$$$, so this gives us a passing complexity of $$$O(n^2)$$$.
Exercise to the Reader: By a similar argument, can you show that any maximal draining single drain is in a maximal pair of drains $$$i',j'$$$?

Boxed Like a Fish
PROGRAMMING
dfs and similar dp games trees

Add tag

Let (n, k) be positive integers. You are given a tree(^{\text{∗}}) with (n) vertices numbered (1, \ldots, n). Cyndaquil is traversing this tree and is trying to reach one of its leaves(^{\text{†}}). Initially, he starts at a non-leaf vertex (v), and in one turn, he may either choose to stay still or move from a vertex (v) along an edge to any of its neighbors (u). However, Snorlax is trying to stop Cyndaquil from doing this by sleeping on an edge. When he picks an edge, Cyndaquil is blocked from traversing it until Snorlax moves again. Furthermore, only one edge may be disallowed at a time, so that only the most recently chosen edge is blocked. Of course, Snorlax is slow and needs some time before he can pick a new edge. He has a cooldown timer, initially at (0). He may only choose a new edge when the cooldown is at (0) or lower, but he doesn't have to do it immediately . When he moves to a new edge, the timer is reset to (k). After each of Cyndaquil's turns (even if he stays still), the cooldown timer decreases by (1). They take turns acting as previously described, with Snorlax starting first, and initially, he is not sleeping on any edge. Assuming both of them play optimally, can Cyndaquil always reach a leaf after a finite number of turns? (^{\text{∗}})A tree is a connected graph without cycles. (^{\text{†}})A vertex with degree 1 is called a leaf. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains three integers (n), (k), and (v) ((3 \leq n \leq 5 \cdot 10^5), (1 \leq k, v \leq n)) — the number of vertices in the tree, Snorlax's cooldown timer, and Cyndaquil's starting vertex. The next (n-1) lines of each test case contain two integers (a) and (b) ((1 \leq a, b \leq n), (a \neq b)), describing an edge b

Suppose Snorlax is winning. Then there exists a neighborhood of $$$v$$$ in the tree (some connected subset of the vertices) with no leaves for which Cyndaquil can be permanently constrained to. Notice that it is sufficient for the distance between any two exits from this neighborhood to be at least $$$k$$$. We additionally claim that it is necessary; if there are two exits less than $$$k$$$ apart, we can just have Cyndaquil move along the path between them and they will eventually escape.
Now, we try to find such a neighborhood of $$$v$$$. Root the tree at the starting vertex; we focus on which nodes are excluded from this neighborhood. Initially, all leaves are excluded. Now, for any path between nodes that have been excluded that are distance at most $$$k + 1$$$ apart, we realize that none of the nodes can possibly be in a valid neighborhood. We keep iterating this, and notice that once no such pair of excluded nodes can be found we have necessarily found a valid neighborhood.
To process these updates to excluded nodes efficiently, we work up the tree. Denote $$$dp[v]$$$ to be the distance to the closest marked node from $$$v$$$. We set $$$dp[v]$$$ to be $$$1 + \min_{\text{children $$$u$$$ of $$$v$$$}}(dp[u])$$$, unless there are two children $$$u_1, u_2$$$ with $$$dp[u_1] + dp[u_2] \leq k-1$$$. If so, $$$v$$$ becomes marked and we set $$$dp[v] = 0$$$ instead.
The answer is now just to check if $$$dp[v] = 0$$$, admitting a linear time solution.

2207E1.editorial_text:
2207E1 - N-MEX (Constructive Version)
Let $$$a_1, ..., a_n$$$ be the array we receive. Then, notice that we can bound $$$n-i \leq a_i \leq n$$$, so any input array that violates this is impossible.
Also, notice that $$$a_i \geq a_{i+1}$$$. This is because adding one number to the collection can only fill in one of the $$$n-i$$$ missing numbers from the previous range.
We now claim any $$$a_i$$$ with these constraints is achievable by doing the following:

Vacuously take $$$b_0 = n$$$. Let $$$S = \{0, \ldots, n\} \setminus a$$$ be the set of integers missing from $$$a$$$. 
To choose $$$b_i$$$, if $$$a_i \lt a_{i-1}$$$, set $$$b_i := \infty$$$ ($$$10^9$$$). 
Otherwise, set it to be the largest element of $$$S$$$ that was not already picked. 
To show that this works, we first claim that if $$$a_i = x$$$, then all elements of $$$S$$$ above $$$x$$$ have been picked already. Indeed, if there are $$$d$$$ distinct numbers above $$$x$$$ in $$$a$$$, then there were $$$i - d$$$ times where $$$a_i = a_{i-1}$$$. Since $$$a_i + i \geq n$$$, we have then taken enough elements from $$$S$$$ for this to be true.
Therefore, when we choose $$$b_i$$$, we are setting it to either a value under $$$a_i$$$ when $$$a_i = a_{i-1}$$$, or a value above $$$a_i$$$ when $$$ai \lt a_{i-1}$$$. When the former happens, we see that the $$$(n+1-i)$$$-mex of $$$[b_1, \ldots, b_i]$$$ will match the $$$(n-i)$$$-mex of $$$[b_1, \ldots, b_{i+1}]$$$. When the latter happens, we see that the $$$(n-i)$$$-mex of $$$[b_1, \ldots, b_{i+1}]$$$ will be the next largest excluded element from $$$S$$$ under the $$$(n+1-i)$$$-mex of $$$[b_1, \ldots, b_i]$$$. By definition, this is $$$a_i$$$.

2207E2.editorial_text:
2207E2 - N-MEX (Counting Version)
Recall the solution to the constructive version. Define $$$a_0 = n$$$ as usual to be the $$$(n+1)$$$-mex of the empty subarray.
Consider the sets of missing numbers $$$S_i := [0, n) \setminus [b_1, \ldots, b_i]$$$. By definition, $$$a_i$$$ is simply the $$$(n+1-i)$$$-th largest element of $$$S_i$$$. Notice that choosing an element $$$b_i$$$ is equivalent to deciding whether or not we remove that corresponding element from $$$S_i$$$.
Now, take some index $$$i$$$; we claim that all elements of $$$S_i$$$ at least $$$a_i$$$ have appeared in $$$[a_1, \ldots, a_i]$$$. In particular, we can work backwards from index $$$i$$$ to $$$0$$$. It is equivalent to have $$$S_{i-1}$$$ be either $$$S_i$$$ or $$$S_i$$$ with an added element, and then $$$a_{i-1}$$$ will simply be the next element after $$$a_i$$$ in the resulting set $$$S_{i-1}$$$. This implies that on any one of these steps $$$j$$$, $$$a_j$$$ will never skip past an element of $$$S_j \supseteq S_i$$$. Since $$$a_0 = n$$$, the claim follows. A corollary of this is that an element $$$x \geq a_i$$$ that isn't in $$$[a_1, \ldots, a_n]$$$ must be removed before step $$$i$$$.
Call an index $$$i$$$ good if $$$a_i = a_{i-1}$$$ and bad otherwise. By definition, $$$|S_n| = n - \text{# of good steps}.$$$ Further recall that $$$a_{i-1} = a_i$$$ if and only if we removed an element under $$$a_{i-1}$$$ from $$$S_{i-1}$$$ to $$$S_i$$$.
We are now ready to count the number of ways to choose the $$$b_i$$$ on good steps, say $$$i_1, \ldots, i_n$$$. Because the number of good steps is precisely $$$n - |S_n|$$$, each of the good steps must remove a unique integer from $$$S_{i_j}$$$, i.e. have a unique choice of $$$b_{i_j}$$$. This means that each element of $$$[0, n) \setminus S_n$$$ is picked exactly once. Furthermore, we have monotonic constraints of the form: for each $$$x \in [0, n) \setminus S_n$$$, if $$$a_{i_j} \lt x$$$, then $$$x$$$ was picked on a step at most $$$i_j$$$. This is now equivalent to counting rook placements on a Young diagram, which can be done in linear time by just multiplying the number of ways to make each of the $$$n - |S_n|$$$ choices.
To choose the $$$b_i$$$ on the $$$|S_n|$$$ bad steps, we need to observe that the size of $$$|S_i \cap [0, a_i]|$$$ is determined for any working construction. In particular, we restrict our attention to only the good steps. Since we know they only ever target elements in $$$[0, n) \setminus S_n$$$, and that all such elements above $$$a_i$$$ have already been removed, we can count exactly how many numbers in $$$[0, a_i] \cap ([0, n) \setminus S_n)$$$ have already been removed based on the rank of $$$a_i$$$ within $$$[0, n) \setminus S_n$$$ and the number of good steps before step $$$i$$$. So, we can just multiply the number of ways to make a choice on each bad step.
Multiplying these two parts together gives a linear time solution.

2207F.editorial_text:
2207F - Hanabi
Consider writing down the sequence of clues that Gi-hun makes without adjacent repeats, and call this a clue string. Our goal is to minimize the length of this string (minus one).
Claim 1. There exists a subfamily of clue strings containing the original optimal strategy where the rank clues are increasing in rank, and additionally, when a rank clue $$$r$$$ is given, it causes all remaining cards of rank (at most) $$$r$$$ to be played.
Proof. First, restrict our attention to strings where each clue plays at least one card.
Suppose there exists a rank clue $$$r$$$ and a color clue $$$c$$$ after it that causes Sang-woo to play a card of rank at most $$$r$$$. Then, the color clue $$$c$$$ could have come before the rank clue $$$r$$$ without affecting legality or increasing the length of the clue string, and we may assume without loss of optimality that color clues always come before rank clues in such scenarios.
Consider any rank clue $$$r$$$. If it is followed by a rank clue $$$r' \leq r$$$, notice that we could have swapped their order without affecting legality; likewise, we can then assume that adjacent rank clues are given in increasing order.
Now, consider an adjacent series of rank clues $$$r_1 \lt \ldots \lt r_k$$$. If $$$r_k$$$ is the end of the clue string, then it must have completed the board, and each of the clues $$$r_1, \ldots, r_k$$$ must have played all the remaining cards of their respective ranks. Otherwise, if $$$r_k$$$ is followed by a color clue $$$c$$$, and $$$c$$$ caused a card of rank at most $$$r_i$$$ to be played for minimal $$$i$$$, then necessarily none of the clues $$$r_{i+1}, \ldots, r_k$$$ caused any cards of color $$$c$$$ to play. Then, we can re-order the clues to be 
$$$$$$r_1, \ldots, r_{i-1}, c, r_i, \ldots, r_k.$$$$$$
without affecting legality. 
We have now restricted our focus to a subfamily of clue strings where no color clue plays cards of rank at most the rank of the previous rank clue, and that all runs of consecutive rank clues are increasing.
We now argue that we can further restrict our focus to assume that for two adjacent runs of rank clues: $$$$$$r_1, \ldots, r_{k_1}, c_1, \ldots, c_\ell, r^{(1)}, \ldots, r^{(k_2)}$$$$$$ we have $$$r_{k_1} \lt r^{(1)}$$$. Since none of the color clues $$$c_1, \ldots, c_{\ell}$$$ play cards of rank at most $$$r_{k_1}$$$, if $$$r^{(1)}$$$ caused any card of colors $$$c_1, \ldots, c_\ell$$$ to play then clearly $$$r^{(1)} \gt r_{k_1}$$$. Otherwise, we could have moved $$$r^{(1)}$$$ in the ordering like so: $$$$$$r_1, \ldots, r_{k_1}, r^{(1)}, c_1, \ldots, c_\ell, r^{(2)}, \ldots, r^{(k_2)}$$$$$$ which keeps the order of cards played legal. Using previous reasoning, we may restrict to assume $$$r_{k_1} \lt r^{(1)}$$$.
This shows that the rank clues can be assumed to be increasing in rank. In particular, since we assumed color clues do not play cards with rank at most the previous rank clue, this means that each rank clue necessarily plays all remaining cards of its rank.
We now work in this restricted set of clue strings. We will optimize in terms of the subsequence of rank clues.
Claim 2. The order of the colors in the input does not matter, and we can focus on just the order of ranks within colors.
Proof. Rank clues play out all remaining cards of their rank, and are colorblind.
With this, we can solve the problem by dynamic programming. Let $$$dp[i][0]$$$ be the minimum length clue string that plays all cards of rank at most $$$i$$$ such that the $$$i$$$-th rank clue is given and $$$dp[i][1]$$$ be the analogous value for not playing the $$$i$$$-th rank clue. It is clear that $$$dp[i][0] = 1 + \min(dp[i-1][0], dp[i-1][1])$$$.
To determine $$$dp[i][1]$$$, we perform casework on the previous color clue $$$j$$$. In particular, for such $$$j$$$, we have
$$$$$$dp[i][1] \xleftarrow{\min} dp[j][1] + (i - j - 1) + \text{number of color clues that could not legally play ranks $i+1, \ldots, j-1$}$$$$$$ where $$$dp[j][1]$$$ counts the previous clues for ranks at most $$$j$$$, the $$$i - j - 1$$$ counts the number of rank clues in between, and the final term accounts for the color clues used for rank $$$j$$$ that don't "bleed over" and need to be clued again.
Notice that sometimes, a rank clue for rank $$$i$$$ must be issued due to some ordering within a color. So, when such a clue is forced, we can just set $$$dp[i][1] = +\infty$$$.
To perform the minimum over all $$$j$$$ efficiently, notice that the last term of this expression takes on values $$$0, \ldots, m$$$. Hence using $$$m$$$ range minimum queries over intervals covering indices $$$1, \ldots, i$$$, each $$$dp$$$ transition can be computed in $$$O(m \log n)$$$ time. As there are $$$n$$$ ranks, this gives an $$$O(nm \log n)$$$ solution.

2207G - Toothless
We first solve in the case of $$$a = b = 1$$$ (i.e., all cells are the same value.) Notice that a set of cells may be colored black iff it is a forest up to edge adjacency, after which we can recover the move order through graph traversal.
Consider the following "stripe" pattern and its three possible shifts:

Among the three shifts, each of the $$$nm$$$ cells is black twice and white once. Now, consider choosing one of the pattern shifts, and take the union of black and needy cells. Our goal is to find a large enough forest among this set of cells. 
Suppose there are $$$p$$$ cells that are black from the pattern and the other $$$v$$$ cells that are needy and not in the pattern. Note that first the edge adjacency graph is planar. 
Claim. There are at most $$$3v$$$ minimal planar cycles among this set of cells. 
Proof. We can focus on adjacent stripes in the pattern:

If we then associate each minimal cycle with the needy cell not on its lower-left corner, we get the desired bound.
Now, pick some minimal cycle, and cut one un-needy cell from it; the number of minimal cycles decreases by $$$1$$$. So, if we do this until there are no cycles remaining, we will get a forest of $$$p + v - 3v = p - 2v$$$ cells. Now, the sum over all three shifts of $$$p - 2v$$$ is equal to $$$2 \cdot (nm - \text{number of needy cells})$$$, so by Pigeonhole at least one of the three shifts will give us a construction with enough shaded cells.
To adapt this to the case of $$$a, b \geq 1$$$, notice that we can choose to cut only non-special cells from each cycle, which is always guaranteed to exist because no special cell is adjacent to a needy cell.
Fun fact: the only reason why the $$$a, b \geq 1$$$ case is not the given form of the problem is that it is possible to cheese the $$$a, b = 1$$$ case with the following algorithm:

Iterate over the cells in reading order. While adding the current cell does not make a cycle, add it to the construction. 
Amazingly, it will obtain an even better bound of $$$\frac 23 \cdot nm - \frac 13 \cdot k$$$ where $$$k$$$ is the number of needy cells, which is asymptotically optimal! Note that such an algorithm is not guaranteed to work in any meaningful generalizations of the problem.
