Seek the Truth
PROGRAMMING
binary search bitmasks interactive

Add tag

This is an interactive problem. There are two hidden integers (k) and (c) such that (k\in \{1,2,3\}) and (1\le c\le 2^n-1). Note that (c\neq 0). Before any interaction, you need to tell the jury a non-negative integer (a\le 2^n-1). The grader will then use (a) as the initial element in the set (S), that is, initially (S = \{a\}). Next, you can make at most (n+3) queries of the following two types: Select an integer (x) such that (0\leq x\le 2^n-1). The jury will insert (f(x)) into (S) and then respond with (|S|) (i. e., the size of (S) after the insertion); Select an integer (y) such that (0\leq y\le 2^n-1). The jury will respond with the number of integers (z) such that (z\in S) and (z\geq y). The definition of (f(x)) is as follows: () f(x)= \begin{cases} x\,\&\,c & \text{if}\, k=1,\\ x\,|\,c & \text{if}\, k=2,\\ x\oplus c & \text{if}\, k=3.\\ \end{cases} () Here, (\&) denotes the bitwise AND operation , (|) denotes the bitwise OR operation , and (\oplus) denotes the bitwise XOR operation . Your task is to determine the values of (k) and (c) using at most (n+3) interactions. Please note that reporting the answer does not count towards the (n+3) interactions. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((2 \leq n \leq 60)). Then, interaction follows. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (10^5). First, you need to output an integer (a) ((0\leq a\le 2^n-1)) — the initial element you chose for set (S). To make an interaction, output a single line in the following format: (\mathtt{I}\;x) ((0\leq x\le 2^n-1)) — Insert (f(x)) into set (S). After that, the jury will return $$$|S|$$

2222E.editorial_text:
2222E - Seek the Truth
First, consider the value of $$$a$$$. Since $$$a$$$ might conflict with a later $$$f(x)$$$, making it impossible to determine the value of $$$f(x)$$$, we want $$$a$$$ to be as different as possible from being equal to a later $$$f(x)$$$. Let's assume $$$a=0$$$, so that it will definitely not be equal to $$$f(x)$$$ when $$$k=2$$$.
Next, consider inserting an $$$f(x)$$$ into $$$S$$$. We find that if we assume $$$x=0$$$, we can easily distinguish between the cases when $$$k=1$$$ and $$$k=2$$$, $$$k=3$$$. Therefore, after inserting $$$f(0)$$$ into $$$S$$$, we can discuss the cases separately:

If $$$|S|=1$$$, it means $$$f(0)=0$$$, then $$$k=1$$$, and $$$c=f(2^n-1)$$$. Since $$$c \gt 0$$$, we know that $$$f(2^n-1) \neq 0$$$. 
If $$$|S|=2$$$, it means $$$f(0) \neq 0$$$, then $$$k = 2$$$ or $$$k = 3$$$, and $$$c = f(0)$$$. 
How do we find the value of $$$f(x)$$$? We only need to know the specific elements in $$$S$$$ before inserting $$$f(x)$$$, and then perform a binary search on the value $$$z$$$ of $$$f(x)$$$ after inserting $$$f(x)$$$. If the number of elements in $$$S$$$ that are $$$\geq z$$$ is different from the number of elements in $$$S$$$ that are $$$\geq z$$$ before inserting $$$f(x)$$$, then $$$f(x) \geq z$$$; otherwise, $$$f(x) \lt z$$$. The number of queries required to find $$$f(x)$$$ by binary search is $$$\log_2 2^n = n$$$.
For case 2 above, we still need to determine whether $$$k=2$$$ or $$$k=3$$$. Observation shows that when $$$c\neq 2^n-1$$$, $$$0$$$, $$$c$$$, $$$2^n-1 | c$$$, and $$$(2^n-1)\oplus c$$$ are all different. Therefore, we can directly insert $$$f(2^n-1)$$$ to distinguish between the cases of $$$k=2$$$ and $$$k=3$$$.
Here, we don't need to know the specific value of $$$f(2^n-1)$$$, only whether the value of $$$f(2^n-1)$$$ is $$$2^n-1$$$, so only one query operation is needed.
For the case of $$$c=2^n-1$$$, we only need to determine whether the value of $$$f(1)$$$ is $$$2^n-1$$$.
When $$$k=1$$$, a total of $$$1+1+n=n+2$$$ interactions are required.
When $$$k=2$$$ or $$$k=3$$$, a total of $$$1+n+1+1=n+3$$$ interactions are required.
Bonus: How to handle the situation where $$$c$$$ is in the range $$$0\leq c \lt 2^n-1$$$.

Statistics on Tree
PROGRAMMING
binary search brute force dfs and similar divide and conquer graphs trees

Add tag

You are given a tree of (n) vertices. We define the value of a pair ((u,v)) ((1\leq u\leq v\leq n)) as the size of the largest component after removing all edges on the path from (u) to (v) in the original tree. For every (1\leq i\leq n), you have to find the number of pairs ((u,v)) satisfying that its value is (i). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1\leq n \leq 10^5)) — the number of vertices. Then (n-1) lines follow, the (i)-th line containing two integers (u) and (v) ((1\leq u,v\leq n)) — the two vertices that the (i)-th edge connects. It is guaranteed that the given edges form a tree. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (5\cdot 10^5). For each test case, output (n) integers, the (i)-th of which denotes the number of distinct pairs ((u,v)) satisfying its value is (i). In the first test case, the value of pair ((1, 1)) is (1). In the second test case, the values of pairs ((1, 1)) and ((2, 2)) are both (2), because no edges will be removed. The value of pair ((1, 2)) is (1), because edge ((1, 2)) is on the path from (1) to (2) in the tree, and after removing it, there will be (2) components left, which are (\{1\}) and (\{2\}), and the size of the largest component is (1). In the sixth test case, the value of pair ((4, 6)) is (3), because edges ((3, 4)), ((2, 3)), and ((2, 6)) are on the path from (4) to (6) in the tree, and after removing them, there will be (4) components left, which are (\{1, 2, 5\}), (\{3, 7\}), (\{4\}), and (\{6\}), and the size of the largest component is (3).

We consider rooting the tree at any of its centroids. Then, we enumerate the LCA of the paths (denoted as $$$o$$$).
For a path $$$(x, y)$$$ where $$$\mathrm{LCA}(x, y) = o$$$ (where $$$x \ne o$$$ and $$$y \ne o$$$), its value is clearly $$$\max(a_x, a_y, n - b_x - b_y)$$$. Here:

$$$a_u$$$ represents the maximum size of the components (other than the one containing $$$o$$$) when the edges along the path $$$(u, o)$$$ are removed. 
$$$b_u$$$ represents the size of the component containing $$$u$$$ after removing $$$o$$$ from the tree. 
By definition, we have $$$a_u \le b_u$$$.
The maximum value among $$$a_x$$$, $$$a_y$$$, and $$$n - b_x - b_y$$$ determines the path's value. We analyze each case separately.

Handling $$$a_x$$$ or $$$a_y$$$ as Maximum:
If $$$a_x$$$ is the maximum, then $$$a_x \ge n - b_x - b_y$$$. Since $$$b_x \ge a_x$$$, this implies $$$2b_x + b_y \ge n$$$. Thus, either $$$b_x \ge \frac{n}{3}$$$ or $$$b_y \ge \frac{n}{3}$$$. After removing $$$o$$$, the sum of the sizes of the remaining connected components is $$$n - 1$$$. Hence, there are at most two connected components with size $$$\ge \frac{n}{3}$$$.
Assume without loss of generality that $$$x$$$ lies in a connected component of size $$$\ge \frac{n}{3}$$$. We enumerate the components in the tree after removing $$$o$$$. For each pair of connected components $$$(X, Y)$$$, we sort the values of $$$a_*$$$ within each component. For each $$$y \in Y$$$, if $$$n - b_x - b_y \lt a_y$$$, we use binary search to count the number of $$$x \in X$$$ where $$$a_x \le a_y$$$ and add this to the answer. For $$$x \in X$$$ where $$$a_x \gt \max(a_y, n - b_x - b_y)$$$, we increment a counter $$$c_x$$$ (maintained via difference arrays). Finally, we add the contributions from $$$c_x$$$ to the answer. The condition $$$a_x$$$ or $$$a_y$$$ being the maximum only holds when $$$o$$$ is the root. Otherwise, $$$n - b_x - b_y \ge \frac{n}{2}$$$, which implies $$$a_x + a_y \le b_x + b_y \le \frac{n}{2}$$$. Thus, each node is processed $$$O(1)$$$ times, leading to an $$$O(n \log n)$$$ time complexity for this part.

Handling $$$n - b_x - b_y$$$ as Maximum:
This case resembles a convolution, which is complex. Instead of considering $$$a_x$$$ and $$$a_y$$$, we first assume $$$n - b_x - b_y$$$ is the maximum and later correct the answer during handling $$$a_x$$$ or $$$a_y$$$ as maximum when $$$o$$$ is the root. Treating this as a polynomial, the highest-degree term is $$$O(sz_o)$$$, where $$$sz_o$$$ is the size of the subtree rooted at $$$o$$$. Direct polynomial multiplication would lead to $$$O(n^2 \log n)$$$ time, but we exploit sparsity properties to optimize.
Proof of $$$O(n \log n)$$$ Time: 

For each $$$o$$$, let the largest child subtree be the "heavy" subtree and the others be "light". 
Contribution between heavy and light subtrees costs $$$O(deg_o)$$$ complexity per node, where $$$deg_o$$$ is the degree of $$$o$$$, totaling $$$O(n)$$$. 
For light subtrees, the number of distinct sizes is $$$O(\sqrt{sm_o})$$$, where $$$sm_o$$$ is the sum of light subtree sizes. So the convolution costs $$$O(sm_o)$$$ complexity, and according to DSU on tree, the sum of $$$sm_o$$$ is $$$O(n \log n)$$$. 

We can simply add contributions when either $$$x=o$$$ or $$$y=o$$$. So the overall time complexity is $$$O(n \log n)$$$.

2222H.editorial_text:
2222H - Counting Sort?
After connecting all arrays $$$ a $$$ to $$$ f(a) $$$ with directed edges, we obtain a directed pseudoforest (a collection of directed trees where each tree has a single cycle at its root). Specifically, the array $$$ a = [0, 0, 0, \dots, 0] $$$ forms an isolated node, while $$$ a = [1, 0, 0, \dots, 0] $$$ serves as the root for all other nodes. Here, $$$ g(a) $$$ corresponds to the depth of $$$ a $$$ in its tree plus one. 
Directly characterizing $$$ g $$$ is quite challenging, so we resort to a more brute-force approach. We observe that after removing two layers of leaves, the number of remaining nodes in the tree becomes manageable. Specifically, we focus on counting the number of arrays $$$ a $$$ such that there exists a array $$$b$$$ that satisfies $$$ f(f(b)) = a $$$.
It turns out that this constraint is equivalent to $$$ \sum_{i=1}^n i \times a_i \le n $$$. Let $$$ P(n) $$$ denote the number of integer partitions of $$$ n $$$. Then, the number of such arrays $$$ a $$$ is $$$ \sum_{i=0}^n P(i) $$$. For $$$ n = 50 $$$, this count is at most $$$ 1.3 \times 10^6 $$$.
We first preprocess all such arrays $$$ a $$$ along with their depths. Then, for each $$$ a $$$, we compute the number of arrays $$$ b $$$ satisfying $$$ f(f(b)) = a $$$ and $$$ \forall 1 \le i \le n, b_i \le r_i $$$. Except for the case where $$$ a = [1, 0, 0, \dots, 0] $$$, we have $$$ g(b) = g(a) + 2 $$$. We accumulate these counts into the final answer and handle the special cases where $$$ g(*) \le 3 $$$ separately.
Next, we discuss how to compute these counts. First, for a given $$$ a $$$, we determine the number of arrays $$$ b $$$ such that $$$ f(b) = a $$$ and $$$ \forall 1 \le i \le n, b_i \le r_i $$$. This can be done by filling the array $$$ b $$$ from the largest value to the smallest, with the coefficients being products of several binomial coefficients. 
We incorporate this process into a dynamic programming (DP) approach. Let $$$ dp_{i, a} $$$ denote the number of valid arrays $$$ b $$$ where we have already determined $$$ f(b)_i, f(b)_{i+1}, \dots, f(b)_n $$$, and $$$ f(f(b)) = a $$$. The DP can be updated in $$$ \mathcal{O}(n) $$$ time per state by enumerating the possible values of $$$ f(b)_i $$$. Thus, for a given $$$ a $$$, the total number of valid arrays $$$ b $$$ is $$$ dp_{1, a} $$$. 
The overall time complexity is $$$ \mathcal{O}(n^2 \sum_{i=0}^n P(i)) $$$. In practice, the number of possible transitions is only about $$$ 2.5 \times 10^8 $$$, which is significantly smaller than this upper bound, making the solution feasible.

You are given an array (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n). You wish to make the array empty by performing the following operation any number of times: Select any sequence of indices (1 \le i_1 \lt i_2 \lt \ldots \lt i_k \le |a|) (note that (|a|) denotes the current length of the array (a)) such that ()a_{i_1} \le a_{i_2} \le \ldots \le a_{i_k}() Remove the elements (a_{i_1}, a_{i_2}, \ldots, a_{i_k}) from the array (a). This operation incurs a cost equal to (a_{i_1} \times a_{i_2} \times \cdots \times a_{i_k}). Determine the minimum total cost required to remove all the elements from the array (a). Note that the total cost is equal to the sum of costs incurred over all the operations performed. As the answer can be very large, report the answer modulo (676\,767\,677). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 500)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each testcase contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 100)) — the length of the array (a). The second line of each testcase contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le 100)) — the elements of the array. For each testcase, output a single integer — the minimum total cost required to make the array (a) empty. As the answer may be large, output the answer modulo (676\,767\,677). For the first testcase, Operation 1 : Choose (i_1 = 1), (i_2 = 2), and (i_3 = 4). This incurs a cost of (1 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 4). After deleting the elements at these indices, the array becomes (a = 1, 3). Operation 2 : Choose (i_1 = 1) and (i_2 = 2). This incurs a cost of (1 \cdot 3 = 3). After deleting the elements at these indices, the array becomes empty. Thus, the total cost is equal to (4 + 3 = 7). It can be shown that this is the minimum possible total cost.

2226B.statement_text:
Problems

Solved
Index
Name
Type
Tags
Community Tag
Rating

( 15167 ) 
B
Everything Everywhere
PROGRAMMING
greedy math number theory

Add tag

An array is called good if the difference between the maximum value and the minimum value in the array is equal to the greatest common divisor (GCD) of all the elements in the array. Note that an empty array is considered to be not good. More formally, an array (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m) is good if and only if () \max(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m) - \min(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m) = \gcd(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m).() You are given a permutation(^{\text{∗}}) (p) of length (n). Determine the number of good subarrays(^{\text{†}}) in the given permutation. (^{\text{∗}})A permutation of length (m) is an array consisting of (m) distinct integers from (1) to (m) in arbitrary order. For example, (2,3,1,5,4) is a permutation, but (1,2,2) is not a permutation ((2) appears twice in the array), and (1,3,4) is also not a permutation ((m=3) but there is (4) in the array). (^{\text{†}})An array (b) is a subarray of an array (a) if (b) can be obtained from (a) by the deletion of several (possibly, zero or all) elements from the beginning and several (possibly, zero or all) elements from the end. In particular, an array is a subarray of itself. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each testcase contains a single integer (n) ((2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the length of the permutation (p). The second line of each testcase contains (n) integers (p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n) ((1 \le p_i \le n)) — the permutation (p). It is guaranteed that (p) is a permutation. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all the test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each testcase, print a single integer — the number of good subarrays in the given permutation. For the first testcase, only one subarray is good, which is $$$1, 2$

Formally, () \begin{aligned} m(l,r) &= \min(a_l, a_{l+1}, \ldots, a_r),\\ M(l,r) &= \max(a_l, a_{l+1}, \ldots, a_r).\\ \end{aligned} () You may perform the following operation any number of times (possibly zero): Select two indices (l) and (r) ((1 \le l \le r \le n)) such that (m(l, r) + M(l, r)) is odd ; Reverse the entire segment (a_l, a_{l+1}, \ldots, a_r). In other words, for every (i) with (l \le i \le r), set (a_i := a_{l+r-i}) simultaneously. Deep in the wilderness, Zhily and Jily discovered two sequences composed of brackets. Each sequence carries some logical structure, but neither of them is necessarily a regular bracket sequence on its own. They found that by swapping brackets between the two sequences, they could repair them. They wish to make both sequences regular bracket sequences by swapping brackets between them. A regular bracket sequence is a sequence consisting of '(' and ')', which can be turned into a valid math expression by inserting 1 and + any number of times into the sequence. For example, the sequence "()(()())" is a regular bracket sequence, while "())((" or "(()" are not regular bracket sequences. You are given two bracket sequences (a) and (b) of even length (n). You can perform the following operation any number of times: Choose a position (i) ((1 \leq i \leq n)) and swap (a_i) and (b_i). Determine whether you can turn both (a) and (b) into regular bracket sequences. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((2 \leq n \leq 2\cdot 10^5), (n) is even) — the length of the strings (a) and (b). The second line of each test case contains a sequence (a) of length (n) consisting only of characters '(' and ')'. The third line of each test case contains a sequence (b) of length (n) consisting only of characters '(' and ')'. 2223A.editorial_text:
2224C - Zhily and Bracket Swapping
If $$$a_i=b_i$$$, it doesn't matter; we ignore them. Otherwise, half of the $$$a_i$$$ should be '(', since there should be same number of '(' in $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$.
After that, the number of '(' and ')' in both $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ are determined. Thus, we just need to ensure for each prefix, the number of ')' is no more than '('. So we can just set $$$a_i$$$ = '(' if there are more ')' in $$$a$$$ before index $$$i$$$, and set $$$a_i$$$ = ')' otherwise.
We can see that it equals to simply set the odd indices of $$$i$$$ such that $$$a_i \neq b_i$$$ as $$$a_i$$$ = '(', vice versa. Just check if it's legal.

Zhily developed a game called Barknights, and she is preparing to release a major update on March (25). Specifically, she plans to add a Module to each Operator in the game, multiplying their power level by the Module's power. After the update is released, the famous game streamer Jily will evaluate the Operators' power levels and rank them in a tier list. Whenever an earlier-released Operator is ranked higher than a later-released Operator, it will cause a wave of drama. Unfortunately, Zhily accidentally knocked over a hot water kettle and broke her computer, which caused all the Modules to be randomly rearranged. Now Zhily wants to know the expected number of waves of drama that will be generated, but since she has to move on to the next problem, she has entrusted this task to you. You are given two arrays (a) and (b) of (n) positive integers. Let (b') be a permutation of array (b) chosen uniformly at random among all (n!) possible permutations. Define (c_i = a_i \cdot b'_i) for (1\le i \le n). Find the expected number of inversions(^{\text{∗}}) of array (c). (^{\text{∗}})An inversion in array (c) is a pair of indices ((i, j)) such that (1 \le i \lt j \le n) and (c_i \gt c_j). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 100)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2000)) — the length of the arrays (a) and (b). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le 10^9)) — the array (a). The third line of each test case contains (n) integers (b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n) ((1 \le b_i \le 10^9)) — the array (b). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2000). For each test case, output the expected number of inversions i

2223B.editorial_text:
2224D - Zhily and Barknights
Fix $$$i \lt j$$$. After randomly permuting $$$b$$$, each ordered pair $$$(b_k, b_l)$$$ with $$$k \ne l$$$ is assigned to positions $$$(i, j)$$$ with probability $$$\frac{1}{n (n - 1)}$$$.
Therefore, the expected number of inversions equals
$$$$$$ \frac{1}{n (n - 1)}\sum_{i \lt j, k \ne l}[a_i b_k \gt a_j b_l]. $$$$$$
The square brackets in $$$[a_i b_k \gt a_j b_l]$$$ denote the Iverson bracket, an indicator function that evaluates to $$$1$$$ if the inequality is true and $$$0$$$ otherwise.
Solution 1:
Rewrite the inequality $$$a_i b_k \gt a_j b_l$$$ as $$$\frac{a_i}{a_j} \gt \frac{b_l}{b_k}.$$$
Compute all values $$$\frac{a_i}{a_j}$$$ for $$$i \lt j$$$, and all values $$$\frac{b_l}{b_k}$$$ for $$$k \ne l$$$. Sort both of these resulting sequences and use a two-pointer technique to count the number of valid pairs.
The time complexity depends on the sorting method. For example, using std::sort, we can achieve an $$$O(n^2\log n)$$$ approach, which can solve the problem within $$$0.6\text{s}$$$ and $$$50\text{MB}$$$.
Solution 2:
Consider all pairs $$$(i, k)$$$ and form a list of 2D elements $$$(a_i b_k, i)$$$.
Counting the number of quadruples $$$(i, j, k, l)$$$ with $$$i \lt j$$$ and $$$a_i b_k \gt a_j b_l$$$ is equivalent to counting dominating pairs among these elements. However, we must subtract the cases where $$$k = l$$$. The number of such cases is equal to $$$n$$$ times the inversion count of sequence $$$a$$$.
Dominating pairs can be counted using a Fenwick tree or merge sort in $$$O(n^2\log n)$$$ time, and this approach takes only $$$0.4\text{s}$$$.

2223C.editorial_text:
2224E - Zhily and Signpost
Let $$$dis_u$$$ denote the total time from the root to node $$$u$$$. Each move $$$u \to son_{u,r}$$$ corresponds to a congruence equation $$$m + dis_u \equiv r\ (\mathrm{mod}\ d_u)$$$. Therefore, when we walk from the root to node $$$u$$$, we must satisfy a system of congruence equations. If it has a solution, we denote the solution by $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$.
For node $$$u$$$ and its child $$$v$$$, we try to derive $$$M_v, R_v$$$ from $$$M_u, R_u$$$.
Specifically, we have $$$M_v = \mathrm{lcm}(M_u, d_u)$$$. Then $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$ implies $$$m \equiv kM_u + R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_v),\ k \in [0,\frac{d_u}{\mathrm{gcd}(M_u, d_u)}-1]$$$. By enumerating all $$$k$$$ and computing the corresponding $$$r$$$, we can obtain the congruence equation for $$$s_{u,r}$$$. If some $$$r$$$ is not obtained, then the congruence equation corresponding to $$$s_{u,r}$$$ has no solution.
Next, we compress the depth of the tree.
Notice that if $$$d_u \mid M_u$$$, then $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$ actually implies $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ d_u)$$$, so the child that $$$u$$$ can move to is unique. Then we can directly merge $$$u$$$ and this child into one node.
In the new tree obtained this way, every node $$$u$$$ satisfies $$$d_u \nmid M_u$$$. Then we have $$$M_v = \mathrm{lcm}(M_u, d_u) \ge 2M_u$$$. Let the upper bound of $$$m$$$ be $$$V = 10^{18}$$$. That is, any node $$$u$$$ with depth $$$\ge \log V + 2$$$ in this tree must satisfy $$$M_u \gt V$$$. Since the queries guarantee $$$m \le V$$$, there is at most one $$$m$$$ satisfying $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$. This determines a unique leaf node reachable through $$$u$$$, so we can directly replace $$$u$$$ with this leaf node. Finally, the depth of this tree does not exceed $$$\log V + 2$$$, and the queries can be answered directly using the naive algorithm, with time complexity $$$O(q\log V)$$$.
We can prove that the preprocessing time complexity is $$$O(n)$$$. Therefore, the total time complexity is $$$O(n + q \log V)$$$.
Furthermore, we do not need to preprocess all $$$R_u$$$. We can perform the node-compression operation while processing the queries. When needed, we only need to use $$$m \equiv R_u\ (\mathrm{mod}\ M_u)$$$ to obtain the current node's $$$R_u$$$. The total time complexity is still $$$O(n + q \log V)$$$.

Zhily and Jily resolved to travel across the entire world to eliminate all chaos. They start from a certain place and wish to visit every region exactly once. You are given a directed graph with (n) vertices numbered from (1) to (n). For each vertex (i) ((1 \le i \le n)), there are directed edges from (i) to all vertices (j) such that (a_i \le j \le n). Find a Hamiltonian cycle (^{\text{∗}}) of the graph. (^{\text{∗}})A Hamiltonian cycle is a cycle that visits each vertex exactly once. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n\,(1 \leq n \leq 10^5)) — the number of vertices. The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_n\,(1 \leq a_i \leq n)) describing the graph. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) across all test cases does not exceed (10^6). For each test case, if no Hamiltonian cycle exists, output " No " in one line. Otherwise, output " Yes " on the first line. On the second line, output a permutation (p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n) ((1\le p_i\le n)) representing the order of vertices visited in the cycle. If there are multiple solutions, print any of them. You can output the answer in any case (upper or lower). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES " will be recognized as positive responses. In the first test case, the figure below illustrates a Hamiltonian cycle: (1 \to 7 \to 5 \to 2 \to 4 \to 3 \to 6 \to 1). In the second test case, no Hamiltonian cycle exists because there are no incoming edges to vertex (1) (i.e., no vertex can reach vertex (1)).

2223D.editorial_text:
2223D - Zhily and Cycle
Assume there exists a Hamiltonian cycle, where point $$$i$$$ connects to $$$u_i$$$. Then, the edge $$$(i, u_i)$$$ can be split into two edges: $$$(i, a_i)$$$ and $$$(a_i, u_i)$$$, noting that $$$a_i \le u_i$$$ always holds.
Consider constructing a graph $$$G = (V, E)$$$, where $$$V = \{1, 2, \cdots, n\}$$$ and $$$E = \{(i, a_i) | 1 \le i \le n\}$$$. And if there exists a Hamiltonian cycle, there should exist an Eulerian circuit after adding some edges of the form $$$(a_i, u_i)$$$ to this graph. We only need to determine whether it is possible to add $$$n$$$ edges of the form $$$(a_i, u_i)$$$ to make $$$G$$$ an Eulerian graph.
Note that relaxing the restriction on adding edges does not affect the determination result. We can allow the addition of any number of edges $$$(u, v)$$$ satisfying $$$u \lt v$$$. Under such conditions, whether $$$G$$$ can become an Eulerian graph is equivalent to whether $$$G$$$ can become an Eulerian graph under the original conditions.
Consider how to determine whether there exists a scheme for adding edges. The conditions for an Eulerian graph are that the out-degree and in-degree of each vertex are equal and the graph is connected. Let the out-degree and in-degree of vertex $$$i$$$ be denoted as $$$out_i$$$ and $$$in_i$$$, respectively, and define $$$deg_i = out_i - in_i$$$. Consider the degree sequence of $$$G$$$: $$$deg_1, deg_2, \cdots, deg_n$$$. Each time, we can choose $$$i \lt j$$$ and update $$$deg_i \leftarrow deg_i + 1$$$ and $$$deg_j \leftarrow deg_j - 1$$$. Ultimately, we need to make all $$$deg_i$$$ equal to $$$0$$$ while ensuring the graph remains connected.
Let $$$sum_i = \sum_{u = 1}^{n} deg_u$$$. It is important to note that the condition for all $$$deg_i$$$ to be $$$0$$$ can be satisfied if and only if $$$\forall 1 \le i \le n, sum_i \le 0$$$. Therefore, we can add edges arbitrarily under this condition and see if we can make the graph connected.
Find all indices where $$$sum_i = 0$$$, denoting them as $$$t_0 = 0 \lt 1 \le t_1 \lt t_2 \lt \cdots \lt t_m = n$$$ (it is clear that $$$sum_n = 0$$$). Any edge we add cannot cross over $$$t_i$$$. Otherwise, if there exists $$$u \le t_i \lt v$$$ and we add $$$(u, v)$$$, then it must be the case that $$$sum_{t_i} \gt 0$$$, making it impossible to satisfy the degree constraints with any subsequent edge additions.
On the other hand, we can add all edges of the form $$$(i, i + 1)$$$ where $$$i \neq t_j$$$. If the graph is still not connected at this point, then it will never be possible to connect it regardless of how edges are added. Thus, we first add all such edges, and then greedily pair the remaining vertices with unbalanced in-degrees and out-degrees, adding no more than $$$3n$$$ edges in total.
If the above process is completed successfully, we will have obtained an Eulerian graph. We only need to find any Eulerian circuit in it to reconstruct a Hamiltonian cycle in the original graph.
The total complexity is $$$O(n)$$$
Also, there's an another solution given by gemini as follows.
We first sort $$$1, \cdots, n$$$ according to $$$a_i$$$ in increasing order, and denote the result sequence by $$$u_1, \cdots, u_n$$$, satisfying $$$a_{u_i} \lt a_{u_{i + 1}}$$$ for all $$$1\le i \lt n$$$. Then we simply link all the edges $$$(u_i, i)$$$. If the result doesn't meet the constraint $$$i \ge a_{u_i}$$$, it can be easily proved that the constraint can never be met and thus there isn't a Hamiltonian cycle in the graph.
And if the constraint is met, all left for us to do is to adjust the graph into one component. We check all pairs $$$(i, i + 1)$$$. If $$$i$$$ and $$$i + 1$$$ are not in the same component and $$$a_{u_{i + 1}} \le i$$$ (which means the following operation won't obey the constraint given by $$$a_i$$$), we alter the end points of $$$u_i$$$ and $$$u_{i + 1}$$$. Now let's prove that we can always find a Hamiltonian cycle after these operations if there is one in the graph.
Denote the node pointing to $$$i$$$ in the graph after the operations by $$$v_i$$$, and then we get the sequence $$$v_i$$$. If the graph still isn't connected, we denote the component containing $$$1$$$ with $$$S$$$ and all the other nodes as $$$T$$$($$$T = \{1, \cdots, n\} - S$$$), and they will form several consecutive segments on both the sequence $$$1, \cdots, n$$$ and $$$v_1, \cdots, v_n$$$(the indexes are corresponding). Since all valid operations have been done, the beginning of every segment will always satisfy that $$$a_{v_i} = i$$$. We claim that under these conditions there can never be a Hamiltonian cycle in the graph.
Consider how could we adjust the result to build a Hamiltonian cycle. To do this, we must build an edge pointing from $$$T$$$ to $$$S$$$, and let's assume it's $$$(v_i, j)$$$, where $$$v_i\in T, j\in S, i \lt j$$$. Consider which node will $$$v_j$$$ point to. It will be in either the segment containing $$$j$$$ or the following segments. If is the former, trace the augment path and the destination will always be in the following segments, which is the latter case. Thus, we will always have to build the edge $$$(v_j, k)$$$ where $$$v_j\in S, k\in T, j \lt k$$$. Doing the operation repeatedly and we will find conflict in the last segment.
So in summary, we can always find the Hamiltonian cycle if there is one. The whole algorithm can be implemented by DSU with time complexity $$$O(n\log n)$$$ bounding on the sort.

2223E.editorial_text:
2223E - Zhily and Permutation
For convenience, we use $$$q$$$ to denote the operation count $$$m$$$ in the statement.
Brief: Through analysis of its properties, we can transform the maintenance of information regarding the left endpoint into a one-dimensional problem on a tree. During implementation, this transformation can be achieved during sweep line processes by maintaining sets using Binary Indexed Trees, resulting in a time complexity of $$$\Theta((n + q) \log n)$$$. After the transformation, the problem can be solved using various powerful data structures in $$$\Theta(n + q \log n)$$$ or using Heavy-Light Decomposition in $$$\Theta(n + q \log^2 n)$$$. This solution can be easily extended to handle online operations by introducing persistent data structures.
For convenience of notation, let $$$F = \{(l, r) \in ([0, n + 1] \cap \mathbb{N})^2 | r - l \gt 1\}$$$, and for $$$(l, r) \in F$$$ define $$$A(l, r) = \operatorname*{argmax} \{a_i\}_{i \in I}, B(l, r) = \operatorname*{argmax} \{b_j\}_{j \in I}, \varphi(l, r) = (\min(A(l, r), B(l, r)), \max(A(l, r), B(l, r)))$$$. Note that the equality between endpoint pairs $$$(1, 2) = (2, 3)$$$ does not hold.
We can consider enumerating $$$l$$$ from large to small, maintaining the state of $$$\varphi(l, \cdot)$$$.
Let $$$\{u_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|u_l|} = \{t \in (l, n] \cap \mathbb{N} | a_t = \max_{i = l + 1}^t a_i\}$$$ be the prefix maximum positions of $$$a$$$ in the current suffix $$$(l, n] \cap \mathbb{N}$$$, and similarly let $$$\{v_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|v_l|} = \{t \in (l, n] \cap \mathbb{N} | b_t = \max_{i = l + 1}^t b_i\}$$$. For convenience of notation, set $$$u_{l, |u_l| + 1} = v_{l, |v_l| + 1} = n + 1$$$. In particular, $$$u_{l - 1, 1} = v_{l - 1, 1} = l$$$, and $$$u_{l - 1, 2}, v_{l - 1, 2}$$$ denote the smallest index $$$k \in (l, n] \cap \mathbb{N}$$$ such that $$$a_k \gt a_l, b_k \gt b_l$$$, respectively (if no such $$$k$$$ exists, take $$$n + 1$$$).
From the definitions, we have:

Proposition 1: For $$$(l, r) \in F$$$, if $$$r \leqslant n$$$, $$$\left(\varphi(l, r) \neq \varphi(l, r + 1)\right) \Leftrightarrow \left(r \in \{u_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|u_l|} \cup \{v_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|v_l|}\right)$$$, and if $$$l \gt 0$$$, $$$\left(\varphi(l, r) \neq \varphi(l - 1, r) \right) \Leftrightarrow \left((u_{l - 1, 2} \geqslant r) \lor (v_{l - 1, 2} \geqslant r)\right)$$$. 
Thus, we can obtain:

Proposition 2: For $$$(l, r) \in F$$$ satisfying $$$1 \leqslant l \lt r \leqslant n$$$, if $$$\varphi(l, r) = \varphi(l, r + 1)$$$, then $$$\varphi(l - 1, r) = \varphi(l - 1, r + 1)$$$; if $$$\varphi(l, r) = \varphi(l - 1, r)$$$, then $$$\varphi(l, r + 1) = \varphi(l - 1, r + 1)$$$. 
It is also obvious that:

Proposition 3: For $$$(l, r) \in F$$$ satisfying $$$r - l \gt 2$$$, if $$$\varphi(l, r) \neq \varphi(l, r - 1)$$$ and $$$\varphi(l, r) \neq \varphi(l + 1, r)$$$, then $$$\varphi(l, r) = (l + 1, r - 1)$$$. 
Propositions 4 to 7 can all be deduced from Propositions 2 and 3, independent of the specific content of $$$\varphi$$$.
Let $$$S = \{(l, r) \in F | (\exists (u, v) \in F)(\varphi(u, v) = (l, r))\}$$$. Then since $$$\varphi(S) \cap F \subseteq S$$$, it is obvious that after at least one transformation under $$$\varphi$$$, the endpoint pairs always lie in $$$S$$$. Since the first transformation under $$$\varphi$$$ is trivial to handle, we only need to focus on the endpoint pairs in $$$S$$$.
According to Propositions 2 and 3, we have:

Proposition 4: For $$$(x, y) \in S$$$, there exist $$$0 \leqslant L \lt x \leqslant y \lt R \leqslant n + 1$$$ such that $$$\left(\varphi(l, r) = (x, y)\right) \Leftrightarrow \left((l \in [L, x)) \land (r \in (y, R])\right)$$$. 
According to Propositions 2 and 4, we have:

Proposition 5: For $$$(x, y) \in S$$$, $$$\varphi(x, y), \varphi(x - 1, y), \varphi(x, y + 1), \varphi(x - 1, y + 1)$$$ are pairwise distinct. 
According to Propositions 4 and 5, we have:

Proposition 6: For $$$(l, r) \in S$$$, there is at most one $$$(x, y) \in S$$$ such that $$$\varphi(x, y) = (l, r)$$$. 
In other words, if we connect elements of $$$S$$$ by directed edges according to the transformation under $$$\varphi$$$, then $$$S$$$ consists of several chains.
These chains can be easily ordered according to the endpoint pairs of the empty intervals obtained by applying $$$\varphi$$$ once more to the chain tails. By mathematical induction, it is easy to prove that:

Proposition 7: There exists a numbering function $$$\psi: F \to \mathbb{N}$$$ such that for $$$(l, r) \in F$$$, if $$$\varphi(l, r) \in F$$$ then $$$\psi(l, r) = \psi(\varphi(l, r))$$$; and if $$$(l, r), (x, y) \in F$$$ satisfy $$$l \leqslant x$$$ and $$$r \leqslant y$$$, then $$$\psi(l, r) \leqslant \psi(x, y)$$$. 
Since Propositions 2 and 3 are local properties, the above property analysis from Proposition 2 to Proposition 7 can also be directly observed during the sweep line process. They can also be directly proved using other methods.
During the sweep line process, for disappearances of right endpoints from $$$\{u_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|u_l|} \cup \{v_{l, i}\}_{i = 1}^{|v_l|}$$$, they are associated with the termination of a chain; similarly at endpoint pairs $$$(l, \max(u_{l, 2}, v_{l, 2})) \notin S$$$. According to Proposition 7, the rank of the terminated chain is the same as the rank of the disappearing endpoint. Hence we can separately maintain the set of current non-terminated chains.
Thus, for each left endpoint, during the sweep line we process an interval of chains such that any chain in this interval that has not terminated before must contain this left endpoint.
All sets can be maintained using binary indexed trees, and thus the time complexity of the above sweep line process is $$$\Theta(n \log n)$$$.
We can perform a second sweep line process in the order of the chains, with point insertions of left endpoints, so we can maintain the set of left endpoints for each chain in $$$\Theta(n \log n)$$$ time, and for each query compute the final interval reached within $$$k$$$ iterations of $$$\operatorname{next}$$$ in $$$\Theta(\log n)$$$ time.
If the queried information is commutative and associative, then the problem can be solved directly using 2D orthogonal range counting methods. However, when a generalized semigroup operation rather than the general addition is utilized, we can construct another $$$\varphi'$$$ that also satisfies Propositions 2 and 3, such that under the APSP hypothesis and when $$$q = \Theta(n)$$$, the corresponding problem cannot be solved in $$$O(n^{1.5-\varepsilon})$$$ time, where $$$\varepsilon$$$ is any positive constant. In other words, we need more properties concerning $$$\varphi$$$ than those given in Propositions 2 to 7 to solve the problem when utilizing generalized semigroup operations (or the semigroup operation in the statement).
We prove the following property independently of Propositions 2 and 3:

Proposition 8: If for $$$(r, x), (s, y), (t, z)\in F$$$, we have $$$r \lt t \lt s$$$, $$$(t, z) \in S$$$ and $$$\varphi(r, x) = (s, y)$$$, then $$$z \leqslant s$$$. 
From $$$\varphi(r, x) = (s, y)$$$, we have either $$$s = A(r, x)$$$ or $$$s = B(r, x)$$$; consider the former case without loss of generality. Since $$$(t, z) \in S$$$, let $$$(t, z) = \varphi(\alpha, \beta)$$$, then $$$t = A(\alpha, \beta)$$$ or $$$t = B(\alpha, \beta)$$$.
If $$$t = A(\alpha, \beta)$$$, then because $$$t \in (r, s) \subseteq (r, x)$$$ and $$$s = A(r, x)$$$, we have $$$a_s \geqslant a_t$$$, and for $$$A(\alpha, \beta) = t$$$ to hold, we must have $$$s \geqslant \beta \gt z$$$.
If $$$t = B(\alpha, \beta)$$$, then similarly $$$b_y \geqslant b_t$$$ and $$$y \geqslant \beta$$$, and since $$$\alpha \lt t \lt s$$$ and for $$$u \in (t, y)$$$ we have $$$a_u \lt a_t$$$, we must have $$$z = A(\alpha, \beta) \leqslant s$$$.
Thus we must have $$$z \leqslant s$$$.
Then it immediately follows that for $$$(d, w) = \varphi(t, z)$$$ we have $$$d \lt z \leqslant s$$$.
Therefore:

Proposition 9: The paths of left endpoints in $$$S$$$ under the transformation of $$$\varphi$$$ are on a forest. (With a virtual root, we get a tree.) 
In fact, during the problem preparation, this conclusion is naturally obtained from a more complex but powerful structure; for simplicity, we now consider the direct proof above.
In the first sweep line process, we can directly process which new left endpoints a left endpoint in $$$S$$$ can reach via $$$\varphi$$$. So the tree can be determined.
The endpoints of the tree paths can also be determined, so we only need to solve the problem of point updates and path sum queries on the tree.
The time complexity is $$$\Theta((n + q) \log n)$$$, and the space complexity of the offline algorithm is $$$\Theta(n + q)$$$. Since the sweep line process is independent of updates, we can extend it to an online algorithm using persistent segment trees, in which case the space complexity becomes $$$\Theta(n \log n)$$$.
The standard solution runs in 546ms at its slowest point on Polygon. For the Heavy-Light Decomposition implementation, since we have not yet constructed targeted adversarial data, the slowest point is currently 510ms. The time limit 2.5s was set by the coordinator after considering several other potential solutions.
Due to slight time constraints during preparation, the design of this problem still has certain shortcomings (though they did not manifest during the contest). We hope for your understanding and forgiveness.

Let $$$n_i = k_i d_i$$$, where $$$k_i$$$ is a non-negative integer; otherwise, there is no solution.
We first consider how to check if a string is valid. Note that we can remove the characters in any order, while it will not change the validity.
Therefore, we can use a stack storing triples like $$$(i, j, t)$$$ meaning there remain $$$t$$$ consecutive characters in the $$$j$$$-th color of the $$$i$$$-th type. For a new character, we consider whether it will push or pop the top, or let the $$$t$$$ of the top increase by $$$1$$$.
Note that this procedure forms a matching structure like a bracket sequence: $$$d_i$$$ characters of the $$$i$$$-th type we removed at once are like a tuple of brackets containing $$$d_i-1$$$ substrings among them.
Now, to count the result, we first consider the bracket structure and then count the coloring ways in which the stack-using procedure can form it. This requires that each bracket should not be the same kind and the same color as the element below in the stack.
For convenience, we can calculate the sum of the valid coloring probabilities of all bracket sequences and then multiply by $$$c_1^{k_1} c_2^{k_2} \dots c_m^{k_m}$$$. Let $$$q_i = \frac1{c_i}$$$.
Let $$$F_i(\mathbf x)$$$ be the number of bracket sequences with an outermost bracket that is of the $$$i$$$-th type. We can derive the equation:
$$$$$$ F_i = \frac{x_i}{(1-(F_1+F_2+\dots+F_m-q_i F_i))^{d_i-1}} $$$$$$
This means that in the $$$d_i$$$ brackets, we can insert a bracket sequence in the $$$d_i-1$$$ gaps, but we need to exclude the cases where they are the same color.
To apply the multivariate Lagrange inversion, we rearrange it into a suitable form:
$$$$$$ \begin{aligned} G_i(\mathbf x) &= \frac1{(1-x_1-\dots-x_m+q_ix_i)^{d_i-1}} \\ &= \frac1{(1-x_1-\dots-x_m)^{d_i-1}\left(1+\frac{q_ix_i}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m}\right)^{d_i-1}} \\ F_i(\mathbf x) &= x_i G_i(\mathbf F) \\ \frac{x_j}{G_i(\mathbf x)} \frac{\partial G_i(\mathbf x)}{\partial x_j} &= \frac{(d_i-1)(1-[i=j]q_i) x_j}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m+q_ix_i} \\ &= (d_i-1)(1-[i=j]q_i) \frac{x_j}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m} \frac1{1+\frac{q_ix_i}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m}}\\ H(\mathbf x) &= \frac1{1-x_1-\dots-x_m} \end{aligned} $$$$$$
We want to find
$$$$$$ [\mathbf x^{\mathbf k}] H(\mathbf F) = [\mathbf x^{\mathbf k}] H \mathbf G^{\mathbf k} \left\Vert[i=j]-\frac{x_j}{G_i(\mathbf x)} \frac{\partial G_i(\mathbf x)}{\partial x_j}\right\Vert $$$$$$
Notice that the expression on the right side is of the form
$$$$$$ [\mathbf x^{\mathbf k}] \frac1{(1-x_1-\dots-x_m)^{1+\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf d-\mathbf 1)}} P\left(\frac{x_1}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m},\dots,\frac{x_m}{1-x_1-\dots-x_m}\right) $$$$$$
We first calculate $$$P(t_1,t_2,\dots,t_m)$$$. It should be
$$$$$$ \begin{aligned} P &= \prod_{i=1}^m \frac1{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)}} \cdot \left\Vert[i=j]-(d_i-1)(1-[i=j]q_i)\frac{t_j}{1+q_it_i}\right\Vert \\ &= \prod_{i=1}^m \frac1{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)+1}} \cdot \left\Vert[i=j](1+d_iq_it_i)-(d_i-1)t_j\right\Vert \\ &= \prod_{i=1}^m \frac1{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)+1}} \cdot \left(1-\sum_{i=1}^m \frac{(d_i-1)t_i}{1+d_iq_it_i}\right) \cdot \prod_{i=1}^m (1+d_iq_it_i) \\ &= [u^1] (1+u)\prod_{i=1}^m \frac{1+d_iq_it_i-(d_i-1)ut_i}{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)+1}} \end{aligned} $$$$$$
The third equality holds because for invertible matrices $$$\mathbf A, \mathbf W$$$, we have
$$$$$$ \det(\mathbf A + \mathbf U\mathbf W\mathbf V) = \det(\mathbf W^{-1} + \mathbf V\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf U) \det(\mathbf W) \det(\mathbf A) $$$$$$
which can be simply proven using block matrices.
Next, we consider what contribution an item $$$\mathbf t^{\mathbf e}$$$ in $$$P(\mathbf t)$$$ will bring to the answer:
$$$$$$ [\mathbf x^{\mathbf k-\mathbf e}] \frac1{(1-x_1-\dots-x_m)^{1+\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf d-\mathbf 1)+\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf 1}} = \binom{\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf d}{\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf d-\mathbf 1)+\mathbf e\cdot\mathbf 1,k_1-e_1,k_2-e_2,\dots,k_m-e_m} $$$$$$
Thus, we only care about $$$\sum e_i$$$ and $$$\prod \frac1{(k_i-e_i)!}$$$.
Now considering the comprehensive calculation, note that we have already organized $$$P$$$ into a form where each variable is independent, so we can introduce a dummy variable $$$w$$$ to measure $$$\sum e_i$$$:
$$$$$$ \sum_{s\ge 0} \frac{(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf d)!}{(\mathbf k\cdot(\mathbf d-1)+s)!}[w^s] \left([u^1](1+u)\prod_{i=1}^m \sum_{e=0}^{k_i} \frac{w^e}{(k_i-e)!} \cdot [t_i^e] \frac{1+d_iq_it_i-(d_i-1)ut_i}{(1+q_it_i)^{k_i(d_i-1)+1}}\right) $$$$$$
Of course, we also need to multiply by $$$\mathbf c^{\mathbf k}$$$

Zhily and Array Operating
PROGRAMMING

Add tag

Deep in the wilderness, Zhily and Jily discovered a series of gathering places that contain abstract logic. Some of these gathering places harbor inconsistent errors in their logic, which may collapse at any moment. They hope to transmit logic between adjacent gathering places through reasonable transfer arrangements so that as many gathering places as possible can eventually restore logical stability. You are given an array (a) of (n) integers. You can perform the following operation any number of times: Choose an index (i) ((1 \le i \lt n)) and assign (a_i\gets a_i+a_{i+1}). Each index can be chosen at most once . Find the maximum number of positive integers in the final array after all operations. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((2\leq n \leq 2\cdot 10^5)). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) ((-10^9\leq a_i\leq 10^9)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2\cdot10^5). For each test case, you should output a single line containing an integer (k), the number of positive numbers in the final sequence. In the first test case, the array (a) is operated on by the following process: (0,-1,3,-3,0\to 0,\color{red}{2},3,-3,0\to \color{red}{2},2,3,-3,0). There are (3) positive numbers in the final array, and it can be proven that this is the maximum count of positive integers. 2224A.editorial_text:
2224A - Zhily and Array Operating
We want to maximize every single number so that the final goodness is the best.
An operation at $$$i$$$ only changes $$$a_i$$$; it never harms positivity elsewhere, but may make $$$a_j$$$ bigger for $$$j \lt i$$$.So we greedily judge every $$$i=n-1$$$ down to $$$1$$$. If $$$a_{i+1} \gt 0$$$, adding it strictly increases, increasing the chance of having more positives. Otherwise, adding it would not help, so we skip it.

Zhily and Mex and Max
PROGRAMMING
constructive algorithms greedy math sortings

Add tag

Deeper in the wilderness, Zhily and Jily discovered a mysterious sequence of numbers. Each prefix of the sequence has an important characteristic value, known as the mex and the max. By rearranging the sequence, it can generate a special kind of magic. You are given an array (a) of (n) non-negative integers. You can rearrange it arbitrarily. Find the maximum possible value of the sum of the MEX(^{\text{∗}}) and the maximum value over all prefixes. Formally, you need to maximize the following expression: (\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (\operatorname{mex}(a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_i)+\max(a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_i))). (^{\text{∗}})The minimum excluded (MEX) of a collection of integers (c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_k) is defined as the smallest non-negative integer (x) which does not occur in the collection (c). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \leq n \leq 2\cdot 10^5)) — the length of the array (a). The second line contains (n) integers (a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_n) ((0\leq a_i \leq 10^9)) — the array (a). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2\cdot 10^5). For each test case, output the maximum sum on a new line. In the first test case, no matter how you rearrange (a), the MEX and the maximum value for each prefix will always be (1) and (0), respectively. In the third test case, you can rearrange (a) into (0,1,1,1,1), so that (\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (\operatorname{mex}(a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_i)+\max(a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_i))=(1+0)+(2+1)+(2+1)+(2+1)+(2+1)=13). It can be shown that this is the optimal solution.

2224B.editorial_text:
2224B - Zhily and Mex and Max
First, we demonstrate that the maximum element ($$$max$$$) must be placed in the first position. After that, we can put the smallest number that does not appear in the new array to maximize the mex.
Suppose this is not the case, and $$$max$$$ first appears at index $$$i+1$$$. Let $$$t$$$ be the MEX of the first $$$i$$$ positions; it follows that $$$t \leq i$$$.
If we move $$$max$$$ directly to the first position (shifting the original elements one step back), consider the changes in the first $$$i$$$ prefix sets (the sets from position $$$i+1$$$ onwards remain unchanged):
Contribution of prefix maximums: The sum increases by at least $$$i$$$, as the original maximum for each of the first $$$i$$$ prefixes was strictly less than $$$max$$$.
Contribution of prefix MEX: The sum decreases by at most $$$t$$$. This is because the original MEX at position $$$p$$$ is no greater than the new MEX at position $$$p+1$$$, and the new MEX at the first position is at most $$$t$$$ smaller than the original MEX at position $$$i$$$.
Since $$$t \leq i$$$, placing $$$max$$$ at the first position is always an optimal strategy. Consequently, the remaining elements should be arranged in ascending order starting from 0, with any duplicate values moved to the end of the sequence.

Marisa Steals Reimu's Takeout
PROGRAMMING
greedy implementation

Add tag

Marisa is a girl of integrity who always helps others safeguard their belongings. Over a period of (n) days, she comes each day to take one of Reimu's takeouts. The (i)-th takeout is described by its deliciousness value — an integer (w_i) ((0\le w_i\le 2)), forming a sequence (w) of length (n). Marisa has a special fondness for the number (3). She can perform the following operation zero or more times: Select a non-empty subsequence(^{\text{∗}}) of (w) whose sum is divisible by (3), and remove the elements of the subsequence from (w). Determine the maximum number of operations Marisa can perform. (^{\text{∗}})A sequence (a) is a subsequence of a sequence (b) if (a) can be obtained from (b) by the deletion of several (possibly, zero or all) element from arbitrary positions. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 500)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1\le n \le 100)). The second line contains (n) integers (w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n) ((0\leq w_i \leq 2)), denoting the deliciousness values of the takeouts. For each test case, output the maximum number of operations Marisa can perform. In the first test case, Marisa can perform four operations: ()\underline{0},0,0,0\to\underline{0},0,0\to\underline{0},0\to\underline{0}\to [].() In the second test case, Marisa can perform two operations: ()\underline{1},\underline{2},0- \gt \underline{0}- \gt [].() In the third test case, Marisa can perform two operations: ()\underline{1},2,1,\underline{2},1- \gt \underline{2},1,\underline{1}- \gt 1.()

2228A.editorial_text:
2228A - Marisa Steals Reimu's Takeout
Author: Sanae
Solution: Sanae

Step 1
Lemma 1. There exists an optimal solution in which each zero is divided separately.
Proof. Suppose in some optimal solution, a zero is grouped with other elements. Separating it into a singleton group does not decrease the total score. Hence, we can transform any optimal solution into one where all zeros are divided separately without worsening the objective. $$$\blacksquare$$$
Therefore, we can restrict our attention to the subsequence consisting only of $1$s and $2$s.

Step 2
Lemma 2. There exists an optimal solution in which any group containing both $$$1$$$ and $$$2$$$ is exactly either $$$[1,2]$$$ or $$$[2,1]$$$.
Proof. Consider a group that contains $$$1$$$, $$$2$$$, and possibly other elements. Splitting it into $$$[1,2]$$$ (or $$$[2,1]$$$) and the remaining part does not decrease the total score. Consequently, we can transform any optimal solution into the desired form. $$$\blacksquare$$$
By Lemma 2, we can greedily extract all $$$[1,2]$$$ or $$$[2,1]$$$ pairs from the remaining sequence.

Step 3
Finally, for the leftover elements, the best strategy is clearly to take triplets $$$[1,1,1]$$$ and $$$[2,2,2]$$$ whenever possible.

Remilia Plays Soku
PROGRAMMING
games implementation

Add tag

Remilia is trying to escape, while Reimu wants to land the final hit. The playing field consists of (n) positions arranged in a circle. For each (1 \le i \lt n), positions (i) and (i+1) are adjacent, and positions (1) and (n) are also adjacent. Initially, at time (0), Reimu is at position (x_1) and Remilia is at position (x_2), where (x_1 \ne x_2). Each second, the following happens in order: Remilia either moves to an adjacent position or stays in place. Over the entire game, she may move to an adjacent position at most (k) times. After observing Remilia's action, Reimu either moves to an adjacent position or stays in place. If they are at the same position after both actions, Reimu catches Remilia and the game ends. Assuming both players play optimally, Reimu always tries to minimize the catching time, while Remilia tries to maximize it. Find the number of seconds until Reimu catches Remilia. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains four integers (n), (x_1), (x_2) and (k) ((2\le n\le10^8), (1\le x_1,x_2\le n), (x_1\ne x_2), (0\le k\le 10^8)). For each test case, output the number of seconds until Reimu catches Remilia, assuming both players play optimally. In the first test case, one possible sequence of actions is: In the first second, Remilia stays in place, and then Reimu moves to (2) and catches Remilia. In the second test case, one possible sequence of actions is: In the first second, Remilia moves to (1), and then Reimu moves to (2). In the second second, Remilia cannot move and has to stay in place, and then Reimu moves to (1) and catches Remilia.

2228B.editorial_text:
2228B - Remilia Plays Soku
Author: Sanae
Solution: Sanae

Solution
We assume $$$n\geq 4$$$ in what follows.
Let us analyze the strategies of both players. Reimu aims to get as close to Remilia as possible, while Remilia aims to get as far away from Reimu as possible. Remilia will use her moves to increase the distance without being caught, and indeed it is optimal for her to use as many moves as possible.
The distance on the circle can be measured with $$$d=min(|x_1-x_2|,n-|x_1-x_2|)$$$. Once $$$d=1$$$, Remilia can increase $$$d$$$ by $$$1$$$ since the circle is large enough ($$$n\geq 4$$$). Similarly, Reimu can decrease $$$d$$$ by $$$1$$$ each turn.
Therefore, we can calculate the outcome directly. The answer is the initial distance plus the extra time gained by Remilia's moves, $$$min(|x_1-x_2|,n-|x_1-x_2|)+k$$$.
Note that when $$$n\leq 3$$$, the answer is always $$$1$$$, because Reimu can always catch Remilia in one step.

2228C2.editorial_text:
2228C2 - Cirno and Number (Hard Version)
Author: Sanae, Sugar_fan
Solution: Sanae, Sugar_fan

Solution
The case $$$a=b$$$ is trivial. We consider two cases separately: $$$a \gt b$$$ and $$$a \lt b$$$. 
We first discuss $$$a \lt b$$$ in what follows. Consider the longest common prefix of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$, scanning from the highest digit to the lowest significant digit. Let $$$x$$$ be the digit of $$$a$$$ be at that position and $$$y$$$ be the digit of $$$b$$$ be at that position. If $$$d_n \gt x$$$, choose $$$y$$$ as the smallest $$$d_i$$$ such that $$$d_i \gt x$$$. Then set the digits beneath in $$$b$$$ to $$$d_1$$$. This guarantees that $$$b$$$ is the smallest number greater than $$$a$$$ and the decimal representation of $$$b$$$ contains only digits from $$$d$$$. Otherwise, if $$$d_n \lt x$$$,we should change an earlier digit to satisfy the inequality. Note that we can make the number of digits in $$$b$$$ more than $$$a$$$.
Similarly, we assume $$$a \gt b$$$. Consider the longest common prefix of $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$, scanning from the highest digit to the lowest significant digit. Let $$$x$$$ be the digit of $$$a$$$ be at that position and $$$y$$$ be the digit of $$$b$$$ be at that position. If $$$d_1 \lt x$$$, choose $$$y$$$ as the largest $$$d_i$$$ such that $$$d_i \lt x$$$. Then set the digits beneath in $$$b$$$ to $$$d_n$$$. This guarantees that $$$b$$$ is the largest number smaller than $$$a$$$ and the decimal representation of $$$b$$$ contains only digits from $$$d$$$. Otherwise, if $$$d_1 \gt x$$$,we should change an earlier digit to satisfy the inequality. Note that if $$$d=[1,2,3]$$$, then $$$b=0$$$ is invalid, because $$$0$$$ dosn't belongs to $$$d$$$.
Depending on the implementation, the time complexity can be $$$O(10n\log a)$$$, $$$O(10n\log^2 a)$$$, $$$O(n\log a)$$$ or $$$O(n\log^2 a)$$$.

2228D.editorial_text:
2228D - Sanae, Cross and Color
Author: Sanae
Solution: Sanae, fanhuaxingyu

Solution 1
We can apply the principle of inclusion--exclusion to compute the answer. First, enumerate a vertical dividing line at integer coordinate $$$x$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$; the contribution is recalculated only when the set of points on the left side changes ~---otherwise, we skip redundant computations.
For each such $$$x$$$, we then enumerate a horizontal dividing line at integer $$$y$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, while carefully excluding overlapping cases to avoid double-counting. Let the y-coordinates of the points on the left side be $$${y_1,y_2,\dots,y_k}$$$, sorted in increasing order. For consecutive y-values $$$y_i$$$ and $$$y_{i+1}$$$, all values in the form $$$k+0.5$$$ in the interval $$$(y_i+0.5,\;y_{i+1}-0.5)$$$ give the same left-side point set. Thus, the left side produces a set of y-intervals, and similarly, the right side also forms a set of y-intervals. To count all valid configurations, we need to count the number of interval-pairs (one interval from the left, one from the right) that intersect in at least one point. This can be computed efficiently using a Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) and a set data structure.
The overall time complexity is $$$O(n\log n)$$$.

Solution 2
An observation is that any valid dividing line must cross at least one of the two groups determined by the smaller y-coordinate.
Suppose the line crosses the group with smaller $$$x$$$ and smaller $$$y$$$. Enumerate the point whose $$$y$$$-coordinate is maximal within this group (and among those with the same maximal $$$y$$$, take the one with the larger $$$x$$$). Using appropriate pre-computation, we can efficiently determine the feasible vertical dividing position $$$x$$$.
The case where the line crosses the group with larger $$$x$$$ but smaller $$$y$$$ is symmetric to the above.
The overall time complexity is $$$O(n)$$$.

For a non-negative integer sequence (c), define (f(c)) as the sum of the squares of its prefix sums: () f(c)=\sum_{i=1}^{|c|}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{i} c_j\right)^2. () Now define (g(b,m)) as follows. Let (b) be an integer sequence such that (b_i\ge -1) for every (i), and let (m) be a non-negative integer. 2228E2.editorial_text:
2228E2 - Amanojaku and Sequence (Hard Version)
Author: Sanae
Solution: Sanae
Tutorial: CirnoNine, fanhuaxingyu

Sanae's Solution
First, consider solving the whole array. We can first compute the total number of possible configurations of $$$a$$$ using stars and bars. Let this number be $$$tot$$$. The remaining sum to be freely distributed is $$$sum= m - \sum_{i} a_i[a_i\neq -1]$$$, and the number of undetermined positions is $$$cnt=\sum_{i} [a_i = -1]$$$. It is obvious $$$tot=\binom{sum+cnt-1}{cnt-1}$$$. We adopt the convention $$$\binom{-1}{-1}=1$$$ to simplify boundary cases.
$$$ \begin{aligned} g(a,m)= {} & \sum_{b \text{ is valid}}\sum_{1\leq i \leq n}(\sum_{1\leq j\leq i}b_j)^2\\ = & \sum_{b \text{ is valid}}\sum_{1\leq i \leq n}\sum_{1\leq j\leq n}b_ib_j (n+1-\max(i,j))\\ = & 2\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}\sum_{1\leq i \lt j\leq n}b_ib_j (n+1-j)\\ &\quad + \sum_{b \text{ is valid}}\sum_{1\leq i \leq n}b_i^2 (n+1-i))\\ \end{aligned} $$$
Denote $$$S_1=2\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}\sum_{1\leq i \lt j\leq n}b_ib_j (n+1-j)$$$ and $$$S_2=\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}\sum_{1\leq i \leq n}b_i^2 (n+1-i))$$$. We should compute each part individually.
To do the computation, we need to first introduce some useful math conclusions. We give the $$$T_0,T_1,T_2$$$.
We recall the following standard combinatorial identities: \begin{enumerate} \item If $$$n\geq 0$$$, then $$$\binom{n}{m}=\binom{n}{n-m}$$$
\item For any $$$n,m$$$,then $$$m\binom{n}{m}=n\binom{n-1}{m-1}$$$
\item If $$$n,m\geq 0$$$, then $$$n\binom{n+m}{n}=(m+1)\binom{n+m}{m+1}$$$ \end{enumerate}
The $$$T_0$$$ is classic,while $$$T_1,T_2$$$ need some work.
$$$ \begin{aligned} T_0(n,m) = &\sum_{x=0}^n \binom{x+m}{m}\\ = & \binom{n+m+1}{m+1} \end{aligned} $$$
The computation of $$$T_1$$$ is straightforward.
$$$ \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} T_1(n,m) = & \sum_{x=0}^n x\binom{x+m}{m}\\ = & \sum_{x=0}^n x\binom{x+m}{m}\\ = & \sum_{x=0}^n x\binom{x+m}{x}\\ = & \sum_{x=0}^n (m+1)\binom{x+m}{m+1}\\ = & (m+1)\binom{n+m+1}{m+2}\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} $$$
Similarly, we compute $$$T_2$$$:
$$$ \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} T_2(n,m) = {}&\sum_{x=0}^n x^2\binom{x+m}{m}\\ = & \sum_{x=1}^n (m+1)x\binom{x+m}{m+1}\\ = & (m+1)\sum_{x=0}^{n-1} (x+1)\binom{x+m+1}{m+1}\\ = & (m+1)(m+2)\binom{n+m+1}{m+3}+(m+1)\binom{n+m+1}{m+2}\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} $$$
We now derive $$$T_3$$$:
$$$ \begin{aligned} T_3(n,m) &= {}\sum_{x=0}^n x^3\binom{x+m}{m}\\ &= \sum_{x=1}^n (m+1)x^2\binom{x+m}{m+1}\\ &= (m+1)\sum_{x=0}^{n-1} (x+1)^2\binom{x+m+1}{m+1}\\
&= (m+1)(\sum_{x=0}^{n-1} x^2\binom{x+m+1}{m+1}+2\sum_{x=0}^{n-1} x\binom{x+m+1}{m+1}+\sum_{x=0}^{n-1} \binom{x+m+1}{m+1})\\ &= (m+1)(T_2(n-1,m+1)+2T_1(n-1,m+1)+T_0(n-1,m+1)) \\\\ &\quad \text{Note: It can be further simplified, but we can just stop here.} \end{aligned} $$$
We first deal with $$$S_2$$$.$$$S_2=\sum_{1\leq i \leq n}\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}b_i^2 (n+1-i))$$$.If $$$a_i\geq 0$$$, $$$b_i=a_i$$$, so the formula can be written like $$$a_i^2(n+1-i) tot$$$. If $$$a_i=-1$$$,the formula can be written like 
$$$ \begin{aligned} &(n-i+1)\sum_{x=0}^{sum}x^2\binom{sum-x+cnt-2}{cnt-2}\\ =&(n-i+1)\sum_{x=0}^{sum} (sum-x)^2\binom{x+cnt-2}{cnt-2}\\ =&(n-i+1)(T_2(sum,cnt-2)-2sum\cdot T_1(sum,cnt-2)+sum^2\cdot T_0(sum,cnt-2)) \end{aligned} $$$
Second, we cope with $$$S_1$$$.
$$$S_1=2\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}\sum_{1\leq i \lt j\leq n}b_ib_j (n+1-j)$$$
After selecting $$$i,j$$$, we only need to compute $$$\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}b_ib_j$$$.
There are three cases:
\begin{enumerate} \item $$$a_i\neq -1 \text{ and } a_j\neq -1$$$.
$$$\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}b_ib_j=tot\cdot a_ia_j$$$
\item $$$a_i\neq -1 \text{ and } a_j = -1$$$, $$$a_i\neq -1 \text{ and } a_j = -1$$$.
It remains to consider $$$a_i\neq -1 \text{ and } a_j = -1$$$, because another case is similar.
$$$ \begin{aligned} &\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}b_ib_j\\ =&\sum_{b_j=0}^{sum}a_ib_j\binom{sum-b_j+cnt-2}{cnt-2}\\ =&a_i\sum_{b_j=0}^{sum}(sum-b_j)\binom{b_j+cnt-2}{cnt-2}\\ =&a_i(sum\binom{sum+cnt-1}{cnt-1}-\sum_{b_j=0}^{sum}b_j\binom{b_j+cnt-2}{cnt-2})\\ =&a_i(sum\binom{sum+cnt-1}{cnt-1}-(cnt-1)\binom{sum+cnt-1}{cnt})\\ =&a_i\frac{sum\binom{sum+cnt-1}{cnt-1}}{cnt}\\ \end{aligned} $$$
It can also be computed by the expectation of each position.
\item $$$a_i = -1 \text{ and } a_j = -1$$$.
It is the trickiest part of the solution. We analyze this case carefully.
$$$ \begin{aligned} &\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}b_ib_j\\ =&\sum_{b_i=0}^{sum}\sum_{b_j=0}^{sum}[b_i+b_j\leq sum]b_ib_j\binom{sum-b_i-b_j+cnt-3}{cnt-3}\\ =&\sum_{s=b_i+b_j=0}^{sum}(\sum_{b_j=0}^{s}b_i(s-b_i))\binom{sum-s+cnt-3}{cnt-3}\\ =&\sum_{s=b_i+b_j=0}^{sum}\frac{s^3-s}{6}\binom{sum-s+cnt-3}{cnt-3}\\ =&\frac{1}{6}(\sum_{s=0}^{sum}s^3\binom{sum-s+cnt-3}{cnt-3}-\sum_{s=0}^{sum}s\binom{sum-s+cnt-3}{cnt-3})\\ =&\frac{1}{6}(\sum_{s=0}^{sum}(sum-s)^3\binom{s+cnt-3}{cnt-3}-\sum_{s=0}^{sum}(sum-s)\binom{s+cnt-3}{cnt-3})\\ =&\frac{1}{6}(\sum_{s=0}^{sum}(sum^3-3s\cdot sum^2+3s^2\cdot sum - s^3)\binom{s+cnt-3}{cnt-3}\\ &\quad -sum\cdot T_0(sum,cnt-3)+T_1(sum,cnt-3))\\ =&\frac{1}{6}(sum^3\cdot T_0(sum,cnt-3)-3sum^2\cdot T_1(sum,cnt-3)+3sum\cdot T_2(sum,cnt-3)-T_3(sum,cnt-3)\\ &\quad -sum\cdot T_0(sum,cnt-3)+T_1(sum,cnt-3))\\ \end{aligned} $$$
It is just a constant, which is easy to compute.
\end{enumerate}
Then, it is time to cope with $$$S_1$$$.
$$$S_1=2\sum_{b \text{ is valid}}\sum_{1\leq i \lt j\leq n}b_ib_j (n+1-j)$$$
For type $$$1$$$, it suffices to compute 
$$$\sum_{1\leq i \lt j\leq n}a_ia_j[a_i\neq -1 \text{ and } a_j\neq -1](n-j+1)$$$
. 
For type $$$2$$$, it suffices to compute 
$$$\sum_{1\leq i \lt j\leq n}a_i[a_i\neq -1 \text{ and } a_j = -1](n-j+1)+a_j[a_i= -1 \text{ and } a_j \neq -1](n-j+1)$$$
.
For type $$$3$$$, it suffices to compute 
$$$\sum_{1\leq i \lt j\leq n}[a_i= -1 \text{ and } a_j = -1](n-j+1)$$$
.
All required quantities can be maintained using a segment tree, and the interval queries and modifications can be processed easily. Note that $$$n-j+1=(n+1)-j$$$. So process $$$X \cdot(n+1)$$$ and $$$X \cdot j$$$ in two data structures. Implementation details are omitted for brevity; see the accompanying code.
By querying on the tree, we can get the answer. And the information can also be modified efficiently. 
After all, we can solve the problem in the total time complexity $$$O(1\ 000\ 000)-O((n+q)\log n)$$$ and total space complexity $$$O(1\ 000\ 000+n)$$$.
Note $$$\binom{-1}{-1}=1$$$ in the code.

CirnoNine's Solution
For a fixed query interval, denote it by $$$b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_L$$$.
Define
$$$A_i=\sum_{j=1}^{i} b_j[b_j\ge 0]$$$
and
$$$T_i=\sum_{j=1}^{i} [b_j=-1]$$$
Here, $$$A_i$$$ is the prefix sum contributed by fixed positions, and $$$T_i$$$ is the number of free positions in the first $$$i$$$ elements.
Let
$$$S=\sum_{i:b_i\ge 0} b_i,\qquad k=\#\{i\mid b_i=-1\}$$$
The total value that must be assigned to all free positions is
$$$N=m-S$$$
If $$$N \lt 0$$$, there is no valid sequence, so the answer is $$$0$$$.
If $$$k=0$$$, there is only one possible sequence. The answer is $$$\sum_i A_i^2$$$ if $$$N=0$$$, and $$$0$$$ otherwise.
Now assume $$$k \gt 0$$$ and $$$N\ge 0$$$.
Let the values assigned to the $$$k$$$ free positions be
$$$x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k$$$
where
$$$x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_k=N,\qquad x_i\ge 0$$$
The number of such assignments is
$$$C=\binom{N+k-1}{k-1}$$$
For prefix $$$i$$$, there are exactly $$$T_i$$$ free positions inside it. Therefore, the contribution of assigned values to this prefix is
$$$X_{T_i}=x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_{T_i}$$$
So the real prefix sum at position $$$i$$$ is
$$$A_i+X_{T_i}$$$
Therefore, we need to calculate
$$$\sum_{\text{valid }x}\sum_{i=1}^{L}(A_i+X_{T_i})^2$$$
Expanding the square gives
$$$(A_i+X_{T_i})^2=A_i^2+2A_iX_{T_i}+X_{T_i}^2$$$
Now we calculate these three parts separately.
First, consider the $$$A_i^2$$$ part.
Since $$$A_i$$$ does not depend on the assignment, every valid assignment contributes the same value. Hence this part contributes
$$$C\sum_i A_i^2$$$
Second, consider the $$$2A_iX_{T_i}$$$ part.
By symmetry, among all weak compositions of $$$N$$$ into $$$k$$$ parts, every variable has the same total contribution. Thus
$$$\sum_{\text{valid }x}x_j=C\cdot\frac{N}{k}$$$
Therefore,
$$$\sum_{\text{valid }x}X_t=C\cdot\frac{Nt}{k}$$$
Substituting $$$t=T_i$$$, we get
$$$\sum_{\text{valid }x}2A_iX_{T_i}=C\cdot\frac{2N}{k}A_iT_i$$$
After summing over all $$$i$$$, this part contributes
$$$C\cdot\frac{2N}{k}\sum_i A_iT_i$$$
Third, consider the $$$X_{T_i}^2$$$ part.
We need the second moment of
$$$X_t=x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_t$$$
For all weak compositions of $$$N$$$ into $$$k$$$ parts, we have
$$$\sum_{\text{valid }x}x_p(x_p-1)=C\cdot\frac{2N(N-1)}{k(k+1)}$$$
and for $$$p\ne q$$$,
$$$\sum_{\text{valid }x}x_px_q=C\cdot\frac{N(N-1)}{k(k+1)}$$$
Since
$$$X_t^2=\sum_{p=1}^{t}x_p^2+2\sum_{1\le p \lt q\le t}x_px_q$$$
we get
$$$\sum_{\text{valid }x}X_t^2=C\left(\frac{N}{k}t+\frac{N(N-1)}{k(k+1)}(t^2+t)\right)$$$
Equivalently,
$$$\sum_{\text{valid }x}X_t^2=C\left(\left(\frac{N}{k}+\frac{N(N-1)}{k(k+1)}\right)t+\frac{N(N-1)}{k(k+1)}t^2\right)$$$
Substituting $$$t=T_i$$$ and summing over all positions, the final formula is
$$$g(b,m)=\binom{N+k-1}{k-1}\left(\sum_i A_i^2+\frac{2N}{k}\sum_i A_iT_i+\left(\frac{N}{k}+\frac{N(N-1)}{k(k+1)}\right)\sum_i T_i+\frac{N(N-1)}{k(k+1)}\sum_i T_i^2\right)$$$
All divisions are done modulo $$$998244353$$$ using modular inverses.
Now we explain why this can be maintained by a segment tree.
For every interval, the formula only needs the following values:
$$$S,\quad k,\quad \sum A_i,\quad \sum T_i,\quad \sum A_i^2,\quad \sum A_iT_i,\quad \sum T_i^2$$$
Therefore, each segment tree node maintains:
$$$len,\quad sum,\quad cnt,\quad sumA,\quad sumT,\quad sumA2,\quad sumAT,\quad sumT2$$$
Here, $$$len$$$ is the length of the segment, $$$sum$$$ is the total fixed value in the segment, and $$$cnt$$$ is the number of $$$-1$$$ positions in the segment.
The other values are:
$$$sumA=\sum_i A_i$$$ $$$sumT=\sum_i T_i$$$ $$$sumA2=\sum_i A_i^2$$$ $$$sumAT=\sum_i A_iT_i$$$ $$$sumT2=\sum_i T_i^2$$$
All prefix values are defined relative to the left end of the current segment.
When merging two adjacent segments $$$L$$$ and $$$R$$$, every prefix inside $$$L$$$ remains unchanged.
For a prefix inside $$$R$$$, the entire left segment is already before it. Therefore,
$$$A'_i=L.sum+A_i$$$
and
$$$T'_i=L.cnt+T_i$$$
So the merge formulas are:
$$$sum=sum_L+sum_R$$$ $$$cnt=cnt_L+cnt_R$$$ $$$sumA=sumA_L+sumA_R+len_R\cdot sum_L$$$ $$$sumT=sumT_L+sumT_R+len_R\cdot cnt_L$$$ $$$sumA2=sumA2_L+sumA2_R+2sum_L\cdot sumA_R+len_R\cdot sum_L^2$$$ $$$sumAT=sumAT_L+sumAT_R+sum_L\cdot sumT_R+cnt_L\cdot sumA_R+len_R\cdot sum_L\cdot cnt_L$$$ $$$sumT2=sumT2_L+sumT2_R+2cnt_L\cdot sumT_R+len_R\cdot cnt_L^2$$$
Thus, the maintained information is closed under concatenation, so it is suitable for a segment tree.
A point update only changes one leaf, and then all nodes on the path to the root are recomputed.
For a range query, we merge $$$O(\log n)$$$ segment tree nodes in left-to-right order. This gives all values required by the formula above.
After precomputing factorials and inverse factorials for combinations, the total complexity is
$$$O((n+q)\log n)$$$

fanhuaxingyu's Solution
Solution
Let sum be the sum of all fixed values in the interval, and let cnt be the number of -1's.
If:

sum > m; or

cnt = 0 and sum ≠ m;

then no valid sequence exists, and the answer is 0.
The following discussion focuses only on valid cases.
For a single query, we have a simple brute-force approach with complexity $$$O(nm)$$$.
Let:

$$$A_i$$$: The sum of fixed values among the first $$$i$$$ positions;

$$$C_i$$$: The count of -1's among the first $$$i$$$ positions;

$$$rem = m - sum$$$.

Then:
$$$ \begin{aligned} f(c) &=\sum_{i=1}^n(A_i+x_i)^2 \\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=0}^{rem}\binom{j+C_i-1}{C_i-1} \binom{rem-j+cnt-C_i-1}{cnt-C_i-1}(A_i+j)^2 \end{aligned} $$$
Here, $$$x_i$$$ represents the total sum distributed to the first $$$C_i$$$ unknown variables (the -1's).
Fixing a prefix $$$i$$$, if the unknowns in this prefix are assigned a sum of $$$j$$$, then the suffix unknowns must be assigned $$$rem-j$$$.
The number of ways is given by the classic Stars and Bars method:
$$$ W_i(j)= \binom{j+C_i-1}{C_i-1} \binom{rem-j+cnt-C_i-1}{cnt-C_i-1}. $$$
However, this approach still has excessive complexity. We consider further optimization.
$$$ \begin{aligned} f(c) &=\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=0}^{rem}W_i(j)(A_i+j)^2 \\ &=\sum_{i=1}^nA_i^2\sum_{j=0}^{rem}W_i(j) +\sum_{i=1}^n2A_i\sum_{j=0}^{rem}jW_i(j) +\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=0}^{rem}jW_i(j) +\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=0}^{rem}j(j-1)W_i(j) \\ &=\binom{rem-1+cnt}{cnt-1}\sum_{i=1}^nA_i^2 +\binom{rem-1+cnt}{cnt}\sum_{i=1}^n(2A_i+1)C_i +\binom{rem-1+cnt}{cnt+1}\sum_{i=1}^nC_i(C_i+1) \end{aligned} $$$
This recurrence uses identity transformations: - $$$n\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}= k\binom{n+k-1}{k}$$$, - $$$n(n-1)\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}= k(k+1)\binom{n+k-1}{k+1}$$$, - $$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{k}{a}\binom{n-k}{m-a}=\binom{n+1}{m+1}$$$.
Thus, we obtain an $$$O(n)$$$ solution for the problem, which corresponds to the solution for E1.
How can we optimize further?
Observing the formula above, it becomes clear that if we can quickly maintain interval information such as:

$$$sum$$$,

$$$cnt$$$,

$$$\sum_{i=1}^nA_i^2$$$,

$$$\sum_{i=1}^nA_iC_i$$$,

$$$\sum_{i=1}^nC_i$$$,

$$$\sum_{i=1}^nC_i^2$$$,

a Segment Tree can handle these operations within $$$O(\log n)$$$ time complexity.
Therefore, the solution for E2 is to use a Segment Tree to optimize the recurrence formula, achieving a total time complexity of $$$O(M+(n+q)\log n)$$$.

Momoyo and the Network
PROGRAMMING
binary search dfs and similar divide and conquer dp trees

Add tag

The Underground Great Line Network is a grand transit system connecting all corners of Gensokyo. Momoyo noticed that the network's layout resembled a tree(^{\text{∗}}) structure. She couldn't help but imagine the most effective way to dismantle that tree. Given a tree with (n) nodes where node (i) has weight (a_i), select a simple path of exactly (k) edges and remove all edges on it. This splits the tree into (k+1) connected components, each with weight equal to the sum of its nodes' weights. You need to maximize the minimum component weight, or output (-1) if no simple path of exactly (k) edges exists. (^{\text{∗}})A tree is a connected graph without cycles. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (k) ((1 \le k \le n-1), (2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)). The second line contains (n) integers, where the (i)-th integer represents (a_i) ((1 \le a_i \le 10^9)). The next (n-1) lines each contain two integers (u) and (v), representing an edge of the tree. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2\cdot 10^5). For each test case, output the maximum possible minimum component weight, or (-1) if no such path exists. In the first test case, consider the path (3\to4). Removing this path yields components of weights (6) and (4). In the fourth test case, take the path (1\to2\to5). Removing this path yields components of weights (7), (6), and (9).
