2233A.title: AI Project Development
2233A.statement_text: Maxim and Nikita are working together on a project consisting of (n) lines of code. Maxim starts working immediately and writes at a speed of (x) lines per hour until the very end. Nikita has two options: not use AI and write from the very beginning at a speed of (y) lines per hour; spend (z) hours first setting up an AI agent, writing nothing during that time, and then write at a speed of (10 \cdot y) lines per hour. Nikita makes this choice before work begins and does not change it later. While Nikita is setting up the AI, he does not write any code at all, but Maxim continues working at the speed of (x) lines per hour. The project is considered completed as soon as Maxim and Nikita together have written at least (n) lines of code. If the project can be completed before the AI setup ends, then the work ends at that moment. Time is measured using full hours: if a project is completed in the middle of an hour, this hour is counted fully. Nikita chooses whether to use AI or not. Determine the minimum number of full hours after which the project will be completed. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 100)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains four integers (n), (x), (y), and (z) ((1 \le n, x, y, z \le 10\,000)) — the number of lines in the project, Maxim's speed, Nikita's speed without AI, and the AI setup time, respectively. For each test case, output one integer — the minimum number of full hours after which the project will be completed if Nikita acts optimally. In the first example, without using AI, Nikita and Maxim will write (2) lines of code in (1) hour, and since the project requires only (1) line to finish, it will be completed in (1) hour. In the fourth example, Nikita spends the first hour setting up the AI, while Maxim writes (10) lines during that time,
2233A.editorial_text:
2233A - AI Project Development
Let us consider both options and choose the minimum:

If Nikita does not use AI, then code is written at a rate of $$$(x + y)$$$ lines per hour, so the total number of hours is $$$\left\lceil\frac{n}{(x + y)}\right\rceil$$$; 
If Nikita uses AI, then during the first $$$z$$$ hours Maxim will write $$$x \cdot z$$$ lines and there will remain $$$n - x \cdot z$$$ lines to write, after which the total speed will be $$$(x + 10 \cdot y)$$$ lines per hour, so the total number of hours will be $$$z + \max(0, \left\lceil\frac{n - x \cdot z}{(x + 10 \cdot y)}\right\rceil)$$$. 
This solution works in $$$O(1)$$$.

2233B.title: Different Distances
2233B.statement_text: Construct an array of (4 \cdot n) integers such that: each number (1, 2, \dots, n) appears in the array exactly (4) times; let (p_{x, i}) be the position of the (i)-th occurrence of number (x) in the array; then, for each (x) from (1) to (n), the numbers ((p_{x, 2} - p_{x, 1}), (p_{x, 3} - p_{x, 2}), (p_{x, 4} - p_{x, 3})) must be pairwise distinct. For example, for (n = 3), one possible array is (1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3), because: (p_{1, 2} - p_{1, 1} = 1, p_{1, 3} - p_{1, 2} = 2, p_{1, 4} - p_{1, 3} = 3) — all numbers are distinct; (p_{2, 2} - p_{2, 1} = 2, p_{2, 3} - p_{2, 2} = 4, p_{2, 4} - p_{2, 3} = 1) — all numbers are distinct; (p_{3, 2} - p_{3, 1} = 2, p_{3, 3} - p_{3, 2} = 3, p_{3, 4} - p_{3, 3} = 1) — all numbers are distinct. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 200)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains one integer (n) ((2 \le n \le 200)). For each test case, output the required array. If there are several suitable arrays, output any of them. It can be shown that at least one suitable array always exists under the constraints of the problem.
2233B.editorial_text:
2233B - Different Distances
One solution is to construct a valid arrangement.
For $$$n = 2$$$, the following works: $$$[1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2]$$$, which means that for any even $$$n$$$ we can construct a solution of the form:
$$$$$$ [\color{red}{1}, \color{red}{2}, \color{red}{2}, \color{red}{1}, \color{red}{2}, \color{red}{1}, \color{red}{1}, \color{red}{2}, \color{blue}{3}, \color{blue}{4}, \color{blue}{4}, \color{blue}{3}, \color{blue}{4}, \color{blue}{3}, \color{blue}{3}, \color{blue}{4}, \ldots, \color{green}{n - 1}, \color{green}{n}, \color{green}{n}, \color{green}{n - 1}, \color{green}{n}, \color{green}{n - 1}, \color{green}{n - 1}, \color{green}{n}] $$$$$$
Blocks of the same color simply repeat the pattern.
For odd $$$n$$$, we proceed similarly: find an answer for $$$n = 3$$$ (for example, take the one from the statement) and construct a solution of the form:
$$$$$$ [\color{red}{1}, \color{red}{1}, \color{red}{2}, \color{red}{1}, \color{red}{2}, \color{red}{3}, \color{red}{1}, \color{red}{3}, \color{red}{2}, \color{red}{2}, \color{red}{3}, \color{red}{3}, \color{blue}{4}, \color{blue}{5}, \color{blue}{5}, \color{blue}{4}, \color{blue}{5}, \color{blue}{4}, \color{blue}{4}, \color{blue}{5}, \ldots, \color{green}{n - 1}, \color{green}{n}, \color{green}{n}, \color{green}{n - 1}, \color{green}{n}, \color{green}{n - 1}, \color{green}{n - 1}, \color{green}{n}] $$$$$$
An alternative solution is to honestly implement a check for the correctness of the array and then simply shuffle the array randomly. You remember problem $$$\texttt{E}$$$ from edu189, right? :)
It turns out that the probability of obtaining a correct array after one shuffle in the worst case is approximately $$$0.1$$$ for $$$n = 3$$$. For larger values of $$$n$$$, this probability is higher (this can be estimated using the Monte Carlo method).

2233C.title: Cost of a Bracket Sequence
2233C.statement_text: Let the cost of an arbitrary bracket string be the length of it's longest subsequence(^{\text{∗}}) that is a regular bracket sequence(^{\text{†}}). You are given a bracket string (s) and an integer (k). Your task is to remove at most (k) characters from the string (s) so that the cost of the resulting string is minimized. (^{\text{∗}})A sequence (a) is a subsequence of a sequence (b) if (a) can be obtained from (b) by the deletion of several (possibly, zero or all) element from arbitrary positions. (^{\text{†}})A bracket sequence is called regular if it is possible to obtain a correct arithmetic expression by inserting the characters (+) and (1) into this sequence. For example, the sequences "((())())", "(())", and "((()(())))" are regular, while "()()", "((())", and "((()))()" — are not. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^3)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (k) ((1 \le n \le 5\,000); (0 \le k \le n)) — the length of the string (s) and the maximum number of deletions. The second line of each test case contains a string (s) of length (n) consisting of the characters "(()" and/or "())". Additional input constraints: the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (5\,000). For each test case, output a binary string of length (n). The (i)-th character should be equal to " 1 " if the corresponding character of the string (s) is removed, and " 0 " otherwise. The number of ones in the string must not exceed (k). The cost of the string obtained after removing the marked characters must be as small as possible. If there are several answers, output any of them. In the first test case, the cost of th
2233C.editorial_text:
2233C - Cost of a Bracket Sequence
Solution $$$O(n^2)$$$:
The length of the maximum regular bracket subsequence (RBS) in the string depends on the maximum number of non-overlapping pairs of the following form: the bracket "$$$\texttt{(}$$$" is to the left of "$$$\texttt{)}$$$".
Each such pair contributes $$$2$$$ to the cost. Therefore, instead of minimizing the cost, we can minimize the number of such pairs. In the end, the cost will simply be twice as large.
Notice the following: to decrease the number of such pairs, it is beneficial to remove either the leftmost opening bracket or the rightmost closing bracket. Let us show this.
Suppose we have found the maximum number of pairs, and the leftmost opening bracket at position $$$i$$$ does not belong to any of the pairs. Consider one of the pairs $$$(j, k)$$$. Its opening bracket $$$j$$$ is to the right of the leftmost opening bracket $$$i \lt j$$$, which means that instead of the pair $$$(j, k)$$$, we can take the pair $$$(i, k)$$$. Therefore, there is no point in removing any opening bracket other than the leftmost one in order to decrease the maximum number of pairs.
Analogous reasoning can be applied to the rightmost closing bracket.
This observation allows us to write a simple solution in $$$O(n^2)$$$.
Let us iterate over the number $$$x$$$ — how many opening brackets on the prefix we remove. Then, on the suffix, we remove no more than $$$(k - x)$$$ closing brackets. The maximum subsequence that is an RBS in the string can be found in $$$O(n)$$$ using a simple greedy algorithm.
Solution $$$O(n)$$$:
For a faster solution, we need a not entirely trivial observation: the maximum number of pairs of the form where the bracket "$$$\texttt{(}$$$" is to the left of "$$$\texttt{)}$$$" is:
$$$$$$ \min_{i = 0}^{n} \,\,\,\texttt{pref_open}_{i} + \texttt{suff_close}_{i} $$$$$$
Let us prove this observation.
Denote the maximum number of pairs as $$$\texttt{pairs}$$$, and the minimum value of $$$\texttt{pref_open}_{i} + \texttt{suff_close}_{i}$$$ for some $$$i$$$ as $$$\min f$$$. Also denote
$$$$$$ \texttt{balance}_{i} = \texttt{pref_open}_{i} - \texttt{pref_close}_{i} $$$$$$
Then
$$$$$$ \texttt{suff_close}_{i} = \texttt{total_close} - \texttt{pref_close}_{i} $$$$$$
Therefore,
$$$$$$ \texttt{pref_open}_{i} + \texttt{suff_close}_{i} = \texttt{pref_open}_{i} + \texttt{total_close} - \texttt{pref_close}_{i} \\ = \texttt{total_close} + \texttt{balance}_{i} $$$$$$
Hence,
$$$$$$ \min f = \texttt{total_close} + \min_i \texttt{balance}_{i} $$$$$$
Now let us look at the greedy algorithm for finding the maximum number of pairs. We go from left to right: if we see "$$$\texttt{(}$$$", we put it into the reserve, and if we see "$$$\texttt{)}$$$" and there is an opening bracket in the reserve, then we form a pair.
A closing bracket remains unmatched only if, at the moment it is processed, there were more closing brackets than opening brackets before it. The total number of such unmatched closing brackets is equal to
$$$$$$ -\min_i \texttt{balance}_{i} $$$$$$
There are $$$\texttt{total_close}$$$ closing brackets in total, so the number of closing brackets that entered pairs is equal to
$$$$$$ \texttt{total_close} - (-\min_i \texttt{balance}_{i}) = \texttt{total_close} + \min_i \texttt{balance}_{i} $$$$$$
Each such closing bracket corresponds to exactly one pair, therefore
$$$$$$ \texttt{pairs} = \texttt{total_close} + \min_i \texttt{balance}_{i} = \min f $$$$$$
The observation is proven. $$$\blacksquare$$$
Therefore, in the solution, we find the corresponding cut $$$i$$$ that minimizes $$$\texttt{pref_open}_{i} + \texttt{suff_close}_{i}$$$, and remove $$$\le k$$$ arbitrary symbols from the set {opening brackets to the left of $$$i$$$ + closing brackets to the right of $$$i$$$}. Using prefix sums, this can be done in $$$O(n)$$$.

2233D.title: Goods on the Shelf
2233D.statement_text: In a supermarket, goods of the same type are usually placed next to each other so that the shelf looks neat and it is easier for customers to find what they need. The shelf is described by an array (a) of (n) elements, where (a_i) is the type of the good at position (i). We will say that the shelf is arranged correctly if for every two positions (i) and (j) such that (1 \le i \lt j \le n) and (a_i = a_j), the following condition holds: for each (k) from (i) to (j), it is true that (a_k = a_i). In other words, goods of each type on the shelf must form one contiguous block. You are allowed to choose two different positions at most once and swap the goods at these positions. You may also choose not to perform any swap. Determine whether it is possible to make the shelf arranged correctly after that. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains an integer (n) ((2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^{5})) — the number of goods on the shelf. The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_{i}) ((1 \le a_{i} \le 10^{9})), where (a_{i}) denotes the type of the good at position (i). Additional input constraints: the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^{5}). 2233E2.editorial_text:
2233E2 - Permutation Transmission (Difficult Version)
The main observation for solving the problem is that, for any permutation, the strings must be in nondecreasing order of the number of ones.
Let us prove this statement. Let $$$\texttt{cnt}_{k}$$$ denote the number of ones in the $$$k$$$-th bit among the numbers $$$1, 2, \ldots, n$$$. It is convenient to add the number $$$0$$$ as well. This changes nothing, because it adds a zero column. So we will prove the statement for the set of numbers $$$0, 1, 2, \ldots, n$$$.
We will prove that $$$\texttt{cnt}_{k} \ge \texttt{cnt}_{k + 1}$$$ for any $$$k$$$.
Consider only bits $$$k$$$ and $$$k + 1$$$. Split the numbers into blocks of length $$$2^{k + 2}$$$. Inside each full block, these two bits look like this by quarters:

$$$Q_{0}$$$: $$$00$$$ 
$$$Q_{1}$$$: $$$01$$$ 
$$$Q_{2}$$$: $$$10$$$ 
$$$Q_{3}$$$: $$$11$$$ 
where each quarter has length $$$2^{k}$$$.
In each full block:

in bit $$$k$$$, the ones are in quarters $$$Q_{1}$$$ and $$$Q_{3}$$$, and their total count is $$$2^{k} + 2^{k} = 2^{k + 1}$$$; 
in bit $$$k + 1$$$, the ones are in quarters $$$Q_{2}$$$ and $$$Q_{3}$$$, and their total count is $$$2^{k} + 2^{k} = 2^{k + 1}$$$. 
So full blocks contribute equally.
Only the last incomplete block remains. In it, the number of ones in each bit grows as follows:

in $$$Q_{0}$$$, no ones are added to either bit; 
in $$$Q_{1}$$$, ones are added only to bit $$$k$$$; 
in $$$Q_{2}$$$, ones are added only to bit $$$k + 1$$$, but bit $$$k$$$ has already gained an advantage in $$$Q_{1}$$$; 
in $$$Q_{3}$$$, ones are added to both bits simultaneously. 
Therefore, for any incomplete block, the number of ones in bit $$$k$$$ is at least the number of ones in bit $$$k + 1$$$.
Hence, $$$\texttt{cnt}_{k} \ge \texttt{cnt}_{k + 1}$$$. $$$\blacksquare$$$
The next useful observation is that if $$$\texttt{cnt}_{k} = \texttt{cnt}_{k + 1}$$$, then bits $$$k$$$ and $$$k + 1$$$ can be swapped and the set of numbers $$$0, 1, 2, \ldots, n$$$ does not change.
To prove this, we use the same idea and again consider blocks of length $$$2^{k + 2}$$$. Swapping bits $$$k$$$ and $$$k + 1$$$ inside a block does the following:

$$$Q_{0}$$$ remains $$$Q_{0}$$$; 
$$$Q_{1}$$$ becomes $$$Q_{2}$$$; 
$$$Q_{2}$$$ becomes $$$Q_{1}$$$; 
$$$Q_{3}$$$ remains $$$Q_{3}$$$. 
So inside a block, this is just a swap of the two middle quarters.
If $$$\texttt{cnt}_{k} = \texttt{cnt}_{k + 1}$$$, then from the reasoning above the last incomplete block must end either in $$$Q_{0}$$$ or in $$$Q_{3}$$$. In either case, the last block is invariant under swapping the middle quarters:

if the last block ends in $$$Q_{0}$$$, then $$$Q_{1}$$$ and $$$Q_{2}$$$ do not exist; 
if the last block ends in $$$Q_{3}$$$, then $$$Q_{1}$$$ and $$$Q_{2}$$$ are complete, and swapping them changes nothing. 
Therefore, swapping bits $$$k$$$ and $$$k + 1$$$ for which $$$\texttt{cnt}_{k} = \texttt{cnt}_{k + 1}$$$ does not change the set $$$0, 1, 2, \ldots, n$$$. $$$\blacksquare$$$
After proving these facts, the solution becomes very simple. Sort all strings by non-increasing number of ones and check that in this order they form a permutation of the numbers $$$1, 2, \ldots, n$$$; if not, the answer is $$$0$$$.
Then compute the array $$$c_i$$$ — the number of strings containing exactly $$$i$$$ ones. The answer is:
$$$$$$ \prod_i c_i! $$$$$$

2233F.title: Shortest GCD Paths
2233F.statement_text: You are given three integers (n), (a), (b). Consider a weighted undirected graph with (n) vertices, where for every pair of distinct vertices ((u, v)) there is an edge with weight: () w(u, v) = \frac{\max(u, v)}{\gcd(u, v)} () Here (\gcd(x, y)) denotes the greatest common divisor (GCD) of integers (x) and (y). Find the shortest path from vertex (a) to vertex (b) in this graph. The only line contains three integers (n), (a), (b) ((2 \le n \le 10^{9}, 1 \le a, b \le n, a \neq b)). Print one integer — the length of the shortest path from vertex (a) to vertex (b). Consider the first example. The shortest path in it is (9 \to 6 \to 8) with total cost (w(9, 6) + w(6, 8) = 3 + 4 = 7).
2233F.editorial_text:
2233F - Shortest GCD Paths
We cannot build the graph directly and search for the shortest path in it, because $$$n$$$ can be very large. Instead, let us look for useful properties of such a graph.
Notice that for any vertices $$$u, v$$$ and any natural number $$$x$$$, we have $$$w(u \cdot x, v \cdot x) = w(u, v)$$$, because both the maximum and the gcd are multiplied by the same value $$$x$$$.
As a consequence, we may assume that $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ can be divided by $$$\gcd(a, b)$$$. That is, if $$$g = \gcd(a, b)$$$, then the shortest path between $$$a' = \frac{a}{g}$$$ and $$$b' = \frac{b}{g}$$$ has the same length as the shortest path between $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$.
Let us prove this carefully. Our proof will consist of two parts:

from a shortest path for ($$$a'$$$, $$$b'$$$), we can obtain a path of the same length for ($$$a$$$, $$$b$$$); 
from a shortest path for ($$$a$$$, $$$b$$$), we can obtain a path of no greater length for ($$$a'$$$, $$$b'$$$). 
The first part follows easily from our property: take all vertices on the shortest path for ($$$a'$$$, $$$b'$$$) and multiply them by $$$g$$$. The weight of every edge on this path remains unchanged.
Now let us prove the second part. Define the operation $$$f(x, y)$$$ for a natural number $$$x$$$ and a positive prime number $$$y$$$ as follows:
$$$$$$ f(x, y) = \begin{cases} x & \quad \text{if } x \text{ is not divisible by } y \\ \frac{x}{y} & \quad \text{if } x \text{ is divisible by } y \end{cases} $$$$$$
We claim that this operation does not increase the weight of an edge if applied to both endpoints of the edge. That is, for any vertices $$$u, v$$$ and any positive prime $$$x$$$, we have $$$w(u, v) \ge w(f(u, x), f(v, x))$$$:

if $$$x$$$ divides both endpoints of the edge, then both $$$\max$$$ and $$$\gcd$$$ are divided by $$$x$$$, so the weight does not change; 
if $$$x$$$ divides neither endpoint, then nothing changes; 
if $$$x$$$ divides exactly one endpoint, then $$$\max$$$ does not increase, while $$$\gcd$$$ does not decrease, so the weight does not increase. 
Also define the operation $$$f'(x, y)$$$ for natural numbers $$$x$$$, $$$y$$$ as follows:
$$$$$$ f'(x, y) = f(f(\ldots f(f(x, p_1), p_2) \ldots), p_k) $$$$$$
for such $$$p_{i}$$$ that $$$\displaystyle\prod_{i = 1}^{k} p_{i} = y$$$. In other words, $$$f'(x, y)$$$ removes from $$$x$$$ the prime factors that are present in $$$y$$$.
Now let us apply the operation $$$f'$$$ to every vertex $$$v$$$ of the shortest path for ($$$a$$$, $$$b$$$), that is, replace every vertex $$$v$$$ with $$$f'(v, g)$$$. If two neighboring vertices become equal after this replacement, simply remove one of them from the path.
We obtain a path for ($$$\frac{a}{g}$$$, $$$\frac{b}{g}$$$) whose length has not increased, and this is exactly a path for ($$$a'$$$, $$$b'$$$).
Thus, we have proved that:

the shortest path for ($$$a$$$, $$$b$$$) is no longer than the shortest path for ($$$a'$$$, $$$b'$$$); 
the shortest path for ($$$a'$$$, $$$b'$$$) is no longer than the shortest path for ($$$a$$$, $$$b$$$). 
Therefore, the lengths of the shortest paths for ($$$a$$$, $$$b$$$) and ($$$a'$$$, $$$b'$$$) are equal. $$$\blacksquare$$$
From now on, we will assume that $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ are coprime.
The next observation is that the shortest path will use only vertices that are divisors of $$$a \cdot b$$$. Indeed, if some intermediate vertices on the path are divisible by some factor that is not present in $$$a \cdot b$$$, then for each such vertex $$$v$$$, replace it with $$$\gcd(v, a \cdot b)$$$. This replacement does not increase the weight of any edge: we are only removing extra prime factors from the endpoints of edges. Therefore, there exists an optimal path in which all vertices are divisors of $$$a \cdot b$$$.
Taking all observations above into account, we can view a transition along some edge as an operation that removes some factor $$$d_{a}$$$ from $$$a$$$ and adds some factor $$$d_{b}$$$ from $$$b$$$, where these factors are coprime. The cost of such an operation is $$$\max(d_{a}, d_{b})$$$. Let us show why this is true.
Suppose the current vertex has the form $$$\frac{a}{d_a} \cdot d_b$$$. If we additionally remove a factor $$$p$$$ from $$$a$$$ and add a factor $$$q$$$ from $$$b$$$, then the new vertex is $$$\frac{a}{d_a \cdot p} \cdot d_b \cdot q$$$. The two vertices share the common part $$$\frac{a}{d_a \cdot p} \cdot d_b$$$, so the weight of the edge is equal to $$$\max(p, q)$$$.
Let us write the following dynamic programming solution: let $$$\texttt{dp}[d_{a}][d_{b}]$$$ denote the minimum total cost of operations needed to remove the factor $$$d_{a}$$$ from $$$a$$$ and add the factor $$$d_{b}$$$ from $$$b$$$. The answer will be $$$\texttt{dp}[a][b]$$$. The transitions are quite simple: for each state ($$$d_{a}, d_{b}$$$), iterate over $$$p$$$ (it will be a divisor of $$$\frac{a}{d_{a}}$$$) and iterate over $$$q$$$ (it will be a divisor of $$$\frac{b}{d_{b}}$$$), and then transition to the state $$$\texttt{dp}[d_{a} \cdot p][d_{b} \cdot q]$$$.
Why does this work fast? Let $$$\tau(x)$$$ be the number of divisors of $$$x$$$. Then the number of states is $$$\tau(a) \cdot \tau(b)$$$, and the number of transitions is:
$$$$$$ \displaystyle\sum_{d_{a} | a} \sum_{d_{b} | b} \tau(\frac{a}{d_{a}}) \cdot \tau(\frac{b}{d_{b}}) = \displaystyle\sum_{d_{a} | a} \sum_{d_{b} | b} \tau(d_{a}) \cdot \tau(d_{b}) $$$$$$
This can be transformed into:
$$$$$$ \displaystyle\sum_{d_{a} | a} \tau(d_{a}) \cdot \sum_{d_{b} | b} \tau(d_{b}) $$$$$$
$$$\tau(x)$$$ is an arithmetic function with the important property $$$\tau(x \cdot y) = \tau(x) \cdot \tau(y)$$$ if $$$\gcd(x, y) = 1$$$, so from the expression
$$$$$$ \displaystyle\sum_{d_{a} | a} \tau(d_{a}) $$$$$$
we can move to the expression
$$$$$$ \displaystyle\prod_{p_{i}} \sum_{e = 0}^{k_{i}} \tau(p_{i}^{e}) $$$$$$
for such $$$p_{i}$$$ that $$$a = p_{0}^{k_{0}} \cdot p_{1}^{k_{1}} \cdot \ldots$$$, where $$$p_{i}$$$ is some prime number from the prime factorization of $$$a$$$.
It is known that $$$\tau(p^e) = e + 1$$$, where $$$p$$$ is prime.
Therefore:
$$$$$$ \displaystyle\prod_{p_{i}} \sum_{e = 0}^{k_{i}} \tau(p_{i}^{e}) = \displaystyle\prod_{p_{i}} \frac{(k_{i} + 1) \cdot (k_{i} + 2)}{2} $$$$$$
Since $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ are coprime, the number of transitions is:
$$$$$$ \displaystyle\sum_{d_{a} | a} \tau(d_{a}) \cdot \sum_{d_{b} | b} \tau(d_{b}) = \displaystyle\prod_{p_{i}} \frac{(k_{i} + 1) \cdot (k_{i} + 2)}{2} $$$$$$
where $$$p_{i}$$$ is a prime number in the factorization of $$$a \cdot b$$$, and $$$k_{i}$$$ is its corresponding exponent.
By the constraints of the problem, $$$a, b \le 10^{9}$$$, hence $$$a \cdot b \le 10^{18}$$$. The maximum value of this function for numbers up to $$$10^{18}$$$ can be found by brute-forcing possible sets of exponents in the factorization, similarly to how highly composite numbers are found. Coincidentally, the maximum value of the function is attained at the same number $$$897612484786617600$$$, which has the maximum number of divisors ($$$103680$$$). The number of transitions for this number is approximately $$$1.6 \cdot 10^{8}$$$. Thus, with a careful implementation, this easily fits within the time limit.
P.S.
The most attentive readers may have noticed an inaccuracy in the proof of the validity of dividing $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$ by $$$g$$$: when multiplying by $$$g$$$, some vertex of the path for ($$$a'$$$, $$$b'$$$) could become greater than $$$n$$$. However, this will not happen, because our solution is able to construct a path such that every intermediate vertex is no greater than $$$\max(a', b')$$$.

2236A.title: Games on the Train
2236A.statement_text: Dabir, Egor, and Arseniy just got on the train and decided to play a game. Dabir has a backpack with an infinite number of cubes. He built (n) towers from them, where the (i)-th tower has height (h_i) cubes. Egor and Arseniy must choose an integer (x_i) for each tower (i) and increase its height by (x_i) exactly once . For example, if (h) = (1, 3, 2, 2), (x) = (3, 2, 2, 8), then after increasing (h) it will become (4, 5, 4, 10). Their goal is to make the heights of all towers equal. To make the game more interesting, Dabir wants to choose an integer (k) and add a restriction: each (x_i) must satisfy (1 \le x_i \le k). Help him find the smallest (k) for which it is possible to finish the game. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. Then (t) test cases follow. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 5)). The second line contains (n) integers (h_1, h_2, \dots, h_n) ((1 \le h_i \le 6)). For each test case, output a single integer — the minimum value of (k) such that it is possible to make all towers have equal height.
2236A.editorial_text:
2236A - Games on the Train
Let the maximum element be $$$mx$$$ and the minimum element be $$$mn$$$. Note that $$$1 \le x_i \le k$$$. After increasing the heights, the new height of the maximum will be at least $$$mx + 1$$$, and the new height of the minimum will be at most $$$mn + k$$$.
After the changes, all heights must become equal, so the new maximum must be equal to the new minimum. Therefore, the game can be finished if $$$k$$$ satisfies $$$mn + k \ge mx + 1$$$, that is, $$$k \ge mx - mn + 1$$$.
It can be shown that it is always possible to make all heights equal with $$$k = mx - mn + 1$$$, so this is the answer.

2236B.title: Tatar TV Show
2236B.statement_text: During the holidays, Egor came to visit his friend Dabir in the city of Kazan. Out of boredom, Dabir and Egor came up with a new business idea: to make their own TV show. The format of the show is very simple: in each episode they invite a guest and play a game with them on a binary string. In today's episode, Egor and Dabir invited Arseniy (aka MAKAN) — the main celebrity of Omsk. For the game, they chose a binary string (s) of length (n) and an integer (k). Arseniy can make an unlimited number of moves. In one move, he can choose an integer (i) ((1 \le i \le n - k)) and invert the characters at positions (i) and (i + k), that is, change (0) to (1) and (1) to (0). For example, if (s = 10110) and (k = 2), then by choosing (i = 2), Arseniy inverts the characters at positions (2) and (4): ( 10110 \rightarrow 11100 ) Arseniy wants to get the main prize — (1\,000\,000) tugriks. To do this, he needs to make the entire string (s) equal to zero. Help Arseniy determine whether he can get his prize, or if he will have to return to Omsk with nothing. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (k) ((1 \le k \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)). The second line of each test case contains a binary string (s) of length (n). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output " YES " if Arseniy can make the string entirely zero, and " NO " otherwise. You can output " YES " and " NO " in any case (for example, " yES ", " yes ", and " Yes " will be accepted).

2236C.title: Omsk Programmers
2236C.statement_text: An annual programmers fair is taking place on the main square of Omsk. You, as the main programmer of Omsk, decided to take part in this wonderful event and went there. At the entrance, a guard decided to check your skills and gave you a problem: You are given three integers (a), (b), (x). You want to make (a) and (b) equal. In order to do so, you can apply the following operations: Choose one of the integers (a) or (b) and add (1) to it. Choose one of the integers (a) or (b) and divide it by (x) with rounding down. You need to find the minimum number of operations after which (a) becomes equal to (b). Can you prove your skills, or will you have to go back home? The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. Then (t) test cases follow. Each test case consists of a single line containing three integers (a), (b), (x) ((1 \le a, b \le 10^9), (2 \le x \le 10^9)). For each test case, output a single integer — the minimum number of operations required to make (a) and (b) equal.
2236C.editorial_text:
2236C - Omsk Programmers
First, we describe an algorithm that finds the optimal answer, and then we prove that it is indeed optimal.
The algorithm is as follows: suppose the current state is described by a pair of numbers $$$(p, q)$$$. Without loss of generality, assume $$$p \leq q$$$, and let $$$cnt$$$ be the number of divisions already performed. We try to update the answer with the value $$$q - p + cnt$$$. If the numbers are equal, we stop. Otherwise, we repeat the process with the pair $$$(p, q / x)$$$.
Now let us prove its correctness. The key idea of the algorithm is that it is optimal to perform all integer divisions first, and only then make the numbers equal using operations of adding $$$+1$$$. Suppose this is not true. Then at some point we applied $$$+1$$$ to a number $$$p$$$, and then applied $$$/= x$$$. Consider two cases:
$$$ \lfloor \frac{p}{x} \rfloor = \lfloor \frac{p + 1}{x} \rfloor $$$.
In this case, the $$$+1$$$ operation had no effect at all, so it could have been skipped, reducing the total number of operations.
$$$ \lfloor \frac{p}{x} \rfloor + 1 = \lfloor \frac{p + 1}{x} \rfloor $$$.
In this case, we can swap the order of operations: first apply $$$/= x$$$, and then apply $$$+1$$$. The result and the number of operations remain the same, while the desired property holds.
Thus, the lemma is proven, which establishes the correctness of the algorithm.
The time complexity of the solution is $$$O(\log_x(a) + \log_x(b))$$$ per test case.

2236D.title: Brand New Tatar TV Show
2236D.statement_text: Dabir and Egor were not satisfied with the fame from the previous episode, so they decided to make another TV show: the guys play their favorite game on an array (a) with their favorite integer (k). Dabir moves first. On the first move, any element from the array can be chosen and removed. Let the previous chosen element be equal to (x). Then on the current move, except the very first one, a player must choose an element (y) from the array such that (0 \leq y - x \leq k) and remove it from the array. The player who cannot make a move loses. But since this was not just a game, but a real show-match, Arseniy (aka MAKAN) — the main celebrity of Omsk was invited again. As a guest celebrity, Arseniy was given the opportunity to make the first move in this match, that is, to make the very first move in the game instead of Dabir . However, it turns out Arseniy is a fan of Egor, so he wants his first move to guarantee Egor a winning strategy against any response from Dabir. Determine whether Arseniy can make the first move for Dabir so that, no matter how Dabir plays, Egor wins. Each test consists of multiple test cases. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (k) ((1 \leq n, k \leq 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the length of the array and the favorite integer of Dabir and Egor. The second line contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) ((1 \leq a_i \leq n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, if there exists such a first move that with optimal play by both players Egor wins, output " YES ", otherwise output " NO ". You can output " YES " and " NO " in any case (for example, " yES ", " yes ", and " Yes " will be accepted). In the first example, the only possible option is to choose the integer (3). After that, the array [
2236D.editorial_text:
2236D - Brand New Tatar TV Show
Observe the following: if the players start taking the maximum element from the array, they will keep taking it until all its occurrences are exhausted.
Based on this observation, consider the following algorithm:
Let the current maximum in the array be $$$mx$$$, and let its count be $$$cnt$$$. If $$$cnt$$$ is even, then Arseniy can take $$$mx$$$ on the first move. Then, by parity, Egor will win, so the answer is YES.
Otherwise, if the difference between the maximum and the second maximum in the array is not greater than $$$k$$$, then Arseniy can take the second maximum on the first move. After that, Egor will take the maximum and win by parity. The answer is YES.
If there is no second maximum in the array (i.e., all remaining elements are equal), then the answer is NO.
Otherwise, we can remove all occurrences of the maximum from the array and continue the algorithm on the modified array.
Now consider when the answer is NO. This happens if the difference between every pair of consecutive distinct values is greater than $$$k$$$, and the count of each value is odd. In these cases, no valid move sequence can help, and Egor will lose regardless of the play.
In all other cases, Arseniy can choose the first move so that Egor wins.
The overall time complexity is $$$O(n \cdot \log n)$$$ due to sorting and compressing the array.

2236E.title: Friendly Gifts
2236E.statement_text: Arseniy decided to make his friends Dabir and Egor happy. For this, he decided to give each of them an array of numbers of the same length . An array (b) is called good if its elements can be rearranged so that for all (i \gt 1) the condition (b_i - b_{i - 1} = 1) holds. Arseniy wants Dabir and Egor to be able to play with these arrays. For this, the following conditions must be satisfied: Each of the given arrays is good . If you write one array after the other (in other words, concatenate them), the resulting array is also good . Arseniy already has an array (a) of length (n). He plans to cut both arrays from (a), that is, to choose two non-overlapping subsegments of the same length . Help Arseniy determine the maximum possible length of the resulting arrays. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 1000)) — the number of test cases. Then (t) test cases follow. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 6000)). The second line contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) ((1 \le a_i \le n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (6000). For each test case, output a single integer — the maximum possible length of the arrays. In the first sample, it is impossible to select (2) arrays, so the answer is (0). In the second sample, the maximum length of the selected arrays is (1). Arrays (1) and (2) can be selected. In the fourth sample, the maximum length of the selected arrays is (2). You can select arrays (2, 1) and (4, 3). In the fifth sample, the maximum length of the selected arrays is (1). One way to select arrays is (1) and (2). Other methods are arrays (2) and (3), (3) and (4), or (4) and (5).
2236E.editorial_text:
2236E - Friendly Gifts
First, note an important observation: since good arrays must remain good after concatenation, the chosen subsegments of the array must not overlap.
The condition for a segment to be a good array is actually equivalent to the following: all numbers on the segment are distinct and $$$max - min = r - l$$$. Therefore, we can iterate over all subsegments of the array, and if a segment is good, store this information in a separate array: $$$good_{min, max} = 1$$$ (meaning that there exists a good segment with these $$$min$$$ and $$$max$$$). This can be implemented in $$$O(n^2)$$$ time.
Next, iterate over the answer from $$$\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor$$$ down to $$$0$$$, and consider the segment of values that will correspond to the concatenation of two subsegments of the array. To check feasibility, we need to verify that both segments exist, i.e., that $$$good_{l, l + ans - 1}$$$ and $$$good_{l + ans, l + 2 \cdot ans - 1}$$$ hold. If such a segment exists for the current value of $$$ans$$$, we output it and stop; otherwise, we continue.
The overall time complexity of the solution is $$$O(n^2)$$$.

2236F1.title: Elections in Saransk (easy version)
2236F1.statement_text: This is the easy version of the problem. The only difference is that (x = 1) On the way home after buying his favorite soda "Zola Cero", Egor saw that elections for the position of "Best Number" are taking place in Saransk. There are (n) people at the polling station. Each person brought a number (a_i). When the (i)-th person enters the voting booth, they choose a candidate that is a divisor of the number (a_i). Let the chosen candidate be (p_i). After everyone has voted, we get an array of votes (p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n). Egor really likes the number (x) and considers the voting ideal if (x \cdot {lcm}(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n))(^{\text{∗}}) = (p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot p_n). Help him find the number of different(^{\text{†}}) arrays (p) modulo (10^9 + 7) that are ideal. (^{\text{∗}})(lcm) — least common multiple . (^{\text{†}})Two arrays of votes are considered different if there exists an index (i) where the two arrays have different elements. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 10^4)) — the number of test cases. Then (t) test cases follow. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (x) ((1 \leq n \leq 10^5), (x = 1)) — the number of voters at the polling station and Egor's favorite number. The second line of each test case contains (n) integers: (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) ((1 \leq a_i \leq 5 \cdot 10^5)) — the numbers brought by the voters. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (10^5). For each test case, output the number of ways modulo (10^9 + 7) to vote so that the resulting array of votes satisfies the condition.
2236F1.editorial_text:
2236F1 - Elections in Saransk (easy version)
First, observe that for an array $$$p = [p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n]$$$ to satisfy $$$\mathrm{lcm}(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n) = p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot p_n,$$$ it is necessary and sufficient that $$$\gcd(p_i, p_j) = 1$$$ for all pairs $$$i \ne j$$$, i.e., all elements are pairwise coprime.
Now fix a prime number $$$\texttt{prime}$$$. Let $$$v_{\texttt{prime}}(x)$$$ denote the exponent of $$$\texttt{prime}$$$ in the prime factorization of $$$x$$$ (that is, the largest power $$$k$$$ such that $$$\texttt{prime}^k \mid x$$$).
Since all $$$p_i$$$ must be pairwise coprime, for each fixed prime $$$\texttt{prime}$$$, at most one element of the array $$$p$$$ can be divisible by $$$\texttt{prime}$$$.
Let us count the number of ways to assign this prime $$$\texttt{prime}$$$ across the array $$$p$$$. For each index $$$i$$$, the value $$$p_i$$$ must divide $$$a_i$$$, so the exponent of $$$\texttt{prime}$$$ in $$$p_i$$$ can be any integer from $$$0$$$ to $$$v_{\texttt{prime}}(a_i)$$$.
Thus, there are two types of choices: either the prime $$$\texttt{prime}$$$ does not appear in any $$$p_i$$$ (all exponents are $$$0$$$), or we choose exactly one index $$$i$$$, and assign to $$$p_i$$$ a positive exponent from $$$1$$$ to $$$v_{\texttt{prime}}(a_i)$$$.
Therefore, the total number of ways to handle this prime is: $$$1 + \sum_{i=1}^n v_{\texttt{prime}}(a_i)$$$, where: the $$$1$$$ corresponds to the case when the prime is not used at all, and each $$$v_{\texttt{prime}}(a_i)$$$ corresponds to choosing index $$$i$$$ and one of its possible positive exponents.
Finally, since different primes are independent, we multiply the number of ways over all primes that appear in at least one $$$a_i$$$. The final answer is: $$$\prod_{\texttt{pr}: \ \exists i,\ \texttt{pr} \mid a_i} \left(1 + \sum_{i=1}^n v_{\texttt{pr}}(a_i)\right)$$$.

2236F2.title: Elections in Saransk (hard version)
2236F2.statement_text: This is the hard version of the problem. The only difference is that (1 \le x \le 5 \cdot 10^5) . On the way home after buying his favorite soda "Zola Cero", Egor saw that elections for the position of "Best Number" are taking place in Saransk. There are (n) people at the polling station. Each person brought a number (a_i). When the (i)-th person enters the voting booth, they choose a candidate that is a divisor of the number (a_i). Let the chosen candidate be (p_i). After everyone has voted, we get an array of votes (p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n). Egor really likes the number (x) and considers the voting ideal if (x \cdot {lcm}(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n))(^{\text{∗}}) = (p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot p_n). Help him find the number of different(^{\text{†}}) arrays (p) modulo (10^9 + 7) that are ideal. (^{\text{∗}})(lcm) — least common multiple . (^{\text{†}})Two arrays of votes are considered different if there exists an index (i) where the two arrays have different elements. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 10^4)) — the number of test cases. Then (t) test cases follow. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (x) ((1 \leq n \leq 10^5), (1 \leq x \leq 5 \cdot 10^5)) — the number of voters at the polling station and Egor's favorite number. The second line of each test case contains (n) integers: (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) ((1 \leq a_i \leq 5 \cdot 10^5)) — the numbers brought by the voters. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (10^5). For each test case, output the number of ways modulo (10^9 + 7) to vote so that the resulting array of votes satisfies the condition.
2236F2.editorial_text:
2236F2 - Elections in Saransk (hard version)
Let us again fix a prime number $$$pr$$$ and consider the condition for it separately.
For the array $$$p = [p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n]$$$ to satisfy $$$x \cdot \mathrm{lcm}(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n) = p_1 \cdot p_2 \cdot \ldots \cdot p_n$$$, for each prime $$$pr$$$ the following must hold: $$$\max(v_{pr}(p_i)) + v_{pr}(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n v_{pr}(p_i)$$$. Therefore, $$$v_{pr}(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n v_{pr}(p_i) - \max(v_{pr}(p_i))$$$.
Here $$$v_{pr}(x)$$$ denotes the exponent of the prime $$$pr$$$ in the prime factorization of $$$x$$$.
We precompute all values $$$v_{pr}(a_i)$$$ for $$$a_i \le 5 \cdot 10^5$$$ in $$$O(\log a_i)$$$ per number by using a sieve of Eratosthenes to find the smallest prime divisor.
Now consider two cases for each prime $$$pr$$$. As in the easy version, the final answer is the product of contributions over all primes.
1. If $$$pr$$$ does not divide $$$x$$$ (i.e., $$$v_{pr}(x) = 0$$$), then the condition simplifies to $$$\sum_{i=1}^n v_{pr}(p_i) = \max(v_{pr}(p_i))$$$, which means that at most one $$$p_i$$$ can have a positive exponent of $$$pr$$$. This is exactly the same as in the easy version, so the contribution is $$$1 + \sum_{i=1}^n v_{pr}(a_i)$$$.
2. If $$$pr$$$ divides $$$x$$$ (i.e., $$$v_{pr}(x) = vp \gt 0$$$), we solve the subproblem using dynamic programming.
Define $$$dp[i][mx][s]$$$ as the number of ways to choose values for the first $$$i$$$ elements such that: 

the current maximum exponent is $$$mx = \max(v_{pr}(p_1), \ldots, v_{pr}(p_i))$$$, 
the sum of exponents is $$$s = \sum_{j=1}^i v_{pr}(p_j)$$$. 
Here $$$0 \le v_{pr}(p_i) \le v_{pr}(a_i)$$$.
The answer for this prime is: $$$\sum dp[n][mx][vp + mx]$$$, over all $$$mx$$$ such that $$$1 \le vp + mx \le S$$$, where $$$S = \sum_{i=1}^n v_{pr}(a_i)$$$.
Note that in practice $$$vp + mx \le \min(S, 36)$$$, since $$$v_{pr}(a_i) \le 18$$$.
Transitions: 

If the chosen exponent $$$e$$$ does not increase the maximum (i.e., $$$e \le mx$$$): $$$dp[i][mx][s] += dp[i-1][mx][s - e]$$$.
If the chosen exponent becomes a new maximum (i.e., $$$e \gt old_mx$$$, so $$$mx = e$$$): $$$dp[i][mx][s] += dp[i-1][old_mx][s - mx]$$$. 
Initial state: $$$ dp[0][0][0] = 1. $$$
The complexity of this solution is: $$$ O(A \cdot \log(a_i)^3 \cdot n), $$$ where $$$A$$$ is the number of distinct prime divisors of $$$x$$$ (and $$$A \le 7$$$).
Note that in both transitions we can eliminate one loop with prefix sum: 

in the first transition — over $$$e$$$, 
in the second transition — over $$$old_mx$$$. 
This improves the complexity to: $$$O(A \cdot \log(a_i)^2 \cdot n)$$$.

2236G.title: Criterion in Burlandia
2236G.statement_text: Regions in Burlandia form a graph with (n) vertices and (n-1) edges, and there is exactly one path between any two vertices. Formally, the regions form a tree. Each region has a friendliness value (a_i). There are (q) queries. In each query, a pair of friends located in different regions is given. They want to know how many subsegments of the path between these regions are hospitable . It is known that in Burlandia there are two criteria for evaluating relationships — XOR and sum. A subsegment of the path, containing some vertices lying on the path from region (x) to region (y), is called hospitable if it is non-empty and the sum of friendliness values on this subsegment does not exceed their XOR. More formally, for each query you are given two vertices (x) and (y) ((x \neq y)). Consider the shortest path from vertex (x) to vertex (y) in the tree. Let the vertices (v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_k) form this path, where (v_1 = x), (v_k = y). You need to find the number of subsegments of this path for which the following condition holds: () a_{v_{l}} \oplus a_{v_{l+1}} \oplus \ldots \oplus a_{v_{r}} \geq (a_{v_{l}} + a_{v_{l+1}} + \ldots + a_{v_{r}}), () where (1 \leq l \leq r \leq k) — the boundaries of the subsegment of vertices on the path from (x) to (y). Each test consists of multiple test cases. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \leq t \leq 10^4)) — the number of test cases. Then the descriptions of the test cases follow. The first line of each test case contains integers (n) ((2 \leq n \leq 10^5)) — the number of vertices in the tree, and (q) ((1 \leq q \leq 10^5)) — the number of queries. The second line contains an array of (n) non-negative integers — the friendliness values of the regions ((0 \leq a_i \lt 2^{20})). The next (n - 1) lines describe the edges of the tree: each line contains integers (u, v) ((1 \leq u, v \leq n))
2236G.editorial_text:
2236G - Criterion in Burlandia
Let us first analyze the condition. For non-negative integers, the XOR is always less than or equal to their sum. Therefore, since a good segment requires the XOR to be at least the sum, it must be that XOR equals the sum.
This equality holds if and only if each bit appears at most once across all numbers in the segment. Hence, the segment can contain at most $$$log(A)$$$ non-zero elements.
First, for each vertex $$$v$$$, let us find the closest ancestor $$$bad_v$$$ such that on the path from $$$v$$$ to $$$bad_v$$$, there exists a bit that appears at least twice (i.e., the condition of a good segment is violated).
Now consider how to answer a query for a path between vertices $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$. Assume the path is not purely vertical (the vertical case is handled similarly). Let $$$t$$$ be their LCA. We want to separately count: 

segments lying entirely on the path from $$$u$$$ to $$$t$$$, 
segments lying entirely on the path from $$$t$$$ to $$$v$$$, 
segments that pass through $$$t$$$. 
However, if we simply sum values of the form $$$d_x - d_{bad_x}$$$ along the path from $$$u$$$ to $$$t$$$, we may overcount, because for some vertices $$$x$$$, the corresponding $$$bad_x$$$ may lie above $$$t$$$.
To handle this, recall that any valid segment contains at most $$$log(A)$$$ non-zero elements. Therefore, we can move $$$t$$$ down by $$$log(A) + \varepsilon$$$ non-zero elements in both directions (towards $$$u$$$ and towards $$$v$$$). This can be done using level ancestor (LA) queries on a compressed tree.
The resulting middle path has length at most $$$2 \cdot log(A)$$$ and can be processed naively: 

either in $$$O(log(A)^2)$$$ by brute force, 
or in $$$O(log(A))$$$ using a two-pointer technique. 
The remaining parts of the path can be processed by summing values $$$d_x - d_{bad_x}$$$, for example using binary lifting.
The overall complexity of the solution is: $$$O(n \cdot (log(n) + log(A)))$$$ or $$$O(n \cdot (log(n) + log(A)^2))$$$, depending on the implementation.
The official solution uses the two-pointer approach.

2237A.editorial_text:
2237A - Destroying Towers
Optimally, go from left to right in that order. After this, the height of tower $$$i$$$ will be $$$\min(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_i)$$$, so the minimum sum is $$$a_1+\min(a_1,a_2)+\min(a_1,a_2,a_3)+\cdots$$$.
Time complexity: $$$\mathcal O(n)$$$

Annoying the Ghost
PROGRAMMING

Ja the Ghost is playing with rubber ducks. He has (n) piles of rubber ducks arranged in a row, where the (i)-th pile contains (a_i) ducks. Quack the Duck gives Ja a strictly increasing sequence (b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n) and commands him to make the piles (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) become exactly this sequence. Ja performs the process in the following two stages: Ja may add any number of ducks to each pile. Formally, for each pile (i), he chooses a non-negative integer (x_i) and replaces (a_i) with (a_i+x_i). Formally, for each pile (i), he chooses a non-negative integer (x_i) and replaces (a_i) with (a_i+x_i). Ja may repeatedly swap two adjacent piles. Formally, he may perform the following operation any number of times, possibly zero: choose an index (i) such that (1\le i\le n-1), and swap the values of (a_i) and (a_{i+1}). Formally, he may perform the following operation any number of times, possibly zero: choose an index (i) such that (1\le i\le n-1), and swap the values of (a_i) and (a_{i+1}). A process is called valid if, after both stages end, the sequence of pile sizes is exactly (b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_n). Find the minimum possible number of operations performed in the second stage among all valid processes. If there is no valid process, output (-1). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 2000)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains an integer (n) ((1\le n\le 2000)) — the number of piles of rubber ducks. 2237B.editorial_text:
2237B - Annoying the Ghost
Do a greedy algorithm. Maintain a set of $$$\{b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n\}$$$.
Increase $$$a_1$$$ to the smallest possible value of $$$b_i$$$ in the set. This is optimal because if it is increased to $$$b_j \gt b_i$$$, then consider $$$m \gt 1$$$ such that $$$a_m$$$ is increased to $$$b_i$$$. Since $$$a_m \le a_1$$$, we may increase $$$a_1$$$ to $$$b_i$$$ and $$$a_m$$$ to $$$b_j$$$ instead.
Now remove $$$b_i$$$ from the set, and repeat with $$$a_2$$$, then $$$a_3$$$, and so on.
The cost (number of inversions) can be computed in $$$\mathcal O(n^2)$$$ (or $$$\mathcal O(n\log n)$$$ if you want to for some reason)
Time complexity: $$$\mathcal O(n^2)$$$ (or $$$\mathcal O(n\log n)$$$ if you want to for some reason).

Ja the Ghost is playing with rubber ducks again! There are (n) piles of rubber ducks arranged in a row from left to right. Initially, the (i)-th pile contains (a_i) rubber ducks. While the sequence (a) is not sorted in nondecreasing order, Ja must perform the following operation: Choose two adjacent piles such that the left pile contains more ducks than the right pile. Ja swaps these two piles, and then adds the number of ducks in the new left pile to the new right pile. Formally, choose an index (i) such that (1\le i \lt n) and (a_i \gt a_{i+1}). Then replace the adjacent pair ((a_i,a_{i+1})) with ((a_{i+1},a_i+a_{i+1})). Formally, choose an index (i) such that (1\le i \lt n) and (a_i \gt a_{i+1}). Then replace the adjacent pair ((a_i,a_{i+1})) with ((a_{i+1},a_i+a_{i+1})). For example, if two adjacent piles contain (7) and (3) rubber ducks, then after the operation they contain (3) and (10) rubber ducks. Ja may choose any index satisfying the condition above at each step. It can be shown that, regardless of his choices, the process eventually ends with the sequence sorted in nondecreasing order. Ja wants the largest pile at the end of the process to contain as few rubber ducks as possible. Determine the minimum possible value of the largest pile. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the number of piles. The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) ((1\le a_i\le 10^9)) — the number of ducks in each pile. 2237C.editorial_text:
2237C - Duck Surplus
It is useful to view the operation in another way. If we have two adjacent piles $$$x \gt y$$$, then after the operation
$$$$$$ (x,y)\to(y,x+y), $$$$$$
the smaller pile $$$y$$$ moves one position to the left, and the pile it passes through increases by $$$y$$$.
We claim that there is an optimal strategy that always chooses the leftmost inversion.
Indeed, operations on disjoint pairs can be swapped freely. The only nontrivial case is when we have three consecutive piles
$$$$$$ x \gt y \gt z. $$$$$$
If we first operate on the right pair, then this block eventually becomes
$$$$$$ (z,\ y+z,\ x+y+2z). $$$$$$
If we first operate on the left pair, then this block eventually becomes
$$$$$$ (z,\ y+z,\ x+y+z). $$$$$$
The second result is never worse, since the last pile is smaller by $$$z$$$. Therefore, whenever two neighboring inversions compete, processing the left one first is at least as good as processing the right one first. By repeatedly applying this exchange argument, we may assume that an optimal process always takes the leftmost inversion.
Now consider what happens under this strategy.
Suppose we have already processed the prefix $$$a_1,\dots,a_{i-1}$$$. It is sorted, and let $$$m$$$ be its largest pile. Now we append $$$x=a_i$$$.
If $$$m\le x$$$, then the whole prefix is still sorted, so the new largest pile is simply $$$x$$$.
Otherwise, $$$m \gt x$$$. Then $$$x$$$ must move left through all piles greater than $$$x$$$. In particular, it passes through the current largest pile $$$m$$$, so that pile becomes $$$m+x$$$. Every other crossed pile was at most $$$m$$$, so after adding $$$x$$$ it is at most $$$m+x$$$. Hence the new largest pile is exactly $$$m+x$$$.
Therefore the transition is:
$$$$$$ m = \begin{cases} x, & m\le x,\\ m+x, & m \gt x. \end{cases} $$$$$$
We scan the array from left to right and maintain this value $$$m$$$. The final value of $$$m$$$ is the minimum possible largest pile.
The time complexity is $$$O(n)$$$.

A binary string is a string consisting only of characters (0) and (1). The two characters (0) and (1) are called opposite values. Consider a binary string (t). Let (|t|) be the length of (t). When (|t| \ge 2), for every (1 \le i \lt |t|), the characters (t_i) and (t_{i+1}) are adjacent. A binary string (t) is called beautiful if it can be reduced to a string of length exactly (1) by applying the following operation any number of times, possibly zero: Choose two equal adjacent characters, remove both of them, and insert one character with the opposite value in their place. For example, the string (\mathtt{10001}) can become (\mathtt{1101}) by replacing the first adjacent pair (\mathtt{00}) with (\mathtt{1}). Then it can become (\mathtt{001}), then (\mathtt{11}), and finally (\mathtt{0}). Therefore, (\mathtt{10001}) is beautiful. On the other hand, (\mathtt{111}) is not beautiful. After one operation, it becomes (\mathtt{01}), and then no operation can be applied. You are given a binary string (s). Compute the number of non-empty beautiful substrings(^{\text{∗}}) of (s). 2237D.editorial_text:
2237D - Fullmetal Bitchemist
We first characterize when a binary string is beautiful.
For a binary string $$$t$$$, define
$$$$$$ f(t)=\text{the number of }\mathtt{1}\text{s in }t-\text{the number of }\mathtt{0}\text{s in }t. $$$$$$
There are two possible operations:

$$$\mathtt{00} \to \mathtt{1}$$$. In this case, $$$f$$$ changes from $$$-2$$$ to $$$1$$$, so it increases by $$$3$$$. 
$$$\mathtt{11} \to \mathtt{0}$$$. In this case, $$$f$$$ changes from $$$2$$$ to $$$-1$$$, so it decreases by $$$3$$$. 
Therefore, one operation does not change $$$f(t) \bmod 3$$$.
If a string can be reduced to a string of length $$$1$$$, then the final value of $$$f$$$ is either $$$1$$$ or $$$-1$$$. Hence, a necessary condition is
$$$$$$ f(t) \not\equiv 0 \pmod 3. $$$$$$
Also, if a string of length greater than $$$1$$$ is alternating, then it has no two equal adjacent characters, so no operation can be applied. Therefore, it is not beautiful.
We claim that these two conditions are also sufficient.
A non-empty binary string $$$t$$$ is beautiful if and only if:

$$$f(t) \not\equiv 0 \pmod 3$$$; 
$$$t$$$ is not an alternating string of length greater than $$$1$$$. 
Now we prove the sufficiency.
First, consider the short corner cases.
If $$$|t|=1$$$, then $$$t$$$ is already reduced to length $$$1$$$, so it is beautiful.
If $$$|t|=2$$$, then $$$\mathtt{00}$$$ and $$$\mathtt{11}$$$ can be reduced to length $$$1$$$ in one operation, while $$$\mathtt{01}$$$ and $$$\mathtt{10}$$$ are alternating and cannot be operated on. This is exactly consistent with the claim.
Now suppose $$$|t| \gt 2$$$, $$$f(t)\not\equiv 0 \pmod 3$$$, and $$$t$$$ is not alternating. Then $$$t$$$ contains a maximal block of equal characters of length at least $$$2$$$.
If there is a block of length exactly $$$2$$$, we apply the operation to this block. Since the block is maximal, any neighboring character must be the opposite character, which is exactly the character inserted after the operation. Therefore, unless the whole string becomes length $$$1$$$, the new string is still not alternating.
If there is no block of length exactly $$$2$$$, then there is a block of length at least $$$3$$$. If this block has a neighboring character, we choose two equal characters near the boundary of the block. After the operation, the inserted character is equal to the character outside the block, so the new string is still not alternating.
The only remaining case is that the whole string consists of one kind of character. Let its length be $$$len$$$. Since $$$f(t)\not\equiv 0 \pmod 3$$$, $$$len$$$ is not divisible by $$$3$$$. The case $$$len=2$$$ was already handled. For $$$len\ge 4$$$, after applying one operation at one end, at least two equal adjacent characters still remain, so the new string is still not alternating.
In all cases, unless the string already becomes length $$$1$$$, we can perform one operation and keep both properties true:

$$$f(t)\not\equiv 0 \pmod 3$$$; 
the string is not alternating. 
Since each operation decreases the length by $$$1$$$, by induction the string can eventually be reduced to length $$$1$$$.
Therefore, a substring is beautiful exactly when:

the number of $$$\mathtt{1}$$$s minus the number of $$$\mathtt{0}$$$s is not divisible by $$$3$$$; 
it is not an alternating string of length greater than $$$1$$$. 
Now we count such substrings.
Define the prefix value
$$$$$$ p_i=\sum_{j=1}^{i} ([s_j=\mathtt{1}]-[s_j=\mathtt{0}]) \pmod 3. $$$$$$
For a substring $$$s[l..r]$$$,
$$$$$$ f(s[l..r]) \equiv p_r-p_{l-1} \pmod 3. $$$$$$
Thus,
$$$$$$ f(s[l..r]) \not\equiv 0 \pmod 3 $$$$$$
if and only if
$$$$$$ p_r \ne p_{l-1}. $$$$$$
We scan the string from left to right. Let $$$\mathtt{cnt}[0..2]$$$ store the number of previous prefixes with each value modulo $$$3$$$. Initially, $$$\mathtt{cnt}[0]=1$$$, corresponding to the empty prefix.
Suppose the current prefix value is $$$x$$$. Then the number of substrings ending at the current position with $$$f\not\equiv 0 \pmod 3$$$ is
$$$$$$ \mathtt{cnt}[0]+\mathtt{cnt}[1]+\mathtt{cnt}[2]-\mathtt{cnt}[x]. $$$$$$
However, among these substrings, some alternating strings of length greater than $$$1$$$ have been counted, and they must be subtracted.
Let $$$y$$$ be the length of the longest alternating suffix ending at the current position. Then all alternating substrings ending at this position have lengths
$$$$$$ 1,2,\dots,y. $$$$$$
Among them, alternating substrings of even length have the same number of $$$\mathtt{0}$$$s and $$$\mathtt{1}$$$s, so their $$$f$$$ value is $$$0$$$. They were not counted in the first place.
Alternating substrings of odd length have $$$f=\pm 1$$$, so they were counted. The length-$$$1$$$ substring is beautiful, so it should not be subtracted. Therefore, we only need to subtract alternating substrings of lengths
$$$$$$ 3,5,7,\dots. $$$$$$
The number of such substrings is
$$$$$$ \left\lfloor \frac{y-1}{2} \right\rfloor. $$$$$$
So the contribution of each position is
$$$$$$ \left\lfloor \frac{y-1}{2} \right\rfloor. $$$$$$
After processing the current position, we increase $$$\mathtt{cnt}[x]$$$ by $$$1$$$.
The value $$$y$$$ can be maintained while scanning. If the current character is different from the previous one, then the longest alternating suffix is extended by $$$1$$$. Otherwise, it is reset to $$$1$$$.
The important corner cases in the counting part are:

Length-$$$1$$$ substrings must not be subtracted, because they are beautiful. 
Alternating substrings of even length must not be subtracted, because they were never counted by the modulo condition. 
Only alternating substrings of odd length at least $$$3$$$ should be subtracted, which is exactly what $$$\left\lfloor \frac{y-1}{2} \right\rfloor$$$ counts. 
The total time complexity is $$$O(n)$$$.

2237E.editorial_text:
2237E - Permutation Commutation
The condition $$$a_{b_i}=b_{a_i}$$$ means that the completed permutation $$$b$$$ must commute with permutation $$$a$$$.
Decompose $$$a$$$ into cycles. A permutation that commutes with $$$a$$$ maps every cycle of $$$a$$$ to another cycle of the same length, preserving the cyclic shift inside the cycle. Therefore, fixed values already written in $$$b$$$ determine which cycle must map to which cycle and which shift must be used.
For every cycle of $$$a$$$, inspect the known positions in $$$b$$$. If they force two different target cycles, two different shifts, or a target cycle with a different length, the answer is impossible. Otherwise, reserve the forced target cycle.
The remaining cycles can be paired arbitrarily with unused cycles of the same length. To obtain the lexicographically smallest permutation $$$b$$$, we match the still-unmatched cycles greedily: among cycles of the same length, the cycle whose leftmost position in $$$a$$$ is smaller should be matched to the unused target cycle whose leftmost value is smaller. After all pairings are chosen, fill every missing value of $$$b$$$ using the corresponding cyclic shift.
The implementation groups cycles by length and stores unused cycles in buckets. Since each cycle and each element is processed only a constant number of times, the total complexity is $$$O(n)$$$ per test case.

2237F.editorial_text:
2237F - Paint the Array
Conclusion:
An array can be obtained by painting if and only if it satisfies $$$a_1 = 1$$$, $$$a_n = m$$$, and for every pair of adjacent elements $$$(a_i, a_{i+1})$$$, at least one of the following three conditions holds:

$$$a_i = m$$$; 
$$$a_{i+1} = 1$$$; 
$$$a_{i+1} = a_i + 1$$$. 
Proof:
Necessity:
First, $$$a_1 = 1$$$ is clearly necessary, because only $$$1$$$ can be painted at the position $$$a_1$$$. Similarly, we must have $$$a_n = m$$$.
Now consider any adjacent pair $$$a_i$$$ and $$$a_{i+1}$$$. If they are obtained in the same painting operation, then condition 3 clearly holds. Otherwise, they are obtained in different painting operations. If $$$a_i$$$ is painted later, then in order not to overwrite $$$a_{i+1}$$$, $$$a_i$$$ must be the last element of its painted segment, so $$$a_i = m$$$. If $$$a_{i+1}$$$ is painted later, then similarly $$$a_{i+1}$$$ must be the first element of its painted segment, so $$$a_{i+1} = 1$$$. Therefore, at least one of the three conditions above must hold.
Sufficiency:
Contract all maximal consecutive positions that belong to the same painting operation into continuous segments. Process these segments from left to right. If the current segment contains $$$1$$$, insert its painting operation after all previously performed painting operations, so that it overwrites all painting operations that occurred in the prefix. Otherwise, since the last position of the already constructed prefix must be $$$m$$$, we no longer need this operation to overwrite any previous content. Therefore, insert this painting operation before all previously performed painting operations, so that it will be overwritten by the operations in the prefix. In this way, we can always construct a valid sequence of painting operations that produces the final array.
Next, consider computing the answer with dynamic programming from left to right. Equivalently, we want to maximize the number of positions that do not need to be modified. Let $$$dp_i$$$ denote the maximum number of unchanged positions when the last unchanged position is $$$i$$$.
If the DP value at position $$$i$$$ can be transferred to position $$$j$$$ where $$$i \lt j$$$, then one of the following three conditions must hold:

$$$a_j - a_i = j - i$$$, meaning that positions $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ are in the same painting operation. 
$$$m - a_i \lt j - i$$$, meaning that $$$j$$$ lies outside the right boundary of the painting segment containing position $$$i$$$. 
$$$a_j - 1 \lt j - i$$$, meaning that $$$i$$$ lies outside the left boundary of the painting segment containing position $$$j$$$. 
For transition $$$1$$$, we can use buckets to maintain the DP values for each type of painting operation. For transition $$$2$$$, one position can update all positions in a suffix. For transition $$$3$$$, one position can transition from all positions in a prefix. Therefore, transitions $$$2$$$ and $$$3$$$ can be optimized using prefix maxima.
The total time complexity is $$$O(n)$$$.

This is a run-twice (communication) interactive problem. There are two players: Ja the Ghost and Quack the Duck. The jury (otherwise known as the interactor of this problem) will first interact with Ja. After Ja ends the interaction, the jury will interact with Quack. Note that Ja and Quack may not directly pass information to each other; both players are only able to send information to or receive information from the jury. Before the interaction, the jury determines an integer (n) and an array of (n) positive integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n). These values are consistent across both players. Ja receives (n) and an array of (n) positive integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) from the jury, which he wants to send to Quack, where (a_i \le 10^6). To do this, Ja will select an integer (k), where ()k \le \left\lceil \frac{10n}{9} \right\rceil + 150,() and create an array of positive integers (b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k), where (b_i \le 10^6), and send it back to the jury. Then the jury will give Quack the integers (n) and (k). Quack can ask the jury at most (180n + 150) queries in the following form: Choose any two integers (i) and (j) ((1 \le i, j \le k), (i \neq j)), and the jury will respond with (\mathrm{gcd}(b_i, b_j)). Ja wants to ensure that Quack can determine the original array (a). 2237G.editorial_text:
2237G - Send GCDs
We want to encode the original array $$$a$$$ into another array $$$b$$$, so that in the second run we can recover every value of $$$a$$$ using only gcd queries.
The key observation is the following. Consider a prime number $$$p$$$, and let $$$p^k$$$ be the largest power of $$$p$$$ such that $$$p^k \le 10^6$$$. If we query
$$$$$$ \gcd(p^k, x), $$$$$$
then the result gives exactly the power of $$$p$$$ appearing in the prime factorization of $$$x$$$.
Therefore, if a number only contains some small primes in its prime factorization, we can recover this number by querying it against the largest powers of those small primes.
In the implementation, we take the first $$$110$$$ primes. For each such prime $$$p$$$, we put the largest power $$$p^k \le 10^6$$$ into the beginning of array $$$b$$$. These values will be used as "basis" numbers for gcd queries.
Now consider all positive integers not larger than $$$10^6$$$ whose largest prime factor is among the first $$$110$$$ primes. By sieving and checking locally, there are at least $$$2^{18}$$$ such integers. We take the first $$$2^{18}$$$ of them and store them in an array $$$v$$$. Then each index from $$$0$$$ to $$$2^{18}-1$$$ can be represented by one such smooth number.
Since every $$$a_i \le 10^6$$$, each $$$a_i$$$ can be represented as a $$$20$$$-bit binary number. We concatenate all these binary representations into one long binary string. Then we split this string into blocks of length $$$18$$$, padding zeros at the end if necessary.
For each $$$18$$$-bit block, suppose its value is $$$x$$$. We append $$$v_x$$$ to array $$$b$$$. Thus, every encoded number in $$$b$$$ represents $$$18$$$ bits of information.
In the second run, the first $$$110$$$ positions of $$$b$$$ are known to be the prime-power basis numbers. For every later position $$$i$$$, we recover its actual value as follows.
Let this value be $$$y$$$. Since $$$y$$$ is composed only of the first $$$110$$$ primes, we query
$$$$$$ \gcd(y, p_j^{k_j}) $$$$$$
for every one of the $$$110$$$ stored prime powers. Each query returns the contribution of one prime in the factorization of $$$y$$$. Multiplying all these gcd values together gives back $$$y$$$ itself.
After recovering $$$y$$$, we find its index in $$$v$$$. This index is exactly the original $$$18$$$-bit block. Hence we can recover the whole binary string, and then split it back into $$$20$$$-bit blocks to obtain all values of $$$a$$$.
The construction of $$$b$$$ is non-adaptive. In the first run, we only build the array $$$b$$$. In the second run, the query strategy is fixed: for each encoded block, query it with all $$$110$$$ prime-power basis numbers.
Let $$$A = 10^6$$$ and $$$P = 110$$$. The preprocessing complexity depends on the sieve implementation: it is $$$O(A \log \log A)$$$ with a standard sieve, or $$$O(A)$$$ with a linear sieve. After preprocessing, the first run takes $$$O(n)$$$ time. The length of $$$b$$$ is
$$$$$$ P + \left\lceil \frac{20n}{18} \right\rceil, $$$$$$
up to possible small constant differences depending on the implementation. The second run uses
$$$$$$ P \cdot \left\lceil \frac{20n}{18} \right\rceil $$$$$$

2237H.editorial_text:
2237H - Slime and Queries
First, assign a core to the slime. Initially, the core can be placed at any slime node. Each query can be seen as moving the core to the target node. If the node that the core moves to is already inside the slime, the cost is $$$0$$$. Otherwise, we need to pay cost $$$1$$$ to move one slime node there.
Consider the following greedy strategy. For each query, we move the core directly to the target node. However, when we need to remove a node, we do not know which node is optimal to remove, so we do not delete any node immediately. Instead, after each query, we mark all nodes that may currently be slime nodes, and only record that exactly $$$m$$$ of them are real slime nodes.
Later, when we need to move the core to some node, we first check all marks on this node. For every mark, we check whether the number of remaining nodes that can still be slime nodes is positive. If all of them still have remaining capacity, then we can determine that this node currently really contains a slime node. We decrease the target count of all marks on this node by $$$1$$$, and remove all marks from this node. Otherwise, we have to pay cost $$$1$$$ to move some other slime node here, and we also remove all marks from this node.
Let $$$c_i$$$ be the number of remaining undetermined slime nodes for the $$$i$$$-th mark, in chronological order. Since the set of marks owned by any node is always a suffix of all current marks, if $$$c_i \gt c_{i+1}$$$, then the $$$i$$$-th mark cannot actually be used more than $$$c_{i+1}$$$ times. Therefore, we can take suffix minima over $$$c$$$, that is,
$$$$$$ c_i = \min(c_i, c_{i+1}, c_{i+2}, \dots). $$$$$$
Then define
$$$$$$ d_i = c_i - c_{i-1}, $$$$$$
where $$$c_0 = 0$$$. If the earliest mark on a node is $$$x$$$, then checking this node is equivalent to finding the largest $$$i \le x$$$ such that $$$d_i \gt 0$$$, and decreasing $$$d_i$$$ by $$$1$$$. If no such $$$d_i$$$ exists, then we must pay cost $$$1$$$.
Now we prove the correctness of the greedy strategy. First, it is never better to avoid moving the core directly to the target node and instead visit some off-path node in advance to save future movement. This is because we still have to visit the target node eventually; changing the order to visit the target first and then visit that off-path node is no worse. Second, whenever we can determine that the current node contains a slime node, we should do it immediately. Each unit of some $$$d_i$$$ can save at most one unit of cost, so once it can be used to save a cost, we should use it. Keeping it for later cannot bring any extra benefit.
We can maintain this process using std::set and heavy-light decomposition. Each time the core passes through a path, after HLD decomposition, this path becomes $$$O(\log n)$$$ intervals.
Define the color of a node as the index of the earliest mark on this node. We use a set to maintain all maximal continuous segments with the same color. Then assigning a new mark to a tree path becomes range color assignment on several intervals. Before assigning the new color, we extract all continuous color segments inside these intervals. The total number of such extracted segments is amortized $$$O(n \log n)$$$, where we regard $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ as the same order.
For each color segment, we check all its nodes together and determine whether they can save cost $$$1$$$. We use another set to maintain all positions with $$$d_i \gt 0$$$. For a color segment whose color is $$$x$$$, we repeatedly find the largest position $$$i \le x$$$ with $$$d_i \gt 0$$$, and match it with as many nodes in this segment as possible. If no such position exists, then those nodes must contribute cost $$$1$$$.
Each matching operation either consumes all remaining value of one position with $$$d_i \gt 0$$$, or consumes all remaining nodes in the current continuous segment. Also, a new position with $$$d_i \gt 0$$$ only appears after a query, when we add a new mark to all nodes. Therefore, the total number of matching operations is also amortized $$$O(n \log n)$$$.
In conclusion, the total number of accesses to the sets is amortized $$$O(n \log n)$$$, and each access costs an extra logarithmic factor. Therefore, the total time complexity is $$$O(n \log^2 n)$$$.
