2246E.editorial_text:
2246E - lce4113 and Security Game
Let's show that a deterministic solution does not exist. Suppose $$$m_0$$$ and $$$m_1$$$ are fixed and declared beforehand, so that the interactor has access to these values before the interaction (as would be the case for a deterministic solution). The interaction may proceed as follows:

The interactor computes $$$c = (m_0 \oplus m_1)$$$. 
The solution sends $$$x$$$ to the interactor. 
The interactor responds with $$$o = x.$$$ 
The solution sends $$$m_0$$$ and $$$m_1$$$. 
The interactor computes $$$v_0 = x\,\&\,(\sim c)$$$ and $$$v_1 = x\,|\,c.$$$ By construction, $$$v_0$$$ is a submask of $$$x$$$, $$$v_1$$$ is a supermask of $$$x$$$, and $$$v_0 \oplus v_1 = c = m_0 \oplus m_1.$$$ 
The interactor sends $$$v_0 \oplus m_0 = v_1 \oplus m_1$$$ to the solution. In this case, both the triples $$$(v,\mathrm{ty},b) = (v_0,|,0)$$$ and $$$(v,\mathrm{ty},b) = (v_1,\&,1)$$$ are consistent with the interaction, so there is a choice of $$$(v,\mathrm{ty},b)$$$ that will make the solution fail. 
We now provide a nondeterministic solution. We will first solve the problem assuming $$$v$$$ is nonzero. Query $$$x = 1$$$. If the input you receive has a set bit which is not the first bit, you know $$$\mathrm{ty} = |$$$. Otherwise, since $$$v$$$ is nonzero, it is sufficient to assume $$$\mathrm{ty} = \&$$$. In either case you now know some bit of $$$v$$$. 
If you determined $$$\mathrm{ty} = \&$$$, send $$$m_0 = 1, m_1 = 0.$$$ The result determines $$$b$$$ (assuming $$$v$$$ is nonzero), since you know the first bit of $$$v.$$$
If you determined $$$\mathrm{ty} = |$$$, pick some bit $$$p$$$ that you know is $$$1$$$ and send $$$m_0 = 2^p$$$ and $$$m_1 = 0$$$. The result again determines $$$b$$$.
It remains to handle the case $$$v = 0$$$. Note that in this case the interactor responds to the final query with $$$m_b,$$$ which is in the set $$$\{m_0, m_1\}.$$$ Is the converse sufficient (i.e., is it enough to check that the interactor returned either $$$m_0$$$ or $$$m_1$$$)? The answer is yes, unless $$$m_b \oplus v = m_{1-b}.$$$ We can design $$$m_0$$$ and $$$m_1$$$ so that this occurs with negligible probability. 
Note that if $$$v = 0$$$ then our algorithm determines $$$\mathrm{ty} = \&$$$. Additionally, in the algorithm above, the bits in $$$m_0$$$ and $$$m_1$$$ which are not the first bit are irrelevant, so we can choose them randomly in both $$$m_0$$$ and $$$m_1$$$. The probability that $$$m_0 \oplus v = m_1$$$ is then $$$2^{-29}$$$, which is negligible. So we can check before processing this case whether the output given by the interactor matches $$$m_0$$$ or $$$m_1$$$, and if it does, we assume that $$$v = 0$$$ and return the corresponding bit. Otherwise we have $$$v$$$ nonzero, so we proceed as described earlier.

2246F.editorial_text:
2246F - Whoname and Unsorted Array
It is not possible to sort the permutation when $$$n$$$ is even and the inversion count is odd, as the operation changes the inversion parity $$$n-2$$$ times, which is also even (so the inversion count will remain odd, hence nonzero).
Otherwise, we can show that it is always possible in at most $$$4n$$$ moves.
Let $$$\textsf{op}(i)$$$ $$$(1 \leq i \leq n-1)$$$ be an operation on index $$$i$$$. Let $$$\textsf{find}(v)$$$ be the index $$$i$$$ such that $$$p_i = v$$$.
Suppose $$$1,\ldots, x$$$ are sorted on the suffix (i.e. $$$p = [p_1, \ldots, p_{n-x}, 1,2 \ldots,x-1, x]$$$). We will show how to sort $$$1,\ldots,x+1$$$ on the suffix. We consider four cases.
The first case is when $$$p = [n, 1, 2, \ldots, n-1].$$$ In this case $$$n$$$ must be odd, since $$$p$$$ has $$$n-1$$$ inversions. We perform the following sequence of operations: 

Perform $$$\textsf{op}(2)$$$ $$$n-2$$$ times. The permutation becomes $$$[1, n, 2, \ldots, n-1],$$$ since $$$n-2$$$ is odd. 
Perform $$$\textsf{op}(1).$$$ The permutation becomes $$$[1, 2, ..., n]$$$ as desired. 
The second case is $$$p = [n-1, n, 1, 2, \ldots, n-2].$$$ In this case we perform the following operations: 

Perform $$$\textsf{op}(1)$$$. The permutation becomes $$$[n-1, 1, 2, \ldots, n-2, n].$$$ 
Perform $$$\textsf{op}(n-1)$$$ $$$n-2$$$ times. The permutation once again becomes $$$[1,2,\ldots,n].$$$ 
The third case is when $$$\textsf{find}(x+1) \neq 1.$$$ In this case performing the operation on the index $$$\textsf{find}(x+1)-1$$$ moves $$$x+1$$$ to the end of the permutation while preserving the order of the elements $$$1,\ldots,x.$$$
The final case is $$$\textsf{find}(x+1) = 1.$$$ Let $$$p_2 = u$$$ and $$$p_3 = v$$$. We perform the following sequence of operations: 

Perform $$$\textsf{op}(2).$$$ The permutation becomes $$$[u, x+1, \ldots, 1, 2, \ldots, x, v].$$$ 
Perform $$$\textsf{op}(1)$$$, transforming the permutation into $$$[u, \ldots, 1, 2, \ldots, x, v, x+1].$$$ 
Perform $$$\textsf{op}(n-1),$$$ making the permutation $$$[v, u, \ldots, 1, 2, \ldots, x, x+1].$$$ Note that $$$1,\ldots,x+1$$$ are sorted on the suffix as desired. 
Since each case requires at most $$$n$$$ operations, the total number of operations required to make the permutation non-decreasing is at most $$$4n.$$$

2244A.title: Iskander and Drawings
2244A.statement_text: During a geometry lesson, Iskander got very bored, so he decided to draw in Yura's notebook. To do this, he took a row and drew horizontal lines on it. Some lines are long, some are short, and some parts of the page remain empty. The page is represented by a string (s), where the character '*' denotes an empty part of the paper, and the character '#' denotes one centimeter of a drawn line. A continuous sequence of '#' characters forms a single line. Yura decided to erase all the lines and made Iskander help him: they will erase one of the lines from both ends simultaneously. Each second, Iskander erases (1) centimeter from the right end of the line, and Yura erases (1) centimeter from the left end. If the current length of the line is (1) or (2) centimeters, then in the next second it is erased completely, and the process ends. Yura wants to choose a line so that, together with Iskander, they erase it for as long as possible. Help him determine this maximum time. If there are no lines on the page, the answer is (0) seconds. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 2500)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains an integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 10)) — the length of the string (s). The second line of each test case contains a string (s) of length (n), consisting of characters '#' and '*'. For each test case, output a single integer — the maximum time required to erase a line.
2244A.editorial_text:
2244A - Iskander and Drawings
For a segment of length $$$l$$$, the erasing time is $$$\lceil \frac{l}{2} \rceil$$$, that is, $$$\frac{l + 1}{2}$$$, because its length decreases by $$$2$$$ every second, and if the segment length is $$$1$$$ or $$$2$$$, then the segment is erased in $$$1$$$ second. Therefore, the answer — is the erasing time of the longest substring of '#' in $$$s$$$.

2244B.title: Nikita and Books
2244B.statement_text: As is well known, Nikita loves reading. Today, he made a mess in his room and arranged his books into (n) stacks in a row, numbered from (1) to (n) from left to right. The (i)-th stack contains (a_i) books. This arrangement is called neat if, in every stack except the rightmost one, the number of books is strictly less than in the stack to its right; that is, the array (a) is strictly increasing. Yura wants to make the arrangement neat by performing the following operation any number of times: Choose a stack (i) such that (1 \le i \lt n) and (a_i \gt 1). Take (1) book from the top of stack (i), so (a_i) decreases by (1). Put this book on top of stack (i + 1), so (a_{i+1}) increases by (1). Determine whether Yura can make the arrangement neat . The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the number of stacks. The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_i) ((1 \le a_i \le 10^9)) — the initial number of books in each stack. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output " YES " if Yura can make the arrangement neat , and " NO " otherwise. You may output each letter in any case (lowercase or uppercase). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES " will be accepted.
2244B.editorial_text:
2244B - Nikita and Books
Books can only be moved to the right, from tower $$$i$$$ to tower $$$i + 1$$$ (provided that $$$a_i \gt 1$$$). Therefore, the total number of books in any prefix consisting of the first $$$i$$$ towers can never increase; it can only decrease or remain unchanged.
For the final array to be strictly increasing, the minimum possible number of books in the $$$i$$$-th tower is $$$i$$$ (since every $$$a_i \ge 1$$$ and all values must be distinct integers). Therefore, for every prefix of length $$$i$$$, the following condition must hold:
$$$\sum_{j=1}^{i} a_j \ge 1 + 2 + \dots + i = \frac{i(i+1)}{2}.$$$ 
This condition is both necessary and sufficient. The required arrangement can be obtained by greedily moving all extra books to the right.

2244C.title: Stepan and Permutation
2244C.statement_text: Stepan found a permutation (p) of length (n). Of course, he decided to sort it. To make the process more interesting, he chose two positive integers (x) and (y) ((x + y \le n)) and defined a rule for swapping elements. In one move, Stepan can choose two indices (i) and (j) ((1 \le i, j \le n)) and swap the elements (p_i) and (p_j) if at least one of the following conditions holds: (|i - j| = x) (|i - j| = y) Stepan wants to know whether it is possible to sort the permutation in ascending order using any number of such operations. Help him answer this question. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains three integers (n), (x), and (y) ((1 \le x, y \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5), (x + y \le n)) — the length of the array and the numbers chosen by Stepan. The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (p_i) ((1 \le p_i \le n)) — the array (p); it is guaranteed that (p) is a permutation. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output " YES " if it is possible to sort the permutation with the given (x) and (y), and " NO " otherwise. You may output each letter in any case (lowercase or uppercase). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES " will be accepted.
2244C.editorial_text:
2244C - Stepan and Permutation
Consider a graph whose vertices are the positions of the array. Connect two positions by an edge if their difference is equal to $$$x$$$ or $$$y$$$. Then one operation corresponds to swapping along an edge of this graph.
Notice that within each connected component of the graph, the elements can be rearranged arbitrarily. Therefore, the permutation can be sorted if and only if, for every element, its current position and the position where it should end up belong to the same connected component.
It remains to understand what the connected components of this graph look like.
Let $$$g = \gcd(x, y)$$$. Any path in the graph consists of steps of length $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$. Therefore, when moving along edges, we always change the position index by a multiple of $$$g$$$. Hence, we can reach only positions with the same remainder modulo $$$g$$$.
Let us show that this condition is sufficient. Since $$$\gcd(x / g, y / g) = 1$$$, by Bézout's theorem any multiple of $$$g$$$ can be represented as $$$ax + by$$$ for some integers $$$a$$$ and $$$b$$$. In other words, any position with the same remainder modulo $$$g$$$ can be reached by a sequence of steps of $$$\pm x$$$ and $$$\pm y$$$.
It remains only to make sure that such steps can always be performed without leaving the bounds of the array. This is exactly why the condition $$$x + y \le n$$$ is given in the statement: it guarantees that within each residue class there is always enough room to replace "out-of-bounds" steps with equivalent ones and move between any two vertices of this class. Thus, each connected component consists exactly of all positions with the same remainder modulo $$$g$$$.
Therefore, the permutation can be sorted if and only if for all $$$i$$$ we have $$$p_i \equiv i \pmod g$$$.

2244D.title: Yaroslav and Productivity
2244D.statement_text: Yaroslav's productivity during the day is described by an array (a) of length (n). His productivity can be negative if he watches short videos, or positive if he works. The total productivity is defined as the sum of all values in the array. Sometimes Yaroslav reads motivational posts. He has (m) posts, where the (j)-th post has an impact value (b_j). If Yaroslav reads a post with value (b_j), then all productivity values from the beginning of the day up to position (b_j) change sign, that is, all integers (a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots, a_{b_j}) are multiplied by (-1). For example, let (a = 1, -4, 3, -4), and Yaroslav reads a post with value (3). Then the signs of the first three elements are flipped, and the array becomes (-1, 4, -3, -4). If he then reads a post with value (1), the first element changes sign again, and the array becomes (1, 4, -3, -4). What is the maximum possible total productivity Yaroslav can achieve by reading any (possibly none) of the posts? The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (m) ((1 \le m \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the number of measurements and the number of motivational posts. The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_i) ((-10^9 \le a_i \le 10^9)) — the productivity values. The third line of each test case contains (m) integers (b_i) ((1 \le b_i \le n)) — the impact values of the posts. It is guaranteed that all (b_i) are distinct. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the maximum possible total productivity .
2244D.editorial_text:
2244D - Yaroslav and Productivity
Sort the posts in increasing order: $$$b_1 \lt b_2 \lt \dots \lt b_m$$$. Add $$$b_0 = 0$$$. Consider the segments $$$(b_{k-1}, b_k]$$$ for $$$k = 1, \dots, m$$$ and the last segment $$$(b_m, n]$$$.
For the segment $$$(b_{k-1}, b_k]$$$, the sign of all elements is determined by the parity of the number of selected posts from the set $$$\{b_k, b_{k+1}, \dots, b_m\}$$$. Denote this parity by $$$y_k \in \{0,1\}$$$. For the last segment, $$$y_{m+1} = 0$$$.
Since the posts can be chosen arbitrarily, $$$y_1, \dots, y_m$$$ can be anything. Therefore, for each $$$k = 1, \dots, m$$$, we can independently take the sum of the elements on the segment $$$(b_{k-1}, b_k]$$$ with either a $$$+$$$ or a $$$-$$$ sign depending on $$$y_k$$$. It is optimal to take the absolute value of this sum. The sign of the last segment cannot be changed. Then the answer is:
$$$\sum_{k=1}^{m} \left| \sum_{i=b_{k-1}+1}^{b_k} a_i \right| + \sum_{i=b_m+1}^{n} a_i.$$$

2244E.title: Masha and the Garland
2244E.statement_text: Masha has a New Year garland consisting of (n) bulbs. Each bulb can be either off or on. The state of the garland is given by a binary string (s) of length (n), where ' 0 ' denotes an off bulb and ' 1 ' denotes an on bulb. Masha considers the garland beautiful if the states of adjacent bulbs strictly alternate. That is, there are no two adjacent bulbs that are both on or both off. For example, the garlands ' 01010 ' and ' 1010 ' are beautiful, while ' 0110 ' and ' 000 ' are not. Yura can apply the following operation to the garland: choose a subsegment and flip the state of all bulbs in it, that is, turn all on bulbs off and all off bulbs on. Masha invites him to play the following game (q) times: she chooses a segment from the (l)-th to the (r)-th bulb inclusive, and Yura must make this segment beautiful using at most (k) operations. However, Yura is not sure whether this is always possible, so he asks you to determine for each game whether he can make the chosen segment beautiful using no more than (k) operations. Note that the games are independent, and the garland itself is not actually modified. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (q) ((1 \le n, q \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the length of the garland and the number of games. The second line contains a binary string (s) of length (n), consisting only of characters ' 0 ' and ' 1 '. The next (q) lines each contain three integers (l), (r), and (k) ((1 \le l \le r \le n), (0 \le k \le n)) — the boundaries of the segment and the maximum allowed number of operations. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) and the sum of (q) over all test cases do not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each game, output " YES " if the segment can be made beautiful using at most (k) operations, and " NO " otherwise.
2244E.editorial_text:
2244E - Masha and the Garland
For each of the two beautiful strings, consider the positions where it differs from the original string. Split them into maximal contiguous blocks.
Notice that if we completely invert one of the internal blocks, it disappears and merges the two neighboring blocks into one. Thus, the number of blocks decreases by $$$2$$$. If we invert an edge block, the number of blocks decreases only by $$$1$$$, so it is not profitable to do that while there are internal blocks.
Therefore, the optimal strategy is to sequentially invert every second block, starting from the second one. After each operation, the number of blocks decreases by $$$2$$$, so if initially there were $$$cnt$$$ blocks, the minimum number of operations is $$$\lfloor\frac{cnt}{2}\rfloor$$$.
It remains to learn how to quickly find the number of blocks for each query. For this, it is enough to precompute an array marking the beginning of each block and its prefix sums. After computing the minimum required number of operations, compare it with $$$k$$$.

2244F.title: Anya Loves Trees!
2244F.statement_text: Anya considers a rooted tree with the root at vertex (1). The leaves of the tree contain integers from (1) to (k), where (k) is the number of leaves. Each leaf contains exactly one number. For every vertex, its children are ordered from left to right in increasing order of their indices. Anya noticed that if we list the leaves from left to right, their values form a sequence. She wants this sequence to become strictly increasing. To achieve this, Anya can perform the following operation: choose any vertex and cyclically shift its children to the left(^{\text{∗}}). For example, if a vertex has children in the order (1, 2, 3), after the shift the order becomes (2, 3, 1). This operation can be applied to any vertices any number of times. A visual example of a cyclic shift of the children of vertex (1): Help Yura determine whether Anya can make the sequence of integers in the leaves strictly increasing from left to right using such operations. (^{\text{∗}})A cyclic left shift is an operation where all elements are shifted left by (1), and the first element becomes the last. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the number of vertices. The next line contains (n - 1) integers (p_2, p_3, \dots, p_n) ((1 \le p_i \le n)), where (p_i) is the parent of vertex (i). The children of each vertex are ordered from left to right in increasing order of their indices. The third line contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) ((0 \le a_i \le n)). If vertex (i) is not a leaf, then (a_i = 0). If vertex (i) is a leaf, then (a_i \gt 0) and represents the number written in that vertex. It is guaranteed that all positive values (a_i) form a permutation. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not e
2244F.editorial_text:
2244F - Anya Loves Trees!
In every subtree, the leaves must form a contiguous segment of numbers — otherwise, they cannot appear consecutively in the global increasing sequence. Therefore, we will check this property bottom-up. For each vertex, store the minimum, maximum, and number of leaves in its subtree, as well as whether the vertex satisfies the conditions.
For an internal vertex, look at its children in the given order. Count the number of gaps between neighboring children in the cycle (that is, including the last and the first): call it a gap if the minimum of the next child is not equal to the maximum of the previous one $$$+1$$$. If all children satisfy the conditions and there is at most one gap, then a cyclic shift can place the children in the correct order — so the vertex is also good. Otherwise, it is not. If the root satisfies the conditions, then it is possible to sort the values in the leaves; otherwise, it is not.

2244G.title: Yura and Deadlines
2244G.statement_text: Yura has (n) homework assignments. For each assignment, its weight (a_i) is known — the number of course points Yura will receive if he completes it. Yura wants to choose a subset of assignments to maximize the total number of points. However, he has one problem: some assignments are too time-consuming. If Yura works on two assignments at positions (i) and (j) ((i \neq j)), there must be enough other assignments between them; otherwise, he will get distracted and fail to complete them. Formally, for any two chosen assignments with indices (i) and (j), the following condition must hold: (|i - j| \gt \max(a_i, a_j)). Find the maximum total weight Yura can obtain by choosing a subset of assignments satisfying this condition. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)) — the size of the array (a). The second line contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n) ((0 \le a_i \le 10^9)) — the elements of the array. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the maximum total weight of the selected assignments. In the first example, it is optimal to choose assignments with indices (1) and (5). In the third example, it is optimal to choose assignments with indices (1) and (6).
2244G.editorial_text:
2244G - Yura and Deadlines
Note that for any chosen sequence of indices, it is enough to check the condition only for adjacent elements: if for every adjacent pair $$$(i, j)$$$ the condition $$$|i-j| \gt max(a_i, a_j)$$$ holds, then it will also hold for any pair, since the distance between them is the sum of the distances between adjacent elements, and each of those is strictly greater than the corresponding $$$a$$$.
Thus, the problem reduces to choosing a subsequence such that for adjacent $$$i \lt j$$$ we must have $$$j - i \gt max(a_i, a_j)$$$, which is equivalent to the two conditions $$$i + a_i \lt j$$$ and $$$j - a_j \gt i$$$.
For each index $$$j$$$, define $$$l_j = j + a_j$$$. Then the previous chosen index $$$i$$$ for $$$j$$$ must satisfy $$$i \lt j - a_j$$$ and $$$l_i \lt j$$$.
We use dynamic programming: $$$dp[j] = a_j + max(dp[i])$$$ over all $$$i$$$ such that $$$i \lt j - a_j$$$ and $$$l_i \lt j$$$.
Process the indices from left to right. Maintain a data structure (a Fenwick tree or a segment tree for maximum) into which we add $$$i$$$ with value $$$dp[i]$$$ as soon as the current index becomes greater than $$$l_i$$$. Then for the current $$$j$$$, a maximum query on the prefix $$$[1, j - a_j - 1]$$$ gives the desired $$$max(dp[i])$$$.

2245A.editorial_text:
2245A - Who Watches the Watchpig?
If a piggy faces left (L), any watchpig pair it belongs to must involve a piggy to its left facing right (R). Symmetric logic applies if it faces right.
Consider a piggy at index $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i \le k$$$). It cannot face $$$\mathtt{L}$$$ because there are at most $$$i - 1 \lt k$$$ piggies to its left, meaning it cannot form $$$k$$$ watchpig pairs. Thus, the leftmost $$$k$$$ piggies must all face $$$\mathtt{R}$$$. By the same reasoning, the rightmost $$$k$$$ piggies must all face $$$\mathtt{L}$$$. 
Notice that this necessary condition is also sufficient:

For any piggy $$$i$$$ in the prefix ($$$1 \le i \le k$$$), it forms exactly $$$k$$$ watchpig pairs with the rightmost $$$k$$$ piggies (which are guaranteed to face L).

For any piggy $$$i$$$ in the suffix ($$$n - k + 1 \le i \le n$$$), it forms exactly $$$k$$$ watchpig pairs with the leftmost $$$k$$$ piggies (which are guaranteed to face R).

For any piggy in the middle portion (if any), depending on its direction, it will form $$$k$$$ watchpig pairs with either the leftmost prefix or the rightmost suffix. 
Therefore, if $$$2k \gt n$$$, the prefix and suffix overlap, and there is no solution. Otherwise, the optimal strategy is simply to force the leftmost $$$k$$$ piggies to face R and the rightmost $$$k$$$ piggies to face L, leaving the middle piggies completely untouched.
Overall complexity $$$O(n)$$$.

2245B.editorial_text:
2245B - Delete and Concatenate
Let us first consider the base case where $$$c=0$$$. Observe that the final score is always the sum of some subset of elements from $$$a$$$. Let $$$m=\left \lceil \frac{n}{2} \right \rceil$$$. We claim that for any integer $$$k$$$ such that $$$m \le k \le n$$$, there exists a sequence of operations yielding a final score exactly equal to the sum of the $$$k$$$ largest elements in $$$a$$$.
Proof. We can demonstrate this by analyzing the following cases based on the remaining elements:

$$$k \gt n-k$$$: Arbitrarily choose any of the largest $$$k$$$ elements and apply the first operation to remove it. 
$$$k=n-k$$$: There must exist at least one pair of adjacent elements where one belongs to the $$$k$$$ largest elements and the other does not. Select this pair and apply the second operation, which effectively absorbs the smaller element while retaining the larger one. 
$$$k \lt n-k$$$: Given our initial condition $$$k \ge \left \lceil \frac{n}{2} \right \rceil$$$, this scenario is mathematically impossible and will never occur. 
Note that for the first two cases, $$$k$$$ remains greater than or equal to $$$n-k$$$ after an operation. 
Thus, for $$$c=0$$$, if there are $$$p$$$ positive elements in $$$a$$$, the optimal strategy is simply to sum the largest $$$\max(m, p)$$$ elements.
Now, let us generalize to the case where $$$c \ge 0$$$. We can apply a baseline shift by defining a new array $$$a'$$$ such that $$$a'_i = a_i - c$$$. Under this transformation, applying the first operation yields a score of $$$a'_i = a_i - c$$$. Similarly, applying the second operation to adjacent elements yields $$$\max(a'_i, a'_j) = \max(a_i - c, a_j - c) = \max(a_i, a_j) - c$$$. This algebraic translation reduces the general case with cost $$$c$$$ to our previously solved base case with cost $$$0$$$.
The maximum possible final score can be computed by first transforming the array into $$$a'$$$, counting the number of positive elements $$$p'$$$ within it, and then simply returning the sum of the largest $$$\max(m, p')$$$ elements of $$$a'$$$. Overall complexity $$$O(n \log n)$$$.

2245C.editorial_text:
2245C - MEXOR
By definition, a permutation of length $$$n$$$ contains all integers from $$$0$$$ to $$$n-1$$$. Therefore, the MEX of the entire array is always exactly $$$n$$$. This means $$$f(n-1) = n$$$ is fixed for any valid permutation.
The problem requires $$$f(0) \oplus f(1) \oplus \dots \oplus f(n-1) = k$$$. Since $$$f(n-1) = n$$$, we can XOR $$$n$$$ on both sides to find the required XOR sum for the first $$$n-1$$$ prefixes: $$$$$$f(0) \oplus f(1) \oplus \dots \oplus f(n-2) = k \oplus n$$$$$$ Let $$$K' = k \oplus n$$$. Our goal simplifies to constructing a permutation such that the XOR sum of the MEX of all prefixes except the last one equals $$$K'$$$.
A powerful trick when dealing with prefix MEX is to control when $$$0$$$ appears. If we place $$$0$$$ toward the end of the permutation, every prefix before $$$0$$$ will be missing $$$0$$$, making their MEX exactly $$$0$$$. We only need to manipulate the few elements placed after $$$0$$$ to achieve the desired $$$K'$$$.
We can break the construction down into three cases based on the value of $$$K'$$$:

$$$K' = 0$$$: we just place $$$0$$$ at the very end of the permutation.
$$$K' \le n-1$$$: we can place $$$0$$$ at the second to last position, and $$$K'$$$ at the last position. The permutation looks like: $$$[\dots, \text{others}, \dots, 0, K']$$$. Here, $$$f(i)=0$$$ for all $$$i \lt n-2$$$, and $$$f(n-2)=K'$$$.
$$$K' \gt n-1$$$: since the maximum possible MEX for any proper prefix is $$$n-1$$$, we cannot generate a single MEX value equal to $$$K'$$$. 
First, check whether it is even possible. If the highest set bit of $$$K'$$$ is strictly greater than the highest set bit of $$$n-1$$$, it is impossible to form $$$K'$$$ using any combination of values $$$\le n-1$$$. In this case, we output "NO".
If it is possible, $$$K'$$$ and $$$n-1$$$ must have the same bit length. This means their XOR will cancel out the highest bit, strictly reducing the value. Let $$$v = (n-1) \oplus K'$$$. Because the highest bits cancel out, we are guaranteed that $$$0 \lt v \lt n-1$$$. We can construct the end of the permutation as: $$$[\dots, \text{others}, \dots, 0, v, n-1]$$$. Here, $$$f(i)=0$$$ for all $$$i \lt n-3$$$, $$$f(n-3)=v$$$, and $$$f(n-2)=n-1$$$. 
Overall complexity $$$O(n)$$$.

2245D1.editorial_text:
2245D1 - Построение массива (простая версия)
Firstly, we shall prove a small lemma:
Lemma. If there exists a solution for the original problem, there exists one where all $$$|a_i|$$$ are distinct. 
Proof. Consider any valid solution $$$a$$$. We build another array $$$a'$$$ as follows:

If $$$a_i \ge 0$$$, then $$$a'_i=2n \cdot a_i + n + i$$$;
If $$$a_i \lt 0$$$, then $$$a'_i = 2n \cdot a_i - i$$$. 
It is not hard to verify that $$$a'$$$ is also a valid solution, and all $$$|a'_i|$$$ are distinct.
As such, we can safely replace the non-negative constraint with positive.
Notice that we can deduce whether each element $$$a_i$$$ is negative or positive, since there definitely exists an $$$a_i+a_i$$$ restriction for every $$$i$$$.
Consider two elements $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ such that $$$a_i$$$ is positive and $$$a_j$$$ is negative. If $$$a_i+a_j$$$ is positive, we can conclude that $$$|a_i| \gt |a_j|$$$; otherwise, $$$|a_i| \lt |a_j|$$$. 
Build a directed graph $$$G$$$ consisting of $$$n$$$ vertices. Add an edge from vertex $$$i$$$ to $$$j$$$ if $$$|a_i| \lt |a_j|$$$. Run topological sort on $$$G$$$. If no topological sorting exists, there must be a cycle in $$$G$$$, and we can conclude that there is no solution. Otherwise, let $$$t$$$ be any topological sorting. $$$|a_{t_i}|=i$$$ is a valid solution.
Overall complexity $$$O(m+n)=O(n^2)$$$.

PROGRAMMING

This is the hard version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, (n \le 2 \cdot 10^5) and (0 \le m \le \min(10^6,\frac{n(n+1)}{2})). You are given two integers (n) and (m). You need to construct an integer array (a) of length (n) that satisfies (m) restrictions. Each restriction can be represented by a tuple ((o,i,j)) such that (o \in \{1,2\}) and (1 \le i \le j \le n): If (o=1), the sum (a_i+a_j) must be non-negative . If (o=2), the sum (a_i+a_j) must be negative . Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (m) ((1 \le n \le \color{red}{2 \cdot 10^5}), (0 \le m \color{red}{\le} \min(10^6, \frac{n(n+1)}{2}))), representing the length of the array (a) you need to construct and the number of restrictions, respectively. Each of the next (m) lines contains three integers (o), (i), and (j) ((o \in \{1,2\}), (1 \le i \le j \le n)), representing a restriction. It is guaranteed that each pair of integers (i) and (j) such that (1 \le i \le j \le n) occurs in at most one restriction. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). It is guaranteed that the sum of (m) over all test cases does not exceed (10^6). For each test case, if no such array (a) exists, output " NO ". Otherwise, first output " YES " on a single line. Then output (n) integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n) ((|a_i| \le 10^9)), representing the array (a) you constructed. It can be proven that under the problem constraints, if such an array exists, there exists one where all elements in the array do not exceed (10^9) in absolute value. 2245D2.editorial_text:
2245D2 - Construct an Array (Hard Version)
Please read the editorial for D1 first.
The topological sorting approach in D1 relies on the information of whether each $$$a_i$$$ is positive or negative. However, it turns out that we do not need this information at all.
If there exists some $$$i$$$ such that $$$a_i + a_j \gt 0$$$ for all $$$j$$$, $$$a_i$$$ must be the largest element in $$$a$$$. We can simply assign $$$a_i$$$ a very large positive value and move on. The same logic applies if there exists some $$$i$$$ such that $$$a_i + a_j \lt 0$$$ for all $$$j$$$. After we process $$$a_i$$$, we can remove all restrictions involving $$$a_i$$$ and look for the new largest/smallest element. 
This can be done in a topological sorting-like approach. Let $$$d_{1,i}$$$ be the number of restrictions involving $$$i$$$ and $$$o=1$$$. Let $$$d_{2,i}$$$ be defined similarly. In a classic topological sort, we push a vertex into the queue if its in-degree becomes zero. In this case, we push a vertex into the queue if either $$$d_{1,i}$$$ or $$$d_{2,i}$$$ becomes zero. Depending on which one reaches zero first, we can also conclude whether $$$a_i$$$ is positive or negative.
Overall complexity $$$O(n+m)$$$.

You are given an undirected tree consisting of (n) vertices. A simple path (p) of length (k) is defined as a sequence of distinct vertices (p_0,p_1,\ldots,p_k) such that there exists an undirected edge between vertices (p_i) and (p_{i+1}) for every (0 \le i \lt k). A simple path is uniquely identified by the unordered pair of its endpoints, ((p_0,p_k)). That is, ((u,v)) and ((v,u)) represent the same simple path . Tom and Jerry are playing a game on this tree. The players take turns, with Tom going first. In the (i)-th turn ((i \ge 1)), the current player chooses a simple path ((x_i,y_i)) that satisfies the following conditions: (x_i \ne y_i). The path does not share any edges with any of the previously chosen paths. Either (x_i) or (y_i) belongs to the path chosen in the ((i-1))-th turn. Note that this condition only applies when (i \ge 2). The player who is unable to choose a valid path on their turn loses the game. Assuming both Tom and Jerry play optimally, your task is to compute the total number of distinct simple paths Tom can choose in the first turn such that he can guarantee a win. 2245E.editorial_text:
2245E - Tom and Jerry
Let's analyze the game strictly after Tom's first move. Suppose Tom chooses an initial path $$$P_1$$$. We can conceptually root the tree at one of the endpoints of $$$P_1$$$. 
When it is Jerry's turn, he must choose a path $$$P_2$$$ starting from some vertex $$$x \in P_1$$$. Because the edges of $$$P_1$$$ are now deleted, $$$x$$$ effectively becomes the root of an independent connected component in the remaining forest. To avoid traversing deleted edges, Jerry's path $$$P_2$$$ is restricted to traveling strictly downwards (from ancestor to descendant) into $$$x$$$'s subtrees. 
Consequently, $$$P_2$$$ will also be a top-down path. By induction, every valid path chosen in all subsequent turns will strictly flow from an ancestor to a descendant. The game elegantly reduces to a top-down path-picking game.
Let $$$S$$$ be the set of vertices belonging to the path chosen in the immediately preceding turn. We claim that the game state is a winning state (N-state) if and only if at least one vertex in $$$S$$$ has an odd degree in the remaining forest; otherwise, it is a losing state (P-state) where all vertices in $$$S$$$ have an even degree.
We can rigorously prove this via combinatorial game theory:

Base case: If a player has no valid moves, all vertices in $$$S$$$ must have a degree of $$$0$$$. Since $$$0$$$ is an even number and no vertex has an odd degree, the terminal state is strictly a losing state, which perfectly aligns with our definition.

Losing State $$$\to$$$ Winning State: Suppose a player starts their turn in a losing state (all $$$v \in S$$$ have an even degree) and chooses a valid path $$$P$$$. By the rules of the game, the starting vertex $$$x$$$ of $$$P$$$ must belong to $$$S$$$. Because the path extends downwards, $$$x$$$ loses exactly $$$1$$$ outgoing edge. Since its initial degree was even, its new degree after deleting the edges of $$$P$$$ becomes odd. Because $$$x$$$ naturally belongs to the newly formed active set $$$S'$$$ (which comprises the vertices of $$$P$$$), the opponent is guaranteed to receive a state containing at least one odd-degree vertex.

Winning State $$$\to$$$ Losing State: Suppose a player starts in a winning state. There exists at least one vertex $$$u \in S$$$ with an odd degree. The player can start the path at $$$u$$$ and walk downwards following this simple stopping rule:

If we arrive at a vertex with an even degree, we continue extending the path downwards. Because we just consumed one incoming edge and its initial degree was even (meaning it must be $$$\ge 2$$$), there is guaranteed to be at least one outgoing edge available to continue the walk. 
If we arrive at a vertex with an odd degree, we stop and terminate the path there. 
Since the tree is finite and every leaf in a rooted forest has a degree of $$$1$$$ (which is odd), this top-down walk is strictly guaranteed to eventually hit an odd-degree vertex and terminate. Let's examine the degrees of the vertices in this chosen path $$$P$$$ after its edges are deleted: the starting vertex (odd) loses $$$1$$$ edge, becoming even; the terminating vertex (odd) loses $$$1$$$ edge, becoming even; and all intermediate vertices (even) lose exactly $$$2$$$ edges (one incoming, one outgoing), thus remaining even. Consequently, all vertices in the newly formed set $$$S'$$$ will have an even degree, successfully forcing the opponent into a losing state. 
To guarantee a win, Tom (the first player) must ensure he hands Jerry a losing state right from the start. Therefore, Tom's initial path $$$P_1$$$ must satisfy the condition that all vertices in $$$P_1$$$ end up with an even degree after its edges are deleted. 
Working backward to the original tree: 

The two endpoints of $$$P_1$$$ each lose $$$1$$$ edge, so they must initially have an odd degree. 
All intermediate vertices of $$$P_1$$$ each lose $$$2$$$ edges, so they must initially have an even degree. 
The number of such paths can be elegantly and efficiently calculated using a depth-first-search on the connected components of even-degree vertices. 
Overall complexity $$$O(n)$$$.

2245F.editorial_text:
2245F - Familiar?
A crucial observation is that for any permutation, its minimum element divides the monotonic stack process into two independent parts. 
Consider a subsegment of the permutation and let $$$p_k$$$ be the minimum element in this subsegment. When $$$p_k$$$ is pushed into the stack, because it is the absolute minimum of the current range, it will pop all elements currently left in the stack that were pushed by the left part $$$[l, k-1]$$$. After this, $$$p_k$$$ will remain at the bottom of the stack and will never be popped by any element in the right part $$$[k+1, r]$$$. 
This independence between the left and right sides (split by the minimum element) strongly inspires an range DP solution.
Let $$$f_{l,r,c}$$$ be the number of ways to choose $$$r - l + 1$$$ relative values to form a valid permutation for the interval $$$p[l..r]$$$, such that: 

All conditions $$$a_i$$$ for $$$i \in [l, r]$$$ are satisfied. 
Exactly $$$c$$$ elements remain in the stack after processing this interval (assuming the stack was empty before processing $$$p_l$$$). 
Base case: for empty intervals, we leave $$$0$$$ elements in the stack: $$$f_{i,i-1,0} = 1$$$ for all $$$1 \le i \le n+1$$$.
Transition: Let $$$W(l, k)$$$ be the number of valid ways to form the left part $$$[l, k-1]$$$. Because $$$p_k$$$ is the minimum, it will pop all elements left by the left part. Thus, if $$$a_k \neq -1$$$, the left part must leave exactly $$$a_k$$$ elements. If $$$a_k = -1$$$, it can leave any number of elements. $$$$$$W(l, k) = \begin{cases} f_{l, k-1, a_k} & \text{if } a_k \neq -1 \\ \sum_{x} f_{l, k-1, x} & \text{if } a_k = -1 \end{cases}$$$$$$
The right part $$$[k+1, r]$$$ leaves $$$c-1$$$ elements in the stack, and $$$p_k$$$ itself contributes $$$1$$$ to the final stack size, totaling $$$c$$$. We also multiply by the number of ways to distribute the relative values to the left part: $$$$$$f_{l,r,c} = \sum_{k=l}^{r} \binom{r-l}{k-l} W(l, k) f_{k+1, r, c-1}$$$$$$
This transition takes $$$O(n^4)$$$ time: $$$O(n^2)$$$ states for $$$[l, r]$$$, $$$O(n)$$$ for $$$c$$$, and $$$O(n)$$$ to iterate $$$k$$$.
To optimize this, we introduce $$$g_{l,r}$$$, which represents the total number of valid ways to form the interval $$$[l, r]$$$ regardless of how many elements are left in the stack: $$$$$$g_{l,r} = \sum_{c} f_{l,r,c}$$$$$$
By substituting the transition of $$$f_{l,r,c}$$$ into the definition of $$$g_{l,r}$$$, we can elegantly push the summation over $$$c$$$ to the right side of the equation: $$$$$$g_{l,r} = \sum_{c} \sum_{k=l}^{r} \binom{r-l}{k-l} W(l, k) f_{k+1, r, c-1}$$$$$$ $$$$$$g_{l,r} = \sum_{k=l}^{r} \binom{r-l}{k-l} W(l, k) \left( \sum_{c} f_{k+1, r, c-1} \right)$$$$$$ $$$$$$g_{l,r} = \sum_{k=l}^{r} \binom{r-l}{k-l} W(l, k) g_{k+1, r}$$$$$$
Now, we can redefine $$$W(l, k)$$$ utilizing our new array $$$g$$$: $$$$$$W(l, k) = \begin{cases} f_{l, k-1, a_k} & \text{if } a_k \neq -1 \\ g_{l, k-1} & \text{if } a_k = -1 \end{cases}$$$$$$
For every $$$r$$$ such that $$$a_{r+1} \ne -1$$$, we only need to calculate $$$f_{l,r,c}$$$ up to $$$c = a_{r+1}$$$. For every $$$r$$$ such that $$$a_{r+1}=-1$$$, we only need to calculate $$$g_{l,r}$$$. Another observation is that during the monotonic stack process, each element pushed into the stack is popped at most once. This bounds the sum of $$$a$$$ to be at most $$$n$$$, which bounds the complexity to $$$O(n) \cdot O\left(\sum a\right) = O(n^2)$$$ states multiplied by $$$O(n)$$$ transitions per state. Overall complexity $$$O(n^3)$$$.

2245G.editorial_text:
2245G - NPC Challenge
Notice that the set $$$S$$$ returned in any query is always an independent set. The solution relies heavily on properties of independent sets. 
Consider two independent sets $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$. If we query $$$A+B$$$, all elements in $$$A$$$, as well as all elements in $$$B$$$ that do not have any edges with vertices in $$$A$$$, will be in $$$S$$$. Thus, we can identify all vertices in $$$B$$$ that have at least one edge with any vertex in $$$A$$$ with cost $$$k=|A|+|B|$$$. Let this subset of $$$B$$$ be $$$f(A,B)$$$.
We design the following procedure, $$$\operatorname{find}(A,B)$$$, that finds all edges between two independent sets $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$ such that $$$B=f(A,B)$$$.
Base case: $$$|A|=1$$$. All vertices in $$$B$$$ are connected to the only vertex in $$$A$$$.
Recursion: Split $$$A$$$ into two equally sized subsets $$$A_1$$$ and $$$A_2$$$. Let $$$B_1=f(A_1,B)$$$ and $$$B_2=f(A_2,B)$$$. We can recursively call $$$\operatorname{find}(A_1,B_1)$$$ and $$$\operatorname{find}(A_2,B_2)$$$. Note that if a vertex $$$u \in B$$$ is not connected to any vertex in $$$A_1$$$, it must be connected to some vertex in $$$A_2$$$. Thus, we can save some cost by using the equality $$$f(A_2,B)=f(A_2,B_1) \cup (B \setminus B_1)$$$. 
With $$$\operatorname{find}$$$, we can design another procedure $$$\operatorname{dfs(T)}$$$, that finds all edges between vertices in $$$T$$$.
Base case: $$$|T| \le 1$$$. There are no edges between vertices in $$$T$$$.
Recursion: let $$$S$$$ be the subset returned by querying $$$T$$$. $$$S$$$ is an independent set. We recursively call $$$\operatorname{dfs}(T \setminus S)$$$ first. Since the induced graph of $$$T \setminus S$$$ is a forest, which is bipartite, we can partition $$$T \setminus S$$$ into two independent sets $$$W_1$$$ and $$$W_2$$$. Finally, we call $$$\operatorname{find}(S,W_1)$$$ and $$$\operatorname{find}(S,W_2)$$$ to find all crossing edges between $$$S$$$ and $$$T \setminus S$$$.
Some amortized analysis can be done to show that the above solution works in $$$O(n \log n)$$$. A detailed proof that the sum of $$$k$$$ is less than $$$30 \cdot n$$$ is given below. You may refer to the solution code.
Let the repeated dfs process define greedy color classes $$$C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_h$$$. The first dfs query accepts $$$C_1$$$, recurses on the rejected vertices, the next accepts $$$C_2$$$, and so on. This is exactly the usual first-fit greedy coloring in the fixed vertex order.
Let $$$$$$M = \sum_{v}(\operatorname{col}(v)-1).$$$$$$
For every vertex of greedy color $$$c$$$, it has earlier neighbors of all colors $$$1, \ldots, c-1$$$. Choose one such edge for each smaller color. These chosen oriented edges are all distinct, because an edge can only be chosen by its later endpoint. Since the hidden graph is a tree, $$$$$$M \le n - 1.$$$$$$
Therefore the total cost of the raw dfs queries is $$$$$$\sum_v \operatorname{col}(v) = n + M \le 2n - 1.$$$$$$
Now consider the initial work(b[i], p1) calls made after the recursive dfs(p2) returns. Across all levels, the A-side contribution is exactly $$$$$$\sum |p_2| = M \le n - 1.$$$$$$
The B-side contribution queries the current color class once or twice, depending on whether one or two bipartition sides of $$$p_2$$$ are nonempty. Since the color classes partition the vertices, this contributes at most $$$2n$$$. Hence $$$$$$K_{\text{initial work}} \le M + 2n \le 3n - 1.$$$$$$
It remains to bound all recursive find calls.
Consider one call find(A, B), where $$$|A| = m$$$, and let $$$e$$$ be the number of true tree edges between $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$. Every vertex of $$$A$$$ has at least one neighbor in $$$B$$$, so $$$e \ge m$$$.
The recursive split tree of find has leaves $$$A$$$. Define $$$$$$H(m) = \sum_{\text{internal split nodes } U} |U|.$$$$$$
Equivalently, $$$H(m)$$$ is the sum of leaf depths in the balanced split tree. For this code's split, $$$$$$H(m) = m \lceil \log_2 m \rceil - \left(2^{\lceil \log_2 m \rceil} - m\right).$$$$$$
Because $$$m \le n - 1 \le 999$$$, $$$$$$\frac{H(m)}{m} \le \frac{H(999)}{999} = \frac{9965}{999}.$$$$$$
Now split the find query cost into A-parts and B-parts. 
The A-parts contribute exactly $$$H(m)$$$.
For the B-parts, choose one incident "base" edge for every vertex of $$$A$$$. The base edges contribute at most $$$$$$H(m) + \frac{H(m)}{2} = \frac{3}{2}H(m),$$$$$$ because, at every split node $$$U$$$, the first B-query can see at most $$$|U|$$$ base-neighbor labels, and the second B-query can see at most the size of the left child, which is at most $$$|U|/2$$$.
There are $$$e - m$$$ extra edges beyond the one base edge per $$$A$$$-vertex. One extra edge can make a B-vertex appear along at most one root-to-leaf path in the split recursion: at most $$$10$$$ first-query occurrences and at most $$$10$$$ second-query occurrences, since $$$m \le 999$$$. So each extra edge adds at most $$$20$$$.
Thus one find call costs at most $$$$$$H(m) + \frac{3}{2}H(m) + 20(e - m) = \frac{5}{2}H(m) + 20(e - m).$$$$$$
Using $$$H(m)/m \le 9965/999$$$, $$$$$$\frac{5}{2}H(m) + 20(e - m) \le \frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{9965}{999}m + 20(e - m).$$$$$$
Since $$$e \ge m$$$, and $$$$$$20 \le \frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{9965}{999},$$$$$$ we get $$$$$$\text{cost of this find call} \le \frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{9965}{999} \, e.$$$$$$
Every tree edge appears in exactly one such find call: if its endpoints have greedy colors $$$i \lt j$$$, it is processed when level $$$i$$$ handles edges between $$$C_i$$$ and the remaining vertices. Therefore $$$$$$K_{\text{find}} \le \frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{9965}{999} \, (n - 1) \lt 24.938(n - 1).$$$$$$
Combining all three parts: $$$$$$K \le (2n - 1) + (3n - 1) + \frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{9965}{999}(n - 1).$$$$$$
Therefore $$$$$$K \lt \left(5 + \frac{5}{2} \cdot \frac{9965}{999}\right)n = 29.937437\ldots \, n.$$$$$$
So a strict clean statement is $$$$$$\boxed{K \lt 29.938n}$$$$$$ and, in integer form, $$$$$$\boxed{K \lt 30n}$$$$$$

Zero Sum
PROGRAMMING

Add tag

You are given an array (a) of length (n), consisting only of (-1) and (1). You may perform the following operation on (a) any number of times: Choose an index (i) satisfying (1 \le i \le n - 1). Assign (a_i = -a_i) and (a_{i + 1} = -a_{i + 1}). Determine whether it is possible to make the sum of elements of (a) equal to (0). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 200)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 100)) — the length of array (a). The second line of each test case contains (n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n) ((a_i \in \{-1, 1\})) — the array (a). For each test case, print " YES " if it is possible to make the sum of elements of (a) equal to (0), and " NO " otherwise. You can output the answer in any case (upper or lower). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES " will be recognized as positive responses. In the first example, we cannot perform any operations, and the sum of elements of (a) equals (-1 \neq 0), so the answer is " NO ". In the second example, the sum of elements of (a) is already (0), so the answer is " YES ". In the fifth example, we can perform an operation with (i = 3), transforming (a) as follows: (-1, 1, \color{red}{-1, -1}, -1, -1 \rightarrow -1, 1, \color{red}{1, 1}, -1, -1). The sum of the resulting array is (0), so the answer is " YES ".

( 15952 ) 
B
Yet Another Constructive
PROGRAMMING
constructive algorithms

Add tag

You are given three integers (n), (k), and (m). We call an array (a) of length (n), consisting of positive integers, good if the minimum length of a non-empty subarray(^{\text{∗}}) of (a) whose sum is divisible by (m) equals (k). Rank Subsequence

Add tag

You are given (n) elements arranged in a line, numbered (1, 2, \ldots, n) from left to right. You may delete any number of elements (possibly none). The remaining elements form a subsequence and keep their relative order. Let the length of this subsequence be (m). If the element with original index (i) becomes the (j)-th element of the subsequence ((1 \le j \le m)), define its left rank as (j), and its right rank as (m - j + 1). For each element, you are given two integer segments (l_i, r_i) and (u_i, v_i). The (i)-th element is valid in a subsequence of length (m) if and only if, when it occupies position (j) in that subsequence, both of the following hold: Its left rank is not in the range (l_i, r_i) (i.e., (j \notin l_i, r_i)); Its right rank is not in the range (u_i, v_i) (i.e., (m - j + 1 \notin u_i, v_i)). A subsequence is valid if every element remaining in it is valid . Find the maximum possible length of a valid subsequence. The answer may be (0). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 5000)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1\le n\le 5000)) — the number of elements. Then (n) lines follow, the (i)-th line containing the four integers (l_i), (r_i), (u_i), and (v_i) ((1\le i\le n), (1\le l_i\le r_i\le n), (1\le u_i\le v_i\le n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (5000). For each test case, print one integer — the maximum possible length of a valid subsequence. In the first test case, the only element cannot form a valid subsequence of length (1), so the answer is (0). In the second test case, all (4) elements can be kept. Their pairs of left and right ranks are ((1, 4)), ((2, 3)), ((3, 2)), and $$$(4, 1)

2249B.title: Permutation Cuts
2249B.statement_text:
Problems

Solved
Index
Name
Type
Tags
Community Tag
Rating

( 4325 ) 
B
Permutation Cuts
PROGRAMMING
combinatorics implementation math

Add tag

You are given an integer (n) and an array (a) of length (n-1). For a permutation(^{\text{∗}}) (p) of length (n), define () v_i=\min\left(\max_{1\le j\le i}p_j, \max_{i+1\le j\le n}p_j\right), () where (1\le i\le n-1). In other words, cut the permutation between positions (i) and (i+1), take the maximum element on each side, and let (v_i) be the smaller of these two values. Your task is to count the number of permutations (p) of length (n) such that (v_i=a_i) for each (1\le i\le n-1). Output the answer modulo (998\,244\,353). (^{\text{∗}})A permutation of length (n) is an array consisting of (n) distinct integers from (1) to (n) in arbitrary order. For example, (2,3,1,5,4) is a permutation, but (1,2,2) is not a permutation ((2) appears twice in the array), and (1,3,4) is also not a permutation ((n=3) but there is (4) in the array). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains one integer (n) ((2\le n\le 10^6)) — the length of (p). The second line contains (n-1) integers (a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{n-1}) ((1\le a_i\le n)) — the elements of (a). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (10^6). For each test case, output one integer — the number of suitable permutations, modulo (998\,244\,353). In the first test case, both permutations (1,2) and (2,1) satisfy (v_1=1). In the second test case, the only suitable permutations are (2,1,3) and (3,1,2). In the third test case, no suitable permutation exists.

2249D.statement_text:
Problems

Solved
Index
Name
Type
Tags
Community Tag
Rating

( 1091 ) 
D
Xor Permutation Matrix
PROGRAMMING
bitmasks chinese remainder theorem constructive algorithms math

Add tag

You are given two integers (n) and (x) ((0 \le x \le n-1)). Construct a matrix (A) of size (n\times n) satisfying all of the following conditions: For every (1 \le i, j \le n), (0 \le A_{i,j}\le n-1); Every row in (A) forms a permutation of (0, 1, \ldots, n-1); Every column in (A) forms a permutation of (0, 1, \ldots, n-1); For every (1 \le i, j\le n-1), () A_{i,j} \oplus A_{i+1,j} \oplus A_{i,j+1} \oplus A_{i+1,j+1} = x. () Here, (\oplus) denotes the bitwise XOR operation . Here, (\oplus) denotes the bitwise XOR operation . Or determine that no such matrix exists. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 180)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (x) ((2\le n\le 2500), (0\le x \lt n)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2500). For each test case, output (-1) if no such matrix exists. Otherwise, output any valid (n) lines of the matrix. If several valid matrices exist, you may output any of them. In the first test case, the displayed matrix has both rows and columns equal to permutations of (0,1), and its only adjacent (2\times2) submatrix has XOR (0). The second and third test cases are impossible. In the last two test cases, every adjacent (2\times2) submatrix has XOR, respectively, (1) and (0).

( 226 ) 
E1
String (Easy Version)
PROGRAMMING
divide and conquer implementation strings

Add tag

This is the easy version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, the constraints on (k) and (q) are smaller. You can hack only if you solved all versions of this problem. Define (\mathrm{popcount}_k(m)) as the sum of all digits of (m) in base (k). Define a base-(k) integer (s=\overline{s_1s_2\cdots}) of infinite length, where the (i)-th digit of (s) is (s_i=(\mathrm{popcount}_k(i) \bmod k)). There are (q) queries. Each query consists of three integers (l), (r), and (n) (all of them are given in decimal form), as well as a base-(k) integer (t) with (n) digits. Note that (t) may have leading zeros. Consider (t) as a string, and your task is to find the number of occurrences of (t) in the string (s_ls_{l+1}\ldots s_r). For digits greater than or equal to decimal (\mathtt{10}), uppercase and lowercase letters are used. Specifically, the uppercase letters (\{\mathtt{A, B,\ldots,Z}\}) represent the decimal values (\{\mathtt{10, 11,\ldots,35}\}), and the lowercase letters (\{\mathtt{a, b,\ldots,z}\}) represent the decimal values (\{\mathtt{36, 37,\ldots,61}\}). The first line of the input contains two integers (k) and (q) ((2\le k\le 10), (1\le q\le 1000)) — the base and the number of queries. Each query contains two lines. The first line contains the three integers (l), (r), and (n) ((1\le l\le r\le 10^{17}), (1\le n\le 2\cdot 10^6)). The second line contains the base-(k) integer (t) with (n) digits ((t_i\in\{\mathtt{0,1,\ldots,9,A,B,\ldots,Z,a,b,\ldots,z}\})). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^6). For each query, output a single integer — the answer to the query. Denote the string (s_ls_{l+1}\ldots s_r) as (sl;r). In the first example, (k = 3), (s = \mathtt{12120201120201012201120012\ldots}), $$$

E2
String (Hard Version)
PROGRAMMING
divide and conquer implementation strings

Add tag

This is the hard version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, the constraints on (k) and (q) are larger. You can hack only if you solved all versions of this problem. Define (\mathrm{popcount}_k(m)) as the sum of all digits of (m) in base (k). Define a base-(k) integer (s=\overline{s_1s_2\cdots}) of infinite length, where the (i)-th digit of (s) is (s_i=(\mathrm{popcount}_k(i) \bmod k)). There are (q) queries. Each query consists of three integers (l), (r), and (n) (all of them are given in decimal form), as well as a base-(k) integer (t) with (n) digits. Note that (t) may have leading zeros. Consider (t) as a string, and your task is to find the number of occurrences of (t) in the string (s_ls_{l+1}\ldots s_r). For digits greater than or equal to decimal (\mathtt{10}), uppercase and lowercase letters are used. Specifically, the uppercase letters (\{\mathtt{A, B,\ldots,Z}\}) represent the decimal values (\{\mathtt{10, 11,\ldots,35}\}), and the lowercase letters (\{\mathtt{a, b,\ldots,z}\}) represent the decimal values (\{\mathtt{36, 37,\ldots,61}\}). The first line of the input contains two integers (k) and (q) ((2\le k\le 62), (1\le q\le 10^4)) — the base and the number of queries. Each query contains two lines. The first line contains the three integers (l), (r), and (n) ((1\le l\le r\le 10^{17}), (1\le n\le 2\cdot 10^6)). The second line contains the base-(k) integer (t) with (n) digits ((t_i\in\{\mathtt{0,1,\ldots,9,A,B,\ldots,Z,a,b,\ldots,z}\})). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^6). For each query, output a single integer — the answer to the query. Denote the substring (s_ls_{l+1}\ldots s_r) as (sl;r). In the first example, (k = 3), (s = \mathtt{12120201120201012201120012\ldots}), $

You are given a simple undirected graph with (n) vertices and (m) edges. A path is simple if it visits no vertex more than once. The length of a path is the number of edges in it. Find a shortest simple path with even length from vertex (1) to vertex (n), or determine that no such path exists. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (m) ((2\le n\le 1000), (0\le m\le \frac{n(n-1)}2)) — the number of vertices and the number of edges in the graph. Then (m) lines follow, the (i)-th line containing two integers (u_i) and (v_i) ((1\le u_i,v_i\le n), (u_i\ne v_i)) — the two vertices that the (i)-th edge connects. It is guaranteed that there are no self-loops or multiple edges in the graph. It is guaranteed that the sum of (n^3) over all test cases does not exceed (1000^3). It is guaranteed that the sum of (m) over all test cases does not exceed (10^6). For each test case, if no such path exists, print (-1). Otherwise, print any shortest simple path of even length from vertex (1) to vertex (n): On the first line, print its length (k); On the second line, print (k+1) vertices (p_0,p_1,\ldots,p_k) in order, where (p_0=1) and (p_k=n). If there are multiple possible answers, you may print any of them. In the first test case, there is no path from vertex (1) to vertex (2), so there is no answer. In the second test case, the path (1 \to 2 \to 3) has length (2), and it is the shortest simple path with even length. In the third test case, the only simple path from vertex (1) to vertex (4) has length (3), which is not even, so there is no answer. ( 14692 ) 
B
String Construction
PROGRAMMING
constructive algorithms

Add tag

You are given two integers (n) and (k). Construct a binary string(^{\text{∗}}) (s) of length (n), such that both of the following conditions hold: The absolute difference between the number of characters (\mathtt{0}) and the number of characters (\mathtt{1}) in (s) is at most (1). There are exactly (k) pairs of adjacent equal characters in (s). Formally, there are exactly (k) indices (i) ((1 \le i \le n-1)) satisfying (s_i = s_{i + 1}). Or determine that no such string exists. (^{\text{∗}})A binary string is a string where each character is either (\mathtt{0}) or (\mathtt{1}). Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 1000)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains two integers (n) and (k) ((2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5), (0 \le k \le n-1)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a binary string (s) of length (n) — the string you constructed. Print (-1) if such a string does not exist. If there are multiple answers, you may output any of them. In the first test case, one possible answer is (s=\mathtt{01110}). It contains three characters (\mathtt{1}) and two characters (\mathtt{0}), and there are exactly (2) adjacent equal pairs in (s): ((s_2, s_3)) and ((s_3, s_4)). In the second test case, (k=n-1). All characters in (s) should be equal, so the numbers of characters (\mathtt{0}) and (\mathtt{1}) could not differ by at most (1). Thus, the answer is (-1). In the third test case, note that (\mathtt{010110}) is also a possible answer.

A
You Delete, I Delete
PROGRAMMING
greedy

Add tag

Alice and Bob are given a binary string(^{\text{∗}}) (s) of length (n). It contains at least one (\mathtt{0}) and at least one (\mathtt{1}). They each perform exactly one operation in the following order: First, Alice chooses an occurrence of (\mathtt{0}) in (s) and deletes it. Then, Bob chooses an occurrence of (\mathtt{1}) in the resulting string and deletes it. Alice wants the final string to be lexicographically(^{\text{†}}) as large as possible, while Bob wants it to be lexicographically as small as possible. Determine the final string if both players act optimally. (^{\text{∗}})A binary string is a string consisting only of the characters (\mathtt{0}) and (\mathtt{1}). (^{\text{†}})For two distinct binary strings (a) and (b) of the same length, (a) is lexicographically smaller than (b) if, at the first position where they differ, (a) has the smaller digit. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 100)). The description of the test cases follows. The only line of each test case contains a binary string (s) of length (n) ((3 \le n \le 100)). It is guaranteed that (s) contains at least one (\mathtt{0}) and at least one (\mathtt{1}). For each test case, output the final string if both players act optimally. In the first test case, Alice must delete the only (\mathtt{0}). Bob may delete either occurrence of (\mathtt{1}), so the resulting string is (\mathtt{1}). In the second test case, Alice may delete either occurrence of (\mathtt{0}). Bob optimally deletes one of the first two occurrences of (\mathtt{1}), so the resulting string is (\mathtt{101}). In the third test case, Alice may delete any occurrence of (\mathtt{0}). Bob then deletes the only occurrence of (\mathtt{1}), so the resulting string is (\mathtt{00}).

Insert one integer (z) into (a) such that (x \le z \le y). After performing all operations, you may arrange the elements of (a) in any order. It is guaranteed that all (n + m) integers in the arrays (a) and (b) are distinct . It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). It is guaranteed that the sum of (m) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, print " YES " if it is possible to make (a) equal to (b), and " NO " otherwise. 2248C.title: Maximize the Score
2248C.statement_text:
Problems

Solved

Name
Type
Tags
Community Tag

( 9733 ) 
C
Maximize the Score
PROGRAMMING
dp greedy

Add tag

You are given an array (a) of length (2n). Each integer from (1) to (n) occurs exactly twice in (a). Initially, your score is (0). You can repeatedly perform the following operation while (a) is non-empty: Choose an integer (x) that is present in (a). Let (l) and (r) be the indices of the leftmost and rightmost occurrences of (x) in the current array, respectively. If (x) occurs only once, then (l = r). Add ((r - l + 1)^2) to your score. Delete the elements (a_l, a_{l + 1}, \ldots, a_r) from (a). The remaining elements are concatenated without changing their order and re-indexed starting from (1). Find the maximum possible score after making the array empty. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer (n) ((1 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5)). The second line contains (2n) integers (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2n}) ((1 \le a_i \le n)). It is guaranteed that each integer from (1) to (n) occurs exactly twice in (a). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n) over all test cases does not exceed (2 \cdot 10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the maximum possible score. In the second test case, one optimal strategy is to choose (x = 1) first. This deletes the subarray (1, 2, 1) and adds (3^2 = 9) to the score. The remaining array is (2); choosing (x = 2) adds (1). The total score is (10). In the third test case, choosing (x = 1) deletes the whole array and adds (4^2 = 16) to the score. In the fourth test case, choose (x = 1) first and then choose (x = 2). The total score is (2^2 + 4^2 = 20). In the sixth test case, choose (x = 2) first. This deletes the subarray (2, 3, 4, 1, 2) from the middle of the array and adds $$$5

2248E.editorial_text:
2248E - Excuse for Breaks

Hint1
Let $$$S_i = F(I(i))$$$. Since the counter resets at $$$n$$$, $$$S_{i+n} = S_i + S_n$$$.

Hint2
If $$$S_x + S_y \gt S_{x+y+1}$$$ for some $$$x,y$$$, the array $$$I(x),[0],I(y)$$$ already wins. Conversely, if no such pair exists, every array loses.

Hint3
For fixed $$$y$$$, the function $$$S_x + S_y - S_{x+y+1}$$$ changes only when $$$x+1$$$ or $$$x+y+2$$$ is a reward point. Where is its maximum attained?

Solution
Let $$$S_i = F(I(i))$$$ ($$$S_0 = 0$$$). The counter resets exactly at $$$n$$$, so $$$S_{i+n} = S_i + S_n$$$; also $$$F$$$ is additive across a 0: if a string ends with 0, the next part starts from $$$c=0$$$.
Define
$$$ M = \max_{x,y \ge 1} \big(S_x + S_y - S_{x+y+1}\big). $$$
Claim. $$$F(s) \le S_{|s|} + \max(M,0)$$$ for every binary array $$$s$$$, with equality for $$$s = I(x),[0],I(y)$$$ at a maximizing pair. Hence the answer is YES iff $$$M \gt 0$$$.
Induct on the number of runs. If $$$s$$$ has no 0, then $$$F(s) = S_{|s|}$$$. Otherwise write $$$s = I(x),[0],t$$$ with $$$x$$$ leading ones. Then
$$$F(s) = S_x + F(t) \le S_x + S_{|t|} + \max(M,0) \le S_{|s|} + \max(M,0),$$$
because $$$S_x + S_{|t|} - S_{x+|t|+1} \le M$$$.
Only reward thresholds matter. Let $$$g(x,y) = S_x + S_y - S_{x+y+1}$$$. By periodicity $$$g$$$ is $$$n$$$-periodic in each variable. Fix $$$y$$$:
$$$g(x+1,y) - g(x,y) = (S_{x+1}-S_x) - (S_{x+y+2}-S_{x+y+1}),$$$
which is positive only when $$$x+1$$$ is a reward point $$$p_i$$$. On the circle of residues modulo $$$n$$$, the maximum is attained on a plateau whose left end is congruent to some $$$p_i$$$ — so some $$$x = p_i$$$ attains it. The same argument in $$$y$$$ gives
$$$ M = \max_{1 \le i,j \le m} \big(S_{p_i} + S_{p_j} - S_{p_i+p_j+1}\big). $$$
(If $$$m=0$$$, then $$$S_x = dx$$$ and $$$M = -d \le 0$$$.)
Algorithm. All needed values of $$$S$$$ follow from the periodic formula $$$S_i = \lfloor i/n\rfloor S_n + S_{i\bmod n}$$$. For each pair $$$(i,j)$$$, locate $$$p_i+p_j+1$$$ among the sorted points $$${p_1,\dots,p_m, n+p_1,\dots,n+p_m}$$$ with a two-pointer scan; if $$$S_{p_i}+S_{p_j} \gt S_{p_i+p_j+1}$$$ for some pair, print YES.
Complexity: $$$O(m^2)$$$ per test case ($$$\sum m \le 2000$$$).

Code
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

class Point:
def __init__(self, t, v):
self.t = t
self.v = v

srw = [Point(0, 0) for _ in range(4100)]

T = int(input())
for _ in range(T):
n, m, d = map(int, input().split())
for i in range(1, m+1):
t, v = map(int, input().split())
srw[i].t = t
srw[i].v = v + srw[i-1].v
for i in range(1, m+1):
srw[m+i] = Point(n + srw[i].t, srw[m].v + srw[i].v)
ok = False
for i in range(1, m+1):
k = i
for j in range(1, m+1):
st = srw[i].t + 1 + srw[j].t
while k+1 <= 2*m and srw[k+1].t <= st:
k += 1
if srw[i].v + srw[i].t*d + srw[j].v + srw[j].t*d > srw[k].v + st*d:
ok = True
print("Yes" if ok else "No")
for i in range(1, 2*m+1):
srw[i] = Point(0, 0)

You are given an integer (k) and a matrix (v) with (n) rows and (m) columns. The element in row (i) and column (j) is denoted by (v_{i,j}). A cell ((x, y)) is called a peak if its value is greater than or equal to the sum of the values in all other cells in row (x) and column (y). Formally, ((x, y)) is a peak if () v_{x,y} \ge \sum_{\substack{1 \le i \le n \\i \neq x}} v_{i,y} + \sum_{\substack{1 \le j \le m \\j \neq y}} v_{x,j}. () You may perform the following operation any number of times (possibly zero): Choose four integers (x_l), (x_r), (y_l), and (y_r) ((1 \le x_l \le x_r \le n), (1 \le y_l \le y_r \le m)). Subtract (1) from (v_{i,j}) for every (x_l \le i \le x_r) and (y_l \le j \le y_r). Find the minimum number of operations required to obtain a matrix with at least (k) peaks. Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^4)). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains three integers (n), (m), and (k) ((1 \le n, m \le 10^5), (1 \le k \le n \cdot m), (n \cdot m \le 10^5)) — the number of rows, the number of columns, and the required number of peaks. The (i)-th of the next (n) lines contains (m) integers (v_{i,1}, v_{i,2}, \ldots, v_{i,m}) ((-10^9 \le v_{i,j} \le 10^9)). It is guaranteed that the sum of (n \cdot m) over all test cases does not exceed (10^5). For each test case, output a single integer — the minimum number of operations required to obtain at least (k) peaks. If there is no solution, print a single integer (-1). 2248F.editorial_text:
2248F - Matrix Elimination

Hint1
Define the deficit $$$g_{x,y} = \text{rowSum}_x + \text{colSum}_y - 3v_{x,y}$$$ of a cell. A cell is a peak iff its deficit is $$$\le 0$$$. How much can one operation reduce a deficit?

Hint2
For $$$n,m \ge 2$$$, every operation reduces any deficit by at most $$$n+m-3$$$, and full-matrix operations achieve this bound for every cell at once. So the problem reduces to a $$$k$$$-th smallest value.

Hint3
In one dimension a cell is a peak iff $$$2a_i \ge S$$$ (total sum). Only "full" operations and operations that skip one endpoint matter, and the two endpoint types are never both useful. The rest is a couple of linear inequalities solved in $$$O(1)$$$.

Solution
Let $$$R_x = \sum_j v_{x,j}$$$ and $$$C_y = \sum_i v_{i,y}$$$. The peak condition is equivalent to
$$$ g_{x,y} := R_x + C_y - 3v_{x,y} \le 0. $$$
If an operation covers $$$a$$$ cells of row $$$x$$$ and $$$b$$$ cells of column $$$y$$$, it changes the deficit by $$$-(a+b-3)$$$ when it covers $$$(x,y)$$$, and by $$$-(a+b)$$$ otherwise. For $$$n,m \ge 2$$$ this means the deficit is reduced by at most $$$n+m-3$$$ per operation: full coverage gives $$$a+b-3 \le n+m-3$$$, while an operation avoiding $$$(x,y)$$$ can cover cells of only one of the two lines, contributing at most $$$\max(n-1,m-1) \le n+m-3$$$.
Case $$$n,m \ge 2$$$. After $$$T$$$ operations, cell $$$(x,y)$$$ can be a peak only if $$$g_{x,y} \le T(n+m-3)$$$. Conversely, $$$T$$$ full-matrix operations make every cell with $$$\lceil g_{x,y}/(n+m-3)\rceil \le T$$$ a peak simultaneously. Hence the answer is the $$$k$$$-th smallest value of
$$$ \text{need}_{x,y} = \max\left(0,\ \left\lceil \frac{R_x + C_y - 3v_{x,y}}{n+m-3}\right\rceil\right). $$$
Case $$$n=1$$$ or $$$m=1$$$. Rotate to a row of length $$$L=\max(n,m)$$$, sum $$$S$$$.
Peak condition: $$$a_i \ge S-a_i \iff h_i := S-2a_i \le 0$$$.
An operation on a segment of length $$$\ell$$$ subtracts 1 from each element inside.

If $$$i$$$ is inside: $$$h_i$$$ decreases by $$$\ell-2$$$

If $$$i$$$ is outside: $$$h_i$$$ decreases by $$$\ell$$$

Only three segment types are useful (others are dominated):

Full $$$[1,L]$$$: every $$$h_i$$$ reduced by $$$L-2$$$.

Skip‑first $$$[2,L]$$$: $$$h_1$$$ reduced by $$$L-1$$$, others by $$$L-3$$$.

Skip‑last $$$[1,L-1]$$$: $$$h_L$$$ reduced by $$$L-1$$$, others by $$$L-3$$$.

Only full operations: Same as the general formula with $$$n+m-3 = L-2$$$:
Answer = $$$k$$$-th smallest $$$\left\lceil \frac{S-2a_i}{L-2} \right\rceil$$$ (with $$$\max(0,\cdot)$$$). (This is exactly the xlim part in the code).
Full + one skip type, with an endpoint among the peaks: Assume the chosen endpoint is $$$p$$$ (either 1 or $$$L$$$), using $$$x$$$ full and $$$y$$$ skip‑$p$ operations ($$$T=x+y$$$). Take the other $$$k-1$$$ peaks as the cells with the largest $$$a_i$$$ (smallest $$$h_i$$$) among the remaining $$$L-1$$$ cells; let $$$v_k$$$ be the smallest of these. Reductions: - For $$$p$$$: $$$(L-2)x + (L-1)y = (L-2)T + y$$$ - For the other $$$k-1$$$ cells: $$$(L-2)x + (L-3)y = (L-2)T - y$$$
Requirements:
$$$ \begin{aligned} (L-2)T + y &\ge S - 2a_p \quad &(1)\\ (L-2)T - y &\ge S - 2v_k \quad &(2)\\ 0 \le y &\le T . \end{aligned} $$$
From the constraints:

(2) with $$$y=0$$$ gives $$$T \ge \lceil (S-2v_k)/(L-2) \rceil$$$

(1) with $$$y=T$$$ gives $$$T \ge \lceil (S-2a_p)/(L-1) \rceil$$$

Adding (1) and (2): $$$2(L-2)T \ge 2S-2a_p-2v_k \iff T \ge \lceil (S-a_p-v_k)/(L-2) \rceil$$$

Set 
$$$ z = \max\left( \lceil \frac{S-a_p-v_k}{L-2} \rceil,\; \lceil \frac{S-2a_p}{L-1} \rceil \right) $$$
(If the first bound $$$\lceil (S-2v_k)/(L-2) \rceil$$$ were strictly larger, then $$$y=0$$$ is optimal and Strategy of only full operations already covers it.)
Now we must check whether there exists an integer $$$y$$$ satisfying the box constraints:
$$$ \max\bigl(0,\; S-2a_p - (L-2)z\bigr) \;\le\; y \;\le\; \min\bigl(z,\; (L-2)z - (S-2v_k)\bigr). $$$
If this holds, $$$T=z$$$ is feasible and optimal for this endpoint; otherwise the endpoint strategy cannot beat the "only full operations" strategy.
The code’s solveL implements exactly this: it computes $$$z$$$, tests feasibility, and returns $$$z$$$ if valid or $$$\infty$$$ otherwise.
The final answer is $$$\min(\text{Strategy full},\; \text{solveL for left endpoint},\; \text{solveL for right endpoint})$$$.
Complexity: $$$O(nm)$$$ per test case.

Code
import math

def ceil_div(a, b):
return (a + b - 1) // b

def solveL(v, v1, s, k):
n = len(v) + 1
if k == 1:
return max(0, ceil_div(s - 2 * v1, n - 1))
v.sort(reverse=True)
vk = v[k - 2]
z = max(ceil_div(s - v1 - vk, n - 2), ceil_div(s - 2 * v1, n - 1))
if min(z, (n - 2) * z - s + 2 * vk) >= max(0, s - (n - 2) * z - 2 * v1):
return z
return math.inf

T = int(input())
for _ in range(T):
n, m, k = map(int, input().split())
s = 0
u, rs, cs = [], [0] * n, [0] * m
v = []
for _ in range(n):
row = list(map(int, input().split()))
v.append(row)
s += sum(row)
rs[_] = sum(row)
for j in range(m):
cs[j] += row[j]
u.append(row[j])

if n + m <= 3:
u.sort()
if k == 1:
if n + m == 2 and u[0] < 0:
print(-1)
else:
print(0)
else:
print(abs(u[0] - u[1]))
continue

xlim = []
for i in range(n):
for j in range(m):
xlim.append(max(0, ceil_div(rs[i] + cs[j] - 3 * v[i][j], n + m - 3)))

xlim.sort()
ans = xlim[k - 1]

if m == 1 or n == 1:
ans = min(ans, solveL(u[:-1], u[-1], s, k))
ans = min(ans, solveL(u[1:], u[0], s, k))
print(ans)

2254A.title: Riptide
2254A.statement_text: Alice, Bob, and Charlie are playing a game with tokens. They start with (a), (b), and (c) tokens, respectively. The game is played in rounds. Before the beginning of each round, they check the number of tokens everyone has: If any two players have the exact same number of tokens, the game immediately ends. Otherwise, the round begins, all three players have a strictly different number of tokens. The player with the strictly most tokens gives exactly (1) token to the player with the strictly fewest tokens. Given the starting tokens (a), (b), and (c), determine exactly how many rounds the game will last before it ends. The first line contains a single integer (t) ((1 \le t \le 10^3)) — the number of test cases. Each test case consists of a single line containing three integers (a), (b), and (c) ((1 \le a, b, c \le 10)). For each test case, output a single integer — the number of rounds the game will last before it ends. In the first test case: No two players have the same number of tokens. Charlie has the most tokens ((3) tokens), and Alice has the fewest tokens ((1) token). Therefore, Charlie gives Alice a token. Now, Alice has (2) tokens, Bob has (2) tokens, and Charlie has (2) tokens. Since there are two players (or more) with the same number of tokens, the game ends. The game ended after (1) round, so the answer is (1). In the second test case, the game is played as follows: Bob gives Charlie a token, now Alice has (4) tokens, Bob has (5) tokens, and Charlie has (2) tokens. Bob gives Charlie a token, now Alice has (4) tokens, Bob has (4) tokens, and Charlie has (3) tokens. Since two players have the same number of tokens, the game ends. The game lasted (2) rounds. In the third test case, two players already have the same number of tokens. So the answer is (0) since no rounds were played.

2254E.statement_text: Yousef has a hidden array (a) of length (n) consisting entirely of strictly positive integers. An operation was performed exactly once to create an array (b): Set (b_1 = a_1).
